0.body:
Behaviour-based intrusion prevention for a small self-hosted server family: an XMPP server (ejabberd) with Nextcloud, a WireGuard VPN host and a Telegram relay node. Everything is written in Rust and runs as single static binaries on Linux (musl; x86_64, aarch64 and 32-bit ARMv7 with hardware floating point). vpsfort follows the systemd journal (ejabberd, sshd, the UFW or firewalld kernel log, Nextcloud AIO), scores every remote address by what it does, and bans attackers in nftables, firewalld, ufw, iptables or ipset within seconds. It can also drop whole countries or networks (ASNs), by the offline geo database it already uses for labels. Nodes can share bans and suspicion reports over an encrypted cluster link. Six optional bots carry vpsfort's admin alerts, daily digest and weekly abuse report to the admins, and an optional web console shows the whole cluster to its admins, read only. They only carry messages and show data: protection never depends on them. ┌──────────── server ─────────────┐ cluster (XChaCha20-Poly1305, TCP 7946)
journal ─► vpsfort ─► nftables/firewalld/ufw/iptables/ipset ◄─► vpsfort on other nodes │ outboxes (files) ├─► vpsfort-xmpp-bot ─► XMPP, OMEMO-encrypted (client mode: else OpenPGP files) ├─► vpsfort-tg-bot ─► Telegram (pseudonymized, files OpenPGP-encrypted) ├─► vpsfort-mail-bot ─► SMTP, PGP/MIME-encrypted ├─► vpsfort-signal-bot ─► Signal through signal-cli (else OpenPGP files) ├─► vpsfort-matrix-bot ─► Matrix, Olm/Megolm-encrypted (else OpenPGP files) └─► vpsfort-push-bot ─► ntfy, Gotify or a webhook (sanitized, files OpenPGP-encrypted) │ read-only console socket └─► vpsfort-web (agent) ◄─ web key, TCP 7949 ─ vpsfort-web (console) ─► HTTPS ─► the admin's browser How vpsfort compares with fail2ban, sshguard, CrowdSec, CSF, Wazuh and OSSEC, the host integrity and monitoring tools, and commercial products, with pros and cons per category and feature: COMPARISON.md .

10.body: A good fit: One to about ten Linux servers you run yourself: Debian or Ubuntu, or Fedora and RHEL with dnf and firewalld; x86_64 (the ARM builds are untried on servers, see below); systemd. SSH, XMPP (ejabberd), Nextcloud and WireGuard hosts, and the common web, database and mail servers through built-in patterns (Apache, nginx, HAProxy, Prosody, MySQL/MariaDB, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis/Valkey, Postfix, Dovecot, ownCloud). Other services count through regex patterns of your own. Admins who want alerts on their phone, encrypted, with nothing about their users or attackers sent to a vendor. Small machines: it is built to stay within a 128 MB memory limit next to the services it protects. Linux desktops and laptops, with a profile of their own (not yet run on one). Not a good fit today: Fleets of dozens of hosts or more that need fleet management, roles, several users and compliance reports. vpsfort's web console shows dozens of nodes to a few equal admins, read only by design, without fleet management or roles. Look at Wazuh, the CrowdSec Console or a commercial EDR. Web-application-heavy hosts that need a WAF, captchas or CDN integration. vpsfort can enforce a WAF's decisions at the firewall ([waf], with CrowdSec's formats built in), but it inspects no HTTP request itself and answers none: run CrowdSec AppSec, ModSecurity or Coraza for the detection, and a CDN or an HTTP bouncer for captchas. Other platforms: Windows, macOS, BSD, Linux without systemd. ARM bundles (arm64 and 32-bit ARMv7) are built and tested in CI but haven't run on an ARM server yet. Fedora has been tried on one test server; RHEL and its rebuilds not yet. Organisations that need a vendor: a support SLA, certified compliance evidence, or a 24/7 security operations team.

100.body:
The same release has a package per architecture, for the distribution's package manager instead of install.sh: vpsfort-web_<version>-1_<arch>.deb (amd64, arm64, armhf; Debian, Ubuntu and their derivatives) vpsfort-web-<version>-1.<arch>.rpm (x86_64, aarch64, armv7hl; Fedora, RHEL and its rebuilds) and vpsfort-web-<version>-r0.<arch>.apk (x86_64, aarch64, armv7; Alpine, with OpenRC: below), each with its .sha256 and .sigstore.json, downloaded and verified as the bundle above (--pattern "*.deb*", "*.rpm*" or "*.apk*"). CI keeps them for every commit as workflow artifacts, and scripts/package.sh builds them locally (cargo install cargo-deb cargo-generate-rpm --locked once, and python3 for the .apk, which scripts/apk.py at the repository's root writes; none needs dpkg, rpm or apk-tools, so it runs on macOS too; --target aarch64-unknown-linux-musl or armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf for the ARM ones). Or from the signed apt and dnf repository on GitHub Pages, once it is set up (the repository README, "Deployment"), where apt upgrade and dnf upgrade then bring new versions. sudo apt install ./vpsfort-web_0.5.1-1_amd64.deb # Fedora, RHEL: sudo dnf install ./vpsfort-web-0.5.1-1.x86_64.rpm
sudoedit /opt/vpsfort-web/config.env # the first install put the template there; then the keys, password, codes ("Setup")
sudo dpkg-reconfigure vpsfort-web # rpm: sudo dnf reinstall ./vpsfort-web-*.rpm (step 7: owners, modes, the certificate)
/opt/vpsfort-web/vpsfort-web check && sudo systemctl enable --now vpsfort-web The package puts the same files in the same places as install.sh (/opt/vpsfort-web with the binary and config.env.example, the user vpsfort-web), except the unit, which is in /usr/lib/systemd/system. Its post-install step does what install.sh does apart from copying files: the user, config.env from the template the first time, the owners and modes, the self-signed certificate once CONSOLE_LISTEN is set; and it lists what is still missing (the to-do list of "Setup"). dpkg-reconfigure vpsfort-web (rpm: dnf reinstall) runs that step again, as "bash install.sh again" does for the bundle. apt remove vpsfort-web (dnf remove) stops the service and keeps /opt/vpsfort-web; apt purge removes it with the keys, password and certificate (rpm: by hand). Nothing starts on its own. The first install puts the template in place and prints what to fill in; you enable the service once it is filled in. An upgrade keeps the config and restarts the service only if it was running and the config is filled in. Over a bundle or deploy.sh install the package takes over: the config, state and keys stay; the bundle's unit in /etc/systemd/system (it would shadow the package's) and its rollback files go, and the service is enabled again on the package's unit if it was (vpsfort's integrity watch reports the removed unit as a warning once). Replacing the config: when a terminal is there, the install asks whether to replace the config with the new template (the old one kept with the suffix .old); Enter, a timeout of a minute, no terminal or DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive keep it. VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace (or keep) answers without asking: sudo VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace apt install ./<file>.deb. Rollback is installing the previous version's package (apt install ./<old>.deb --allow-downgrades, dnf downgrade ./<old>.rpm): there is no .prev file. Alpine (apk, OpenRC): apk add --allow-untrusted ./vpsfort-web-<version>-r0.x86_64.apk puts the same files in the same places, with the OpenRC script /etc/init.d/vpsfort-web instead of the unit: the settings exported from config.env as EnvironmentFile= does, STATE_DIR /var/lib/vpsfort-web (the console's own, mode 0700) unless config.env says otherwise, the console's own messages in /var/log/vpsfort-web/console.log, supervised by supervise-daemon and started again 5 seconds after a crash; systemd's sandboxing has no equivalent there. The package is unsigned, hence --allow-untrusted: sha256sum -c and the attestation verify it. Its install scripts are POSIX sh and do what the post-install step above does: the user, config.env from the template the first time, the owners and modes; an upgrade restarts a running console. Then rc-update add vpsfort-web default && rc-service vpsfort-web start. apk del vpsfort-web stops it and keeps /opt/vpsfort-web and the state. Not yet run on an Alpine host: CI installs the package in an Alpine container.

102.body: On the Mac , beyond the tests above: runs against snapshots made from real decision logs, through real TLS and the agent protocol, with the page looked at in a browser (light and dark; phone, tablet and desktop widths; keyboard only), and two reviews of the rendered page with the fixes they named. Abuse reports built by vpsfort from a copy of real actions logs and merged from two fake nodes through a real agent, per-provider Copy and .txt, several admins (also against a console without vpsfort), the in-place refresh; the address page, Mail with RDAP (the console's lookup and the browser's fallback both asked rdap.org for real addresses), mailed marks, CSV/JSON exports, links with filters, sessions, the 7-day charts, the table of differences; the proof of work and the account lockout through the demo (a wrong password raised the difficulty from 20 to 21 bits, the next login solved it and got in; 20 bits took 0.7 s in the browser, 22 bits 2.4 s) and in the end-to-end test; the no-JavaScript notice rendered from its markup. On the real cluster (since 2026-10-27; five nodes, all but one through their agents): the unit under systemd's sandboxing, vpsfort's real console socket, install.sh, a browser reaching the console without a tunnel with its self-signed certificate; every node's alerts and bans on one page; a node's stale state during its agent's restart, the "since the last snapshot" line as its data came back, the filters above the tables. Reviewed (2026-10-29): an audit of the whole crate (the proof of work first): six fixes, each with a test, listed in the commit vpsfort-web: audit fixes; the rest of what was read (the HTTP parser, the agent protocol, sessions, the page's handling of what nodes send, the unit's sandbox, the installer's modes) found sound. A second audit the same day, after the page's changes: two small fixes (a locked account's files were read for any login attempt at it, now only for one carrying something shaped like a code; the page's "seen" marks are pruned after 30 days). Known and accepted: someone holding an account's TOTP secret but not its password can keep failing at a locked account (the lock is for password guessers; the secret is the larger loss); /api/v1/session?user=NAME shows a raised difficulty for a name under attack, which says the name is being tried, not that it exists. Found by these runs , fixed the same day: check misread an AGENT_ALLOW list with blanks when config.env was sourced in a shell (the commands now read the file themselves, as systemd does); the installer's new system user raised high alerts in vpsfort (the installers now announce the account files); an empty console socket setting was refused; on the real cluster the Bans, Offenders and Activity tabs had their heading and filters below the table.

104.body: A simulated vpsfort cluster and its web console, in one process, from real decision logs or a console export. For trying the console without servers, for screenshots, for working on the page against a cluster's worth of data, and for showing it around. What runs: A node per decision log (actions.jsonl): its state is what vpsfort's own log reader (tui --actions) makes of the log (the bans active at its end, the decisions, the alerts, the countries and networks), its digest comes from vpsfort's digest renderer, and its abuse reports from vpsfort's live report builder, so the console sees exactly what a daemon's [console] socket would answer. A log is shifted so that it ends now (shift_to_now), and every trickle_secs a new ban (now and then an alert) copied from it, stamped now, keeps the page's "new since your last look" paths busy. A node per snapshot the console saved ("Snapshot" or "Download JSON" on a node's page, or the nodes of an "Export JSON" of the whole cluster): served as it is. No abuse reports (they need a log); the digest is rendered from the snapshot. A real vpsfort-web agent on every node but the first, and a real vpsfort-web console on the first node's socket and the other nodes' agents: the production layout, with the real login (password, one-time code, proof of work), sessions, share links, exports. What a decision log doesn't carry (the cluster as the node sees it, certificates, disk and memory, antivirus, package and cron checks, updates, listeners) is made up when fill = true (the default), varied per node so every card of the console shows something: an infected file here, a failing peer there, a full disk, a certificate about to expire. Don't take those for real; the bans, offenders, alerts, countries and abuse reports are the log's.

105.body:
cargo build --release
./target/release/vpsfort-sim --init # writes vpsfort-sim.toml: an example to edit
./target/release/vpsfort-sim vpsfort-sim.toml The first run makes what the console needs and says so: the web key, the admin's password (vpsfort-sim for the account admin), the one-time secret (printed as an otpauth:// link for an authenticator app, and the current code, which a real console never prints), and a self-signed certificate for 127.0.0.1 and localhost. Files that exist are kept; delete one to have it made again. Then it prints each node, the agents, the console's address and how to log in. Open https://127.0.0.1:7948 and accept the certificate (its fingerprint is printed).
105.title: Run

106.body:
dir = "/tmp/vpsfort-sim" # keys, the admin's files, the certificate, sockets, shifted logs (keep it short; made 0700, and refused if others can reach it)
console_listen = "127.0.0.1:7948"
plain_http = "" # e.g. "127.0.0.1:7950": the same console over plain HTTP, for a browser that can't take the certificate (loopback only)
agent_port = 7960 # the agents: 127.0.0.1:7960, 7961, ... (the first node needs none)
totp = true # logins ask for a one-time code (the secret is made and printed)
login_work = 8 # proof-of-work bits before a login (the real default is 20; 0: off)
refresh_secs = 10
expected_version = "" # EXPECTED_VERSION: a node on another vpsfort-web release is pointed out
shift_to_now = true
trickle_secs = 20 # 0: nothing moves
fill = true # the made-up cards (see above)
export = "" # a console export: its nodes, besides the ones below [[node]]
name = "node1"
actions = "logs/node1.actions.jsonl" # relative to this file
address = "203.0.113.10" # the public address the abuse reports name
backend = "nftables" [[node]]
name = "node2"
snapshot = "vpsfort-node2-snapshot.json" # a snapshot instead of a log Nodes are numbered in the order given, the export's after the [[node]] entries; the first one hosts the console. A node of the export without a snapshot (it was down when exported) is left out, and said. The plain_http door rewrites each request's Host, Origin and Referer to the console's own and drops the HSTS header on the way back, so the page's login works over http://127.0.0.1 (browsers treat that address as secure). It is for automation; use HTTPS otherwise.

107.body: Nothing is enforced: there is no firewall, no journal, no cluster traffic between the nodes. The nodes don't talk to each other; a peer's ban in a log stays a line in that log. The console's own behaviour (sessions, lockouts, share links, the attention history, the digest archive) is the real one, in the real code.

108.body: An XMPP bot for vpsfort, in one of two modes (BOT_MODE in config.env): admin (the default): the Rust rewrite of the Python XMPP admin bot (/opt/xmpp-bot/bot8.py, before the rename below), on the XMPP server itself: the same chat commands over ejabberdctl for the admin and users, the same state.json, the same config.env, plus vpsfort's alerts and weekly report for the admin (vpsfort's [notify] bot_outbox, with vpsfort's plain-text fallback). Most of this README is about it. client : a copy bot like vpsfort-tg-bot or vpsfort-matrix-bot, on any host (a VPN server, a relay node, a desktop with vpsfort's desktop profile) with an account on any XMPP server. It only sends vpsfort's alerts, daily digest and weekly abuse report to its admin, OMEMO-encrypted, and as files encrypted to the admin's OpenPGP key when OMEMO can't reach the admin (vpsfort's [notify] xmpp_outbox). No ejabberd, no commands but /status, /omemo and /help. See "Client mode" below. Both share the login (SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS, certificates verified, stop on a wrong password), the OMEMO code and trust pins, the no-archive hints and the outbox format.

110.body: Login: SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS (SCRAM-SHA-256 bound to the TLS 1.3 session) instead of DIGEST-MD5. At startup the bot refuses a server that doesn't offer SCRAM-SHA-256, so it never falls back to SCRAM-SHA-1 or PLAIN. If the server rejects the channel binding, the bot logs a warning and uses plain SCRAM-SHA-256. ejabberd logs Accepted c2s SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS authentication for bot@.... TLS certificates are verified against the JID's domain, also when connecting to 127.0.0.1. xmpppy didn't verify them. Wrong password: the bot stops (exit 78, which the unit does not restart) instead of retrying until mod_fail2ban (or vpsfort) bans the address. That holds at startup and also when the password changes while the bot runs: it stops after the second failed login (see "Connection drops"). The bot runs as the ejabberd user , the one ejabberd itself runs as, with no root and no capabilities. ejabberdctl then works for it directly, without switching users. The bot's password is removed from the environment of the commands it runs. (Run as root instead, it starts ejabberdctl and openssl as EJABBERD_USER.) Usernames are normalized as ejabberd does (nodeprep): Admin, ADMIN and ａｄｍｉｎ are all admin. The admin's and the bot's own accounts can't be removed, banned, kicked, given a new password or reset link, or reported. /remove also takes the user off the bot allowlist, so a new account of the same name starts without bot access. Late commands are not run. A command that reaches the bot more than 2 minutes after it was sent (held in offline storage while the bot was down) gets "Not run: … send it again" instead. A message delivered twice (same id) runs once. The password is no longer on the command line : the bot reads BOT_PASSWORD (and every other setting) from the environment, i.e. straight from config.env. Nothing the bot sends is archived. Every message it sends (replies, errors, alerts, OMEMO key messages) carries a XEP-0334 <no-permanent-store/> hint. mod_mam (default: always) then archives it on neither side, while offline storage still delivers it. The bot also sets its own account's archive preference to never (XEP-0313). What a user sends to the bot still lands in that user's archive; /purge_bot_chats confirm deletes it, along with the bot's whole archive. Messages are accepted only from exactly the bot's domain (the Python suffix test also let through domains like evilexample.org, although only listed JIDs could run commands). User commands , all about the sender's own account only: /invite points to mod_invites' web page (INVITE_URL, default https://<domain>:5281/invites), where users sign in and create invitations; it replaces /create, which still answers with the same text. /resetlink: a reset link for their own account. /devices: their connected devices, numbered, with address and time online; the one they write from is marked. A footer reminds them to check the list and to disconnect an unknown device with /logout and set a new password with /resetlink. /logout <number|device>: disconnects one of their devices, by its number in /devices or its name. The device the command comes from only with confirm. /storage: how many of their messages the server archive holds and how many wait for delivery. /delete_history confirm: deletes their whole message archive on the server. /motd: the current message of the day. /lang <EN|FR|GE|PL|RU|UA>: the language of the bot's replies. /export: what the server and the bot hold about the user (GDPR art. 15): last login, profile, contacts, group chats, devices, message counts, invitations they created (without tokens, and without who used them), their language and abuse reports, and how many reports there are about them (not by whom). The whole-server XEP-0227 export (export_piefxis) is not used: it writes everyone's data, password hashes included, to disk. With EJABBERD_DB set (ejabberd's sql_database), the full copy follows as a JSON file (GDPR art. 15 and 20), sent like the weekly report: encrypted (OMEMO media, XEP-0454), to the device that asked and the user's other trusted devices, in an OMEMO-encrypted chat only (a plain chat gets a note instead). It holds every row of ejabberd's database about the account: account (hash types, not hashes), last activity, contacts and groups, vCard, private storage, privacy lists, archive settings, the archived messages themselves, offline messages, push registrations (not their secrets), published items (PEP) and their settings, own pubsub subscriptions, room nicknames and subscriptions, invitations created, login tokens' client names (not the tokens), shared roster groups; plus connected devices, joined rooms and what the bot holds. Only the user's own data. sqlite3 -readonly reads the database. Every query matches the account exactly (=, never LIKE, whose _ and % would match other names), and every row is checked again in the bot before it goes into the file: a row owned by anyone else is dropped and logged. Left out on purpose: group chat archives and member lists (other people's messages and accounts), who subscribed to the user's published items, the accounts the user's invitations created, a contact's subscription request text, and every secret. A test (commands/tests.rs) builds a SQLite database with the user, a look-alike account LIKE would match, a group chat and a foreign publisher, and checks the file holds none of them. /privacy (also for the admin): how long the server keeps data. The archive, offline messages and push registrations go after RETENTION_MESSAGE_DAYS (21), uploads (at most UPLOAD_MAX_MB, 500, each) after RETENTION_FILE_DAYS (7), accounts without a login after RETENTION_ACCOUNT_DAYS (90), unused group chats after RETENTION_ROOM_DAYS (90). Keep them in step with cleanup_db.sh and mod_http_upload(_quota). It also covers passwords (SCRAM hashes), OMEMO, server logs and what the bot itself keeps. /help ends with the admin's address (ADMIN_JID) for questions. ejabberd's error texts go to the bot's log, not to users. At startup and then daily, the bot drops from state.json what it holds about accounts that no longer exist (the daily cleanup_db.sh deletes inactive ones without telling it), reports about or by them, and abuse reports older than ABUSE_REPORT_DAYS (90). It skips this when ejabberd's user list lacks the bot's own account, so a failed listing can't wipe the state. /getlim, /setlim and /invited (the old /create quota) are gone; old entries stay in state.json. Replies to users in their language. /allow <username> [language] sets it, and users can change it with /lang: EN (default), FR, GE (German), PL (Polish), RU or UA (Ukrainian), in any case. Everything the bot says to that user is translated: help, errors, usage lines, /invite, /resetlink, /abuse, OMEMO messages and /omemo. Command names stay English. The admin's replies stay English. /allowed shows each user's language. It is kept in state.json (a lang field older versions ignore). Server announcements in the configured languages. /maintenance, /restart and the subject of /warn are written in every language of ANNOUNCE_LANGUAGES, in that order (default EN,FR,RU,UK; GE/DE, PL and UA/UK work too), one paragraph per language with its flag. Times are given in each language's time zone, named as it is then (BST or GMT for English, CET/CEST for French, German and Polish, MSK, EET/ EEST for Ukrainian): /maintenance 'Sun 01:00' 'Sun 02:00' gives "from Sun 02:00 to Sun 03:00 (BST)" and so on. /dt_conv shows a time the same way. The text of /warn itself is the admin's, as typed. Delivery and read receipts. Commands that ask for them get a XEP-0184 receipt and a XEP-0333 "displayed" marker, so Conversations shows them as delivered and read. The bot answers disco#info and puts XEP-0115 caps in its presence, so clients know it supports both. state.json is written to a temporary file and then renamed into place, so a crash never leaves a truncated file. The format is unchanged, so you can roll back. Pings, disco#info and roster pushes are answered; other IQ requests get service-unavailable. Passwords and reset links sent unencrypted carry <no-store/> too, so they never wait in the server's offline storage. With OMEMO=required they are always encrypted. More admin commands , grouped by section in /help: /status, /certs, /sessions, /roster, /storage, /baninfo, /kick, /unban_ip (fail2ban), /resetlink (a mod_invites page where the user sets a new password), /invites, /spam_domains, /block_domain, /unblock_domain. These ask for a final confirm: /purge_mam, /purge_offline (ejabberd's batch purges; /purge_status shows progress), /purge_bot_chats, /restart (restart_kindly: refuses new logins, announces in the ANNOUNCE_LANGUAGES, waits, restarts) and /reload_config. Shutdown, backups, modules and mass deletion stay in the root shell. Replies use Message Styling (XEP-0393), which Conversations renders and other clients show as plain text: generated logins and passwords, commands in /help and usage lines, and OMEMO fingerprints in monospace; listings (/list, /online, …) in a preformatted block. Server announcements (/maintenance, /warn, /announce, MOTD) stay plain. The avatar shows in Conversations. Besides the vCard photo, the bot publishes the avatar with XEP-0084 (PEP, open access), which is the only kind Conversations shows for contacts; it uses vCard photos only for servers. It also approves subscription requests from the admin and allowed users, and asks them for theirs in return: ejabberd sends a contact's PEP items (the avatar) when that contact's presence reaches the publisher, so it takes a subscription in both directions. At startup, and right after /allow, it makes the subscription mutual with the admin and every allowed user, also those who never added the bot as a contact. Conversations shows such a user the bot's request once; accept it. Other subscription requests stay unanswered.
110.breadcrumbs: The bots » XMPP (vpsfort-xmpp-bot) » What changed from the Python bot
110.title: What changed from the Python bot

111.body: The bot speaks OMEMO 0.3 (eu.siacs.conversations.axolotl, what Conversations, Gajim, Dino and Monal use), implemented in src/omemo/ from the X3DH, Double Ratchet and XEdDSA specifications and XEP-0384 v0.3. On login it publishes its device list (only its own device) and its key bundle, with open access. It republishes the bundle when a one-time key gets used, and rotates the signed key every 30 days. An encrypted command gets an encrypted reply, sent to the sender's trusted devices, with the same no-archive hint as every other message of the bot. OMEMO=on (the default) also accepts unencrypted commands. OMEMO=required refuses them, except /omemo. OMEMO=off turns OMEMO off entirely. /omemo shows the bot's fingerprint and your devices' fingerprints with their trust state. Compare the bot's fingerprint with the one in Conversations (contact details) and with the OMEMO on: device …, fingerprint … line in the bot's log. Trust. Keys are pinned in omemo-trust.txt next to state.json (OMEMO_TRUST_FILE), one <jid> <fingerprint> per line, as Conversations shows the fingerprint (spaces and case don't matter). A JID with pinned keys is served only on those keys: an unknown device gets its fingerprint back and no command runs. A JID without pins is trusted on any key, as Conversations does before you verify anything, unless OMEMO_TRUST=pinned, which trusts pinned keys only. The bot warns in its log while the admin has no pin. The file must be owned by root (or the bot's user) and writable by its owner only; otherwise the bot trusts no key at all and says so in its log. Because pinning needs root on the server, a stolen admin password alone cannot run commands once your devices are pinned. The file is re-read on every message, so no restart is needed. Keys. omemo.json next to state.json (OMEMO_STORE, mode 600) holds the bot's identity key and sessions. Deleting it gives the bot a new device and key, which clients then have to trust again. Never restore an old copy: its ratchet state has already been used. Tests. ./scripts/omemo-oracle.sh sets up omemo-dr, Gajim's OMEMO library, in a venv under target/ and runs src/omemo/oracle_tests.rs against it. The tests cover signatures in both directions, sessions started by either side, many messages each way, out-of-order and duplicate messages, key transport messages, tampering, a peer rebuilding its session, and the bot restarting. Once the venv exists, ci.sh runs these tests too. omemo-dr is GPL-3.0 and only runs at test time; none of its code is in the bot. Reminder: OMEMO 2. The bot speaks only OMEMO 0.3. The current XEP-0384 is OMEMO 2 (urn:xmpp:omemo:2: a different wire format, XEP-0420 stanza content encryption, and the whole stanza encrypted instead of just the body), and clients are moving to it. When Conversations, which the admin uses, ships it, add OMEMO 2 next to 0.3: publish both device lists and bundles, and answer each device in the version it uses. Don't switch from one to the other; that would cut off clients that still speak only one. Then test both versions against an oracle as for 0.3.
111.title: OMEMO

112.body: vpsfort's messages to the admin (alerts and the daily digest) come through the bot, OMEMO- encrypted like everything else it sends, instead of from ejabberd's send_message in plain text (which mod_mam would also archive). vpsfort's [notify] bot_outbox points at the bot's outbox. Each message is a file there, alert-*.msg. The bot looks every 5 seconds, claims a message by renaming it to .<name>.sending, sends it to the admin's trusted devices and deletes it. vpsfort falls back to plain text. A message the bot hasn't taken within vpsfort's bot_grace (2 minutes) goes out the old way, with a last line saying why it isn't encrypted. That happens when the bot is down or offline, OMEMO is off, no admin device is trusted, or sending failed (the bot then puts the file back). Admin only. The bot sends only messages addressed to ADMIN_JID. It renames a message for anyone else to .<name>.rejected, and vpsfort sends that one itself right away. Users' warnings never go through the bot. If the bot stops while sending, it puts the message back at its next start (or vpsfort takes it after 10 more minutes). vpsfort also warns the admin (the same way) when another file waits in the outbox longer than bot_stuck_after (1 hour), i.e. a weekly report the bot can't send. Check it as root on the XMPP server: vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml notify-test --bot admin@example.org waits until the bot has sent the test message, and says so.

112.title: Alerts from vpsfort

113.body: Every Monday at 06:00 UTC the admin gets vpsfort's abuse report for both servers as an encrypted file: a line saying what it is (servers, period), then the file itself, which Conversations and Monal show as a downloadable attachment. How it gets there. vpsfort and the bot stay separate programs; they meet only in a directory. vpsfort-abuse-report.timer runs on both servers at the same time (vpsfort's deploy/vpsfort-abuse-report.sh). Each server writes its own JSON report (abuse-report --since 7d --json --all --min-events 1). The VPN server sends its report to the XMPP server over the cluster link (vpsfort cluster-send-report: the same XChaCha20-Poly1305 key and port as the shared bans, nothing new opened), where vpsfort writes it to /var/lib/vpsfort/inbox/. The XMPP server merges both (abuse-report --merge … --contacts: the RDAP lookups, --min-events 3 and --top 50 apply to the merged report) into the text report with one "Hello, …" section per abuse mailbox, and puts it in the bot's outbox, /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/outbox/abuse-report-<date>.txt, owned by the bot. The bot checks the outbox every 5 minutes and right after login. It encrypts each file with AES-256-GCM (a new random key and 12-byte IV per file), uploads the ciphertext with HTTP File Upload (XEP-0363) and sends the admin an OMEMO message whose body is the download URL as aesgcm://…#<IV><key> (OMEMO media sharing, XEP-0454). Then it deletes the file. Why encrypted end to end. The TLS certificate comes from Let's Encrypt, which is fine for transport, but the server (and anyone with access to its disk or backups) would otherwise hold a readable copy of the upload. With XEP-0454 the server only ever stores ciphertext, and the key exists only inside the OMEMO message, encrypted for the admin's trusted devices. The bot never sends a report in plain text, whatever OMEMO says: with no trusted admin device the file waits and is retried. No XEP-0066 <x xmlns='jabber:x:oob'> is added, since it would travel in clear. PEP/pubsub is involved only as it already is, for the OMEMO device list and bundles; the report itself does not use pubsub. Needs on the server: mod_http_upload with the bot allowed to upload (the default access: local is enough). The bot finds the service with disco on the domain; set UPLOAD_SERVICE (e.g. upload.example.org) to skip that. The upload is an HTTPS PUT to the slot URL, verified against the system's root certificates. Retention (GDPR). The report holds attackers' addresses and sanitized log lines; account names are withheld. It is derived from vpsfort's security records, kept 84 days anyway (SECURITY_RECORD_DAYS), and adds no copy that outlives them: the work files on both servers live in a private directory under /run (memory), deleted when the job ends; the VPN report in the XMPP server's inbox is deleted once merged; an unmerged one after 7 days; the outbox file is deleted as soon as it is sent; an unsent one after OUTBOX_MAX_DAYS (7), with a warning in the bot's log; the upload is ciphertext only and goes after RETENTION_FILE_DAYS (7, mod_http_upload_quota); the two messages carry the no-archive hint like everything the bot sends: not in MAM, only in offline storage until delivered. The admin's devices keep what they downloaded; delete the chat or file there when the abuse desks have been written to. /privacy says, in every language, that the admin gets this weekly encrypted report without account names and that the server holds it only encrypted for at most RETENTION_FILE_DAYS days. The legal basis is the legitimate interest in network and information security (GDPR art. 6(1)(f), recital 49). Check it without waiting for Monday, as root on both servers (the VPN server first): systemctl start vpsfort-abuse-report, then journalctl -u vpsfort-abuse-report and the bot's log (outbox: … sent to the admin (OMEMO media)).

113.title: Weekly abuse report

114.body:
BOT_MODE=client (template: deploy/config-client.env.example) makes the bot a copy bot for vpsfort's [notify] xmpp_outbox, as vpsfort-tg-bot is for tg_outbox: for a host without ejabberd, such as the VPN server, a relay node, or a Linux desktop with vpsfort's desktop profile (deploy/vpsfort-desktop.toml in vpsfort names the lines). Any XMPP server, for the bot and the admin. The bot needs an account of its own anywhere (a public server will do) and writes only to ADMIN_JID, on whatever server that is. Without XMPP_SERVER it connects to the JID's domain through its SRV records (_xmpp-client._tcp, or _xmpps-client._tcp with XMPP_TLS=direct), falling back to port 5222 (5223); the certificate is verified against the JID's domain either way. The login is the admin bot's: SCRAM-SHA-256(-PLUS) only, and exit 78 when the server offers nothing else or the password is wrong. Prosody before 13 offers only SCRAM-SHA-1: ALLOW_SCRAM_SHA1=yes accepts it (never PLAIN). OMEMO first. Alerts go out as OMEMO messages, files (the weekly abuse report) as OMEMO media (XEP-0454) through the bot's server's HTTP File Upload, to the admin's trusted devices, exactly as in admin mode: trust pins in omemo-trust.txt, blind trust while there are none (or OMEMO_TRUST=pinned). OpenPGP when OMEMO can't reach the admin : OMEMO=off, the admin's client publishes no OMEMO device, none of the admin's devices is trusted (not pinned under OMEMO_TRUST=pinned, or no key bundle), or encrypting fails. The message or file is then encrypted to the admin's OpenPGP key (OPENPGP_KEY: a v4 RSA or Curve25519 key, as OpenKeychain and iPGMail export it; the same code as vpsfort-matrix-bot's), uploaded under a neutral name (message-<time>.txt.pgp, report-<time>.txt.pgp) and sent as a link (body and XEP-0066 <x xmlns='jabber:x:oob'>), which Conversations shows as a download; open it with OpenKeychain (Android) or iPGMail (iPhone). Without OPENPGP_KEY such messages wait. OMEMO=off without OPENPGP_KEY is refused at the start (exit 78): the bot sends nothing in clear. In clear the server sees only the links to the OpenPGP files (their content is encrypted) and short notices, each kind at most once a day: why messages come as files now ("none of admin@…'s 2 OMEMO device(s) is trusted and reachable …"), why they wait, how many alerts were dropped. Every message carries the no-archive hint, as in admin mode. No fallback on vpsfort's side , as for the other copy bots: an alert waits in the outbox until it is sent or older than ALERT_MAX_HOURS (24; then dropped, and one notice says how many), a file until OUTBOX_MAX_DAYS (7). vpsfort warns when copies wait longer than its bot_stuck_after. The bot accepts any To: in the outbox: it has one admin. It answers only its admin , plain or OMEMO: /status (what was sent since the start, what waits, OMEMO, the fallback key's fingerprint), /omemo (fingerprints, as in admin mode) and /help. Anyone else gets no answer and no presence. It asks the admin for a mutual subscription at every start, as the admin bot does; accept it once. No ejabberdctl, no state.json, no users. BOT_STATE_PATH's directory holds the OMEMO keys, the pins and the outbox. The admin-mode settings (EJABBERDCTL, EJABBERD_DB, INVITE_URL, the retention days, ANNOUNCE_LANGUAGES) are ignored. Install from the release bundle on the host, as root: ./install.sh --client (or plain ./install.sh on a host without the user ejabberd) puts the client template in place as /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/config.env and installs the bot without starting it; fill in BOT_JID, BOT_PASSWORD, ADMIN_JID, copy your OpenPGP public key to /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/admin.asc (or comment OPENPGP_KEY out), then run ./install.sh again. Because the config says BOT_MODE=client, install.sh creates the system user vpsfort-xmpp-bot and installs vpsfort-xmpp-bot-client.service as vpsfort-xmpp-bot.service (the package keeps it under its own name: systemctl enable --now vpsfort-xmpp-bot-client): no ejabberd group, ProtectSystem=strict, MemoryDenyWriteExecute (no Erlang VM to start here). It skips every ejabberd step. Then, in vpsfort's [notify]: enabled = true
xmpp = false # no ejabberd on this host
xmpp_outbox = "/opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/outbox"
xmpp_user = "vpsfort-xmpp-bot" and systemctl restart vpsfort, vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml notify-test --xmpp-client. The weekly abuse report job finds the outbox there too. Switching an existing install between the modes: change BOT_MODE and run install.sh; it moves the files to the other mode's user. The OMEMO device stays the same if the bot's account does. One vpsfort-xmpp-bot per host: vpsfort refuses bot_outbox and xmpp_outbox together.
114.title: Client mode

115.body: tokio-xmpp reconnects by itself, forever (backing off from 1 to 30 s), finds the server again through DNS each time, and resumes the session (XEP-0198) when the server still holds it. Three things it doesn't do are covered by the bot (since 2026-10-26, both modes): Nothing in the outbox is lost. tokio-xmpp counts a stanza as sent once it is in the socket's buffer, also on a connection that died unnoticed (a laptop that just woke up), and drops what the server hadn't acknowledged when it can't resume the session (the server keeps it 5 minutes on ejabberd's default). It reports no disconnection either. So before sending outbox items the bot pings its server (XEP-0199) and waits if there is no answer (asking again after 30 s at the earliest); after each alert or file it pings again and deletes the file only if the answer came on the same session. Otherwise the file stays and goes out again later: an alert may arrive twice, never not at all. Every send waits at most 30 s, so the bot keeps answering stop signals while the connection is down. A dead connection is noticed sooner in client mode: after 60 s of silence the bot asks the server for a sign of life and gives up on the connection 15 s later (tokio-xmpp's tight timeouts; admin mode, on localhost, keeps 5 + 5 minutes). Its timers stop while the machine sleeps, so on a laptop that is 75 s after waking up at most. Failed reconnects can't get the bot banned, and a flaky network can't stop it. The server may be guarded by mod_fail2ban (5 failed logins) and by vpsfort: a failed login is 25 points there, a connection without login 10, a failed TLS handshake 40; vpsfort bans at 100 points of a score halving every 10 minutes, or 200 of one halving every 12 hours. A connection that reached the server but didn't get the session online is followed by a wait of 2, 5, then 10 minutes (30 after six such attempts, 60 after twelve), which keeps even failed TLS handshakes under both scores; attempts that never reach the server (no network, DNS down, connection refused) aren't counted. Before the next attempt, the bot checks the login on a connection of its own: only a rejected password (or no SCRAM-SHA-256) stops it, after two failed logins in all, whereas a network that went away during the login just means trying again. The usual reconnect after a sleep or a Wi-Fi change reaches the server and comes online at once, so it never waits. A server restart can't leave the bot resuming a session the server no longer has. After a restart ejabberd answers the resumption with <failed/> without an h attribute (it knows no count for a session it never had); xmpp-parsers 0.23 rejects that element, and tokio-xmpp then drops the stream but keeps the old session's state, so every reconnect would try the same resumption, logging in each time and never coming online (and stopping after three such logins, as if the password had changed). A login check that passes after a connection that never got the session online makes the bot start a new client, with no session to resume: it is back about two minutes after the server (the wait above, then the check). The same cure covers any other dead end after the login. The bot's account must be a real one, not a vpsfort canary. vpsfort's [canary] xmpp names (its shipped list: test, info, support, user, guest, demo, xmpp, jabber, ...) are account-level tripwires: one failed login bans the address at once (100 points), and every login is a critical alert. The spacing above can't help there. The bot warns at the start when its name is on the shipped list; install.sh checks the list of the vpsfort on the same host and refuses such an account in admin mode (warns in client mode, whose server is usually elsewhere). The cure is another account, or the name in [canary] except on the server. No network at the start (a laptop that boots offline): the login check at startup waits and tries again (5 s, doubling to 5 minutes) instead of exiting. The client unit therefore doesn't pull in network-online.target, which slows booting on desktops. After a long sleep, vpsfort on the same machine may report once that the bot left a message unsent for hours: it measures the wait by the wall clock, which went on during the sleep.

116.body:
Without a Rust toolchain: every version tag vpsfort-xmpp-bot-v<version> gets its bundle, vpsfort-xmpp-bot-<version>-<commit>-<arch>.zip for each architecture (x86_64-linux-musl, aarch64-linux-musl for arm64, armv7-linux-musleabihf for 32-bit ARMv7 with hardware floating point), as an asset of the tag's GitHub Release (see "Releases" in the repository README ); CI also keeps one for every commit as a workflow artifact (they expire and need a GitHub login), and scripts/bundle.sh builds it locally. It holds the static binary, the unit and logrotate files, config.env.example, SHA256SUMS and install.sh. Download and verify (on your machine, then copy the zip over, or on the server): take the zip for the server's architecture (uname -m: x86_64, aarch64, or armv7l for armv7) from the GitHub Release of the version's tag, with the GitHub CLI or from the Releases page (each crate's releases are tagged vpsfort-xmpp-bot-v<version>): arch=x86_64-linux-musl # the server's: aarch64-linux-musl (arm64), armv7-linux-musleabihf (32-bit ARM)
gh release download vpsfort-xmpp-bot-v0.6.1 --repo makhort/vpsfort --pattern "*-$arch.zip*" # the zip, its .sha256 and .sigstore.json
sha256sum -c vpsfort-xmpp-bot-*-$arch.zip.sha256 # the download is intact (macOS: shasum -a 256 -c)
gh attestation verify vpsfort-xmpp-bot-*-$arch.zip --repo makhort/vpsfort --source-ref refs/tags/vpsfort-xmpp-bot-v0.6.1 gh attestation verify (after gh auth login) checks the signed build provenance: that this repository's CI built exactly this zip from that tag. With --bundle vpsfort-xmpp-bot-*-$arch.zip.sigstore.json it checks the attestation attached to the Release instead of fetching it from GitHub. Only a public repository's releases have one (GitHub offers attestations for private repositories only with Enterprise Cloud). On the XMPP server (apt install unzip or dnf install unzip if needed): arch=x86_64-linux-musl # as above: aarch64-linux-musl, armv7-linux-musleabihf on ARM
unzip vpsfort-xmpp-bot-*-$arch.zip && cd vpsfort-xmpp-bot-*-$arch
sudo ./install.sh # first time: installs the bot with /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/config.env from the template, not started
sudoedit /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/config.env # the bot's account, ADMIN_JID, XMPP_DOMAIN ("Settings")
sudo ./install.sh # starts the bot (or: systemctl enable --now vpsfort-xmpp-bot); later: upgrades it
sudo ./install.sh rollback # back to the previous version It doesn't start the bot while config.env still holds REPLACE… placeholders. It checks every file against SHA256SUMS in a copy only root can write, then runs the same install.sh as deploy.sh below (./install.sh --check only checks the files). Without --client, the first install takes the admin template where the user ejabberd exists and the client template elsewhere. An existing /opt/xmpp-bot (the bot's old name) is moved over as with deploy.sh.

117.body:
The same release has a package per architecture, for the distribution's package manager instead of install.sh: vpsfort-xmpp-bot_<version>-1_<arch>.deb (amd64, arm64, armhf; Debian, Ubuntu and their derivatives) vpsfort-xmpp-bot-<version>-1.<arch>.rpm (x86_64, aarch64, armv7hl; Fedora, RHEL and its rebuilds) and vpsfort-xmpp-bot-<version>-r0.<arch>.apk (x86_64, aarch64, armv7; Alpine, with OpenRC: below), each with its .sha256 and .sigstore.json, downloaded and verified as the bundle above (--pattern "*.deb*", "*.rpm*" or "*.apk*"). CI keeps them for every commit as workflow artifacts, and scripts/package.sh builds them locally (cargo install cargo-deb cargo-generate-rpm --locked once, and python3 for the .apk, which scripts/apk.py at the repository's root writes; none needs dpkg, rpm or apk-tools, so it runs on macOS too; --target aarch64-unknown-linux-musl or armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf for the ARM ones). Or from the signed apt and dnf repository on GitHub Pages, once it is set up (the repository README, "Deployment"), where apt upgrade and dnf upgrade then bring new versions. sudo apt install ./vpsfort-xmpp-bot_0.6.1-1_amd64.deb # Fedora, RHEL: sudo dnf install ./vpsfort-xmpp-bot-0.6.1-1.x86_64.rpm
sudoedit /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/config.env # the first install put the template there ("Settings")
sudo systemctl enable --now vpsfort-xmpp-bot # admin mode; client mode: vpsfort-xmpp-bot-client The package puts the same files in the same places as install.sh (/opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot with the binary and both templates, /var/log/vpsfort-xmpp-bot), with two units in /usr/lib/systemd/system: vpsfort-xmpp-bot.service for the admin bot (as the user ejabberd, on the XMPP server) and vpsfort-xmpp-bot-client.service for the client bot (BOT_MODE=client, its own user vpsfort-xmpp-bot, any host); you enable the one for the mode in config.env. The first install takes the admin template where the user ejabberd exists and the client template elsewhere. The post-install step does what install.sh does apart from copying files: the client mode's user, config.env the first time, the owners and modes for the mode's user, the outbox and the log directory, the logrotate rules for the mode (/etc/logrotate.d/vpsfort-xmpp-bot, and in admin mode ejabberd-logs, written from the copies in /usr/share/vpsfort-xmpp-bot), and the canary and CTL_OVER_HTTP checks as warnings. It refuses nothing: with BOT_MODE=admin and no user ejabberd it only says so. Switching modes: change BOT_MODE, run dpkg-reconfigure vpsfort-xmpp-bot (rpm: dnf reinstall ./vpsfort-xmpp-bot-*.rpm), then disable one unit and enable the other. In vpsfort's [sources] services, the client bot is vpsfort-xmpp-bot-client.service. apt remove stops the bot and keeps /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot; apt purge removes it with the state, OMEMO keys and pins, and the logrotate rules it wrote (rpm: by hand). Nothing starts on its own. The first install puts the template in place and prints what to fill in; you enable the service once it is filled in. An upgrade keeps the config and restarts the service only if it was running and the config is filled in. Over a bundle or deploy.sh install the package takes over: the config, state and keys stay; the bundle's unit in /etc/systemd/system (it would shadow the package's) and its rollback files go, and the service is enabled again on the package's unit if it was (vpsfort's integrity watch reports the removed unit as a warning once). Replacing the config: when a terminal is there, the install asks whether to replace the config with the new template (the old one kept with the suffix .old); Enter, a timeout of a minute, no terminal or DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive keep it. VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace (or keep) answers without asking: sudo VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace apt install ./<file>.deb. Rollback is installing the previous version's package (apt install ./<old>.deb --allow-downgrades, dnf downgrade ./<old>.rpm): there is no .prev file. A bundle's client-mode install ran under the admin unit's name; the takeover enables vpsfort-xmpp-bot-client.service instead. Alpine (apk, OpenRC): apk add --allow-untrusted ./vpsfort-xmpp-bot-<version>-r0.x86_64.apk puts the same files in the same places, with two OpenRC scripts instead of the units: /etc/init.d/vpsfort-xmpp-bot (the admin bot, as the ejabberd user) and /etc/init.d/vpsfort-xmpp-bot-client (the client bot, as vpsfort-xmpp-bot), each exporting the settings from config.env as EnvironmentFile= does, supervised by supervise-daemon and started again 5 seconds after a crash; systemd's sandboxing has no equivalent there. The package is unsigned, hence --allow-untrusted: sha256sum -c and the attestation verify it. Its install scripts are POSIX sh and do what the post-install step above does: the user (vpsfort-xmpp-bot, only where there is no ejabberd user to run as), config.env from the template the first time (the admin bot's where ejabberd runs, else the client's), the owners and modes, the log directory; an upgrade restarts a running bot. Then rc-update add vpsfort-xmpp-bot default && rc-service vpsfort-xmpp-bot start (or -client). apk del vpsfort-xmpp-bot stops them and keeps /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot. Not yet run on an Alpine host: CI installs the package in an Alpine container.

118.body:
./scripts/ci.sh # fmt, clippy, tests, cargo audit, static Linux binary
./deploy/deploy.sh # ci.sh, then copies (over SFTP only) to a fresh xmpp:/tmp/vpsfort-xmpp-bot-deploy.XXXX The static Linux build needs rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl (for ARM: aarch64-unknown-linux-musl, armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf, built with TARGET=... ./deploy/deploy.sh) and rustup component add llvm-tools (see .cargo/config.toml). Then paste the command deploy.sh prints into a root shell on the server: it checks the files and runs install.sh (installs /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/vpsfort-xmpp-bot and the unit, restarts). On a clean host that first run creates /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot with config.env from the template (the admin bot's where the user ejabberd exists, the client bot's elsewhere; bash install.sh --client picks the client one), installs the bot for that mode (the client mode's user, the unit, the log directory, the outbox) and stops before starting it while config.env still holds REPLACE… placeholders. Fill it in, then systemctl enable --now vpsfort-xmpp-bot. To go back to the previous binary and unit: bash /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/install.sh rollback Renamed from xmppbot (2026-10-17). The bot was xmppbot, installed as /opt/xmpp-bot/xmppbot, run by xmpp-bot.service, logging to /var/log/xmpp-bot. The first install.sh of the new name moves an old install over on its own, before installing: stops and disables xmpp-bot.service, removes it and /etc/logrotate.d/xmpp-bot (local changes in xmpp-bot.service.d/ move to vpsfort-xmpp-bot.service.d/); moves /opt/xmpp-bot to /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot and /var/log/xmpp-bot to /var/log/vpsfort-xmpp-bot, with owners and modes: state.json, the OMEMO keys and trust pins, the avatar, the outbox and the log carry over, so the XMPP account, the OMEMO device and the admins' pinned fingerprint stay the same; rewrites the old paths in config.env (the previous file stays as config.env.pre-rename) and adds LOG_DIR if it was missing; keeps the old binary as vpsfort-xmpp-bot.prev if it ran cleanly, so rollback works right after the move (with the new unit and paths; the old unit is not kept); in /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml and /etc/default/vpsfort-abuse-report, replaces /opt/xmpp-bot and "xmpp-bot.service" (each changed file stays as <file>.pre-rename-<time>), checks that vpsfort accepts the config (else puts it back and says what to change by hand) and restarts vpsfort. Deploy the current vpsfort first: its vpsfort-abuse-report.service may write only to the new outbox paths, and install.sh warns while the installed one names only the old ones. vpsfort's integrity check reports the changed units in /etc/systemd/system once; that is this move. Running install.sh again changes nothing more; if both /opt/xmpp-bot and /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot exist, it stops and asks you to keep one. Fuzzing. The OMEMO code and the outbox format live in the crate's library (src/lib.rs), which the binary uses too, so fuzz/ can reach them. There are three cargo-fuzz targets (code in src/fuzzing.rs): omemo_wire: libsignal's protobuf messages inside OMEMO keys. Whatever parses must serialize back to the same message. omemo_decrypt: encrypted messages to a bot device, including session starts on its real prekey ids with fuzzed keys (zeros, low-order points) and a fuzzed first message. omemo_stanza: XML from other clients (<encrypted>, device lists, bundles the bot starts sessions from) and vpsfort's outbox messages. tests/fuzz_smoke.rs runs them on stable, over real traffic between two throwaway devices, the seeds in fuzz/seeds/ and fixed mutations, so cargo test keeps them working (VPSFORT_XMPP_BOT_WRITE_SEEDS=1 cargo test --test fuzz_smoke regenerates the seeds; the keys in them are throwaway). The real search needs nightly: rustup toolchain install nightly --profile minimal && cargo install cargo-fuzz --locked # once
cargo +nightly fuzz run omemo_decrypt fuzz/corpus/omemo_decrypt fuzz/seeds/omemo_decrypt -- -max_total_time=600 New inputs collect in fuzz/corpus/, crashes in fuzz/artifacts/ (both git-ignored). The first runs (2026-10-16, 90 s per target, 240,000 to 750,000 inputs each) found nothing. ejabberd's database holds only SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-512 hashes (the bot needs SHA-256). The one-off script that migrated the plain-text passwords (ejabberd_scram_migration.py) ran on 2026-10 and was retired with its backups; it is in the git history. install.sh keeps the previous binary and unit (vpsfort-xmpp-bot.prev, vpsfort-xmpp-bot.service.prev) for rollback (only while the running version runs cleanly), backs up state.json, installs a logrotate rule for /var/log/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/bot.log (weekly, one old copy: 14 days at most, as /privacy says; older copies are deleted). The bot logs only there, not to systemd's journal, which would keep the lines longer (tail -f /var/log/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/bot.log instead of journalctl -u vpsfort-xmpp-bot; the journal still has systemd's own start/stop lines and anything printed before the log opens). It also installs ejabberd-logs, a logrotate rule keeping ejabberd's own log files 14 days at most (weekly, one old copy, reopen_log afterwards), unless another rule already covers /opt/ejabberd/logs, and reminds you to set log_rotate_size: infinity in ejabberd.yml so ejabberd stops rotating by size. With journald limited to 14 days (MaxRetentionSec=14day, MaxFileSec=1day), /privacy can say server logs are deleted after 14 days at the latest. It also checks that ejabberd's unit runs as ejabberd, and shows the bot's log and ejabberd's record of the login. The Python bot can't come back: it only logs in with DIGEST-MD5 or PLAIN, which the server no longer offers. It warns when CTL_OVER_HTTP is set in /opt/ejabberd/conf/ejabberdctl.cfg. In that mode ejabberdctl sends its arguments to ejabberd as JSON without escaping them, so line breaks and quotes (announcements, passwords) break commands, and replies with non-ASCII text (a Cyrillic nickname in a roster) come back empty. The bot needs the classic mode; turning it off doesn't affect ejabberd's socket itself, which other tools may use directly. It also sets owners and modes, so the bot can change only what it has to: Path Owner Mode /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/ root:ejabberd 1770 (sticky: the bot can't replace root's files) config.env (holds the password), omemo-trust.txt, the avatar root:ejabberd 640 state.json, omemo.json ejabberd 600 /var/log/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/, bot.log ejabberd 700, 600 outbox/ (the weekly report waiting to be sent) root:ejabberd 1770; files ejabberd 600 After editing omemo-trust.txt as root, keep it root:ejabberd 640; the bot trusts no key while others than root can write it. The unit drops every capability, keeps /usr and /etc read-only, is held to 512 MB of memory (MemoryMax: the bot is small, but every ejabberdctl command starts an Erlang VM of tens of MB inside the unit; the client unit gets 128 MB), and has KillMode=process, so a pending /restart (ejabberdctl restart_kindly waiting out its delay) carries on when the bot restarts; a second one is refused while it runs.

12.body: Bottom line: for the services it knows, vpsfort detects more, and is more careful about false positives, than the generic tools. For any other service, the others ship far larger rule libraries. feature vpsfort fail2ban sshguard CrowdSec Wazuh CSF/LFD built-in parsers ◐ sshd, ejabberd, kernel log (UFW, firewalld, iptables), Nextcloud, su/sudo, PAM, audit log, and 24 common services (web servers and proxies, databases, mail, a code forge, a password manager, identity providers, Matrix, OpenVPN, FTP, a media server) ✓ dozens of filters ◐ SSH and common mail/FTP daemons ✓ hub of parsers and scenarios ✓ thousands of rules ✓ hosting stack patterns of your own ✓ ✓ – compiled in ✓ ✓ ✓ one score per address across all services ✓ ◐ per jail, plus recidive ✓ ◐ per scenario ◐ correlation rules ◐ per trigger low-and-slow probing over hours ✓ 12 h score ◐ long findtime ◐ ◐ ◐ ◐ escalating ban times ✓ 1 h to 30 d ✓ bantime.increment ✓ ◐ profile expressions ✓ repeated_offenders ✓ LF_PERMBLOCK subnet bans ✓ grow from /24 towards /16 – ◐ fixed prefix ◐ range-scoped scenarios – ◐ LF_NETBLOCK, fixed port scans and tripwire ports ✓ ◐ own filter – ✓ ◐ ✓ honeypot listeners (handshake proves the source; what the scanner sent is evidence) ✓ – – – – – canary account names ✓ ◐ own filter – ◐ own scenario ◐ own rule – per-account alerts (distributed guessing, login after failures, new network, new SSH key) ✓ – – ◐ ◐ success after failures ◐ LF_DISTATTACK a recent login protects an address ✓ per service ◐ ignorecommand script – – – – dry-run mode ✓ shadow mode ◐ dummy action – ✓ simulation ✓ alert-only by default ✓ TESTING replay old logs through the same engine ✓ ◐ fail2ban-regex tests filters – ✓ replay mode ◐ wazuh-logtest – XMPP server attacks ✓ deep ◐ own filter – ◐ own parser ◐ own decoder – feature pros (vpsfort) cons (vpsfort), and who does better Parsers Deep parsers for what it knows. An ejabberd TLS failure is tied to its address through the Erlang PID. OpenSSH 10's sshd-session lines are handled. A line counts only from its real sender, by journald's own fields, so a local user can't log a fake sshd line to get someone banned. [sources] apps adds built-in patterns for Apache, nginx, HAProxy, Prosody, MySQL/MariaDB, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis/Valkey, Nextcloud, ownCloud, Postfix, Dovecot and its own web console, each taking the address only from where the service writes it, so a client can't get another address banned through a user name or path. The built-in services are tested against documented and forged log lines, and Apache's against two honeypots' logs, but not yet run on a host with them. FTP and everything else need [[patterns]]. fail2ban, CrowdSec and Wazuh ship ready filters for hundreds of services. Own patterns Linear-time regex, so no catastrophic backtracking on hostile lines. The sender is pinned by unit, or by identifier and uid. test-pattern and a TUI tab show the lines read, matched, and matched without an address. A pattern is a regex, a kind and a weight. There are no multi-line or stateful scenarios like CrowdSec's leaky buckets or Wazuh's composite rules. Scoring Two decaying scores (10 min and 12 h half-life) add up every signal from every service. A scanner that touches SSH, XMPP and closed ports a little each still reaches a ban. Weights are calibrated on a real month of logs. One model for everything: tuning means weights and thresholds, not per-service rules. At first it is less obvious than fail2ban's "N failures in T minutes". Escalation 1 h → 6 h → 1 d → 7 d → 30 d per repeat offence. Offences are shared, so a repeat attacker escalates on every node of the cluster. fail2ban, sshguard and CSF escalate too, and CSF offers permanent bans. Only the cluster-wide counter is new here. Subnet bans Starts at /24 (IPv6 /64) and grows towards /16 (/48) only as nearby bans appear, at most 2 bits a step. It never covers a protected address. With the geo database, it never grows into another provider's network. The provider boundary needs the [geo] ASN database. A stricter policy, such as blocking a whole network or country now, needs feeds. CSF blocks countries out of the box. Tripwires and honeypots One SYN to an unused telnet, RDP or database port bans. Kernel tripwires log these hits from vpsfort's own nftables rules, so UFW's log limit (about 3 lines a minute) doesn't hide scans. Honeypot ports complete the TCP handshake, so their evidence can't be forged, and keep the scanner's first bytes (a Telnet login, an HTTP request) for the abuse report. A blocked SYN can carry a forged source address. vpsfort limits the damage: such evidence never bans an address that logged in recently, replies always pass, and with honeypots set it is worth half a ban. A spoofer can still get outsiders banned for an hour. Canary accounts No accounts to create. On a key-only host, ssh = ["*"] makes every unknown user name a ban. A successful login to a canary is a critical alert. fail2ban, CrowdSec and Wazuh can do this with a filter of your own. vpsfort just has it built in. Account protection Distributed guessing against one account from several addresses; a login right after failures (possible compromise); a login from a new network or provider for that account; a login with a never-seen SSH key. Covers XMPP, SSH, Nextcloud, the built-in services and your patterns only. Wazuh covers far more authentication sources (PAM, Windows, cloud services). False positives Shadow mode lifts its own "bans" when the address later logs in, and says so. An address that logged in recently isn't banned for that service's typos and reconnects. Private, CGNAT, loopback and link-local addresses are never banned. Login trust is a heuristic. An attacker behind the same carrier NAT as a user gets the same excuse for that service's noise; real failures still raise an alert. Testing replay runs journal exports through the whole pipeline without touching the firewall, and opens the result in the TUI. CrowdSec's replay mode and cscli explain are as capable, and better documented for writing new scenarios.

120.body: A Telegram bot that brings vpsfort's admin messages to the admin's Telegram chat: the alerts, the daily digest (both servers'; the VPN server's arrive through the cluster) and the weekly abuse report. It does for Telegram what vpsfort-xmpp-bot does for XMPP on vpsfort's side, through the same kind of outbox, and nothing else: No link to ejabberd. No ejabberdctl, no database, no XMPP login. It runs as its own user vpsfort-tg-bot, which isn't in the ejabberd group and can't read ejabberd's files. No XMPP account data, and no server addresses, on Telegram. Telegram's servers can read everything a bot sends (bots get no end-to-end encryption). So in alerts and digests account names become pseudonyms and the servers appear only by their node ids (below), and the abuse report goes only as a file encrypted to the admin's OpenPGP key. vpsfort-xmpp-bot's user commands (/invite, /devices, /export, ...) and admin commands (/list, /sessions, ...) are not here. No orders for the servers. Its commands only show its own state; the servers are managed over SSH. Both bots can run side by side. vpsfort feeds vpsfort-tg-bot only when [notify] tg_outbox is set. Without it, nothing changes. Where it runs. On a small VPS of its own that joins the vpsfort cluster (the Telegram relay node , vpsfort's deploy/vpsfort-tg.toml), so the XMPP server never connects to Telegram: the XMPP and VPN nodes relay their admin messages to it over the encrypted cluster link, and may limit what it hands them to notices (it can't ban or allowlist anything there). vpsfort's README, "A Telegram relay node", has the cluster side. It can also run on the XMPP server itself: then that server talks to Telegram.
120.title: vpsfort-tg-bot

122.body: From vpsfort In Telegram an alert or the digest (alert-*.msg in the outbox) a message, account names and server addresses replaced: the subject (server and topic) in bold, the text as a monospace block; long ones split into several messages the weekly abuse report (abuse-report-<date>.txt), or any other file report-<date>.txt.pgp: the whole file encrypted to OPENPGP_KEY, with a fixed caption that says nothing about it. Without a key, files aren't sent alerts older than ALERT_MAX_HOURS (24) when the bot gets to them dropped, and one message says how many an alert Telegram refuses (400 Bad Request) sent again without formatting; refused again, dropped with a note, so it can't hold up the alerts after it Commands, from the admin only: /status (uptime, what was sent, what waits in the outbox, the last error), /privacy (what goes through Telegram and what the bot keeps), /help. The bot sets them as its command menu in the admin's chat only. Messages from anyone else get no answer, and a group or channel someone adds the bot to, it leaves. The log only counts them, with the latest sender's numeric id, at most every 10 minutes.

123.body: vpsfort's admin alerts name XMPP accounts (account alice@example.org registered from …, ejabberd:alice@… under distributed attack, ejabberd log lines as evidence). vpsfort-tg-bot replaces each with [acct:1a2b3c]: the first 24 bits of an HMAC-SHA-256 of the bare address (lower case, resource dropped) under pseudonym.key, a random key made on the first start. It never leaves the server. The same account always gets the same pseudonym, so repeated attacks on one account still show. Without the key, nobody can tell which account it is, Telegram included. A plain hash would not do: account names are few and easy to guess. On the server, vpsfort-tg-bot pseudonym alice@example.org prints an account's pseudonym (as root or vpsfort-tg-bot, with the same PSEUDONYM_KEY). Every address-like local@domain in an alert is replaced (with its /resource), and so is ejabberd:<name> (a bare user name counts as on the first of XMPP_DOMAINS). Alerts never need an e-mail address. A name is everything back to a blank or a character XMPP forbids in account names ("&'/:<>@). Account names may contain ( ) [ ] { } , ; = |, so bob(1)@example.org and a,b@… are hidden whole; brackets in front stay outside ((alice@…) and alice@… get the same pseudonym). Matching too much only hides more. Files are not touched: they go out encrypted as a whole (below).

124.body: SERVER_NAMES lists each server's own addresses and host names under its node id (vpsfort's [cluster] node_id): node1=192.0.2.10,example.org; vpn=198.51.100.20; tg=203.0.113.10. In alerts and digests, after the account names: an address becomes the node id: cluster peer 198.51.100.20:7946 failing → cluster peer vpn:7946 failing. IPv4 matches as any run of digits and dots, wherever it is (dead:…, ::ffff:…:7946); IPv6 as a run of hex digits and colons that is the address (brackets and IPv4-mapped too), or, when the run is no valid address, starts with it before a colon (…: refused, a port). A run that is another valid address stays: attackers' addresses, also 2001:db8::7:5 next to a server's 2001:db8::7; a host name becomes the node id, subdomains keeping their first labels: example.org:5223 → node1:5223, nextcloud.example.org:443 → nextcloud.node1:443. notexample.org and example.org.example.net are left alone. List every public IPv4 and IPv6 address of each server. Loopback and unspecified addresses (127.0.0.1, ::, 0.0.0.0) are refused: they are no server's address and appear in many lines. A node id needs a letter other than a to f (node1, vpn, tg, relay): one of hex digits only would join the colons and digits around it into a new address. Without SERVER_NAMES the bot warns at startup and sends the names as they are. The subjects say which server already ([xmpp]). What does go to Telegram: attackers' addresses, ports, countries and networks; ban decisions; the servers' state (exposure, certificates, cluster) under their node ids; sanitized log lines with account names and server names replaced. A "suspicious login" alert also carries the login's address. That is the point of the alert, but if it was the account owner, it is their address.

125.body: The weekly abuse report (or any file vpsfort puts in the outbox) is sent only as one OpenPGP message encrypted to the admin's public key (OPENPGP_KEY), never in clear, not even in part: the caption is a fixed line saying how to open it, the name is report-<date>.<ext>.pgp. Telegram sees a file of some size, and that it is OpenPGP. Apps. Android: OpenKeychain (F-Droid, Google Play; in maintenance mode, still working). iPhone: iPGMail (paid, updated in 2026). In Telegram, open the file's menu → Share (or Save to Files) → the app; it asks for the key's passphrase and shows or saves report-<date>.txt. The key. Create it in that app (on the phone, so the secret key never leaves it), or use one you have. A v4 key with an RSA (3072 or 4096 bits) or Curve25519 encryption subkey works everywhere; RSA is the safe choice if you switch between Android and iPhone apps. Export the public key as a file (both apps can share or export it from the key's page), copy it to the server and install it as root: install -o root -g vpsfort-tg-bot -m 640 admin.asc /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot/admin.asc, then restart the bot. Its log (and /status) shows the fingerprint: compare it with the one the app shows. The format. What these apps and GnuPG read: a v3 PKESK packet for each encryption subkey, a SEIPD v1 packet (with MDC) under AES-256, no compression, no file name inside (RFC 9580 advises none). Not SEIPD v2 / AEAD or v6 keys: OpenKeychain can't read them. The bot uses rPGP (pure Rust, MIT/Apache). tests/gpg_interop.rs checks every file decrypts with GnuPG, for RSA-4096 and Curve25519 keys made by gpg. Checks at startup. The key must parse, its self-signatures verify, and it must be a v4 key, not revoked or expired, with an encryption subkey of those kinds that was never revoked. Signatures by other keys (gpg --sign-key, web of trust) are ignored, not taken for broken self-signatures (until 2026-10-17 they stopped the bot). Otherwise the bot stops (exit 78) instead of running without a key. Without OPENPGP_KEY it runs, and files wait, unsent, until they expire after OUTBOX_MAX_DAYS. And at every file. A key (or subkey) that expires while the bot runs is no longer used: files wait, /status says why, and the chat gets a note at most once a day. A file Telegram refuses for good (400 Bad Request, 413 too large) is dropped with a note in the chat. Only the public key is on the server: whoever gets into it can't read reports sent before. The report itself still names the servers' addresses, for the abuse desks; that stays inside the encryption. Deleting a key gives every account a new pseudonym; old messages then no longer match.

125.title: Files go out encrypted, as a whole

126.body: They share one directory, /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot/outbox (root:vpsfort-tg-bot 1770, sticky), and vpsfort-xmpp-bot's file format (see src/outbox.rs and vpsfort's src/botbox.rs): vpsfort's notifier writes a copy of each message to the first of [notify] admins (on the relay node, [notify] xmpp = false, or with admins empty: every admin message, its own and the relayed ones, and then only here) as alert-<time>-<n>.msg (To: and Subject: lines, a blank line, the text). It writes under a dot name first, gives the file to tg_user, and renames it into place. This copy is in addition to the XMPP way, which is unchanged. The bot looks every 5 seconds. It claims a message by renaming it to .<name>.sending, sends it and deletes it. If sending fails, it renames the file back and tries again (after Telegram's retry_after, or after 30 s). A message left in .sending by a stop is put back at the next start. Messages over 1 MB (vpsfort's are a few KB) are deleted unread. At startup the bot checks it can write the outbox (an OUTBOX_DIR outside the unit's ReadWritePaths can't be), and says so in its log if not. Unlike the XMPP bot's outbox, vpsfort takes nothing back: there is no plain-text fallback for a copy. When copies wait longer than bot_stuck_after (1h), also ones a bot that died left half-sent (.sending), vpsfort warns the admins the XMPP way, at most once per hour (with no XMPP admins: as a system alert in its journal, relayed to peers with relay_notices). vpsfort-abuse-report.sh (merge role: on the XMPP server, or any server with vpsfort-tg-bot) puts the weekly report into every outbox it knows: vpsfort-xmpp-bot's, and vpsfort-tg-bot's when vpsfort's [notify] tg_outbox (or ABUSE_REPORT_TG_OUTBOX) is set. On the relay node (role relay) it waits for the report the XMPP server merged and forwarded (ABUSE_REPORT_FORWARD_TO there) and puts that in vpsfort-tg-bot's outbox; if none comes, it merges itself. The bot looks every minute, sends the report encrypted and deletes it. A report not sent within OUTBOX_MAX_DAYS (7) is deleted unsent. Check it as root: vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml notify-test --telegram puts a test in the outbox and waits until vpsfort-tg-bot has sent it.

126.title: How vpsfort and the bot meet

127.body:
Instead of deploy.sh (step 2 below), without a Rust toolchain: every version tag vpsfort-tg-bot-v<version> gets its bundle, vpsfort-tg-bot-<version>-<commit>-<arch>.zip for each architecture (x86_64-linux-musl, aarch64-linux-musl for arm64, armv7-linux-musleabihf for 32-bit ARMv7 with hardware floating point), as an asset of the tag's GitHub Release (see "Releases" in the repository README ); CI also keeps one for every commit as a workflow artifact (they expire and need a GitHub login), and scripts/bundle.sh builds it locally. It holds the static binary, the unit, config.env.example, SHA256SUMS and install.sh. Download and verify (on your machine, then copy the zip over, or on the server): take the zip for the server's architecture (uname -m: x86_64, aarch64, or armv7l for armv7) from the GitHub Release of the version's tag, with the GitHub CLI or from the Releases page (each crate's releases are tagged vpsfort-tg-bot-v<version>): arch=x86_64-linux-musl # the server's: aarch64-linux-musl (arm64), armv7-linux-musleabihf (32-bit ARM)
gh release download vpsfort-tg-bot-v0.5.1 --repo makhort/vpsfort --pattern "*-$arch.zip*" # the zip, its .sha256 and .sigstore.json
sha256sum -c vpsfort-tg-bot-*-$arch.zip.sha256 # the download is intact (macOS: shasum -a 256 -c)
gh attestation verify vpsfort-tg-bot-*-$arch.zip --repo makhort/vpsfort --source-ref refs/tags/vpsfort-tg-bot-v0.5.1 gh attestation verify (after gh auth login) checks the signed build provenance: that this repository's CI built exactly this zip from that tag. With --bundle vpsfort-tg-bot-*-$arch.zip.sigstore.json it checks the attestation attached to the Release instead of fetching it from GitHub. Only a public repository's releases have one (GitHub offers attestations for private repositories only with Enterprise Cloud). On the server (apt install unzip or dnf install unzip if needed): arch=x86_64-linux-musl # as above: aarch64-linux-musl, armv7-linux-musleabihf on ARM
unzip vpsfort-tg-bot-*-$arch.zip && cd vpsfort-tg-bot-*-$arch
sudo ./install.sh # install or upgrade; the first time also /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot/config.env
sudo ./install.sh rollback # back to the previous version The first install, as with deploy.sh, doesn't start the bot while the token and admin id are placeholders: continue with step 3. install.sh checks every file against SHA256SUMS in a copy only root can write, then runs the same installer as deploy.sh (./install.sh --check only checks the files).
