128.body:
The same release has a package per architecture, for the distribution's package manager instead of install.sh: vpsfort-tg-bot_<version>-1_<arch>.deb (amd64, arm64, armhf; Debian, Ubuntu and their derivatives) vpsfort-tg-bot-<version>-1.<arch>.rpm (x86_64, aarch64, armv7hl; Fedora, RHEL and its rebuilds) and vpsfort-tg-bot-<version>-r0.<arch>.apk (x86_64, aarch64, armv7; Alpine, with OpenRC: below), each with its .sha256 and .sigstore.json, downloaded and verified as the bundle above (--pattern "*.deb*", "*.rpm*" or "*.apk*"). CI keeps them for every commit as workflow artifacts, and scripts/package.sh builds them locally (cargo install cargo-deb cargo-generate-rpm --locked once, and python3 for the .apk, which scripts/apk.py at the repository's root writes; none needs dpkg, rpm or apk-tools, so it runs on macOS too; --target aarch64-unknown-linux-musl or armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf for the ARM ones). Or from the signed apt and dnf repository on GitHub Pages, once it is set up (the repository README, "Deployment"), where apt upgrade and dnf upgrade then bring new versions. sudo apt install ./vpsfort-tg-bot_0.5.1-1_amd64.deb # Fedora, RHEL: sudo dnf install ./vpsfort-tg-bot-0.5.1-1.x86_64.rpm
sudoedit /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot/config.env # the first install put the template there
sudo systemctl enable --now vpsfort-tg-bot The package puts the same files in the same places as install.sh (/opt/vpsfort-tg-bot with the binary and config.env.example, the user vpsfort-tg-bot, /var/log/vpsfort-tg-bot, the logrotate rule), except the unit, which is in /usr/lib/systemd/system. Its post-install step does what install.sh does apart from copying files: the user, config.env from the template the first time, the owners and modes, the outbox and the log directory; and it prints what is left to do (step 3 of "Setup": the token and ADMIN_CHAT_ID from pair, your OpenPGP key). dpkg-reconfigure vpsfort-tg-bot (rpm: dnf reinstall ./vpsfort-tg-bot-*.rpm) runs that step again, e.g. after copying a key there. apt remove vpsfort-tg-bot (dnf remove) stops the bot and keeps /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot; apt purge vpsfort-tg-bot removes it with the state and keys (rpm: by hand). Nothing starts on its own. The first install puts the template in place and prints what to fill in; you enable the service once it is filled in. An upgrade keeps the config and restarts the service only if it was running and the config is filled in. Over a bundle or deploy.sh install the package takes over: the config, state and keys stay; the bundle's unit in /etc/systemd/system (it would shadow the package's) and its rollback files go, and the service is enabled again on the package's unit if it was (vpsfort's integrity watch reports the removed unit as a warning once). Replacing the config: when a terminal is there, the install asks whether to replace the config with the new template (the old one kept with the suffix .old); Enter, a timeout of a minute, no terminal or DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive keep it. VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace (or keep) answers without asking: sudo VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace apt install ./<file>.deb. Rollback is installing the previous version's package (apt install ./<old>.deb --allow-downgrades, dnf downgrade ./<old>.rpm): there is no .prev file. Alpine (apk, OpenRC): apk add --allow-untrusted ./vpsfort-tg-bot-<version>-r0.x86_64.apk puts the same files in the same places, with the OpenRC script /etc/init.d/vpsfort-tg-bot instead of the unit: the settings exported from config.env as EnvironmentFile= does, supervised by supervise-daemon and started again 5 seconds after a crash; systemd's sandboxing has no equivalent there. The package is unsigned, hence --allow-untrusted: sha256sum -c and the attestation verify it. Its install scripts are POSIX sh and do what the post-install step above does: the user, config.env from the template the first time, the owners and modes, the log directory; an upgrade restarts a running bot. Then rc-update add vpsfort-tg-bot default && rc-service vpsfort-tg-bot start. apk del vpsfort-tg-bot stops it and keeps /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot. Not yet run on an Alpine host: CI installs the package in an Alpine container.

129.body:
Create the bot with @BotFather : /newbot, then /setjoingroups → Disable (it serves one private chat). Keep the token secret. Deploy from the Mac (builds a static Linux binary, runs scripts/ci.sh first), to the relay node: first vpsfort (../vpsfort/deploy/deploy.sh tg deploy/vpsfort-tg.toml, after setting the peers and peer_accept on the other nodes), then the bot: ./deploy/deploy.sh # copies to tg:/tmp/vpsfort-tg-bot-deploy, prints the root command (the XMPP server's ssh alias as argument for that server) The first install creates the vpsfort-tg-bot user, /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot and config.env (from deploy/config.env.example, every option with a reasonable value). It doesn't start the bot while the token and admin id are placeholders. Fill in config.env as root: put the token in TELEGRAM_TOKEN. Then find your user id: set -a; . /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot/config.env; set +a; /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot/vpsfort-tg-bot pair It prints a link and a code. Open the link (or send /start <code> to the bot) from your Telegram account, and it prints ADMIN_CHAT_ID=…. Put that in config.env, check SERVER_NAMES, install your OpenPGP public key as OPENPGP_KEY (above), then systemctl enable --now vpsfort-tg-bot (or run install.sh again). pair reads the bot's updates itself, so the service must be stopped meanwhile. Tell vpsfort (optional, off by default; vpsfort-tg.toml has it already). In [notify] of /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml (a vpsfort with tg_outbox support must be deployed first: older ones reject the key): tg_outbox = "/opt/vpsfort-tg-bot/outbox"
tg_user = "vpsfort-tg-bot" The weekly abuse report job reads tg_outbox from there too. On a server with ejabberd, leaving admins empty sends admin messages to Telegram only (users are still warned over XMPP). For a relay node, in /etc/default/vpsfort-abuse-report: ABUSE_REPORT_SEND_TO=<the XMPP server>:7946 there, and on the XMPP server ABUSE_REPORT_PEERS="vpn tg" and ABUSE_REPORT_FORWARD_TO=<tg>:7946. Then systemctl restart vpsfort and run the notify-test --telegram check above. Adding vpsfort-tg-bot.service to vpsfort's [sources] services gets an alert when the bot fails. install.sh rollback goes back to the previous binary and unit (kept while the running version runs cleanly). Renamed from tgbot (2026-10-17). The bot was tgbot, installed as /opt/tgbot/tgbot, run by tgbot.service as the user tgbot, logging to /var/log/tgbot. The first install.sh of the new name moves an old install over on its own, before installing: stops and disables tgbot.service, removes it and /etc/logrotate.d/tgbot (local changes in tgbot.service.d/ move to vpsfort-tg-bot.service.d/); renames the user and group tgbot to vpsfort-tg-bot (same ids, so every file stays theirs); moves /opt/tgbot to /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot and /var/log/tgbot to /var/log/vpsfort-tg-bot: the state (Telegram's queue position, messages to delete), the pseudonym key (so every account keeps its pseudonym), OPENPGP_KEY, the outbox and the log carry over; rewrites the old paths in config.env (the previous file stays as config.env.pre-rename) and adds BOT_STATE_PATH and LOG_DIR if they were missing; keeps the old binary as vpsfort-tg-bot.prev if it ran cleanly, so rollback works right after the move (with the new unit and paths; the old unit is not kept); in /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml and /etc/default/vpsfort-abuse-report, replaces /opt/tgbot, tg_user = "tgbot", "tgbot.service" and ABUSE_REPORT_TG_OWNER=tgbot (each changed file stays as <file>.pre-rename-<time>), checks that vpsfort accepts the config (else puts it back and says what to change by hand) and restarts vpsfort. Deploy the current vpsfort first (its abuse report unit may write only to the new outbox paths, and its tg_user default is now vpsfort-tg-bot); install.sh warns while the installed abuse report unit names only the old ones. Running it again changes nothing more; if both /opt/tgbot and /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot exist, it stops and asks you to keep one. The bot's token and chat stay the same; Telegram doesn't see the rename. Telegram sees the address of the host vpsfort-tg-bot runs on; in the messages the servers appear by their node ids only, as far as SERVER_NAMES lists them. The host needs outgoing HTTPS to api.telegram.org. TELEGRAM_API_URL can point to a local Bot API server instead (plain HTTP only on localhost).
129.title: Setup

13.body: Bottom line: vpsfort's enforcement takes the most care not to break the server itself (Docker, flushed rulesets, replies, oversized feeds). It covers the Linux firewalls (nftables, firewalld, ipset, ufw, iptables) but no BSD or Windows ones, and CrowdSec reaches the HTTP layer and CDNs. feature vpsfort fail2ban sshguard CrowdSec bouncer Wazuh CSF/LFD firewall backends ◐ nftables, firewalld, ipset, ufw, iptables (Linux only) ✓ iptables, nftables, firewalld, ufw, pf, ipfw, … ✓ iptables, ipset, nftables, firewalld, pf, ipfw ✓ nftables, iptables/ipset, pf, Windows ◐ iptables, firewalld, pf, Windows ◐ iptables bans expire in the kernel, even while the daemon is down ✓ nft and ipset timeouts ◐ some ipset actions – ✓ – – Docker-published ports covered without extra setup ✓ ◐ DOCKER-USER chain by config ◐ ◐ DOCKER-USER or forward hook by config ◐ ◐ DOCKER option per-source connection rate limits in the kernel ✓ – – – – ✓ CONNLIMIT, PORTFLOOD public blocklists loaded into the firewall ✓ with sanity limits – – ✓ console blocklists – ✓ csf.blocklists country blocking ✓ offline, from DB-IP Lite or a commercial database read as it is, plus networks by ASN – – ◐ paid lists or own profiles – ✓ CC_DENY HTTP-level responses (403, captcha, CDN) – ◐ Cloudflare action – ✓ nginx, Traefik, HAProxy, Cloudflare, … – – a WAF's or IPS's decisions blocked at the firewall ✓ [waf]: CrowdSec built in; JSON, CSV, regex, plain lists for others ◐ an action script of your own – ✓ what a bouncer does ◐ active response scripts – feature pros (vpsfort) cons (vpsfort), and who does better Where bans sit Its own nftables table at prerouting, right after connection tracking. It runs before ufw's chains and before Docker's DNAT, so your own ALLOW rules can't shadow a ban, and Docker ports are covered without touching DOCKER-USER. It never edits your rules. On Fedora and RHEL it can keep everything in firewalld instead: its own ipsets, a drop zone and a forwarding policy, visible with firewall-cmd. The ipset backend is iptables with one set lookup however many bans. Linux only: no pf, ipfw or Windows. The ufw fallback loses Docker coverage, rate limits and feeds; the firewalld backend has no rate limits or feeds, and its entries end only while vpsfort runs. The firewalld, ipset and nftables backends ran on a Fedora 44 test server; the plain iptables backend has not yet run on a real host. Expiry Ban timeouts live in the kernel: if vpsfort stops, bans still end on time. After a reboot it re-applies what is still active. CrowdSec's firewall bouncer works the same way. Self-healing Debian's and Ubuntu's nftables.conf starts with flush ruleset, so a restart of nftables deletes every ban. vpsfort notices within 30 s, rebuilds every set and chain, re-adds the bans with their remaining time, and raises a high alert. The same after firewall-cmd --reload or a firewalld restart, and after its iptables chains are flushed (both seen on the Fedora server). A single change the firewall program refuses is kept and tried again every 30 s, with a high alert while it keeps failing. fail2ban restores its chains too, but only at its next ban action. Replies to the server's own connections Bans drop after connection tracking, so replies always pass: DNS, mail relay, update mirrors, federated XMPP servers. A forged packet that gets such an address banned can't cut the server off. The chains dropped a test client on the Fedora server, and on a production server both pings and a TCP connection to addresses banned there got their replies. Rate limits Per-source [[ratelimit]] entries in the kernel, from the first packet, Docker ports included. status shows their drop counters. nftables backend only (status says so under the others). CSF has richer flood controls (SYN floods, per-port and per-connection limits). Feeds Downloads with curl (the binary has no TLS library) and keeps the last good copy. It drops bogons, prefixes wider than /12, and anything overlapping your allowlist or peers. A refresh that suddenly covers far more address space is refused. A few public lists (Spamhaus DROP and ASN-DROP, FireHOL); no curated commercial lists. nftables, ipset and firewalld backends (firewalld: 50,000 networks per list). CrowdSec's blocklists are larger and updated more often. Countries and networks [geoblock] drops whole countries (or all but some) and networks by AS number, from the DB-IP Lite databases it already holds for labels: no download, no second database, about 1 MB while the list is computed. Protected addresses are cut out exactly. China is about 15,000 networks, everything but one country about 28,000. On the Fedora server two blocked countries timed out and a third connected. The free DB-IP Lite data misplaces some addresses and is refreshed monthly: coarse, not a curated list; a commercial database (DB-IP's IP to Country as it is) can replace it. ufw and plain iptables can't hold it; firewalld takes at most 50,000 networks. CSF's CC_DENY and CC_ALLOW have been doing this for years; vpsfort's [geoblock] ports limits a country block to some ports (SSH and XMPP closed, the web site open) the same way. HTTP layer [waf] blocks what a WAF decides at the firewall, for every port and, as bans, on every cluster node: CrowdSec's local API, cscli output and blocklist mirror are read as they are, any other app through JSON, CSV, regex or plain-list formats. Its decisions get the protections of an operator ban (allowlists, peers, recent logins), are lifted when the WAF drops them, and large blocklists go into sets of their own. No WAF of its own, and no HTTP-level response: a banned visitor just times out. No captcha, no ban at the CDN or edge. CrowdSec's remediation components and WAF cover that layer. [waf] is tested against CrowdSec's documented formats, not yet run against a real CrowdSec.

130.body: All in config.env (deploy/config.env.example has each with a reasonable value and a comment; vpsfort-tg-bot --help lists the matching flags): Variable Default TELEGRAM_TOKEN / TELEGRAM_TOKEN_FILE from @BotFather; one of the two ADMIN_CHAT_ID your Telegram user id (vpsfort-tg-bot pair) TELEGRAM_API_URL https://api.telegram.org XMPP_DOMAINS a bare user name in an alert counts as on the first one SERVER_NAMES node=address,...,name; ...: replaced by the node id in alerts OPENPGP_KEY the admin's OpenPGP public key; files go out encrypted to it, or not at all DELETE_AFTER_HOURS 0 (keep) 1–47: the bot deletes the chat's messages, both sides, after that long PROTECT_CONTENT no yes: clients don't allow forwarding, saving or copying alerts ALERT_MAX_HOURS 24 older alerts are dropped unsent OUTBOX_MAX_DAYS 7 older files are deleted unsent BOT_STATE_PATH /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot/state.json OUTBOX_DIR outbox next to the state PSEUDONYM_KEY pseudonym.key next to the state LOG_DIR /var/log/vpsfort-tg-bot bot.log, 14 days Exit status 78 (Telegram refused the token, or a setting is wrong) is not restarted by the unit. Fix config.env and start it again. A token revoked while the bot runs stops it the same way.
130.title: Settings

131.body: On Telegram: messages stay in the chat until deleted. With DELETE_AFTER_HOURS, the bot deletes its own and your messages in the chat after that long. Telegram allows bots this only within 48 hours, so messages from a longer downtime have to be deleted in the app. /privacy says which applies. On the server: bot.log (14 days: weekly rotation, one old copy), state.json (the next update id and, with auto-delete, message ids and times: no text), pseudonym.key, and outbox files until they are sent (or expire). Nothing the bot sends is written anywhere else on the server. Path Owner Mode /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot/ root:vpsfort-tg-bot 1770 (sticky) config.env (the token), OPENPGP_KEY root:vpsfort-tg-bot 640 state.json, pseudonym.key vpsfort-tg-bot 600 outbox/ root:vpsfort-tg-bot 1770; files vpsfort-tg-bot 600 /var/log/vpsfort-tg-bot/, bot.log vpsfort-tg-bot 700, 600 The unit drops every capability, makes the whole file system read-only except /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot and /var/log/vpsfort-tg-bot, allows only IPv4 and IPv6 sockets, denies writable-executable memory, and is held to 128 MB of memory (MemoryMax).

132.body: The suggested telegram-rs-2 (0.1.2) served as a reference for the API's shape but is not a dependency: it has no sendDocument, and its Message lacks from and date; its reqwest uses the default TLS (OpenSSL), which breaks the static musl build; its errors carry reqwest's URL, which holds the token, into logs; it pulls in a proc-macro crate from the same single author (runs at build time), with a few dozen downloads in all. src/api.rs calls the half dozen methods it needs directly, over reqwest with rustls and ring (like vpsfort-xmpp-bot's TLS). It checks the token's shape before it goes into a URL and strips URLs from errors. Formatting goes as entities, never Markdown or HTML, so nothing in a log line can change how a message displays.

133.body:
./scripts/ci.sh # fmt, clippy, tests, cargo audit, static Linux binary The static build needs rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl (for ARM: aarch64-unknown-linux-musl, armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf, built with TARGET=... ./deploy/deploy.sh) and rustup component add llvm-tools (see .cargo/config.toml, the same as vpsfort-xmpp-bot's). tests/fake_telegram.rs runs the delivery code against a fake Bot API server on 127.0.0.1: an alert with account names and server addresses replaced, the report held back without a key and then sent encrypted (nothing of it in the request, the admin's key opens it), flood control (429 retry_after), strangers ignored, the state across a restart, auto-delete and its 48-hour limit. tests/gpg_interop.rs decrypts the files with GnuPG when gpg is installed (brew install gnupg), in a throwaway GNUPGHOME, and checks keys that expire. Not yet tried against the real Telegram or on a phone. Fuzzing. What comes from outside (vpsfort's outbox files with attackers' log text in them, Telegram's replies, the key file, SERVER_NAMES) goes through four cargo-fuzz targets (code in src/fuzzing.rs): alert_text: an outbox file through the whole way to Telegram. Besides no panics, it checks the promises with rules of its own: no name@domain and no ejabberd:<name> left, no configured server address or host name left, nothing left to replace on a second pass, and every message as Telegram takes it unchanged (1 to 4096 UTF-16 units, no blanks at the ends, no control characters, entities inside the text and not splitting a UTF-16 pair). telegram_reply: Bot API replies (updates, errors, sent messages) and state.json; no update with an id may be lost. openpgp_key: the key file; whatever is taken as a key must encrypt, with nothing in clear. server_names: a SERVER_NAMES value and a text (split at the first NUL byte). tests/fuzz_smoke.rs runs them on stable on realistic inputs, the seeds in fuzz/seeds/ and a few thousand mutations, so cargo test keeps them working; a failing input is saved as target/fuzz-smoke-<target>.bin (VPSFORT_TG_BOT_WRITE_SEEDS=1 cargo test --test fuzz_smoke regenerates the seeds; the keys in them are new and throwaway). The real search needs nightly: rustup toolchain install nightly --profile minimal && cargo install cargo-fuzz --locked # once
cargo +nightly fuzz run alert_text fuzz/corpus/alert_text fuzz/seeds/alert_text -- -dict=fuzz/alert_text.dict -max_total_time=600 New inputs collect in fuzz/corpus/, crashes in fuzz/artifacts/ (both git-ignored). The regression-* seeds are inputs the first runs (2026-10-17) failed on, all fixed: a server address inside a longer run (dead:…, …:ad:192.0.2.10, 2001:db8::10.example…), an address with junk after a colon, two addresses touching (a@x{@y), an ejabberd:[acct: that wasn't a pseudonym hiding the name after it, brackets alone taken for an ejabberd: name, a hex-only node id rebuilding an address, an address glued to another (198.51.100.20db8::, now replaced until nothing changes), a long subject cut on a blank. The smoke test found the first of these within a second. Later the same day, vpsfort-mail-bot's fuzzing of the same code found a server address that, replaced by its node id, completed an address (admin@::ffff:192.0.2.10 → admin@node1): the account pass now runs again after the server pass (regression-server-makes-address).

134.body: A send-only mail bot for vpsfort : it mails vpsfort's admin alerts, the daily digest and the weekly abuse report to the admins, each mail OpenPGP-encrypted as a whole , subject included. It goes out through a mail server over SMTP: the local Postfix, or any other server with TLS. It reads no mail and takes no orders; the servers stay managed over SSH. It is the third copy bot next to vpsfort-xmpp-bot (OMEMO) and vpsfort-tg-bot (Telegram), and works like vpsfort-tg-bot: vpsfort puts a copy of every admin message in its outbox, the bot sends it and deletes it. It can run on any vpsfort node, alone or next to the other bots, or on a relay node of its own (as vpsfort-tg-bot does, deploy/vpsfort-tg.toml in vpsfort).
134.title: vpsfort-mail-bot

135.body: What a mail looks like Keys Sanitizing (optional) The mail server How vpsfort and the bot meet Install from a release bundle Install from a package Setup Settings Retention and what the bot keeps Build and test
135.title: Contents

136.body: Every mail is PGP/MIME (RFC 3156): multipart/encrypted, one OpenPGP message holding the whole content. Mail servers on the way, and the mailbox provider, see only: the envelope and the outer headers: From, To, Date, Message-ID (random), the size, and the subject ... (OUTER_SUBJECT); Auto-Submitted: auto-generated (no auto-replies), and, if the bot signs, an Autocrypt header with the bot's public key. Inside, encrypted: the real subject ([vpn] vpsfort: password guessing blocked) and the headers again as "protected headers" (protected-headers="v1"), which Thunderbird, K-9 / Thunderbird for Android, FairEmail and Delta Chat show in place of ..., then the text, quoted-printable (any line length, any character). Text from attackers in alerts (user names they tried, URIs) never reaches a header unencoded and can't start a MIME part. Alerts and the digest : one mail each, the message's text as the mail's text. The weekly abuse report : the report as the mail's text (it is text). A file that isn't UTF-8 text would be attached instead. The OpenPGP format is the one every client reads: v4 keys (RSA, or Ed25519/Curve25519), a v3 PKESK per recipient key, SEIPD v1 with MDC under AES-256, no compression (not AEAD / v6, which many clients can't read yet). tests/gpg_interop.rs has GnuPG decrypt the mails and check the signature, for RSA and Curve25519 keys.
136.breadcrumbs: The bots » Mail (vpsfort-mail-bot) » What a mail looks like
136.title: What a mail looks like

137.body: OPENPGP_KEY (required): the recipients' public keys, in one file (armored or binary, one or more keys). Each address in MAIL_TO gets the key whose user id names it; with a single key, that key serves every address (logged as a warning when the user id differs). An address without a key stops the bot at the start (exit 78): nothing goes out in clear. A key that has expired, at the start or later: that recipient gets nothing (logged every 10 minutes) until the key is replaced; with no usable key at all the bot doesn't start, and when the last one expires while it runs, messages wait and vpsfort warns about them after bot_stuck_after. Only the key's own signatures count: certifications by others (gpg --sign-key, web of trust) are ignored, not taken for broken self-signatures. SIGNING_KEY (optional): the bot's own key, made once with vpsfort-mail-bot keygen (Ed25519, no passphrase: it would sit next to the key anyway). Every mail is then signed, and the public key goes out in the Autocrypt header (autocrypt.org Level 1), so clients that read it (Thunderbird, K-9/FairEmail, Delta Chat) learn it from the first mail and show the signature as valid. Others: import signing.key.pub.asc. The key proves a mail comes from the bot; it can't read anything. Only public keys of the recipients are on the server: whoever gets into it can't read mails already sent.
137.title: Keys

138.body: The mails are encrypted end to end, so by default alerts and digests go out as they are, with XMPP account names and the servers' own addresses. SANITIZE=on replaces them exactly as vpsfort-tg-bot does for Telegram (the same code, src/redact.rs and src/servers.rs): every XMPP address (alice@example.org, ejabberd:alice) becomes a pseudonym [acct:1a2b3c], an HMAC under PSEUDONYM_KEY (made on the first start, the bot's, 600); vpsfort-mail-bot pseudonym alice@example.org on the server tells which is which; the servers' own addresses and host names in SERVER_NAMES become their node ids (nextcloud.example.org:443 → nextcloud.node1:443); attackers' addresses stay. The weekly abuse report is never changed (as on Telegram). The Telegram bot sanitizes always.

139.body: SMTP_TLS port login the local Postfix none (only allowed to 127.0.0.1, ::1, localhost) 25 usually SMTP_AUTH=none a provider or another server tls (TLS from the start) or starttls (required: never falls back to plain) 465 / 587 SMTP_AUTH=auto (PLAIN or LOGIN, whichever is offered), plain, login The server's certificate is checked against the system's CAs (/etc/ssl/certs) and SMTP_TLS_NAME (default: SMTP_HOST), or only against SMTP_CA_FILE (a server with a certificate of its own CA). A login is never sent over plain SMTP to another host: that setting is refused. The password goes in SMTP_PASSWORD_FILE (root:vpsfort-mail-bot 640). What the server says decides what happens: Out of reach, 4xx, TLS failing: the message waits; the bot tries again after 30 s, doubling up to 30 minutes. Alerts older than ALERT_MAX_HOURS (24) are dropped and counted in one mail; files after OUTBOX_MAX_DAYS (7). 5xx for one mail (too large, rejected as spam): the bot sends a short note in its place saying what was refused and where to find it (vpsfort's actions log, or how to make the report again). If the note goes through, the refused mail is dropped. 5xx for every mail (the sender or a recipient refused): the note fails too, the message waits, and the bot tries every 30 minutes. A refused login (530, 534, 535, 538): no note is tried (it would be one more failed login towards the server's ban); the message waits, retried every 30 minutes. At the start it stops the bot with exit 78, which systemd doesn't restart. No STARTTLS offered where SMTP_TLS=starttls: nothing is sent, not even the login, and the bot keeps retrying with backoff rather than giving up for good (someone in the way may be stripping it, and must not be able to stop the bot). The bot opens one connection per mail (a few a day).

14.body: Bottom line: vpsfort shares well among your own servers and keeps every observation private. Like every tool here but CrowdSec, it has no crowd-sourced intelligence; that is CrowdSec's main strength. feature vpsfort fail2ban sshguard CrowdSec Wazuh CSF/LFD bans shared between your own servers ✓ peer to peer, encrypted – scripts – ✓ through one central local API ✓ through the manager ✓ LF_CLUSTER suspicion below the ban threshold adds up across servers ✓ – – – ✓ the manager sees all events – works without a central server ✓ mesh, chain or star – – – – ✓ crowd-sourced global blocklist – ◐ AbuseIPDB actions – ✓ – ◐ third-party lists nothing about attackers leaves your servers by default ✓ ✓ ✓ – signals go to CrowdSec unless turned off ✓ self-hosted ✓ reports to the attackers' abuse desks ✓ weekly, with evidence and contacts ◐ complain and AbuseIPDB actions – – – – offline country and network labels ✓ – – ✓ ✓ ✓ feature pros (vpsfort) cons (vpsfort), and who does better Cluster XChaCha20-Poly1305 under a key derived from a fresh X25519 exchange per connection (the shared key authenticates the exchange; a recording stays unreadable if the key leaks later), and only peers may connect. Facts are de-duplicated and forwarded up to 3 hops. Suspicion is shared too, so an address that probes every server a little still adds up to a ban. A shared ban carries up to three of its evidence lines, worded as the abuse reports word them, so a peer's log and the console say what the source did, not only its score. A limited peer (peer_accept) can send messages but never ban anything. Optional node identities: each node signs its own facts and files with an Ed25519 key of its own, pinned on the others, so a broken-into node (or a stolen cluster key) speaks only for itself, and a node is dropped by deleting its key, without a new cluster key. Key rotation is staged in three rounds, without a gap. Without node identities, every unlimited key holder is fully trusted: a broken-into node can ban on the others under any name, for at most max_remote_ban. With them, it can still ban for itself, and still read what the others share until the cluster key is rotated. Keys are pinned by hand in each node's config, with no PKI or enrollment. Node identities run on the authors' five servers, each pinning the other four's keys and requiring signatures; a fact refused for its signature has not been seen yet. It is sized for a handful of nodes, with no fleet management. Threat intelligence Your data stays yours: no vendor sees your attackers or your users. The static feeds (Spamhaus, FireHOL) need no account. No network effect, as with every tool here but CrowdSec, which blocks addresses that attacked thousands of other servers before they reach yours; vpsfort knows what your own nodes saw, its feeds, and through [waf] what a CrowdSec next to it decides. Abuse reports A weekly report grouped by abuse mailbox (looked up with RDAP), each attacker with UTC log lines and account names withheld. Reports from several nodes are merged, and the result reaches the admin encrypted. The web console shows the last day's or week's at any time, merged across the nodes, one entry per network owner, each copied or saved as the e-mail to its abuse desk, or opened in your mail program with the mailbox looked up (RDAP); a network is marked as mailed, and one banned again after that shows "seen again". An address's page can be handed to its hosting provider as a link that needs no login, cut to what the abuse report would show (account names withheld, nodes numbered), good for a day to a week. You send the mails yourself: vpsfort never mails third parties, by design. There is no AbuseIPDB integration. Geo DB-IP Lite by default, or a commercial database read as it is (DB-IP's CSVs; any CSV with a header row; a city-level one adds cities and coordinates): about 1.2 million ranges in ~40 MB, looked up in memory, with no request per lookup. Used in alerts, to limit subnet growth, to learn each account's providers, and to block countries and networks. Cities, and map markers at the addresses' coordinates, only with a city-level database (DB-IP's city lite needs the unit's memory raised); the free data's accuracy: on the authors' servers, a VPN exit in Vienna (M247) shows as Czechia.

140.body: The outbox (/opt/vpsfort-mail-bot/outbox, root:vpsfort-mail-bot 1770, sticky) has the format of the other bots: alert-*.msg with To: and Subject: lines, a blank line and the text, written under a dot name and renamed into place, owned by the bot's user. The bot claims one by renaming it to .<name>.sending, sends it, deletes it; if sending fails it renames it back (and on the next start it puts back what a stop left half-sent). The weekly report is any other regular file. vpsfort ([notify] mail_outbox, mail_user) puts a copy of every message for the first admin there (every admin message on a node with xmpp = false or no admins), and the abuse report job puts the report there. vpsfort warns the admins (over XMPP and to the Telegram bot, else as a system alert) when the bot leaves something unsent longer than bot_stuck_after.

141.body:
Instead of deploy.sh (below), without a Rust toolchain: every version tag vpsfort-mail-bot-v<version> gets its bundle, vpsfort-mail-bot-<version>-<commit>-<arch>.zip for each architecture (x86_64-linux-musl, aarch64-linux-musl for arm64, armv7-linux-musleabihf for 32-bit ARMv7 with hardware floating point), as an asset of the tag's GitHub Release (see "Releases" in the repository README ); CI also keeps one for every commit as a workflow artifact (they expire and need a GitHub login), and scripts/bundle.sh builds it locally. It holds the static binary, the unit, config.env.example, SHA256SUMS and install.sh. Download and verify (on your machine, then copy the zip over, or on the server): take the zip for the server's architecture (uname -m: x86_64, aarch64, or armv7l for armv7) from the GitHub Release of the version's tag, with the GitHub CLI or from the Releases page (each crate's releases are tagged vpsfort-mail-bot-v<version>): arch=x86_64-linux-musl # the server's: aarch64-linux-musl (arm64), armv7-linux-musleabihf (32-bit ARM)
gh release download vpsfort-mail-bot-v0.5.1 --repo makhort/vpsfort --pattern "*-$arch.zip*" # the zip, its .sha256 and .sigstore.json
sha256sum -c vpsfort-mail-bot-*-$arch.zip.sha256 # the download is intact (macOS: shasum -a 256 -c)
gh attestation verify vpsfort-mail-bot-*-$arch.zip --repo makhort/vpsfort --source-ref refs/tags/vpsfort-mail-bot-v0.5.1 gh attestation verify (after gh auth login) checks the signed build provenance: that this repository's CI built exactly this zip from that tag. With --bundle vpsfort-mail-bot-*-$arch.zip.sigstore.json it checks the attestation attached to the Release instead of fetching it from GitHub. Only a public repository's releases have one (GitHub offers attestations for private repositories only with Enterprise Cloud). On the server (apt install unzip or dnf install unzip if needed): arch=x86_64-linux-musl # as above: aarch64-linux-musl, armv7-linux-musleabihf on ARM
unzip vpsfort-mail-bot-*-$arch.zip && cd vpsfort-mail-bot-*-$arch
sudo ./install.sh # install or upgrade; the first time also /opt/vpsfort-mail-bot/config.env
sudo ./install.sh rollback # back to the previous version The first install, as with deploy.sh, doesn't start the bot until config.env is filled in (then run it again). install.sh checks every file against SHA256SUMS in a copy only root can write, then runs the same installer as deploy.sh (./install.sh --check only checks the files).

142.body:
The same release has a package per architecture, for the distribution's package manager instead of install.sh: vpsfort-mail-bot_<version>-1_<arch>.deb (amd64, arm64, armhf; Debian, Ubuntu and their derivatives) vpsfort-mail-bot-<version>-1.<arch>.rpm (x86_64, aarch64, armv7hl; Fedora, RHEL and its rebuilds) and vpsfort-mail-bot-<version>-r0.<arch>.apk (x86_64, aarch64, armv7; Alpine, with OpenRC: below), each with its .sha256 and .sigstore.json, downloaded and verified as the bundle above (--pattern "*.deb*", "*.rpm*" or "*.apk*"). CI keeps them for every commit as workflow artifacts, and scripts/package.sh builds them locally (cargo install cargo-deb cargo-generate-rpm --locked once, and python3 for the .apk, which scripts/apk.py at the repository's root writes; none needs dpkg, rpm or apk-tools, so it runs on macOS too; --target aarch64-unknown-linux-musl or armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf for the ARM ones). Or from the signed apt and dnf repository on GitHub Pages, once it is set up (the repository README, "Deployment"), where apt upgrade and dnf upgrade then bring new versions. sudo apt install ./vpsfort-mail-bot_0.5.1-1_amd64.deb # Fedora, RHEL: sudo dnf install ./vpsfort-mail-bot-0.5.1-1.x86_64.rpm
sudoedit /opt/vpsfort-mail-bot/config.env # the first install put the template there
sudo systemctl enable --now vpsfort-mail-bot The package puts the same files in the same places as install.sh (/opt/vpsfort-mail-bot with the binary and config.env.example, the user vpsfort-mail-bot, /var/log/vpsfort-mail-bot, the logrotate rule), except the unit, which is in /usr/lib/systemd/system. Its post-install step does what install.sh does apart from copying files: the user, config.env from the template the first time, the owners and modes, the outbox and the log directory; and it prints what is left to do ("Setup": the addresses, the mail server, the recipients' OpenPGP keys). dpkg-reconfigure vpsfort-mail-bot (rpm: dnf reinstall ./vpsfort-mail-bot-*.rpm) runs that step again, e.g. after copying a key there. apt remove vpsfort-mail-bot (dnf remove) stops the bot and keeps /opt/vpsfort-mail-bot; apt purge vpsfort-mail-bot removes it with the state and keys (rpm: by hand). Nothing starts on its own. The first install puts the template in place and prints what to fill in; you enable the service once it is filled in. An upgrade keeps the config and restarts the service only if it was running and the config is filled in. Over a bundle or deploy.sh install the package takes over: the config, state and keys stay; the bundle's unit in /etc/systemd/system (it would shadow the package's) and its rollback files go, and the service is enabled again on the package's unit if it was (vpsfort's integrity watch reports the removed unit as a warning once). Replacing the config: when a terminal is there, the install asks whether to replace the config with the new template (the old one kept with the suffix .old); Enter, a timeout of a minute, no terminal or DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive keep it. VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace (or keep) answers without asking: sudo VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace apt install ./<file>.deb. Rollback is installing the previous version's package (apt install ./<old>.deb --allow-downgrades, dnf downgrade ./<old>.rpm): there is no .prev file. Alpine (apk, OpenRC): apk add --allow-untrusted ./vpsfort-mail-bot-<version>-r0.x86_64.apk puts the same files in the same places, with the OpenRC script /etc/init.d/vpsfort-mail-bot instead of the unit: the settings exported from config.env as EnvironmentFile= does, supervised by supervise-daemon and started again 5 seconds after a crash; systemd's sandboxing has no equivalent there. The package is unsigned, hence --allow-untrusted: sha256sum -c and the attestation verify it. Its install scripts are POSIX sh and do what the post-install step above does: the user, config.env from the template the first time, the owners and modes, the log directory; an upgrade restarts a running bot. Then rc-update add vpsfort-mail-bot default && rc-service vpsfort-mail-bot start. apk del vpsfort-mail-bot stops it and keeps /opt/vpsfort-mail-bot. Not yet run on an Alpine host: CI installs the package in an Alpine container.

On your Mac: ./deploy/deploy.sh vpn It runs scripts/ci.sh, builds the static binary, copies it with the unit and install.sh to the server and prints the command to paste into a root shell there. The first install creates the user vpsfort-mail-bot, /opt/vpsfort-mail-bot/config.env from config.env.example, and doesn't start the bot until it's filled in. Then, as root: Fill in config.env: MAIL_FROM, MAIL_TO, the mail server. Copy the recipients' public keys to /opt/vpsfort-mail-bot/recipients.asc (Thunderbird: Account settings → End-to-end encryption → OpenPGP Key Manager → File → Export; or gpg --armor --export you@example.org), and the SMTP password to smtp-password. /opt/vpsfort-mail-bot/vpsfort-mail-bot check # connects, logs in, sends nothing
/opt/vpsfort-mail-bot/vpsfort-mail-bot send-test # one test mail

For SPF/DKIM, MAIL_FROM should be an address the mail server may send as; otherwise the mails may land in spam. install.sh rollback goes back to the previous binary and unit.

145.body: Outbox files until they are sent (alerts 24 h at most, files 7 days). Its log, /var/log/vpsfort-mail-bot/bot.log (owner only): what was sent to whom, and the mail server's answers; rotated weekly, no line older than 14 days. No message text. Nothing else: no state file. With SANITIZE=on, the pseudonym key. 146.body:
./scripts/ci.sh Format, clippy, the tests, cargo audit, and the static x86_64-unknown-linux-musl binary (TARGET=aarch64-unknown-linux-musl ./scripts/ci.sh, or armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf, for ARM). tests/fake_smtp.rs runs the bot against a fake mail server on 127.0.0.1 (plain, STARTTLS and TLS with a test CA, PLAIN and LOGIN, a server that strips STARTTLS, refusals) and runs the binary as systemd would; it needs to bind 127.0.0.1. tests/gpg_interop.rs needs gpg (skips without it). SMTP is lettre (blocking, rustls with ring: no OpenSSL), OpenPGP is rpgp, both pure Rust. Fuzzing. What comes from outside (vpsfort's outbox files with attackers' log text in them, other files there, the recipients' key file, the signing key) goes through four cargo-fuzz targets (code in src/fuzzing.rs). Besides no panics, each checks the promises with rules of its own: alert_mail: an outbox file to the finished mail, with SANITIZE off and on. The mail is all ASCII with CRLF line ends and lines under 998 characters; it has exactly the bot's own outer headers (subject ...) and, between the boundaries, only the version part and the armored message. Decrypted, it has the fixed protected headers, the subject on one line, and the text back unchanged; with SANITIZE=on, no account address and no server address or host name of the fuzzed setup is left. file_mail: a file (name, NUL, content): text as the mail's text, anything else attached under a safe name, back byte for byte. openpgp_keys: the key file; whatever is taken must encrypt to every usable address. signing_key: whatever is taken signs mails that verify, in a well-formed Autocrypt header. tests/fuzz_smoke.rs runs them on stable on realistic inputs, the seeds in fuzz/seeds/ and a few thousand mutations, so cargo test keeps them working; a failing input is saved as target/fuzz-smoke-<target>.bin (VPSFORT_MAIL_BOT_WRITE_SEEDS=1 cargo test --test fuzz_smoke regenerates the seeds; the keys in them, the signing key's secret part too, are throwaway). The real search needs nightly: rustup toolchain install nightly --profile minimal && cargo install cargo-fuzz --locked # once
cargo +nightly fuzz run alert_mail fuzz/corpus/alert_mail fuzz/seeds/alert_mail -- -dict=fuzz/alert_mail.dict -max_len=8192 -max_total_time=600 New inputs collect in fuzz/corpus/, crashes in fuzz/artifacts/ (both git-ignored). The regression-* seeds are inputs the first runs (2026-10-17) failed on, all fixed: a subject holding =?utf-8?b?…?= went into the header as it was, so mail clients would have shown it decoded, as other text (now encoded); a damaged signing key whose secret part no longer matched its public part was taken, and every mail would have carried a bad signature (now refused at the start); with SANITIZE=on, a server address replaced by its node id completed an address (admin@::ffff:192.0.2.10 → admin@node1; fixed in vpsfort-tg-bot too). One was the oracle's: a pseudonym cut by the 200-character subject limit. Tested on a server (since 2026-10-20): a Debian VPS deployed with deploy.sh, the unit running. check, send-test, vpsfort's notify-test --mail (picked up from the outbox and sent within seconds), a digest (digest --send), real alerts (a source gone quiet, new listeners, a cluster node not responding) and the weekly abuse report, all through a provider (SMTP_TLS=tls, port 465, LOGIN) to a SimpleLogin alias forwarding to Proton Mail. Proton Mail on Android decrypts and shows them; GnuPG on a Mac decrypts the exported mails and shows the bot's signature as good. Proton re-armors the encrypted part and exports it quoted-printable with CRLF line ends, which turns every = in the armor (the base64 padding and the checksum line) into =3D and makes gpg report a CRC error or a malformed CRC. Undo that before decrypting a mail exported from Proton (only there: base64 itself never holds =3D, apart from a checksum that happens to start with 3D): sed 's/=3D/=/g' mail.eml | gpg --decrypt

147.body: A Signal bot that brings vpsfort's admin messages to the admin's Signal account: the alerts, the daily digest and the weekly abuse report. Signal encrypts every message end to end; the bot adds a check that the other end is still the admin (the safety number ), and when it isn't, sends only files encrypted to the admin's OpenPGP key, or nothing. It does for Signal what vpsfort-tg-bot does for Telegram on vpsfort's side, through the same kind of outbox: A client only. It uses an account of its own on Signal's servers through signal-cli , which it runs as its child process. No server runs here, nothing listens. Send only. It reads nothing people send it: no commands. The servers are managed over SSH. No link to ejabberd. It runs as its own user vpsfort-signal-bot. vpsfort feeds it only when [notify] signal_outbox is set. Without it, nothing changes. It can run next to the other bots, on any node; on the relay node (vpsfort's deploy/vpsfort-tg.toml) the XMPP server never connects to Signal.

149.body: Signal's protocol libraries (libsignal, and presage on top of it) are AGPL-3.0, and Signal's service (registration, sealed sender, its key servers) can't reasonably be reimplemented from specifications, as vpsfort-xmpp-bot's OMEMO was. So the bot, which stays MIT, talks to signal-cli (GPL-3.0, a separate program) over its JSON-RPC interface (signal-cli jsonRpc on stdin and stdout, src/rpc.rs), and signal-cli does the Signal protocol. The bot holds no Signal keys itself; signal-cli keeps them in its data directory (SIGNAL_CLI_DATA, the bot's user only, mode 700).

15.body: Bottom line: vpsfort covers the practical "how would someone stay in?" checklist on Debian and Ubuntu with no extra tools. It is not a kernel-level runtime sensor and not a compliance-grade FIM. feature vpsfort Wazuh AIDE rkhunter, debsums Falco, Tetragon osquery persistence points watched out of the box (cron, at, timers, system and user units, SSH keys and host keys, PAM, sudoers, ld.so.preload, apt and dnf hooks and sources, network hooks, shell start-up files, ...) ✓ every minute ◐ default directories, 12 h scans; real time by config ◐ distribution config, typically daily ◐ some startup files ✓ rules, real time ◐ tables, scheduled queries changed lines shown in the alert ✓ ✓ report_changes – – – – package files told apart from foreign ones (dpkg or rpm origin) ✓ – – ✓ debsums – ◐ deb_packages, rpm_packages package files checked against dpkg's or rpm's hashes ✓ weekly – ◐ own baseline ✓ debsums – – set-uid program inventory ✓ ◐ rootcheck ◐ baseline ◐ ◐ rules ✓ suid_bin outbound connections and reverse shells ◐ checked every 60 s, containers' too ◐ command monitoring – – ✓ syscall events ◐ snapshots new kernel modules, containers (privileged, host network, risky mounts), WireGuard peers ✓ every 60 s, after a learning period ◐ rootcheck, rules – ◐ rkhunter: modules ✓ rules ◐ kernel_modules, docker_containers tables programs running from /tmp, from memory or from deleted files ✓ checked every 60 s ◐ rootcheck – ◐ ✓ ◐ by query failed su and sudo ✓ ✓ – – – – PAM failures (console, polkit, Cockpit), account changes, auditd stopped ✓ ✓ – – ◐ rules ◐ by query a login with a never-seen SSH key ✓ – – – – – malware signatures ◐ ClamAV results; changed files scanned with ClamAV or YARA ◐ ClamAV, YARA, VirusTotal integrations – ◐ rootkit signatures – – real-time kernel events – ◐ who-data through auditd – – ✓ eBPF ◐ evented tables events copied off the host as they happen ◐ alerts through bots and peers; the decision log mirrored to a peer at every sync, and a daily hash of it kept by the peers ✓ ◐ Samhain's server – ◐ falcosidekick ◐ fleet server signs of journal tampering (lost position, sealed-journal check) ✓ – – – – – feature pros (vpsfort) cons (vpsfort), and who does better Persistence watch It knows where intruders hide, including the scripts crontab lines run (also behind sudo -u, flock, timeout), at-jobs, user-level units, every user's shell start-up, the network stack's hooks, the resolver and the host keys, the package sources and the CA store. It keeps fingerprints only, never contents, so no password hashes in alerts or state. Alert severity knows whether dpkg or rpm installed the file unchanged. A file reached under two names (Fedora's merged /usr/local/sbin) is watched once. Installers announce their changes (expect-change) so upgrades don't alert. One local account can raise at most 5 alerts an hour, so it can't flood the channel. The kernel wakes it (inotify on the watched directories), so a change is scanned within seconds and one undone within the minute is still seen. It doesn't see which process made the write: Falco and Tetragon do. The list of places is fixed, plus your own [cron] files; AIDE and Wazuh FIM cover any directory tree. Package and set-uid check A debsums-like check (or rpm -Va-like, with each package's own digest algorithm) plus a set-uid inventory. It reads at most 20 MB/s and drops what it read from the page cache, so it stays within the 128 MB unit. Diverted files, rpm's %config files and upgrades in progress are handled. On the Fedora server it matched 7,472 files and caught a tampered binary; with dpkg on a production server no file differed, with 17 set-uid programs listed. Once a week. A root attacker who also rewrites the package database defeats it, as with debsums. Process watch A baseline of outbound connections per program and port, containers' network namespaces included (a connection out of a container is named with its id). A shell or network tool talking out, or a miner or reverse-shell port, is always high. Programs from /tmp, from memory (memfd) or from deleted files are reported. Baselines of the kernel modules loaded, the containers running (from Docker's own files: a privileged one, or one on the host's network or mounting the Docker socket, is high) and WireGuard's peers: a new one after the learning period is reported. A snapshot every 60 s misses short-lived connections. eBPF tools are much stronger here. Privilege and keys Failed su and sudo, each with the account's last SSH login and its place (su seen on the XMPP server; neither server has sudo). New-SSH-key alerts start after a learning period. PAM failures of the programs no other parser reads (the console, desktops, polkit, Cockpit, FTP), account changes (useradd, usermod, passwd, groups), auditd stopping, and authentication failures in the audit log. Wazuh's ruleset covers far more event types, and Windows and cloud logins. Account changes (a new account and group) have been reported on hosts; PAM failures and auditd alerts not yet. Malware Turns ClamAV's runs into alerts: infected files, scans killed for memory, stale signatures, missing runs. It ships a scan timer that runs at low priority and dies first when memory runs out. Files its watches see change can be scanned at once with ClamAV, YARA or both, outside vpsfort's memory limit, and are checked again just before the scanner reads them. No scanning engine of its own: ClamAV or YARA must be installed. The changed-file scans have run on hosts with ClamAV (a changed sshd_config, clean) and with ClamAV and YARA together (Debian's yara 4.5 with YARA Forge's core set compiled by yarac, a new file in /usr/local/bin: clean). An infected file's alert has not yet been seen on a host. Tamper resistance Alerts leave the host at once (encrypted bots, peers). The decision log can be mirrored to a peer at every sync ([cluster] mirror_to), and the peers hold each day's hash of it, so an edit shows and the lines survive a wiped node. A lost journal position and failed journalctl --verify checks are reported. Peers report a node that stops answering for 5 minutes, and a fact that fails its signature check is an alert (a node broken into, or a stolen key). vpsfort checks its own files daily: a key, config or state another user can read, a directory another user can write to, a binary that isn't root's. The daemon runs under a capability bound of nine. The raw journal stays on the host. A root attacker can stop vpsfort: the systemd watchdog restarts a hung daemon, not a deliberately stopped one. EDRs add tamper protection, and Wazuh ships every event off the host.

151.body: The first time the bot writes to the admin, it sends a message without content (vpsfort-signal-bot: connected...): that makes the Signal session, so signal-cli knows the admin's identity key before anything real goes out. The bot then pins the safety number (the number the Signal app shows under the chat's "View safety number") in state.json, or takes it from ADMIN_SAFETY_NUMBER, and logs it: compare it with your app. Before each message it asks signal-cli for the admin's current identity: the pinned safety number: the message goes as a Signal message. If signal-cli had marked the identity untrusted (after a change you then confirmed with ADMIN_SAFETY_NUMBER), the bot tells signal-cli it is verified first. another one (you reinstalled Signal or changed phones, or someone took over your number): nothing readable goes to the new identity. The bot tells signal-cli to accept the new key for transport only, and sends each message and file as an attachment encrypted to OPENPGP_KEY, with one notice a day naming both safety numbers. Without OPENPGP_KEY, messages wait (alerts for ALERT_MAX_HOURS, files for OUTBOX_MAX_DAYS). It stays so until you check the new safety number in the app, set ADMIN_SAFETY_NUMBER to it in config.env and restart the bot. The OpenPGP files are v4 / SEIPD v1 with AES-256 (what OpenKeychain on Android and iPGMail on iPhone read), with a neutral name and caption.

155.body:
The same release has a package per architecture, for the distribution's package manager instead of install.sh: vpsfort-signal-bot_<version>-1_<arch>.deb (amd64, arm64, armhf; Debian, Ubuntu and their derivatives) vpsfort-signal-bot-<version>-1.<arch>.rpm (x86_64, aarch64, armv7hl; Fedora, RHEL and its rebuilds) and vpsfort-signal-bot-<version>-r0.<arch>.apk (x86_64, aarch64, armv7; Alpine, with OpenRC: below), each with its .sha256 and .sigstore.json, downloaded and verified as the bundle above (--pattern "*.deb*", "*.rpm*" or "*.apk*"). CI keeps them for every commit as workflow artifacts, and scripts/package.sh builds them locally (cargo install cargo-deb cargo-generate-rpm --locked once, and python3 for the .apk, which scripts/apk.py at the repository's root writes; none needs dpkg, rpm or apk-tools, so it runs on macOS too; --target aarch64-unknown-linux-musl or armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf for the ARM ones). Or from the signed apt and dnf repository on GitHub Pages, once it is set up (the repository README, "Deployment"), where apt upgrade and dnf upgrade then bring new versions. sudo apt install ./vpsfort-signal-bot_0.3.1-1_amd64.deb # Fedora, RHEL: sudo dnf install ./vpsfort-signal-bot-0.3.1-1.x86_64.rpm
sudoedit /opt/vpsfort-signal-bot/config.env # the first install put the template there
sudo systemctl enable --now vpsfort-signal-bot The package puts the same files in the same places as install.sh (/opt/vpsfort-signal-bot with the binary and config.env.example, the user vpsfort-signal-bot, /var/log/vpsfort-signal-bot, the logrotate rule), except the unit, which is in /usr/lib/systemd/system. Its post-install step does what install.sh does apart from copying files: the user, config.env from the template the first time, the owners and modes, the outbox and the log directory; and it prints what is left to do ("Setup": the numbers, your OpenPGP key, then signal-cli's registration as the bot's user (the install prints the commands; signal-cli itself is installed separately)). dpkg-reconfigure vpsfort-signal-bot (rpm: dnf reinstall ./vpsfort-signal-bot-*.rpm) runs that step again, e.g. after copying a key there. apt remove vpsfort-signal-bot (dnf remove) stops the bot and keeps /opt/vpsfort-signal-bot; apt purge vpsfort-signal-bot removes it with the state and keys (rpm: by hand). Nothing starts on its own. The first install puts the template in place and prints what to fill in; you enable the service once it is filled in. An upgrade keeps the config and restarts the service only if it was running and the config is filled in. Over a bundle or deploy.sh install the package takes over: the config, state and keys stay; the bundle's unit in /etc/systemd/system (it would shadow the package's) and its rollback files go, and the service is enabled again on the package's unit if it was (vpsfort's integrity watch reports the removed unit as a warning once). Replacing the config: when a terminal is there, the install asks whether to replace the config with the new template (the old one kept with the suffix .old); Enter, a timeout of a minute, no terminal or DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive keep it. VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace (or keep) answers without asking: sudo VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace apt install ./<file>.deb. Rollback is installing the previous version's package (apt install ./<old>.deb --allow-downgrades, dnf downgrade ./<old>.rpm): there is no .prev file. Alpine (apk, OpenRC): apk add --allow-untrusted ./vpsfort-signal-bot-<version>-r0.x86_64.apk puts the same files in the same places, with the OpenRC script /etc/init.d/vpsfort-signal-bot instead of the unit: the settings exported from config.env as EnvironmentFile= does, supervised by supervise-daemon and started again 5 seconds after a crash; systemd's sandboxing has no equivalent there. The package is unsigned, hence --allow-untrusted: sha256sum -c and the attestation verify it. Its install scripts are POSIX sh and do what the post-install step above does: the user, config.env from the template the first time, the owners and modes, the log directory; an upgrade restarts a running bot. Then rc-update add vpsfort-signal-bot default && rc-service vpsfort-signal-bot start. apk del vpsfort-signal-bot stops it and keeps /opt/vpsfort-signal-bot. Not yet run on an Alpine host: CI installs the package in an Alpine container.

A phone number for the bot that can receive one SMS or call (not your own Signal number), or a Signal account of its own on a phone to link signal-cli to. Install signal-cli (above). Deploy from the Mac (runs scripts/ci.sh first, builds the static binary): ./deploy/deploy.sh # to the relay node "tg"; name another host as the argument The first install creates the user, /opt/vpsfort-signal-bot (with signal-cli's data directory) and config.env. Fill in config.env as root (SIGNAL_ACCOUNT, ADMIN, your OpenPGP public key as OPENPGP_KEY, root:vpsfort-signal-bot 640) and run bash install.sh again. It prints the commands for the next step with the settings filled in. Register the bot's number, as the bot's user (the signal-cli subcommand runs signal-cli with the bot's data directory and account): runuser -u vpsfort-signal-bot -- env SIGNAL_ACCOUNT=+49... /opt/vpsfort-signal-bot/vpsfort-signal-bot signal-cli register --captcha 'signalcaptcha://...'
runuser -u vpsfort-signal-bot -- env SIGNAL_ACCOUNT=+49... /opt/vpsfort-signal-bot/vpsfort-signal-bot signal-cli verify 123456 The captcha token comes from https://signalcaptchas.org/registration/generate.html (signal-cli's wiki, "Registration with captcha"). Optionally ... signal-cli updateProfile --given-name vpsfort. Then systemctl enable --now vpsfort-signal-bot (or bash install.sh again). Check the safety number : the first message pins it (pinned the safety number in /var/log/vpsfort-signal-bot/bot.log); compare it with the one your app shows for the bot's chat, or set ADMIN_SAFETY_NUMBER before the first message. Tell vpsfort , in [notify] of /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml (deploy a vpsfort that knows the key first): signal_outbox = "/opt/vpsfort-signal-bot/outbox"
signal_user = "vpsfort-signal-bot" then systemctl restart vpsfort and vpsfort ... notify-test --signal. 157.body: All in config.env (deploy/config.env.example has each with a comment; --help lists the matching flags): Variable Default SIGNAL_CLI /usr/local/bin/signal-cli the program SIGNAL_CLI_DATA /opt/vpsfort-signal-bot/signal-cli its data directory (700) SIGNAL_CLI_ARGS --ignore-attachments --ignore-stories more arguments for jsonRpc SIGNAL_ACCOUNT the bot's number ADMIN your number or ACI: the only one the bot writes to ADMIN_SAFETY_NUMBER (pinned on first sight) the safety number with you OPENPGP_KEY your OpenPGP public key, for the fallback; without it messages wait SANITIZE no yes: pseudonyms and node ids in alerts (XMPP_DOMAINS, SERVER_NAMES, PSEUDONYM_KEY) ALERT_MAX_HOURS 24 older alerts are dropped unsent OUTBOX_MAX_DAYS 7 older files are deleted unsent BOT_STATE_PATH /opt/vpsfort-signal-bot/state.json OUTBOX_DIR outbox next to the state LOG_DIR /var/log/vpsfort-signal-bot bot.log, 14 days (signal-cli's own lines included) Exit status 78 (a setting is wrong, or signal-cli didn't start: the account isn't registered, an option it doesn't know) is not restarted by the unit; the log has signal-cli's last lines. 16.body: Bottom line: vpsfort explains, port by port, what the internet can reach and why, and catches certificate mistakes other monitors miss. It audits sshd, and alerts when its settings weaken. Use Wazuh or Lynis for CVE matching and whole-host hardening benchmarks, and unattended-upgrades to apply updates. feature vpsfort Wazuh Lynis unattended-upgrades, needrestart Uptime Kuma, blackbox_exporter external scan (nmap, Shodan) each listener compared with the firewall rule that lets it in ✓ ufw, firewalld zones, iptables, nftables rulesets, docker-proxy ◐ port inventory ◐ once per run – – ◐ outside view Docker ports that bypass ufw ✓ – – – – ◐ seen as open alerts: new public listener, listener gone, dead allow rule, no firewall ✓ ◐ listening-port change rule – – ◐ port down – pending security updates, reboot needed, processes on replaced libraries ✓ in the digest ✓ ◐ ✓ installs and restarts – – CVE matching – ✓ ◐ – – ◐ service versions SSH hardening audit, with alerts when settings weaken ✓ sshd only ✓ SCA ◐ once per run – – ◐ algorithms only hardening benchmark (CIS style), sysctls ◐ the kernel's hardening sysctls, with alerts when one weakens; no benchmark ✓ SCA ✓ – – – live certificate expiry, STARTTLS included ✓ – – – ✓ ◐ "renewed but not in use", DANE TLSA value at each renewal ✓ – – – – – feature pros (vpsfort) cons (vpsfort), and who does better Exposure Reads the listeners from /proc and follows the firewall's own logic: rules in order, jumps, policies, rate limits. The TUI names the rule that lets each port in. It flags Docker-published ports, which ufw doesn't filter, and allow rules for ports nothing listens on: the kind of dead rules that were found by hand on the authors' hosts before. Under firewalld it reads the zones (services, ports, rich rules, source-bound zones), and nftables rulesets of your own as nft prints them (base chains in priority order, verdict maps). With peer_probe, the cluster's peers try the host's public ports from outside hourly: a port the firewall should block that a peer reaches is a high alert, one a provider's firewall in front blocks an info. A view from the host, plus its peers' (your own servers, not the internet at large); an external scan remains the ground truth. Patches A simulated apt-get, or dnf check-update from the cached metadata (no lock taken either way), in a unit of its own; a newer installed kernel than the running one; programs still running replaced libraries. All of it is in the daily digest. Reports only: it doesn't apply updates (use unattended-upgrades or dnf-automatic). No CVE database. apt and dnf only. Certificates Live endpoints every 6 h, XMPP STARTTLS included, plus the certificates on disk. It warns when a renewed certificate isn't served yet, explains ejabberd's ACME failures, gives the new DANE 3 1 1 value at each renewal, and compares the TLSA records published for each endpoint with the certificate served (a warning when none matches). This matters more since Let's Encrypt stopped sending expiry e-mails in June 2025. The host's own names are resolved hourly: one that no longer points here (a changed record, a hijack) is a high alert. Checked from the host itself, so routing problems elsewhere are not seen. Hardening sshd's settings as sshd -T applies them (Match blocks included), checked against the host's layout: a plain VPS, a hosting panel, or a key-only gateway user forced into a su/sftp wrapper. It names the file each setting comes from (cloud-init's override) and alerts when a setting weakens. The kernel's hardening sysctls the same way (forwarding, redirects, source routing, rp_filter, SYN cookies, ASLR, kptr_restrict, ptrace_scope, unprivileged BPF, protected links, ...), with the line to set. sshd and sysctls only: no other services, no CIS benchmark or score. Run Lynis or Wazuh SCA for the rest of the host.

160.body: A Matrix bot that brings vpsfort's admin messages to the admin's Matrix account: the alerts, the daily digest and the weekly abuse report, end-to-end encrypted (Olm and Megolm, as Element, FluffyChat and other clients do it). When end-to-end encryption to the admin isn't possible, a message goes out as a file encrypted to the admin's OpenPGP key instead, or waits. It does for Matrix what vpsfort-tg-bot does for Telegram on vpsfort's side, through the same kind of outbox, and nothing else: A client only. It logs in to an existing homeserver (matrix.org or your own) with an account of its own. No homeserver runs here, nothing listens. Send only. It doesn't read the room (no /sync): no commands, and nothing anyone writes there reaches it. The servers are managed over SSH. No link to ejabberd. It runs as its own user vpsfort-matrix-bot, which can't read ejabberd's files. vpsfort feeds it only when [notify] matrix_outbox is set. Without it, nothing changes. It can run next to the other bots, on any node: on the relay node (vpsfort's deploy/vpsfort-tg.toml), the XMPP server never connects to the homeserver.

163.body: The bot is a Matrix device of its own (vpsfort-matrix-bot login makes it). It makes a direct chat with the admin (ADMIN), encrypted from its first event, and invites them. For each message it: asks the homeserver for the admin's devices and cross-signing keys, and checks every signature itself (src/crypto.rs): a device must sign its own keys; with cross-signing, the admin's self-signing key must carry their master key's signature and the device the self-signing key's. The homeserver can withhold keys, not forge them. decides which devices are the admin's: with cross-signing (the usual case: every current client sets it up): only the devices the admin verified, under the admin's master key , which the bot pins the first time it sees it (or takes from ADMIN_MASTER_KEY). A changed master key, as after a reset of your cross-signing or a homeserver handing out keys of its own, gets nothing: messages come as OpenPGP files until you set ADMIN_MASTER_KEY to the new key (the bot logs it, and so does its notice) and restart the bot. without cross-signing: every device that signs its own keys, each pinned by device id on first sight (a device id that comes back with other keys gets nothing). The bot logs a warning: anyone who controls the homeserver could add a device then. shares the room's Megolm session key with those devices over Olm (a one-time key claimed for each, checked against the device's signature), and sends the message as a Megolm event. A new session is made after 100 messages, after a week, and whenever a device that had the key is no longer trusted (removed, or unverified), so it can't read what follows. The bot's own device is signed by the bot account's cross-signing keys (made at the first login), so clients show its messages as from a device its owner verified rather than with a red warning. You can also verify the bot user in your client; the bot doesn't need it. The Olm and Megolm code is vodozemac (matrix.org's pure-Rust implementation, Apache-2.0, audited); the rest (key checks, sharing, the client API calls) is in this crate. state.json keeps the device's keys, the sessions and the pins (mode 0600); a Megolm ratchet is saved before each message leaves, so no message index is ever used twice.

164.body: E2EE=no; the admin's master key changed or vanished (above); with cross-signing, none of the admin's devices is verified; no device could take the room key (no one-time key to start an Olm session with); the room isn't encrypted (it always is, unless someone with power in it changed that). Then a message or file goes out as one OpenPGP message to OPENPGP_KEY (v4, RSA or Curve25519, SEIPD v1 with AES-256: what OpenKeychain on Android and iPGMail on iPhone read), uploaded as a file in a plain event, with a notice at most once a day saying why. Without OPENPGP_KEY messages wait in the outbox (alerts for ALERT_MAX_HOURS, files for OUTBOX_MAX_DAYS), and the notice says that instead. Nothing goes to the homeserver in clear but these notices, which name keys, never content. vpsfort warns the admins over its other ways when copies wait longer than bot_stuck_after.

Or from the signed apt and dnf repository on GitHub Pages, once it is set up (the repository README, "Deployment"), where apt upgrade and dnf upgrade then bring new versions. sudo apt install ./vpsfort-matrix-bot_0.3.1-1_amd64.deb # Fedora, RHEL: sudo dnf install ./vpsfort-matrix-bot-0.3.1-1.x86_64.rpm
sudoedit /opt/vpsfort-matrix-bot/config.env # the first install put the template there
sudo systemctl enable --now vpsfort-matrix-bot The package puts the same files in the same places as install.sh (/opt/vpsfort-matrix-bot with the binary and config.env.example, the user vpsfort-matrix-bot, /var/log/vpsfort-matrix-bot, the logrotate rule), except the unit, which is in /usr/lib/systemd/system. Its post-install step does what install.sh does apart from copying files: the user, config.env from the template the first time, the owners and modes, the outbox and the log directory; and it prints what is left to do ("Setup": the homeserver and accounts, your OpenPGP key, then login as the bot's user (the install prints the command)). dpkg-reconfigure vpsfort-matrix-bot (rpm: dnf reinstall ./vpsfort-matrix-bot-*.rpm) runs that step again, e.g. after copying a key there. apt remove vpsfort-matrix-bot (dnf remove) stops the bot and keeps /opt/vpsfort-matrix-bot; apt purge vpsfort-matrix-bot removes it with the state and keys (rpm: by hand). Nothing starts on its own. The first install puts the template in place and prints what to fill in; you enable the service once it is filled in. An upgrade keeps the config and restarts the service only if it was running and the config is filled in. Over a bundle or deploy.sh install the package takes over: the config, state and keys stay; the bundle's unit in /etc/systemd/system (it would shadow the package's) and its rollback files go, and the service is enabled again on the package's unit if it was (vpsfort's integrity watch reports the removed unit as a warning once). Replacing the config: when a terminal is there, the install asks whether to replace the config with the new template (the old one kept with the suffix .old); Enter, a timeout of a minute, no terminal or DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive keep it. VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace (or keep) answers without asking: sudo VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace apt install ./<file>.deb. Rollback is installing the previous version's package (apt install ./<old>.deb --allow-downgrades, dnf downgrade ./<old>.rpm): there is no .prev file. Alpine (apk, OpenRC): apk add --allow-untrusted ./vpsfort-matrix-bot-<version>-r0.x86_64.apk puts the same files in the same places, with the OpenRC script /etc/init.d/vpsfort-matrix-bot instead of the unit: the settings exported from config.env as EnvironmentFile= does, supervised by supervise-daemon and started again 5 seconds after a crash; systemd's sandboxing has no equivalent there. The package is unsigned, hence --allow-untrusted: sha256sum -c and the attestation verify it. Its install scripts are POSIX sh and do what the post-install step above does: the user, config.env from the template the first time, the owners and modes, the log directory; an upgrade restarts a running bot. Then rc-update add vpsfort-matrix-bot default && rc-service vpsfort-matrix-bot start. apk del vpsfort-matrix-bot stops it and keeps /opt/vpsfort-matrix-bot. Not yet run on an Alpine host: CI installs the package in an Alpine container.

168.body:
An account for the bot on a homeserver, made in any client (not your own account). Note its user id (@vpsfort:example.org) and password. Your own client should have cross-signing set up (current Element, Element X, FluffyChat do it by default) and your devices verified. Deploy from the Mac (runs scripts/ci.sh first, builds the static binary): ./deploy/deploy.sh # to the relay node "tg"; name another host as the argument The first install creates the user, /opt/vpsfort-matrix-bot and config.env. Fill in config.env as root: MATRIX_HOMESERVER, MATRIX_USER, ADMIN, and your OpenPGP public key as OPENPGP_KEY (/opt/vpsfort-matrix-bot/admin.asc, root:vpsfort-matrix-bot 640), then log the bot in, as its own user (it asks for the password, which it doesn't keep): runuser -u vpsfort-matrix-bot -- sh -c 'set -a; . /opt/vpsfort-matrix-bot/config.env; exec /opt/vpsfort-matrix-bot/vpsfort-matrix-bot login' It prints the bot's device and keys (vpsfort-matrix-bot info again later). If the account already has cross-signing keys from another client, login --reset-cross-signing replaces them; a homeserver behind Matrix Authentication Service then asks you to approve the reset in the account's web page (the bot prints the link). Run bash install.sh again (or systemctl enable --now vpsfort-matrix-bot). Accept the invitation in your client. The first message pins your master key; check it in the bot's log (pinned ... master cross-signing key) against your client's, or set ADMIN_MASTER_KEY before the first message. Tell vpsfort , in [notify] of /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml (deploy a vpsfort that knows the key first): matrix_outbox = "/opt/vpsfort-matrix-bot/outbox"
matrix_user = "vpsfort-matrix-bot" then systemctl restart vpsfort and vpsfort ... notify-test --matrix. Adding vpsfort-matrix-bot.service to vpsfort's [sources] services gets an alert when it fails. install.sh rollback goes back to the previous binary and unit. The host needs outgoing HTTPS to the homeserver; the homeserver sees the host's address.
168.title: Setup

169.body: All in config.env (deploy/config.env.example has each with a comment; --help lists the matching flags): Variable Default MATRIX_HOMESERVER the client URL, https (http only to localhost) MATRIX_USER the bot's account, for login ADMIN your user id: the only one the bot writes to ADMIN_MASTER_KEY (pinned on first sight) your master cross-signing key E2EE yes no: everything as OpenPGP files OPENPGP_KEY your OpenPGP public key, for the fallback; without it messages wait SANITIZE no yes: pseudonyms and node ids in alerts (XMPP_DOMAINS, SERVER_NAMES, PSEUDONYM_KEY) ALERT_MAX_HOURS 24 older alerts are dropped unsent OUTBOX_MAX_DAYS 7 older files are deleted unsent BOT_STATE_PATH /opt/vpsfort-matrix-bot/state.json OUTBOX_DIR outbox next to the state LOG_DIR /var/log/vpsfort-matrix-bot bot.log, 14 days Exit status 78 (a setting is wrong, no login yet, or the homeserver no longer knows the login: a device deleted in a client, a password change that logged out every device) is not restarted by the unit: run login again, then start it.

17.body: Bottom line: vpsfort covers the alerts a small server needs, and knows when its own view has gone dark. It is not a metrics system, but its web console hands what it sees to Prometheus. feature vpsfort Monit Netdata Prometheus, Alertmanager Logwatch, logcheck a log source goes quiet, or stops naming addresses ✓ ◐ file timestamps – ◐ absent() on your own metrics – OOM kills, with process and size ✓ – ✓ ◐ a counter only ◐ in the daily mail disk space, memory pressure (PSI) ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ – failed systemd units that are not restarted ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ – restarts services itself – ✓ – – – daily digest ✓ security and health – – – ✓ graphs and history ◐ TUI trends; web console charts (3 hours to 7 days), what needed attention and the digests kept on disk (7 and 14 days by default, settable); Prometheus export with alerting rules shipped ◐ M/Monit ✓ ✓ with Grafana – feature pros (vpsfort) cons (vpsfort), and who does better Silence Tells "no attacks" from "not seeing logs", with thresholds measured per source on a real month. It also notices lines that arrive but name no address (ejabberd's hide_sensitive_log_data, a changed log format). An optional heartbeat URL (healthchecks.io, Uptime Kuma) lets a service outside notice when a node, or the whole cluster, goes dark. For its own sources only. Resources OOM kills (they revealed weeks of a nightly ClamAV scan being killed), disk under 10 % and 5 %, memory availability and pressure stalls, failed units after a restart grace period, a clock that isn't synchronised, and its own state file and actions log when they can't be written. Basic: no per-process graphs; the console's own history (7 days of problems, 14 days of digests) is kept, but longer history needs Prometheus (vpsfort-web's /metrics, with deploy/prometheus-rules.yml to start from). Netdata and Prometheus are far richer. Digest One message a day per server, marked ⚠ when something needs attention: certificates, peers, feeds, dead rules, patches, top offenders. A fixed format, with no report builder.

170.body: On the homeserver: the room's events (encrypted) and uploads (encrypted) stay as long as the homeserver keeps them; delete the room in your client to drop them for you. On the server: bot.log (14 days), state.json (login token, device keys, Olm and Megolm sessions, the bot's self-signing key, your pinned keys: no message text), with SANITIZE the pseudonym key, and outbox files until they are sent or expire. Whoever reads state.json (root) could read what the bot sends while the current Megolm session lasts. Path Owner Mode /opt/vpsfort-matrix-bot/ root:vpsfort-matrix-bot 1770 (sticky) config.env, OPENPGP_KEY root:vpsfort-matrix-bot 640 state.json, pseudonym.key vpsfort-matrix-bot 600 outbox/ root:vpsfort-matrix-bot 1770; files vpsfort-matrix-bot 600 /var/log/vpsfort-matrix-bot/, bot.log vpsfort-matrix-bot 700, 600 The unit drops every capability, makes the file system read-only except its two directories, allows only IPv4 and IPv6 sockets, denies writable-executable memory, and is held to 128 MB of memory (MemoryMax).
