172.body: ./scripts/ci.sh # fmt, clippy, tests, cargo audit, static Linux binary The static build needs rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl (or the ARM targets) and rustup component add llvm-tools, as the other crates. tests/fake_homeserver.rs runs the bot against a fake homeserver on 127.0.0.1 whose admin devices are vodozemac accounts of their own: login (device keys that verify, cross-signing keys, the device signed by them, the password step when the homeserver asks), the room made encrypted with the admin invited, an alert and the report that decrypt on the verified phone and not on the unverified laptop (nothing of them in any request), a newly verified device getting the current key, a removed one forcing a new session, rate limiting, a changed master key giving OpenPGP files that the admin's key opens (and ADMIN_MASTER_KEY bringing end-to-end back), messages that wait without any route, E2EE=no, an admin without cross-signing, a device id with new keys left out, a second login keeping the room and pins, a wrong password leaving the working device alone, and a revoked token stopping the bot. On matrix.org (since 2026-10-29): notify-test --matrix, real alerts and a daily digest arrived in Element X end-to-end encrypted, without warnings, and so did the weekly abuse report (51 KB, covering two nodes) as an encrypted attachment, which Element X decrypted and opened in its file viewer. Its event shows the file encrypted with AES-256-CTR and the key inside the Megolm-encrypted event, as above; Element X lists the bot's identity as unverified (the admin never verified the bot account) without warning about it. Not yet seen for real: the OpenPGP files (a changed master key, no verified device), and a homeserver other than matrix.org. Fuzzing. fuzz/ has cargo-fuzz targets (code in src/fuzzing.rs): keys_query (the homeserver's key replies: only self-signed devices come out, cross-signed ones only under a master key), alert_file (outbox files), attachment (encrypt and decrypt, damage caught). Under cargo-fuzz vodozemac accepts every signature (its fuzzing cfg), so the targets reach past the checks; the signature checks themselves are in src/crypto.rs's tests. tests/fuzz_smoke.rs runs the targets on stable over realistic inputs, fuzz/seeds/ and thousands of mutations (VPSFORT_MATRIX_BOT_WRITE_SEEDS=1 regenerates the seeds). cargo +nightly fuzz run keys_query fuzz/corpus/keys_query fuzz/seeds/keys_query -- -max_total_time=600

173.body: A send-only bot that brings vpsfort's admin messages (the alerts, the daily digest and the weekly abuse report) to a push service you run or trust, or to any webhook: ntfy ( https://ntfy.sh , or a server of your own): a message per alert, the report as an attachment; Gotify (a server of your own): a message per alert; it takes no attachments, so files stay on the server and the admin is told once a day; a webhook : a JSON POST per alert and per file, with a Bearer token. None of these encrypts end to end: the service's server reads what the bot sends. So, as on Telegram (vpsfort-tg-bot, whose code this bot shares), account names become pseudonyms and the servers appear only by their node ids , and files go out only OpenPGP-encrypted to the admin's key, or not at all. It does for push services what vpsfort-tg-bot does for Telegram on vpsfort's side, through the same kind of outbox, and nothing else: it reads nothing back, takes no orders for the servers, and runs as its own user vpsfort-push-bot. vpsfort feeds it only when [notify] push_outbox is set. Without it, nothing changes. It can run next to the other bots, on any node; on a relay node (vpsfort's deploy/vpsfort-tg.toml), the XMPP server never connects to the service.

175.body: From vpsfort ntfy Gotify webhook an alert or the digest (alert-*.msg) a message: the subject as the title, the text as the message; longer ones in pieces of 4000 characters (the later ones marked "continued"); the priority from vpsfort's severity ([High] 4, [Critical] 5) the same, priorities 8 and 10 {"kind": "alert", "subject", "text", "priority"} the weekly abuse report (abuse-report-<date>.txt), or any other file a PUT with the file encrypted to OPENPGP_KEY, named report-<date>.txt.pgp, a fixed caption not sent: the file waits on the server, a message once a day says so {"kind": "file", "name", "caption", "content_base64"} (encrypted) alerts older than ALERT_MAX_HOURS (24) when the bot gets to them dropped, and one message says how many an alert the service refuses for good (400, 413, ...) dropped with a note, so it can't hold up the alerts after it A refused token (401, 403) stops the bot with exit 78, which the unit doesn't restart: fix PUSH_TOKEN and start it again. 176.body: Account names never reach it. Every XMPP address in an alert (alice@example.org, ejabberd:alice) becomes a pseudonym [acct:1a2b3c]: an HMAC under pseudonym.key, made on the first start and kept on the server (vpsfort-push-bot pseudonym <address> there tells which account is which). The same account always gets the same pseudonym. The servers appear by their node ids (SERVER_NAMES): their own addresses and host names in alerts become xmpp, vpn, ... (nextcloud.example.org:443 becomes nextcloud.xmpp:443). Attackers' addresses, ports, countries and networks stay: that is what the alert is about. Files go out encrypted as a whole (OpenPGP, OPENPGP_KEY: a v4 RSA or Curve25519 key as OpenKeychain and iPGMail export it, SEIPD v1 with AES-256, no name inside): the service holds a file of some size and a neutral name. Open it on the phone with OpenKeychain (Android) or iPGMail (iPhone). Without a key, files wait and expire unsent. The topic is the secret, on ntfy. Whoever knows a topic's name reads it: pick a long random one, and on ntfy.sh or any server with access control give the bot an access token (ntfy token add) and keep the topic private. Gotify needs an application token; a webhook gets a Bearer token. Every request is HTTPS (plain HTTP only to localhost). Redirects are never followed: one would carry the message and the token elsewhere.

177.body: They share one directory, /opt/vpsfort-push-bot/outbox (root:vpsfort-push-bot 1770, sticky), in vpsfort-xmpp-bot's file format (vpsfort's src/botbox.rs, the shared vpsfort-botlib's outbox): vpsfort writes a copy of each message to the first of [notify] admins (every admin message when admins is empty or xmpp = false) as alert-<time>-<n>.msg; the bot looks every 5 seconds, claims one by renaming it to .<name>.sending, sends it and deletes it, or renames it back to try again. The abuse report job puts the weekly report there too when [notify] push_outbox (or ABUSE_REPORT_PUSH_OUTBOX) is set; the bot looks every minute. There is no fallback on vpsfort's side: vpsfort warns the admins its other ways when copies wait longer than bot_stuck_after. Check it as root: vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml notify-test --push.

18.body: Bottom line: no other tool here encrypts alerts end to end, pseudonymizes them for an untrusted channel, or warns the user whose account is attacked. In exchange, vpsfort offers six channels where the others offer dozens. feature vpsfort fail2ban CrowdSec Wazuh commercial EDR, SIEM admin channels ◐ XMPP, Telegram, e-mail, Signal, Matrix, ntfy/Gotify/webhooks ◐ e-mail, scripts ✓ Slack, e-mail, webhooks, Splunk, Elastic, Sentinel, … ✓ e-mail, Slack, PagerDuty, custom ✓ end-to-end encryption ✓ OMEMO, Signal, Olm/Megolm, OpenPGP – – – – pseudonymized copies for an untrusted channel ✓ Telegram – – – – warns the attacked user, in their language ✓ XMPP and Nextcloud accounts, 6 languages – – – – budgets per topic, so a flood can't hide a critical alert ✓ – ◐ grouping ◐ e-mails per hour ✓ feature pros (vpsfort) cons (vpsfort), and who does better Channels XMPP through the admin bot, OMEMO-encrypted and kept out of the server's archive, or from any host through any XMPP server with the bot's client mode (OMEMO, else OpenPGP files). Telegram, with account names pseudonymized and servers named only by node id. E-mail, OpenPGP-encrypted as a whole, subject included. Signal (through signal-cli) while the admin's safety number is the pinned one, and Matrix, Olm/Megolm-encrypted to the devices the admin verified; both send OpenPGP files instead when they can't reach that identity. ntfy, Gotify or any webhook through the push bot, sanitized as for Telegram (files only encrypted). Any mix of the six. The XMPP bot survives sleep, Wi-Fi changes and server restarts without losing a message and without getting itself banned (back about two minutes after an ejabberd restart, seen on the XMPP server). Delivered for real: the XMPP bot (OMEMO), the Matrix bot (alerts, a digest and the weekly report as an encrypted attachment, through matrix.org to Element X) and the mail bot (alerts and the weekly report, read in Proton Mail on Android). No Slack, Teams or PagerDuty of their own (a webhook reaches them through a relay of yours). A new channel means a new bot, though the bots now share one library. The push bot is untried against a real ntfy or Gotify. The Signal bot needs signal-cli (Java on ARM) installed beside it. The Signal bot and the XMPP bot's client mode are untried against the real services. Privacy Built for operators who take GDPR seriously: nothing about users goes to a vendor, Telegram never sees account names, and reports travel as encrypted files. Encryption takes setup (OMEMO device trust, OpenPGP keys). If the XMPP bot doesn't take a message within 2 minutes, it goes out over plain XMPP, saying why. Users Account holders learn when their account is attacked: password guessing, a possible compromise, and (opt-in) a login from a new network. No other tool here does this. XMPP accounts over XMPP, Nextcloud accounts through Nextcloud's own notifications (occ). SSH and the other services' users aren't messaged. Noise control One message per incident and account every 6 h, hourly caps per topic for admins, hourly budgets per local user for host changes. Alerts relayed from peers are tagged with the node's name. A bot that stops sending is itself reported over the other channels. Fixed policies: routing is less flexible than Alertmanager's or CrowdSec's profiles.

The service. ntfy: a topic with a long random name on your server or ntfy.sh, and an access token for the bot (ntfy token add, or a user and password). Gotify: an application (its token). A webhook: an HTTPS endpoint that takes a JSON POST. Deploy from the Mac (runs scripts/ci.sh first, builds the static binary): ./deploy/deploy.sh # to the relay node "tg"; name another host as the argument The first install creates the user, /opt/vpsfort-push-bot and config.env (from deploy/config.env.example, every option with a reasonable value). It doesn't start the bot while PUSH_URL is the placeholder. Fill in config.env as root: PUSH_KIND, PUSH_URL, PUSH_TOKEN (or PUSH_TOKEN_FILE), SERVER_NAMES, XMPP_DOMAINS, and your OpenPGP public key as OPENPGP_KEY (/opt/vpsfort-push-bot/admin.asc, root:vpsfort-push-bot 640; as for vpsfort-tg-bot). Then: set -a; . /opt/vpsfort-push-bot/config.env; set +a
/opt/vpsfort-push-bot/vpsfort-push-bot check # the settings, the key, the outbox; sends nothing
/opt/vpsfort-push-bot/vpsfort-push-bot send-test # one test message to the service

182.body: On the service: messages stay as the service keeps them (ntfy's cache, 12 hours by default on ntfy.sh; Gotify's database until deleted in the app; a webhook's own). On the server: bot.log (14 days: weekly rotation, one old copy), pseudonym.key, and outbox files until they are sent (or expire). No state file: nothing the bot sends is written anywhere else on the server. Path Owner Mode /opt/vpsfort-push-bot/ root:vpsfort-push-bot 1770 (sticky) config.env (the token), OPENPGP_KEY root:vpsfort-push-bot 640 pseudonym.key vpsfort-push-bot 600 outbox/ root:vpsfort-push-bot 1770; files vpsfort-push-bot 600 /var/log/vpsfort-push-bot/, bot.log vpsfort-push-bot 700, 600 The unit is hardened like vpsfort-tg-bot's: no capabilities, a read-only system but its two directories, IPv4 and IPv6 sockets only, no writable-executable memory, and 128 MB of memory at most (MemoryMax).

184.body: A first run of what is new for Fedora and RHEL, none of which has run on a real host yet: package_manager = "dnf" (rpm package checks, dnf patch status), the -dnf config templates, the firewalld backend, firewalld's denied-packet log lines, the exposure watch reading firewalld's zones, the optional ipset backend, and on an arm64 VPS the aarch64 build. Each step says what to run and what you should see. Note what differs (paste the output) and send it back: that is the test result. Placeholders: VPS_IP is the server's public address, ADMIN_IP the address you connect from (curl -s https://ifconfig.me on your machine), PROBE_IP the probe's (the same command there), SSH_PORT the server's SSH port (22 unless you changed it). Commands run on the VPS as root (sudo -i) unless they say "on the Mac" or "on the probe". You need: the VPS, with your SSH key, and the provider's web console in case you lock yourself out; a probe : a second machine with another public address that never logs in to the VPS (a phone hotspot, or another VPS). It plays the attacker. Your own address is allowlisted, so it can't. about 2 hours, mostly waiting (the package check starts 15 minutes after vpsfort). Shortcut used below: lg() { vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml "$@"; }

188.body:
Give it 3 minutes, then: lg status Note the whole output. Check in it: Exposure (firewalld's zones): the firewall line says firewalld running, not nftables, rules not read. sshd is allowed by firewalld with [ALLOW ssh (public)] (or [ALLOW SSH_PORT/tcp (public)]). Patch status (dnf): a patches line: up to date, N updates pending, none for security, or what needs doing (N security updates pending (...): dnf upgrade, a newer kernel than the running one, programs still running replaced code), then N other updates pending. Compare with dnf --cacheonly --quiet check-update --security. An error here (e.g. dnf check-update: ...) is a finding: paste it. Firewall signals: a public VPS gets scanned within minutes. Check firewalld logs them, and vpsfort counts them: journalctl -k -g 'filter_IN_public_REJECT' -n 3 --no-pager
journalctl -u vpsfort -b | grep '\[shadow\]' | tail -n 5 Expect kernel lines filter_IN_public_REJECT: IN=eth0 OUT= ... SRC=..., and after a while would-be bans of scanners, tagged [shadow] (also in /var/log/vpsfort/actions.jsonl). Exposure, step by step (python3 comes with Fedora): lg status lists only exposed listeners; the TUI's Exposure tab (lg tui, key 6, q to quit) lists all of them, blocked ones too. python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 0.0.0.0 > /dev/null 2>&1 &
sleep 70; lg status | grep 8080 # nothing: not exposed
lg tui # tab 6: 0.0.0.0:8080/tcp python3 blocked by firewalld
firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp firewalld's zones are re-read every 5 minutes (sooner when a file in /etc/firewalld changes; this runtime change touches none), so: sleep 300; lg status | grep 8080 # 0.0.0.0:8080/tcp python3 allowed by firewalld [ALLOW 8080/tcp (public)]
kill %1
sleep 70; lg status | grep -i dead # dead firewalld rule: 8080/tcp (public) (nothing listens)
firewall-cmd --remove-port=8080/tcp A source-only rule: firewall-cmd --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="ADMIN_IP" port port="8081" protocol="tcp" accept'
python3 -m http.server 8081 --bind 0.0.0.0 > /dev/null 2>&1 &
sleep 360; lg tui # tab 6: 8081 allowed by firewalld from some sources only, # rule "ALLOW rich rule 8081/tcp (public) from ADMIN_IP"
kill %1
firewall-cmd --remove-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="ADMIN_IP" port port="8081" protocol="tcp" accept' Package origins (rpm): lg integrity | head -40 Expect watched files with their rpm package (package pam for /etc/pam.d/*, package openssh-server for sshd_config), and files of your own (e.g. /etc/sudoers.d/90-cloud-init-users, if your image has it) as local. Then a modified one: cp -a /etc/pam.d/sudo /root/pam-sudo.bak
echo '# vpsfort test' >> /etc/pam.d/sudo
lg integrity | grep pam.d/sudo # package sudo, MODIFIED
cp -a /root/pam-sudo.bak /etc/pam.d/sudo

189.body:
First check your own address is allowlisted: grep -A3 '^nets' /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml must show ADMIN_IP. Then edit the config: mode = "enforce", and in [enforce] backend = "firewalld". Then: systemctl restart vpsfort
journalctl -u vpsfort -b | grep -E 'started|firewalld' | tail -n 5 Expect mode=Enforce backend=firewalld, and no firewalld unavailable line. The first start reloads firewalld once (it creates vpsfort's ipsets and zone in firewalld's permanent configuration). Your second SSH session must still be alive. vpsfort's firewalld objects: firewall-cmd --get-ipsets # vpsfort-alive vpsfort-ban4 vpsfort-ban6
firewall-cmd --info-zone=vpsfort # target: DROP, sources: ipset:vpsfort-ban4 ipset:vpsfort-ban6
firewall-cmd --info-policy=vpsfort-fwd # ingress-zones: vpsfort, egress-zones: ANY, target: DROP
firewall-cmd --ipset=vpsfort-alive --get-entries # 192.0.2.1
firewall-cmd --permanent --list-all --zone=public # unchanged by vpsfort An operator ban of the probe (documentation addresses like 192.0.2.x are refused: vpsfort never bans non-routable addresses): lg ban PROBE_IP --for 10m --note test
firewall-cmd --ipset=vpsfort-ban4 --get-entries # PROBE_IP (plus any bans vpsfort decided) On the probe, nc -vz -w 3 VPS_IP 22 now times out. Then: lg unban PROBE_IP
firewall-cmd --ipset=vpsfort-ban4 --get-entries # PROBE_IP gone; the probe connects again A real ban, from the probe (on the probe, which has never logged in): nc -vz -w 3 VPS_IP 22 # on the probe: succeeds (or "open") before
nc -vz -w 3 VPS_IP 23 # on the probe: a tripwire port; refused or times out
sleep 5
nc -vz -w 3 VPS_IP 22 # on the probe: now times out: banned On the VPS: tail -n 3 /var/log/vpsfort/actions.jsonl # a ban of the probe's address, tripwire 23/tcp
firewall-cmd --ipset=vpsfort-ban4 --get-entries # the probe's address
journalctl -k -g filter_IN_vpsfort -n 3 --no-pager # (only if logged) these are not counted again (If the probe's first nc ... 22 was itself refused, sshd listens elsewhere: use SSH_PORT.) Healing after a firewalld reload: firewall-cmd --reload
firewall-cmd --ipset=vpsfort-ban4 --get-entries # empty: firewalld forgot them
sleep 40
firewall-cmd --ipset=vpsfort-ban4 --get-entries # the probe's address is back
grep -c 'firewalld forgot' /var/log/vpsfort/actions.jsonl # 1 (a high "system" alert) Do the same with systemctl restart firewalld. Exposure under enforce: lg status still says firewalld running; the vpsfort zone must not make anything look open (its whitelist ports are for banned sources only). Lift the probe's ban: lg unban PROBE_IP, and nc -vz -w 3 VPS_IP 22 from the probe works again.

19.body: Bottom line: a capable terminal UI on each node, a read-only web console for the whole cluster with a REST API and Prometheus metrics, and careful upgrade tooling. Nothing changes from the web, by design: bans and settings stay on the servers, behind SSH. A browser, with its extensions and the exploits written for it, is no place to hold a firewall's controls, whatever the login method; a console broken into shows what its page shows and nothing more. feature vpsfort fail2ban sshguard CrowdSec Wazuh CSF/LFD live dashboard ✓ terminal UI, web console – – ◐ cscli; web console (SaaS) ✓ web ✓ panel UI web UI and fleet view ✓ read only by design; dozens of nodes; a few equal admins (no roles) with a one-time code or a passkey, and proof of work, at the login – – ✓ ✓ ◐ per server ban, unban, temporary allow ✓ CLI and TUI, shared with peers ✓ – ✓ ◐ API ✓ pattern tester ✓ test-pattern ✓ fail2ban-regex – ✓ cscli explain ✓ wazuh-logtest – REST API ✓ read only by design – – ✓ local API ✓ – metrics for Prometheus ✓ through the web console, or a textfile for node_exporter ◐ community exporters – ✓ ◐ API – community, Q&A, third-party guides ◐ one detailed README ✓ ◐ ✓ ✓ ◐ forks feature pros (vpsfort) cons (vpsfort), and who does better TUI Works over SSH in an 80-column terminal. Up to 10 tabs: offenders with evidence, bans, decisions, accounts, exposure, countries with port histograms, a world map, alerts and patterns. Ban, unban and allow with a confirmation. It also reads saved decision logs of several servers offline. One node at a time (the web console shows them all); no roles, no multi-tenant view. Tooling status (also as JSON), explain for one address, quiet to hold the admins' messages back during an upgrade, baseline export/import so a reinstalled host skips the learning days, replay, print-nft, notify-test for each channel, a digest preview. config-diff runs after every upgrade and lists new options, changed defaults and unknown keys. The installer dry-runs the nftables ruleset against the kernel first. vpsfort-sim runs a simulated cluster and the real web console on a laptop from a few days of decision logs, for trying the console without servers. No OpenTelemetry export, and no API that changes anything: the control socket is root-only, and the web console reads through a separate read-only socket. Web console vpsfort-web shows every node's bans, alerts, decisions, offenders, countries and networks, peers, certificates, disks and updates on one HTTPS page, with what needs attention first (as a queue, with 7 days of history of what appeared and went), activity charts over 3 hours to 7 days, a world map (bans at their coordinates with a city-level database, else at capitals; countries [geoblock] blocks hatched), a page per address, the nodes' settings side by side with the differences marked, each node's digests of the last two weeks, saved views and keyboard navigation; every table exports as CSV or JSON, and the whole cluster as one JSON file for a ticket. It only reads, by design: it holds a web key of its own, never the cluster key, and reaches vpsfort through a read-only socket, so a break-in at the console or in an admin's browser gives a view, never a ban, an unban or a setting. TLS 1.3; a password and a one-time code or a passkey (WebAuthn) per admin (one or several, all equal); a proof of work before each login that grows with failed attempts; sessions in memory that an admin can list and end; failed logins are locked out and banned by vpsfort itself. About 110 Prometheus metric families, with alerting rules shipped. Asked only while someone looks (plus each node's digest once a day). No roles: every admin sees everything. Its own history (a week of what needed attention, two weeks of digests, the marks) is kept on disk now; longer history needs Prometheus. A self-signed certificate unless you give it one. New, with two audits of its own so far; it runs on the authors' five servers, all but one through their agents. The CrowdSec Console and Wazuh's dashboard manage fleets and keep history on disk. Docs One README that explains every default, often with the measurement behind it. One long document: no website, no forum or chat. Some answers are only in the code.

2.body: Each directory is its own Cargo project with a README that covers setup, settings and design in detail. crate what it does vpsfort The daemon and its CLI/TUI: log parsers, the scoring and ban engine, firewall backends, cluster, exposure/cron/antivirus watches, package checks (dpkg or rpm), blocklist feeds, country and network blocking, daily digest, weekly abuse reports. vpsfort-xmpp-bot XMPP bot in two modes. Admin (on the XMPP server): curated ejabberdctl commands in chat, plus vpsfort's admin messages over OMEMO. Client (BOT_MODE=client, any host and XMPP server, e.g. a desktop): send-only, vpsfort's admin messages over OMEMO, else as OpenPGP-encrypted files. SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS login. vpsfort-tg-bot Telegram transport for vpsfort's admin messages. Account names become pseudonyms and servers appear only by node id. Reports go out as OpenPGP-encrypted files. vpsfort-mail-bot Send-only SMTP bot that mails vpsfort's admin messages, each OpenPGP-encrypted as a whole (subject included). vpsfort-signal-bot Send-only Signal bot over signal-cli (installed separately): vpsfort's admin messages while the safety number with the admin is the pinned one, else as OpenPGP-encrypted files. vpsfort-web Read-only web console for the whole cluster: an agent on every node hands its vpsfort's data (through a read-only socket) to the console, sealed with a web key of its own (never the cluster key) and forward-secret; the console shows bans, alerts, offenders, places and every node's health and every node's abuse report split per network owner, ready to mail, over HTTPS (TLS 1.3) to its admins (one or a few, all equal), each with a password and a one-time code or a passkey, plus /metrics for Prometheus. It also runs alone on a host without vpsfort, as an aggregator. vpsfort-sim A simulated cluster and its web console in one process, from real decision logs (each node's state from vpsfort's own log reader, digest renderer and abuse report builder) or a console export, with real vpsfort-web agents and console: for trying the console without servers, screenshots and page work. Makes the web key, the admin's password and one-time secret and a certificate when missing, and says so. vpsfort-matrix-bot Send-only Matrix client: vpsfort's admin messages end-to-end encrypted (Olm/Megolm, vodozemac) to the devices the admin verified, else as OpenPGP-encrypted files. vpsfort-push-bot Send-only push bot for ntfy, Gotify or any webhook: vpsfort's admin messages sanitized as for Telegram (the service reads them), files only OpenPGP-encrypted. vpsfort-botlib What the Telegram, mail, Signal, Matrix and push bots share: the outbox format, the pseudonyms and server names, the OpenPGP files, the log. A library, not shipped on its own. The supported combinations of bots and cluster peers are described in vpsfort's README, "Deployment layouts". vpsfort/tests/layouts.rs runs each layout end to end.

20.body: Bottom line: the smallest and most self-contained option here after sshguard, written in a memory-safe language. It runs on fewer platforms, is packaged in fewer ways, and has the shortest track record. feature vpsfort fail2ban sshguard CrowdSec Wazuh CSF/LFD runtime static binary, ~10 MB (web console ~4 MB more) Python 3 C Go: engine and bouncer C agent; manager; OpenSearch-based indexer; dashboard Perl memory ~10 MB for a real month, ~50 MB with geo; capped at 128 MB moderate a few MB moderate light agent; the indexer needs ≥ 4 GB RAM (8 GB in the 5.0 beta) moderate memory-safe language ✓ ✓ – ✓ – C agent ✓ platforms Linux with systemd: x86_64, arm64, 32-bit ARMv7 Linux, BSD Linux, BSD, macOS Linux, FreeBSD, Windows, containers, Kubernetes Linux, Windows, macOS and more Linux ARM builds ◐ arm64 and ARMv7 bundles, tested in CI only ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ distribution packages or apt repository ✓ .deb, .rpm and Alpine .apk (OpenRC) from the releases, a signed apt and dnf repository on GitHub Pages (built by CI after each release), or a zip bundle with install.sh ✓ ✓ ✓ vendor repositories ✓ vendor repositories ◐ forks signed releases ✓ build provenance (Sigstore), SHA256SUMS, a CycloneDX SBOM ✓ distribution-signed ✓ distribution-signed ✓ signed repositories ✓ signed repositories ◐ license MIT GPL-2.0 BSD-style MIT (engine) GPL-2.0 GPL-3.0 in use since October 2026 2004 the 2000s 2020 2015 about two decades, until 2025 feature pros (vpsfort) cons (vpsfort), and who does better Footprint Fits a 1 GB VPS next to the services it protects. The memory limit is backed by flood tests, per-address state is capped (max_tracked_ips), and the apt or dnf query runs in a unit of its own, outside the limit. Country blocking costs about 1 MB while its list is computed; the list itself sits in the kernel's sets. – Platforms The static musl binary needs no matching libc: the same file runs on Debian 13, Ubuntu 22.04 and Fedora 44. Package checks with dpkg or rpm, patches with apt or dnf. Bundles for arm64 and 32-bit ARMv7 (hard-float), from the same CI. Linux with systemd only. The ARM bundles haven't run on an ARM server yet; RHEL and its rebuilds are untried. Supply chain Few dependencies, cargo audit and cargo deny (permissive licenses, crates.io only) on every CI run, and a CycloneDX SBOM attached to every release next to the build provenance attestation. No TLS library in the binary: curl does the downloads. The parsers, the decision-log readers and their hourly index, the console's HTTP and agent protocols and abuse reports, and the bots' inputs are fuzzed (23 cargo-fuzz targets across the crates, each with a smoke run in every cargo test). Log text never reaches a shell: firewall changes are built from parsed addresses and fed to nft -f -. That class of bug is real elsewhere: fail2ban's CVE-2021-32749 (the mail-whois action), Wazuh's CVE-2026-54085 (active response scripts, fixed in 4.14.7). Nine internal security reviews in October and November 2026, the later ones covering the web console, the simulator, the bots and the packages too, each finding fixed with a test. No independent third-party audit yet, and no distribution maintainers reviewing its packages. A project this young has no CVE history to judge it by.

22.title: 14. Scorecard

23.body: Know these before you adopt it: No HTTP layer of its own: no WAF, captcha or CDN integration. It can enforce a WAF's decisions at the firewall ([waf]: CrowdSec, or any app that gives out a list). A limited set of built-in sources: sshd, ejabberd, the kernel log, Nextcloud, su and sudo, PAM and the audit log, and 24 common services (web servers and proxies, HAProxy, Prosody, Synapse, databases, Redis, mail, ownCloud, Forgejo, Vaultwarden, Keycloak, authentik, OpenVPN, FTP, Jellyfin), the latter tested against log lines but not yet on a host. Everything else needs regex patterns of your own. One platform family: Linux with systemd and journald. Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora have run it; ARM builds exist but haven't run on an ARM server. No control from a browser, by design: vpsfort-web shows the cluster to a few admins, with a REST API and Prometheus metrics, and changes nothing on the servers: a browser, with its extensions and the exploits aimed at it, is no place to hold the firewall's controls, whatever the login method. What it lacks: roles (every admin sees everything), and age. No crowd-sourced intelligence (only CrowdSec has one). It has static public feeds, country and network blocking from a free database that misplaces some addresses (a commercial one, read as it is, can take its place), and a CrowdSec's decisions through [waf]. Host watches poll (every minute, with inotify waking the file watch at once) or run once a week; they don't see which process did what. There is no tamper protection against root. No CVE matching, hardening benchmark or compliance reports (the hardening audit covers sshd and the kernel's sysctls only). Six alert channels: XMPP, Telegram, e-mail, Signal, Matrix, and ntfy, Gotify or a webhook. A young package repository: the signed apt and dnf repository on GitHub Pages is built by CI after each release (it needs a signing key in the repository's secrets); apt and dnf have installed from it, on one server each. Without it: .deb and .rpm files from the releases, installed one by one, or a release zip with install.sh. Young: version 0.6.1, running on the authors' own servers only, written by one maintainer in collaboration with an AI model (see the README ). It has had internal security reviews, but no independent audit. Covered by tests, not yet run on a host: the plain iptables backend, sudo and new-SSH-key alerts, PAM failures and audit alerts, the built-in sources for common services, [waf] against a real CrowdSec, the Telegram relay node and the Telegram, Signal and XMPP-client bots against their real services, the desktop profile, and the ARM builds ( Evidence so far ). Users' own warnings work in tests but have not yet been confirmed reaching a user. Forged sources: evidence that rests only on blocked packets can name a forged source. vpsfort limits the harm, but someone who forges packets can still get outsiders banned for an hour.

24.body: In production. Five servers run in enforce mode: one Ubuntu 22.04 (a VPN host, kernel 5.15), three Debian 13 (an XMPP and Nextcloud server, kernel 6.12, since mid-October 2026 after a shadow-mode period, and two more that joined in late October) and one Fedora 44 (the test server below, which stayed on). Seen there, with the details in the README's Verified on the servers : Input and blocking: live journal input, and the warning when a source goes quiet; bans in nftables with kernel timeouts, placed after connection tracking, so the servers' own pings and TCP connections to banned addresses get their replies; IPv4 and IPv6 bans, and subnet bans growing from a /24 to a /22; the table rebuilt within 30 s after it was deleted; kernel rate limits; SSH canary bans; blocklist feeds and the geo database; operator controls. Cluster: facts in both directions, with repeat offences escalating across nodes; node identities (every node signs its facts and pins the others' keys); forward secrecy between the real nodes (every peer answers the key exchange); a node reported when it stopped answering during a reinstall. Host watches: the exposure watch (Docker ports recognised; a new listener and an allow rule with nothing behind it reported); the process watch (a new outbound connection); certificate checks; the cron watch and antivirus results; OOM alerts; changed files scanned with ClamAV, and with ClamAV and YARA (YARA Forge's core set, compiled); su alerts with the account's last SSH login and its place; account changes reported, and an installer's new system user logged as announced; the package and set-uid check with dpkg (no file differs, 17 set-uid programs) and the patch status with apt (the old kernel still running after an upgrade); the SSH audit (a hardened gateway found clean; on a cloud image, root's password login and cloud-init's override of PasswordAuthentication found, then logged as fixed); the systemd watchdog. Channels: the XMPP bot delivering OMEMO-encrypted, and back online about two minutes after an ejabberd restart; the Matrix bot delivering alerts, a digest and the weekly abuse report (as an encrypted attachment) end-to-end encrypted through matrix.org to Element X; the mail bot delivering alerts and the weekly report PGP-encrypted, read in Proton Mail on Android. Packages: vpsfort installed from the signed apt and dnf repositories on GitHub Pages, on the XMPP server and the Fedora server, each taking over a running bundle install: config, bans, scores and alerts kept across the restart, and vpsfort's self-audit of its own files clean afterwards. The web console showing every node, all but one through their agents. These runs found thirteen problems, all fixed the same day: two misleading SSH audit messages, an installer's new user raising high alerts, the web console's check misreading lists with blanks, an empty console socket setting refused, no way to correct a country the geo database gets wrong (now [geo] places), the XMPP bot never coming back after an ejabberd restart (a session it could not resume), the console's filters drawn below their tables, a package upgrade's new config template raising a high integrity alert, the repository's signing key saved unreadable for apt under a strict umask, the TUI's count of the running process's decisions labelled as if it counted everything, the packages' config question hidden by dnf until it timed out, and the sysctl audit's advice putting the sysctl -w command in a sysctl.d file, which ignores it at boot. On the Fedora 44 server's first evening (2026-10-25, x86_64, firewalld 2.4.4, rpm 6 and dnf5, real scanners and a VPN as the test client), following TESTING-fedora.md : install from the release bundle with a -dnf template; firewalld's denied-packet log as a signal source: real scanners banned on their first tripwire hit; honeypot ports 22 and 23, tried with nc from the VPN's exits; the exposure watch reading firewalld's zones, rich rules and dead rules included; rpm origins, the package check (7,472 files; a tampered binary caught) and the dnf patch status (the newer kernel waiting for a reboot); the firewalld, nftables and ipset backends: bans, expiry, operator ban and unban, recovery within 30 s after firewall-cmd --reload, a firewalld restart or flushed chains; country blocking: two countries' 137,000 networks loaded, test clients there timed out and one elsewhere connected. The run found nine bugs (a bundle could carry an older binary, two misleading status lines, a failed start logged too quietly, a merged /usr/sbin doubling integrity alerts, and more), all fixed the same day. Not yet seen on a server (covered by tests; the README's Not yet verified has the full list): the plain iptables backend, a change the firewall program refused being tried again, the self-audit of vpsfort's own files finding a problem, the clock warning, and the kernel module, container and WireGuard peer baselines; sudo and new-SSH-key alerts, PAM failures and audit alerts, an infected file's alert; the built-in sources for common services on a host that runs one; patterns of your own on a live journal; a kernel tripwire hit, and country blocking under the nftables and firewalld backends; [waf] against a real CrowdSec; users' own warnings reaching a user; the Telegram relay node, and the Telegram, Signal and XMPP-client bots against their real services; the desktop profile; the ARM builds, RHEL and SELinux in enforcing mode. On a real month of logs (Sep 11 to Oct 11, 2026, about 210,000 records from ejabberd, sshd and UFW): 185 bans of 93 targets. None of them ever authenticated, and no user's address was banned. 13,480 tripwire hits banned about 7,500 scanners on first contact. The OOM alerts revealed a nightly virus scan that had been killed for weeks, and a disabled signature updater. The old setup's generated UFW deny rules sat below the ALLOW rules, so they never matched: 4,438 XMPP connections and 106 SSH sessions came from addresses they were meant to block. This is why vpsfort's bans sit in their own table, ahead of everything else. In tests: About 390 tests in vpsfort, about 220 more in the bots, 60 in the web console (an agent and a console against a stand-in vpsfort, logged into over TLS like a browser, proof of work included) plus the page's own JavaScript tests, and a few in the simulator. The firewalld, ipset and rpm code is also tested against stand-in firewall-cmd, ipset, iptables and rpm programs. tests/layouts.rs runs the real daemon in each of the 16 supported layouts of bots and peers, end to end. The parsers, the decision-log readers and their index, the console's protocols and abuse reports, and the bots' inputs are fuzzed (23 targets). CI enforces on its runner's own kernel with the real nft, as root: a ban with its timeout, feeds, the table deleted and rebuilt with the bans still active, from the library and through the installed daemon. CI runs clippy with warnings as errors, cargo audit, cargo deny, and static musl builds for every commit: the tests on x86_64 and arm64, the ARMv7 binary started under qemu.

26.body: vpsfort works well next to: unattended-upgrades or dnf-automatic , to install what vpsfort's patch status reports. An external uptime and certificate monitor , which sees the host from outside, even when it is down. Cluster peers already report a node that stops answering for 5 minutes. A WAF for web applications: Coraza or ModSecurity, or CrowdSec AppSec with an HTTP-level bouncer only. Keep one ban manager per host: running fail2ban or CrowdSec's firewall bouncer next to vpsfort bans twice and splits the evidence between them. Lynis , for a periodic hardening audit. Falco or Tetragon , where containers matter. ClamAV , whose results vpsfort reads and reports. An off-host log archive (systemd-journal-remote, rsyslog) and backups, for forensics.

27.body: Check the requirements: Linux with systemd (x86_64; ARM builds untried on servers), and one of nftables (recommended), firewalld, ufw, iptables or ipset ( Requirements ). Download a release bundle and verify its checksum and build provenance ( Install from a release bundle ). Install with a template: vpsfort.toml for an XMPP server, vpsfort-standalone.toml for a host with SSH and UFW only, vpsfort-tg.toml for a Telegram relay node; each has a -dnf variant for Fedora and RHEL. Run in shadow mode (the default) for one to two weeks: it decides, but bans nothing. Watch vpsfort tui, and look for "likely false positive" alerts. You can replay a week of your journal first: journalctl -u ssh -k --since -7d -o json > week.json && vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml replay week.json Enforce: set mode = "enforce", restart, and check nft list table inet vpsfort (or firewall-cmd --info-zone=vpsfort). To roll back, switch to shadow mode and delete the table ( Rollout ). Add more when you want it: cluster peers, the bots, the web console ( vpsfort-web ), blocklist feeds, country blocking, honeypot ports, built-in sources and patterns for your other services. Before the console goes on a server, vpsfort-sim runs it on your laptop from a few days of your decision logs (the health cards it can't read from a log are made up, and say so).

29.body: A Rust daemon that protects a Linux server, in real time, with the logs it already writes. It follows the systemd journal for ejabberd (optional), sshd and the firewall's log ( UFW , firewalld ), scores each remote address by its behaviour, and bans attackers through nftables , firewalld , ufw , iptables or ipset (see "Firewall backends"), and can drop whole countries or networks by the same offline database it labels addresses with. Apache, nginx, Caddy, Traefik, HAProxy, Prosody, Nextcloud, ownCloud, MySQL/MariaDB, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis/Valkey, Postfix, Dovecot, Exim, Forgejo/Gitea, Vaultwarden, Synapse, Keycloak, authentik, OpenVPN, vsftpd/ProFTPD and Jellyfin have built-in sources ("Built-in sources for common services"), other services count through patterns of your own ("Patterns of your own"). Besides attackers it watches the host: su and sudo, scheduled tasks and other ways back in, package files and set-uid programs, outbound connections and odd processes, patch status, listeners and firewall rules. It is a single static binary of about 10 MB. journalctl -f -o json ──► parsers ──► events ──► engine ──► decisions ──► nftables / firewalld / ufw / iptables / ipset (cursor-resumed) ejabberd PID correlation decaying scores ban ladder, expiry ssh / ufw subnet + account actions.jsonl, journal analysis snapshot socket ──► TUI

3.body:
You need Rust stable and the x86_64-unknown-linux-musl target (for ARM also aarch64-unknown-linux-musl, armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf; TARGET=<target> ./scripts/ci.sh builds one). The bots and vpsfort-web also need the llvm-tools component. Each crate builds and tests on its own: cd vpsfort # or vpsfort-xmpp-bot, vpsfort-tg-bot, vpsfort-mail-bot, vpsfort-signal-bot, vpsfort-matrix-bot, vpsfort-push-bot, vpsfort-web
./scripts/ci.sh # fmt, clippy -D warnings, tests, cargo audit, cargo deny, static musl build
./scripts/bundle.sh # the release bundle (zip); ./scripts/package.sh: the .deb, .rpm and .apk (both take --target TRIPLE) package.sh needs cargo install cargo-deb cargo-generate-rpm --locked once; they write the packages without dpkg or rpm, so the packages build on macOS too. The static Linux binary also builds from macOS without a C cross toolchain (see each crate's .cargo/config.toml). Some tests listen on 127.0.0.1, so they need a machine or sandbox that allows local sockets. .github/workflows/ runs the same ci.sh per crate on GitHub Actions and uploads the bundles: the tests on x86_64 and on GitHub's arm64 runners, the 32-bit ARM binary cross-built, linted for its target and started under qemu. Each crate has fuzz/ targets for cargo-fuzz (nightly). tests/fuzz_smoke.rs runs the same targets on stable over their seeds.

31.body: The binary is static (musl): no Rust, libc version or packages are needed to run it. What it works with on the host: what needed for notes Linux on x86_64, aarch64 (arm64) or 32-bit ARMv7 with hardware floating point, systemd everything runs as a Type=notify unit; tested on Debian 13 (kernel 6.12), Ubuntu 22.04 (kernel 5.15) and Fedora 44 (kernel 7.2), all x86_64. The ARM binaries pass CI (the tests natively on aarch64; armv7 is linted and started under qemu) but haven't run on an ARM server yet journalctl (systemd-journald) all log input follows the journal as JSON; journald must keep the logs of sshd, the kernel and ejabberd. Lines count only from their real senders, by journald's own fields: sshd's from root, ejabberd's from a unit named ejabberd*, the kernel's and systemd's (PID 1). A host without a journal (Alpine) follows a syslog text file instead, [journal] syslog_file, without that check (below) one firewall backend enforce mode nft (the default; nft 1.0 on kernel 5.15 and Debian 13's on 6.12 are verified), or firewall-cmd (firewalld running; policies from 0.9), or ufw, or iptables + ip6tables (legacy or nf_tables flavour, with the mangle table, conntrack and multiport), the latter with ipset too for the ipset backend. Shadow mode needs none. nft rate limits, blocklist feeds, [waf] lists only the nftables backend has rate limits; feeds and [waf] lists also with ipset ([waf] bans work with every backend) firewall logging firewall signals (port scans, tripwires) ufw logging low, or firewall-cmd --set-log-denied=unicast, or with plain iptables a LOG rule with the prefix [VPSFORT BLOCK] (see "Firewall backends") ufw, else firewall-cmd, else iptables + ip6tables, else nft exposure watch's firewall view without an active ufw, firewalld's zones (firewall-cmd --list-all-zones, every 5 minutes), else the filter table's INPUT chain (iptables -S), else nftables rulesets of their own (nft -j list chain per input-hook chain); with no firewall at all, listeners are still watched and the TUI says so in red ejabberdctl, or ejabberd's HTTP API on loopback XMPP notifications see "XMPP notifications"; reading ejabberd's log needs nothing extra openssl certificate checks in the daily digest curl blocklist feeds, geo database downloads, [waf] sources read from a URL 7.55 or later for [waf] api_key_file (-H @-) docker the Nextcloud AIO source reads docker logs -f of the Apache container df disk space watch coreutils apt-get, or dnf patch status ([patches]) apt: a simulation (-s) only (Debian, Ubuntu); without it, they are read from the files auditd, or journald's audit socket the audit log's alerts ([sources] audit) optional; journald reads audit records where its audit socket runs, audit_log names auditd's file instead nftables fib and dynamic sets kernel tripwires ([ports] kernel_tripwires) in Debian's and Ubuntu's kernels; where missing, vpsfort runs without them and says so ClamAV (clamscan/clamdscan) the vpsfort-avscan timer; [antivirus] scan_changed "clamav"/"both" optional YARA (yara 4.1 or later) and rules [antivirus] scan_changed "yara"/"both" optional; systemd-run (systemd 235 or later) runs the scanners outside vpsfort's memory limit the XMPP admin bot (vpsfort-xmpp-bot) encrypted admin messages optional, [notify] bot_outbox the XMPP client bot (vpsfort-xmpp-bot with BOT_MODE=client) a copy of admin messages over XMPP, OMEMO-encrypted, from an account on any server; no ejabberd needed (a VPN server, a relay node, a desktop) optional, [notify] xmpp_outbox the Telegram admin bot (vpsfort-tg-bot) a copy of admin messages on Telegram optional, [notify] tg_outbox the mail bot (vpsfort-mail-bot) a copy of admin messages by mail, OpenPGP-encrypted optional, [notify] mail_outbox the Signal bot (vpsfort-signal-bot, with signal-cli) a copy of admin messages on Signal optional, [notify] signal_outbox the Matrix bot (vpsfort-matrix-bot) a copy of admin messages on Matrix, end-to-end encrypted optional, [notify] matrix_outbox the push bot (vpsfort-push-bot) a copy of admin messages to ntfy, Gotify or a webhook, sanitized as for Telegram optional, [notify] push_outbox To build: Rust (stable) with the x86_64-unknown-linux-musl target (aarch64-unknown-linux-musl, armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf for ARM); deploy/deploy.sh builds on a Mac. Alpine, or any host without a journal: [journal] syslog_file = "/var/log/messages" makes vpsfort follow that syslog text file (Aug 16 21:20:19 host sshd[123]: ..., busybox syslogd's or rsyslog's format) instead of running journalctl; the Alpine package's template (vpsfort-alpine.toml) sets it. Lines are stamped when read (the file's own times have no year or zone), so what was written while vpsfort was down is scored as new, up to 24 hours back (file-positions.json, "Files"). What the journal gives and syslog can't: a line counts from whoever wrote it, since syslog records no sender, so a local user's logger -t sshd "Failed password for root from 203.0.113.5 ..." is an sshd line here and can get an address banned (the same weakness /var/log/mail.log has, "Built-in sources for common services"); and no journal means no [sources] services, no verify_every, no [patches] or [verify] without apt or dnf (the template turns them off). The sshd, kernel (UFW), su/sudo, PAM and audit parsers read the same lines in syslog form; ejabberd's lines too, where it logs to syslog. Not yet run on such a host. Fedora and RHEL: set package_manager = "dnf" (top of the config, before any section), or start from a -dnf template (vpsfort-dnf.toml, vpsfort-standalone-dnf.toml, vpsfort-tg-dnf.toml; scripts/template-variants.sh writes them from the others). Package lookups then ask rpm, pending updates dnf. Tried on a Fedora 44 server ("Verified on the servers"). Fedora has no ufw (firewalld instead): use the nft backend, and [sources] ufw sees no firewall lines unless something logs them with ufw's prefix.

33.body:
[enforce] backend picks how bans are applied. auto (the default) tries nftables first, then firewalld if it runs, then ufw if it is installed, then iptables (ipset only when named). If none works, vpsfort stays in shadow mode and says why. A fallback after nftables failed raises a high system alert. nft firewalld ufw iptables ipset where own table inet vpsfort, prerouting right after connection tracking ipsets vpsfort-ban4/-ban6, the sources of a zone vpsfort with target DROP ufw prepend deny rules own chains vpsfort and vpsfort-ban in the mangle table, jumped to from the top of PREROUTING the same chains, matching ipset sets vpsfort-ban4/-ban6, vpsfort-feed4/-feed6, vpsfort-waf4/-waf6 before Docker's published ports yes yes, with a policy vpsfort-fwd (firewalld 0.9 and later) no yes yes bans end in the kernel (set timeouts), also while vpsfort is down when vpsfort removes the entry when vpsfort removes the rule when vpsfort removes the rule in the kernel (ipset timeouts, up to 24 days; longer ones when vpsfort lifts them) whitelisted ports stay open for banned addresses yes yes (the zone's ports) no yes yes rate limits yes no no no no blocklist feeds yes no no no yes many bans one set lookup one set lookup one rule each one rule each one set lookup self-healing table rebuilt within 30 s entries restored within 30 s of a reload – chains rebuilt within 30 s chains and sets rebuilt within 30 s No backend drops replies to connections the server opened itself. A banned address can be forged (one SYN to a tripwire port names any source), and the server must not lose its DNS resolver, mail relay, update mirrors or federated XMPP servers that way. nftables and iptables therefore drop after connection tracking, which tells replies apart; ufw's own rules accept them before vpsfort's. Versions before 2026-10-24 dropped earlier (nftables chain pre at raw priority, iptables chains in the raw table), replies included; at its first start, this version removes those. iptables is meant for hosts that manage their firewall with plain iptables, e.g. with iptables-persistent (netfilter-persistent), instead of ufw. vpsfort never touches your own rules or chains; it only adds its two chains to the mangle table and one jump at the top of the mangle PREROUTING chain, for IPv4 (iptables) and IPv6 (ip6tables): vpsfort: allowlisted networks, whitelisted ports and replies to the server's own connections RETURN, then a jump to vpsfort-ban. Rebuilt when the allowlist changes. vpsfort-ban: operator allows (RETURN) at the top, then one DROP rule per ban. Allowed traffic RETURNs rather than ACCEPTs, so other rules in the mangle table still apply. At start vpsfort empties vpsfort-ban and re-adds the bans and allows that are still active from its state file. So if netfilter-persistent save stored them while vpsfort ran, a reboot or netfilter-persistent reload restoring stale bans does no harm: they're replaced as soon as vpsfort starts. If a reload removes the chains or the jump, vpsfort rebuilds them within 30 s (high system alert). Bans don't expire in the kernel: one stays until vpsfort (running) lifts it. Paths and the chain name are set in [enforce] (iptables, ip6tables, iptables_chain). For firewall signals, iptables must log what it drops, with the prefix vpsfort reads ([sources] ufw covers these lines too). Add it as the last rules of INPUT, before its DROP policy or final DROP rule, and save it with your other rules: iptables -A INPUT -m limit --limit 10/second -j LOG --log-prefix '[VPSFORT BLOCK] '
ip6tables -A INPUT -m limit --limit 10/second -j LOG --log-prefix '[VPSFORT BLOCK] ' For the cluster port, vpsfort cluster-ufw-rules --iptables prints the rules that open it to the peers only; install.sh shows them when there is no ufw. firewalld (Fedora, RHEL and its rebuilds) keeps its own objects, so firewall-cmd --list-all-zones shows what vpsfort does. At its first start vpsfort adds to firewalld's permanent configuration (firewalld makes ipsets and zones nowhere else) and reloads it once: ipsets vpsfort-ban4 and vpsfort-ban6 (hash:net), the sources of a zone vpsfort whose target is DROP. A source-bound zone comes before the interfaces' zones, so firewalld drops everything from a banned network, except the zone's ports ([ports] whitelist, kept in step at each start) and replies to the server's own connections (firewalld accepts established traffic before any zone). a policy vpsfort-fwd from that zone to ANY, target DROP: their forwarded traffic too (ports published by Docker or Podman). firewalld before 0.9 has no policies: vpsfort says so and goes on without it. an ipset vpsfort-alive no rule uses, holding one entry (192.0.2.1). The bans themselves are runtime entries (firewall-cmd --ipset=vpsfort-ban4 --add-entry=...), never permanent: at start vpsfort empties the sets and re-adds the active bans from its state file, so nothing of a ban outlives vpsfort. firewall-cmd --reload or a firewalld restart forgets them, the sentinel entry with them: within 30 s vpsfort notices and re-adds them (high system alert). An operator allow lifts the bans inside it, as with ufw, but can't open a gap in a wider ban (a zone's sources have no exceptions). No rate limits, blocklist feeds or kernel tripwires (nftables only). With nftables, auto still prefers its own table, which works next to firewalld's; name firewalld to have firewalld hold everything. Its log lines: firewall-cmd --set-log-denied=unicast makes firewalld log what its zones reject or drop (filter_IN_public_REJECT: ...), which [sources] ufw reads as firewall signals, like UFW's (not those of the vpsfort zone: its sources are banned already). install.sh opens the cluster port to the peers with permanent rich rules (cluster-ufw-rules --firewalld prints them) and says when denied packets aren't logged. ipset is the iptables backend for many bans: the same chains and allow rules, but vpsfort-ban matches its ipset sets (bans, feeds, [waf] lists, [geoblock]; IPv4 and IPv6), one rule each, instead of one rule per ban. Bans carry their time in the kernel (ipset add ... timeout), so they end while vpsfort is down too; a ban longer than ipset's limit (2,147,483 s, about 24 days) goes in without one and vpsfort lifts it. Blocklist feeds load into vpsfort-feed4/-feed6, [waf] lists into vpsfort-waf4/-waf6. At start the ban sets are emptied and refilled from the state file. Needs ipset and the xt_set match; the set names start with iptables_chain.
33.title: Firewall backends

34.body: Each address has two exponentially decaying scores: score half-life threshold catches fast 10 min 100 bursts: 3 TLS failures, 5 SSH password failures, a port sweep slow 12 h 200 low-and-slow probing, e.g. one TLS failure every 30 min Events add points: signal weight source xmpp_tls_fail 40 TLS handshake failure (old protocol, no shared cipher), attributed to an IP via the Erlang PID xmpp_auth_fail 25 failed SASL login xmpp_no_auth 10 5222/5223 connection that never authenticated within 90 s xmpp_conn 2 connection to 5269/5280/5443/5349… xmpp_s2s_bad 25 inbound s2s rejected: not-well-formed, syntax error, host-unknown… xmpp_http_miss 4 request for a missing upload file xmpp_token_fail 5 rejected FAST token (HT-*): almost always a legitimate client with an expired token xmpp_register 15 in-band account registration (each also raises an info alert) ssh_auth_fail / ssh_invalid_user 25 / 40 failed password, gave up authenticating / unknown user ssh_preauth 8 disconnected before auth, failed key exchange, banner garbage (a close/reset from an sshd-session that never authenticated counts too, even without [preauth]) ssh_penalty 25 OpenSSH PerSourcePenalties fired fw_block / fw_limit 1 / 20 UFW BLOCK / UFW LIMIT BLOCK: kernel lines that start with the prefix and go on with IN=... OUT=..., as only the packet logger writes them (other kernel lines start with a name any user picks, such as a crashing program's) fw_tripwire 100 UFW BLOCK on a [ports] tripwire port (telnet, mail, RDP, VNC, SMB, databases, ...), or the same SYN logged by vpsfort's own rule ("Kernel tripwires"): one hit = ban. 50 when [ports] honeypot is set tripwire_connect 100 a completed TCP handshake with a [ports] honeypot listener ("Honeypot ports"): its source isn't forged peer_report reported points × 0.5 suspicion reported by another cluster node web_probe 40 Nextcloud: request for secrets refused (/config/.env, aws.yml, secrets.yml…) or path traversal (/../.env) nc_auth_fail 25 Nextcloud: failed login pam_auth_fail 25 a failed login PAM logs from an address on the internet, at a service with no parser of its own (vsftpd, Cockpit, ...; "PAM, account changes and auditd") custom_failure / custom_probe the pattern's weight a line a pattern of your own or a built-in one of [sources] apps matched ("Patterns of your own", "Built-in sources for common services"); custom_success is a login Weights are calibrated against the 10-minute half-life: 40 means three strikes within about 5 minutes ban; 25 means five strikes within about 5 minutes. With 34, three strikes only added up when all came within about 25 seconds, so a scanner pausing 30 s between requests was never banned. Bonuses: +60 when one address touches 3 or more XMPP ports within 10 min (port spread), and +60 when UFW drops it on 8 or more distinct ports (port scan). Protection. Private, loopback, link-local and CGNAT addresses are ignored entirely; for example, a Docker container hitting the host's public IP is blocked by UFW about once a minute. Allowlisted addresses are never banned. Addresses that authenticated successfully within trust_ttl (24 h) aren't banned for that service's noise and typos, nor for blocked packets on any port (see "Canary accounts"). Noise signals from them score 0. Real failures still raise an alert. A subnet containing a protected address is never banned. Subnets. Every 60 s a /24 (or IPv6 /64) is banned in either of two cases: 3 or more of its addresses are individually bad (concentrated attack). 5 or more addresses together reach a summed score of 100 (distributed scanning, e.g. 12.23.48.0/24 probing once per IP). A banned /24 then grows step by step, up to a /16 (v4_wide_prefix). It grows to the narrowest network that also holds the next ban nearby, either an address or another subnet, and at most 2 prefix bits at a time (wide_max_step). For example, 11.145.59.0/24 plus a banned 11.145.57.7 becomes 11.145.56.0/22, and that /22 grows to a /20 with the next ban inside the /20. An address 5 bits away (11.145.36.5, common network /19) stays a host ban until the range has grown close enough. Growth stops before any network with a protected address. With the [geo] network database loaded, it also stops before a network that holds another provider's (ASN's) addresses. The rest of a cloud provider's /16 stays reachable: other customers, VPN exits. The TUI's status and the daily digest show how many addresses the subnet bans cover, and the widest one. This replaces the earlier single step from 12 bad addresses over 4 /24s straight to the whole /16. wide_min_bad_ips and wide_min_subnets are still accepted in old config files, but they are ignored, and config-diff lists them. IPv6 /64 bans grow the same way, up to v6_wide_prefix (/48), wide_max_step_v6 (4) bits at a time: providers hand out /64s, /60s, /56s and /48s, and an attacker rotating through a /56 shows up as /64 after /64. 3fff:180:1:2::/64 plus a ban in 3fff:180:1:3::/64 becomes 3fff:180:1:2::/63; a ban in 3fff:180:1:8::/64 then takes it to the /60. v6_wide_prefix = 64 keeps IPv6 bans at /64. A peer's IPv6 ban wider than this node's own widest is ignored, as for IPv4. Ban ladder. Bans last 1h → 6h → 1d → 7d → 30d per repeat offence. The offence counter resets after 30 days without a new ban. Accounts. Alerts are raised for: Distributed password guessing against one account: about 20 failures from 3 or more IPs within an hour. A login right after suspicious activity from the same IP: critical , possible compromise. A login from a new /16, after a 7-day learning period. An SSH login with a key the account never used before ( high ): the key is in sshd's Accepted publickey ... ssh2: ED25519 SHA256:... line. Each account's keys are learned silently for learning_period (7 days) after the first one is seen, then a new one is reported once and becomes known. If nobody added a key, the account's authorized_keys was changed (the cron watch reports that file too). [accounts] new_key_alerts = false turns it off. Shadow-mode self-check. If a "banned" address later logs in successfully, a likely false positive alert is raised and, in shadow mode, the ban is lifted (here and at the peers). In enforce mode a banned address can't connect, so a login line naming one is suspect: the alert says so and the ban stays (vpsfort unban it if it is a false positive).

35.body: ./deploy/deploy.sh vpn deploy/vpsfort-standalone.toml # ssh alias "vpn"; then paste the printed command into a root shell there deploy/vpsfort-standalone.toml sets three things: [sources] ejabberd = false: the journal filter and the pipeline skip ejabberd entirely. [ports] whitelist = ["51820/udp"]: wg-easy's WG_PORT. The panel (PORT=51821) is no longer published, so it is not whitelisted. notify.enabled = false: there is no ejabberdctl on that host. Whitelisted ports (PORT/udp, PORT/tcp, or a bare PORT for both) work as follows: Never scored: UFW blocks or other events on them don't count towards a ban. Never blocked in enforce mode: an accept for them precedes the ban drop, so even a banned address can still reach them. Docker: ports published with docker run -p bypass UFW and the host INPUT chain. vpsfort therefore hooks nftables at prerouting (right after connection tracking, before Docker's DNAT), so bans do cover Docker-published ports. The iptables backend covers them the same way (mangle PREROUTING). The ufw fallback can't do this, and it can't keep whitelisted ports open either; vpsfort warns about this at startup. The wg-easy panel: the WireGuard port is safe to whitelist, because it silently ignores unauthenticated packets. The admin panel is not: whitelisting it lets banned scanners keep trying its login page. Prefer not exposing it at all. Drop --publish 0.0.0.0:51821:51821/tcp and open http://10.8.0.1:51821 while connected to the VPN: the panel listens inside the container, which owns the WireGuard interface. Alternatively publish it as 127.0.0.1:51821:51821/tcp and use an SSH tunnel. Then remove 51821/tcp from the whitelist.

36.body: For a Nextcloud without AIO (distribution packages, the snap, your own web server) and for ownCloud 10, use [sources] apps = ["nextcloud"] or ["owncloud"] instead ("Built-in sources for common services"). [sources] nextcloud_aio = true reads two things, with no change to Docker or AIO (until 2026-10-26 the option was called nextcloud, and its section [nextcloud_aio] was [nextcloud]; both old names still work, and config-diff points them out): docker logs --follow --timestamps nextcloud-aio-apache. Apache's error log shows every refused request with the client IP. It's restarted automatically when the container is recreated (AIO updates, reboots), resuming after the last line seen. tail -F of nextcloud.log (/var/lib/docker/volumes/nextcloud_aio_nextcloud/_data/data/nextcloud.log; occ log:file shows the path inside the container) for Login failed: user (Remote IP: …). This is the same file AIO's own fail2ban container reads; failures count per account like XMPP and SSH ones. Restarts lose nothing: the time of the last line read from each of the two is kept in the state file. After a restart, docker logs resumes from that moment and nextcloud.log is re-read from its last 2,000 lines; lines already seen are skipped by their timestamps. Login names from these logs are attacker-chosen: control characters are removed before they reach alerts or a terminal. On the Oct 2–11 Apache log this bans each Google-Cloud .env/aws.yml/config.js prober on its third request. The daily 12.195.52.117 escalates 1h → 6h → 1d → 7d. Docker-published ports bypass UFW, but vpsfort's nftables chain sits in prerouting, so these bans apply to Nextcloud too.

Web servers and proxies, a load balancer, Prosody and Synapse, Nextcloud and ownCloud, databases, in-memory stores, mail, a code forge, a password manager, two identity providers, OpenVPN, FTP, a media server and vpsfort's own web console need no patterns of your own: name them in [sources] apps and vpsfort reads their logs with built-in patterns (src/parse/apps.rs, each tested against real and forged lines): [sources]
apps = ["nginx", "postgresql", "redis"] [sources.app_logs] # only for a log that isn't in the usual places
nginx_access = ["/srv/www/logs/access.log", "/srv/www/logs/api-access.log"] # absolute paths, * in a file name
postgresql = "postgresql@17-main.service" # or a unit: its journal [sources.app_weights] # points of a built-in pattern, if not its default
nginx_limit = 0
nginx_survey = 100 # ban internet survey scanners at once app log (key in app_logs), where it is looked for patterns: what counts, points apache (httpd 2.2 and 2.4) apache_access: /var/log/apache2/*access.log, /var/log/httpd/*access_log; apache_error: *error.log, *error_log there apache_probe 40: requests for secrets and exploits (below); apache_proxy 20: absolute URLs and CONNECT (open-proxy tests); apache_scanner 40 / apache_survey 20: user agents of attack tools / survey scanners (below); apache_auth 25: Basic auth wrong password or unknown user (AH01617/AH01618); apache_traversal 40 (AH10244); apache_badreq 10: invalid method, URI too long, no Host; apache_denied 20: refused by Require (AH01630/AH01797) nginx nginx_access: /var/log/nginx/*access.log; nginx_error: /var/log/nginx/*error.log nginx_probe, nginx_proxy, nginx_scanner, nginx_survey as for Apache; nginx_auth 25: auth_basic password mismatch, unknown user; nginx_denied 20: deny; nginx_limit 8: limit_req/limit_conn rejections haproxy haproxy: /var/log/haproxy.log, else haproxy.service haproxy_probe 40 (option httplog); haproxy_denied 20: termination state PR/PT (http-request deny, tarpit, bad request); haproxy_tls 10: TLS handshake failures prosody prosody: /var/log/prosody/prosody.log, else prosody.service prosody_auth 25: failed logins, as mod_log_auth logs them (enable it: Prosody itself logs no address) mysql (MySQL, MariaDB, Percona) mysql: /var/log/mysql/error.log, /var/log/mysqld.log, /var/log/mariadb/mariadb.log, else the journal of mariadb.service, mysql.service or mysqld.service mysql_auth 25: Access denied for user; mysql_preauth 8: connections closed before authenticating. Needs skip_name_resolve = ON (else the log names hosts, not addresses); MySQL 8 also log_error_verbosity = 3 (MariaDB logs them by default) postgresql postgresql: /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-*.log, /var/lib/pgsql/data/log/postgresql-*.log, else postgresql.service postgresql_auth / postgresql_role 25: wrong password, unknown role; postgresql_hba 25: no pg_hba.conf entry; postgresql_preauth 8: broken startup packets, failed TLS. Needs the client in the prefix right after the pid: log_line_prefix = '%m [%p] %h %q%u@%d ', and English messages (lc_messages = 'C') mongodb (4.4 and later) mongodb: /var/log/mongodb/mongod.log, else mongod.service mongodb_auth, mongodb_auth_v6 25: failed authentication (both message forms) redis (Redis, Valkey, KeyDB) redis: /var/log/redis/redis-server.log, redis.log, the Valkey and KeyDB ones, else their units redis_attack 40: HTTP sent to the Redis port ("Possible SECURITY ATTACK"); redis_tls 10: failed TLS handshakes. Redis doesn't log failed AUTH (only ACL LOG shows them): keep it off the internet nextcloud (without AIO: packages, the snap, your own web server) nextcloud: nextcloud.log in /var/www/nextcloud/data/, /var/www/html/nextcloud/data/, /var/www/html/data/, /srv/nextcloud/data/, the snap's /var/snap/nextcloud/current/logs/, /var/log/nextcloud/, /var/log/ (occ log:file shows yours) nextcloud_auth 25: Login failed; nextcloud_bruteforce 40: its own brute-force protection slowing an address down (logged at loglevel 1 and below). Its web server's probes come from apache or nginx (the snap's Apache logs are among the places apache looks). Behind a reverse proxy, set trusted_proxies, or every line names the proxy. Names in [canary] nextcloud are canaries. Not together with [sources] nextcloud_aio: both read the same failed logins owncloud (ownCloud 10) owncloud: owncloud.log in /var/www/owncloud/data/, /var/www/html/owncloud/data/, /var/www/html/data/, the Docker image's /mnt/data/files/, /var/log/owncloud/ owncloud_auth 25: Login failed; names in [canary] nextcloud are canaries. Not ownCloud Infinite Scale (oCIS), whose log is another postfix postfix: the journal of postfix@-.service or postfix.service, else /var/log/mail.log, /var/log/maillog postfix_sasl 25: SASL login failures; postfix_relay 25: relay attempts dovecot dovecot: the journal of dovecot.service, else the mail log dovecot_auth 25: IMAP/POP3/ManageSieve logins that failed caddy caddy: /var/log/caddy/access.log (JSON), else caddy.service caddy_probe 40, caddy_scanner 40, caddy_survey 20, as for Apache; the address is the request's remote_ip, which Caddy writes first traefik traefik: /var/log/traefik/access.log, else traefik.service traefik_probe 40, traefik_scanner 40 (the common format, with Traefik's router, backend and duration at the end), traefik_probe_json 40 (the JSON format: ClientHost and RequestPath) forgejo (also gitea) forgejo: /var/lib/forgejo/log/forgejo.log, /var/lib/gitea/log/gitea.log, /var/log/gitea/gitea.log, else forgejo.service, gitea.service forgejo_auth 25: a failed web login (Failed authentication attempt for <user> from <address>); forgejo_ssh 25: a failed SSH key login at its built-in SSH server vaultwarden vaultwarden: /var/log/vaultwarden/vaultwarden.log, /var/log/vaultwarden.log, else vaultwarden.service vaultwarden_auth 25: Username or password is incorrect; vaultwarden_2fa 25: a wrong TOTP code synapse (Matrix) synapse: /var/log/matrix-synapse/homeserver.log, else matrix-synapse.service synapse_auth 25: a login request answered 403 in the access log (synapse.access.http) keycloak keycloak: /opt/keycloak/data/log/keycloak.log, else keycloak.service keycloak_auth 25: a LOGIN_ERROR event (invalid_user_credentials, user_not_found, ...) with its ipAddress; needs the events logged (--log-level=org.keycloak.events:debug, or the jboss-logging event listener) authentik authentik: /var/log/authentik/server.log, else authentik-server.service authentik_auth 25: a login_failed event (JSON) with its client_ip openvpn openvpn: /var/log/openvpn/openvpn.log, /var/log/openvpn/*.log, else openvpn-server@server.service, openvpn@server.service openvpn_auth 25: Auth Username/Password verification failed; openvpn_tls 20: a failed TLS handshake or certificate check; openvpn_hmac 40: a packet without the tls-auth/tls-crypt key (what every scanner sends) ftp (vsftpd, ProFTPD; also vsftpd, proftpd) vsftpd: /var/log/vsftpd.log, else vsftpd.service; proftpd: the journal of proftpd.service, else /var/log/proftpd/proftpd.log vsftpd_auth 25: FAIL LOGIN; proftpd_auth 25: Login failed; proftpd_user 25: no such user found exim exim: /var/log/exim4/mainlog, /var/log/exim/main.log, else exim4.service exim_auth 25: authenticator failed ... 535 Incorrect authentication data; exim_relay 25: rejected RCPT ...: relay not permitted jellyfin jellyfin: /var/log/jellyfin/jellyfin*.log, else jellyfin.service jellyfin_auth 25: Authentication request for "<user>" has been denied (IP: "<address>") vpsfort-web (the web console, below) vpsfort_web: the journal of vpsfort-web.service vpsfort_web_login 25: failed console logins (wrong password or one-time code), and attempts while the address is locked out; vpsfort_web_probe 40: probes (as for Apache) for paths the console doesn't have; vpsfort_web_refused 20: connections from outside CONSOLE_ALLOW/AGENT_ALLOW; vpsfort_web_agent 20: requests to an agent without the web key; vpsfort_web_share 20: a share link's token guessed or expired, or its page hammered Where: a log with several files in the usual place (Apache's and nginx's per-site example.org-access.log) is followed in all of them, up to 16, found when vpsfort starts. Without one, the installed unit's journal is read. Postfix and Dovecot prefer the journal: /var/log/mail.log is written by syslog, where any local user can log lines in Postfix's name, while journald names the real sender. HAProxy usually logs only to /var/log/haproxy.log (from a chroot), which has the same weakness: if local users aren't trusted, send its log to the journal and set haproxy = "haproxy.service". At start, vpsfort's journal says where it reads each log ([sources] apps: nginx access log: ...), and the Patterns tab shows each built-in pattern with its lines: none means the log isn't where vpsfort looks. Probes are requests no legitimate client sends: secrets (/.env, /.git/, /.aws/, /.ssh/, .htpasswd, wp-config.php, id_rsa, docker-compose.yml), path traversal (../, %2e%2e, ..;/), well-known exploits (Log4Shell ${jndi:, PHPUnit's eval-stdin.php, router and IIS worms such as cmd.exe, root.exe, Code Red's .ida?, FrontPage's _vti_aut, awstats' configdir=, wget+http in a URL). Not wp-login.php, xmlrpc.php or /phpmyadmin/: a site may have them. Tested on two Honeynet Project honeypots' Apache logs (SotM 34 and the 2005 honeynet bundle, log-sharing.dreamhosters.com ): every match was an attack. Scanners by user agent (from nginx-hardening's list ): attack tools (nuclei, nikto, sqlmap, gobuster, ffuf, wpscan, masscan, zgrab, nmap, LeakIX, ...) score 40; internet survey scanners (Censys, Shodan, Palo Alto Expanse, BitSight, ...) 20, as they only map. HTTP libraries (okhttp, curl, python-requests, Go-http-client) aren't on it: Android XMPP clients upload with okhttp, monitoring uses curl. Scan your own server only from an allowlisted address. Forged addresses: these logs carry text the client chose (user names, paths, headers). Each pattern takes the address only from where the service writes it: the first field of an access log line, after fixed fields only the service fills (nginx's client:, Apache's [client ...], PostgreSQL's prefix, Nextcloud's and ownCloud's remoteAddr), or at the end of the line (MySQL, Prosody, Dovecot's last rip=). Prosody's message must also start right after its source and level, so a client's text ending another message (a stream error's) can't pass for one. A Basic auth user name can't hold a :, a JSON value can't hold an unescaped ", and PostgreSQL starts the lines of a message with a tab. The tests try made-up user names, paths and headers naming other addresses. Behind a proxy or CDN the web server's logs show the proxy's address, not the client's: vpsfort would score the proxy. Private and loopback addresses are ignored anyway; for a CDN's public ones, log the real client (nginx real_ip_header, Apache mod_remoteip) or allowlist the CDN's networks. Docker: a container logging to stdout reaches none of these files. Mount its log directory on the host and name the files in app_logs. Or use Docker's journald log driver and set the logs to "docker.service" (dockerd writes them, access and error lines alike): then every container's lines are read, so only where all containers are yours. All built-in patterns are probes or failures (none trusts an address after a login). Their events are custom_probe and custom_failure, their accounts <pattern>:<user>, as for the patterns of your own; vpsfort test-pattern runs them too (--pattern nginx_probe). A pattern of your own may not take the name of a built-in pattern of an app in apps; yours are tried first.
