38.body:
A service vpsfort has no parser for counts through [[patterns]]: a regular expression over the lines of a systemd unit (journal) or of a log file, with the client address in a group named ip and, optionally, the account in user: Postfix is built in (above); its SASL failures as a pattern of your own would be: [[patterns]]
name = "smtp_sasl"
unit = "postfix@-.service" # journal lines of this unit; or identifier + uid; or file = "/var/log/..."
regex = 'warning: [^\[]*\[(?P<ip>[0-9A-Fa-f.:]+)\]: SASL \S+ authentication failed(: [^,]*, sasl_username=(?P<user>\S+))?'
kind = "failure" # failure, probe or success
weight = 25 # points per line (not for success)
port = 587 # optional: the local port, for the dashboard's statistics Kinds: failure is a failed login (custom_failure): counted per account, so distributed guessing and a login right after failures are noticed as for XMPP and SSH. probe (custom_probe) is hostile without a login. success (custom_success) is a login: its address is trusted for these lines (all patterns' lines together) like a login to XMPP or SSH. Whose lines: any local user can log lines with any SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER, so a journal pattern names its sender by journald's own fields: unit (_SYSTEMD_UNIT, exactly), or identifier together with uid (_UID). Lines the built-in parsers read (ejabberd, sshd, the kernel's firewall lines) don't reach the patterns. A file is followed by vpsfort itself, from where the last run left it (file-positions.json, "Files"): lines written during a restart or an upgrade are read too, and a file rotated meanwhile from its new start; only a position older than a day is left alone (the lines would be scored as new). The first pattern that is for a line's sender and finds an address in it wins. Safe with any line: the regex crate matches in linear time, whatever an attacker puts into a line (no catastrophic backtracking); a pattern compiling to more than 1 MB is refused. But it is matched anywhere in a line, and lines carry text attackers choose (user names, URLs): anchor it (^, or the text the service writes right before the address) so that a made-up user name can't put someone else's address into group ip. Accounts are kept as <pattern>:<user> and get no user notifications (only XMPP accounts do); the evidence kept for a ban (which abuse reports quote) shows [account] in place of group user. On the dashboard: the TUI's Patterns tab (key 0) shows what each pattern found since vpsfort started counting: lines read from its unit or file (none: the service isn't installed, or the unit name or path is wrong, and the tab says so), matched lines, the last match, the busiest addresses with their bans, and the lines it matched without finding an address (a regex that needs a fix: they score nothing). The counts are kept in the state file; up to 200 addresses per pattern are kept (the busiest, and none unseen for 30 days). port only labels the lines for the Countries tab's port statistics: vpsfort opens no port for a pattern. Try it first: vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml test-pattern --pattern smtp_sasl /var/log/mail.log (journal JSON, journalctl short output, a log file's lines, .gz too; stdin without a file) prints, per pattern, how many lines it matched, the addresses and accounts it found, and the lines with no address in group ip; -v prints every match. The sender checks need the live journal and are left out there.

4.body:
From a release bundle (no Rust needed): one zip per crate and architecture, <crate>-<version>-<commit>-<arch>.zip, <arch> one of x86_64-linux-musl, aarch64-linux-musl (arm64) and armv7-linux-musleabihf (32-bit ARMv7, hard-float). It holds the static binary, the systemd units, logrotate files and config templates, SHA256SUMS, and an install.sh. Unzip it on the server and run sudo ./install.sh (the first run of each puts a config in place to edit, then you run it again). Each crate's README has a section "Install from a release bundle", with how to download and verify one. From a package (Debian, Ubuntu and their derivatives; Fedora, RHEL and its rebuilds; Alpine): the same releases carry <crate>_<version>-1_<arch>.deb (amd64, arm64, armhf), <crate>-<version>-1.<arch>.rpm (x86_64, aarch64, armv7hl) and <crate>-<version>-r0.<arch>.apk (x86_64, aarch64, armv7), the same static binary and deploy files for the package manager: sudo apt install ./<file>.deb, sudo dnf install ./<file>.rpm or apk add --allow-untrusted ./<file>.apk (the .apk is unsigned; its .sha256 and attestation verify it, and it brings OpenRC scripts instead of the units: Alpine has no systemd, and no journal, so vpsfort follows /var/log/messages there). vpsfort goes to /usr/bin with its units in /usr/lib/systemd/system and the templates in /usr/share/vpsfort/templates; the bots and vpsfort-web stay in /opt/<crate>. Nothing starts on its own: the first install puts the config template in place to edit, then you enable the service. An upgrade keeps the config (asking, when a terminal is there, whether to replace it with the new template) and restarts a running service when its config is valid. The packages also install over a bundle or deploy.sh install and take it over, keeping its config, keys and state. Rollback is installing the previous version's package. Each crate's README has a section "Install from a package". From the repository (a public repository with GitHub Pages): .github/workflows/repository.yml runs after every release is published, gathers the newest .deb and .rpm of every crate from the releases, builds a signed apt repository (deb/, suite stable, component main) and a signed dnf repository per architecture (rpm/<arch>/) with scripts/repo.sh, and pushes them to the gh-pages branch, which Pages serves at https://makhort.github.io/vpsfort/ with the instructions on its index page; the rpms in it are signed with the same key (dnf checks each package, gpgcheck=1), the debs are covered by the signed InRelease. The same workflow builds the documentation site under docs/ there (the READMEs and COMPARISON.md with mdBook, scripts/docs-site.sh) after every push to main that changes them, also without a signing key. It needs the repository secret REPO_GPG_KEY (an armored OpenPGP private key made for this: gpg --quick-generate-key "vpsfort packages <you@example.org>" rsa4096 sign 0; RSA, since rpm before 4.16 (RHEL 8) can't verify ed25519 signatures; exported with --export-secret-keys), REPO_GPG_PASSPHRASE if it has one, and Pages set to deploy from the gh-pages branch (the workflow's first run creates it: choose it in Settings → Pages after that); without the key, or before the first release, only the documentation is published. Then: sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://makhort.github.io/vpsfort/vpsfort.asc | sudo install -m 0644 /dev/stdin /etc/apt/keyrings/vpsfort.asc
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/vpsfort.asc] https://makhort.github.io/vpsfort/deb stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/vpsfort.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install vpsfort and on Fedora or RHEL sudo curl -fsSL https://makhort.github.io/vpsfort/vpsfort.repo -o /etc/yum.repos.d/vpsfort.repo && sudo dnf install vpsfort. Compare the key's fingerprint on the index page with the one you made. apt upgrade and dnf upgrade then bring new versions, with the same post-install steps as a single package. The signing key's fingerprint is 12A75B42C4ADD340896F5E7A2F64B712E37F3CEC; compare it with the downloaded key's before the first apt update: gpg --show-keys /etc/apt/keyrings/vpsfort.asc. Releases: a version is a tag <crate>-v<version> (vpsfort-v0.6.1, vpsfort-xmpp-bot-v0.6.1, ...), with the version in that crate's Cargo.toml and the release notes as that version's ## <version> section in the crate's CHANGELOG.md (./scripts/bundle.sh --check-tag TAG checks both). Pushing the tag runs that crate's workflow, which refuses a tag that doesn't match or has no notes, tests, builds and installs the bundles and packages as on every commit (the .deb on the runner, over the bundle's install; the .rpm in Fedora and AlmaLinux containers, the .apk in an Alpine container), then attaches them to the GitHub Release of the tag, each with its .sha256 and (in a public repository) a signed build provenance attestation, .sigstore.json, that gh attestation verify checks, and a software bill of materials, <crate>-<version>.cdx.json (CycloneDX, from cargo cyclonedx: every crate in the binary with its version, license and pkg:cargo identifier, with its .sha256 and covered by the attestation). Every CI run, tagged or not, also keeps its zip, .deb, .rpm, .apk and SBOM as workflow artifacts. Dependencies: cargo audit (known vulnerabilities, unsound code, yanked versions) and cargo deny ( deny.toml : permissive licenses only, crates from crates.io only, two versions of one crate reported) run in every crate's ci.sh, locally and on every CI run. vpsfort's workflow also enforces on the runner's own kernel with the real nft, as root (tests/real_nft.rs, and the installed daemon in enforce mode: a ban, the table deleted and rebuilt, an unban); the other enforcement tests use a stand-in nft. Fedora and RHEL: vpsfort's package_manager = "dnf" (its -dnf config templates, the .rpm's default on a host with dnf) reads rpm's database and asks dnf for pending updates instead of dpkg and apt; with firewalld as the firewall. Tried on a Fedora 44 server, step by step in vpsfort/TESTING-fedora.md ; the results are in vpsfort's README, "Verified on the servers". From a checkout: each crate has a deploy/ directory: a deploy.sh that runs ci.sh, builds the binary and copies everything to a host over SSH, and an install.sh to run there as root. It also holds the systemd units, logrotate files and config templates. scripts/bundle.sh builds the release bundle locally. vpsfort ships config templates for four roles: vpsfort.toml (XMPP server), vpsfort-standalone.toml (a host with SSH and UFW only, e.g. a VPN server), vpsfort-tg.toml (Telegram relay node) and vpsfort-desktop.toml (a Linux desktop or laptop), each also as a -dnf variant for Fedora and RHEL. The templates use placeholder names and addresses (example.org, documentation ranges). Replace them, and the allowlist entries, with your own before deploying. Start in mode = "shadow", review the decisions, then switch to "enforce". SSH hardening: hardening/harden-vps.sh, run from your laptop, turns SSH on a VPS (Debian/Ubuntu or Fedora/RHEL-like) into the gateway layout vpsfort's SSH audit checks: one key-only user forced into su or sftp, keys in a root-owned file, su limited by pam_wheel. It takes over a server hardened partly by hand too (-g keeps its user, --su works without root login or sudo). It tests the new login before it commits and rolls back otherwise; hardening/harden-vps.sh --help lists the options.

40.body: UFW logs blocked packets at most about 3 lines a minute for the whole host (ufw logging low: --limit 3/min), so most scans never reach vpsfort: the Sep–Oct month's 141,772 UFW lines are exactly that limit. With [ports] kernel_tripwires = true (the default) and the nftables backend in enforce mode, vpsfort's own table logs tripwire hits itself: What: a new TCP connection (ct state new) to this host (fib daddr type local: not what it forwards, such as a VPN server's clients reaching mail servers elsewhere) on a TCP tripwire port nothing listens on. A port something listens on (on an address other than loopback: a local exim on 127.0.0.1:25 leaves port 25 closed from outside) is taken out, checked every 30 seconds: a mail server started on 25 later stops it within that time. Honeypot ports are taken out too. With Docker's userland proxy disabled ("userland-proxy": false), a published port has no listener: keep such ports out of tripwire. How much: the first such connection per source address every 10 minutes (dynamic sets tripseen4/tripseen6), at most kernel_tripwire_rate (60/minute) for the whole host. A flood of forged SYNs from random addresses can't produce more than that. Where: in the bans chain after the drops (banned, blocklisted and allowlisted sources aren't logged), with the prefix [VPSFORT BLOCK] UFW-format lines are read with, so a hit is a fw_tripwire event like UFW's. When UFW logs the same SYN too, it counts once. Its source address may be forged just the same, and is judged the same way: never against an address that logged in within trust_ttl, and shared with peers as forgeable evidence. Needs [sources] ufw (the kernel log), and an nft and kernel with fib and dynamic sets (Debian 13, Ubuntu 22.04). The rules are loaded on their own after the table: where they are rejected, vpsfort runs without them and raises a warning; install.sh says so in its dry run (print-nft prints them, print-nft --no-tripwires leaves them out). Not with the ufw or iptables backends, nor in shadow mode.
40.title: Kernel tripwires

41.body:
A blocked SYN names any source address its sender wants, and a forged tripwire hit can get an outsider banned for an hour (see "Forged sources"). [ports] honeypot = ["2323/tcp", "5900/tcp"] makes vpsfort listen on those ports itself, never send a byte, and close every connection after reading what the sender says first. A connection is only accepted after the TCP handshake, which a forged address can't complete (the SYN-ACK goes to the real owner), so a hit scores tripwire_connect (100, a ban) and is shared with peers as evidence they apply even to their own logged-in users. Scanners that complete connections (Mirai and its kind on 23/2323, nmap -sT) are caught for certain; SYN scanners (masscan, zmap) never complete one and still show up only as blocked SYNs. What they sent: honeypot_capture = 512 (bytes; the default) keeps the first bytes of each connection, waited for up to 3 seconds: a Telnet login (root
1234
), an HTTP request, a protocol banner. They go into the ban's evidence, the cluster's shared evidence and the abuse report as one line of plain ASCII (sent 14 bytes: "root
1234
"; control characters and bytes outside ASCII as \xNN, cut at 120 characters), so an abuse desk sees what the scanner was after and not just that it connected. Sources that send nothing (they wait for a banner) show as sent nothing. honeypot_capture = 0 closes every connection at once without reading, as before; at most 4096. At most 64 connections are read at a time; beyond that, and for a source's repeat connections within the minute, the connection is closed at once. With any honeypot port set, fw_tripwire (a blocked SYN to a tripwire port) scores 50 instead of 100 unless [scoring.weights] sets it: two such hits within minutes ban, one doesn't. Open the ports in the firewall (ufw allow 2323/tcp), and leave them out of tripwire (a port with a listener can't trip anyway). TCP only. A port something else listens on is reported at startup (high system alert) and skipped. A logged-in address (a carrier NAT neighbour) is still excused, as for blocked SYNs. Each source counts once a minute per port, and a banned one can't connect any more. The Exposure tab lists them as honeypots (magenta; red when the firewall blocks one: it catches nothing then), vpsfort status and the digest name them, and they never make a new or gone listener alert.
41.title: Honeypot ports

42.body:
Account names attackers guess but nobody here uses are tripwires too. One login attempt on one is an immediate ban: [canary]
xmpp = ["test", "info", "support", "root", "administrator", "webmaster", "guest", "demo"]
ssh = ["*"] # key-only server with a single user: every other name is a probe
except = ["admin", "<gateway user>"] # real accounts are never canaries, whatever the lists say No accounts to create. ejabberd logs Failed c2s … authentication for test@…: Invalid username or password for a non-existent account exactly as for a wrong password, and sshd logs Invalid user / User root from … not allowed because not listed in AllowUsers. If in-band registration is open, a registration of a canary name also trips. The account would still be created, though, so keep registration closed or create the canary accounts yourself with long random passwords to reserve the names. A successful login to a canary (e.g. an account you forgot existed) is a critical compromise alert, and the address earns no trust. Your own mistakes (a typo from an allowlisted address, or from one that recently logged in to the same service) raise a "protected address" alert instead of a ban. A login never excuses a canary name. It does excuse blocked packets from that address, tripwire ports and port scans included, whatever service it logged in to: one forged SYN names any source address, and a carrier NAT may share one with others. Trust from a login is per service ([allowlist] trust_ttl, default 24 h after the last login): an XMPP login excuses that address's XMPP reconnects and typos, not SSH guessing or peers' reports, so one account (or a shared carrier NAT) can't shield an attacker. It is not shared with cluster peers, and what it excuses isn't reported to them either. A peer's ban or report that rests on blocked packets alone isn't applied to an address that logged in here within trust_ttl. An XMPP login earns trust only on a client connection vpsfort saw open (5222/5223): one it can't tie to its connection (a web client over BOSH or WebSocket, or a forged log line) counts for the account and its alerts, but protects nothing. Nextcloud and ownCloud: nextcloud = [...] covers Nextcloud AIO and the apps nextcloud and owncloud ([sources] apps), whose failed logins become nc_canary (100 points) like AIO's. Don't list admin: it's AIO's initial admin account, and often ownCloud's. Expect few hits. In the Sep–Oct month nobody guessed SSH user names at all, and all 8 failed XMPP logins were real users with expired tokens. Canaries are cheap insurance for the day someone starts. Your own account must not be a canary. With ssh = ["*"], a gateway user missing from except bans the admin's address at the next login and raises the critical alert (seen on a real node: the admin then needed the provider's console). So vpsfort canary-check lists the accounts that can log in over SSH on this host (a login shell in /etc/passwd, or an authorized_keys file; not a shell-less system account that only shares a login account's home, as Fedora's operator shares /root) that the canary list matches, with the except line to add; the installers (install.sh, the package) run it after the config check and after the restart and print a loud warning to fix it while the SSH session is still open; the daemon checks at start and daily (a high system alert); and the "LOGGED IN to canary account" alert says when the account exists here and can log in, with the fix, instead of only "lock it".
42.title: Canary accounts

43.body: [sources] privilege = true (the default) follows su and sudo (journal identifiers su, sudo; only from /usr/bin/su and /usr/bin/sudo, or as root: any user can log a line tagged su): line alert FAILED SU (to root) gateway on pts/0, gateway : 3 incorrect password attempts ; ..., pam_unix(sudo:auth): authentication failure, user NOT in sudoers high , compromise topic: if it wasn't you, someone has that account and is trying for root. Repeats by the same user within 10 minutes, whatever account they try, are counted into the next one (one user trying every account can't use up the hour's messages). sudo's line holds the directory and command the user chose: one with two USER= names the target ? a switch within 30 minutes after failures warning: su to root by gateway succeeded after 2 failed attempts any other switch info, on record (TUI, actions log), not sent Each alert names the account's latest SSH login, with its place: (gateway's last SSH login: 13.46.43.31 (Ukraine / ...), 2m ago). Where root is reached only through one SSH account and su, a failed su is the moment someone holding that account's key tries the second factor. The Sep–Oct month's export of sshd's unit had 5 failed and 26 successful su to root.

43.title: su and sudo

44.body: [sources] pam = true and audit = true (the defaults) report what logins and account changes leave in PAM's, the account tools' and the audit log's lines (src/parse/auth.rs): line what happens a failed login at the console, a desktop or its screen locker, polkit (pkexec, run0) or the web console (Cockpit): pam_unix(login:auth): authentication failure; ... tty=/dev/tty1 ... user=root, audit USER_AUTH ... res=failed high , compromise topic: login as root on tty1 failed (login) - if it wasn't you, someone is trying root's password. Counted per service and who asked (polkit's user) or where (the terminal), one message per 10 minutes, the next one with the count; PAM's line and its audit record are one failure a failed login PAM logs from an address on the internet, at a service with no parser of its own (vsftpd, Cockpit, xrdp, ...) pam_auth_fail, 25 points: five strikes ban, as for SSH. Its account is <service>:<user> the same from no address or a private one, at any other service info, on record only session opened at the console or a desktop, audit USER_LOGIN on a tty warning: root logged in at the console or a desktop (login) (Cockpit's: info) pam_faillock/pam_tally2 locked an account, audit ANOM_LOGIN_FAILURES warning: account root locked after repeated failed logins a changed password (pam_unix(passwd:chauthtok): password changed for root, usermod -p, audit USER_CHAUTHTOK) high for root (one per minute), warning for others (one per account and hour: any user can change their own password every minute), integrity topic a new account (useradd, audit ADD_USER) high for a person's account (UID 1000 and up, or a login shell) and for a second UID 0; a package's own system account is on record only added to an admin group (root, sudo, wheel, admin, adm, docker, lxd, incus-admin, libvirt, disk, shadow) by useradd -G, usermod -aG, gpasswd, audit GRP_MGMT high : its members are admins or can become root; other groups on record only a UID changed to 0, a shell changed from nologin to one that logs in high ; other changes of the account tools: info, or warning for a deleted account auditd stopped (audit SERVICE_STOP unit=auditd, DAEMON_END) / aborted / auditing switched off (auditctl -e 0: CONFIG_CHANGE audit_enabled=0) warning / high / high : nothing is recorded until it runs again a rule of yours fired whose key is in audit_keys (-w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity, audit_keys = ["identity"], "*" for any key) warning: audit rule identity: vim (/usr/bin/vim.basic) as uid 0 by gateway (auid 1000) on pts0, one per key per 10 minutes. Fields are read only where the record has them, never from inside a quoted value: a program named 'key=x', or an account typed as 'addr=203.0.113.9', can't hide a rule's key or name another address Whose lines: any local user can log a line saying pam_unix(login:auth): authentication failure or tagged useradd. PAM's and the account tools' lines count only from programs running as root, or from the set-uid programs the system installs (passwd, chsh, chfn, newgrp, gpasswd, pkexec, polkit's helper, run0). Audit records come only from the kernel and from programs allowed to write them (CAP_AUDIT_WRITE): journald's own (_TRANSPORT=audit), the kernel's log, or auditd's file. sshd's, su's and sudo's lines stay with their own parsers (sshd's lockouts are read here too). Typed names: the user name of a failed login is whatever someone typed, and comes last in PAM's line: a line naming more than one rhost= names no address (from an unclear address), and scores nothing. The audit library writes odd names in hex (acct=726F6F7420...), which are decoded and cleaned. Where: PAM's and the account tools' lines through journalctl matches on their syslog facilities (SYSLOG_FACILITY=10 authpriv, 4 auth); audit records through _TRANSPORT=audit. Where journald doesn't read the audit log (Audit=no, or journald's audit socket off), set audit_log = "/var/log/audit/audit.log": vpsfort then follows auditd's file instead, the journal's copies are left out, and auditd's own stop and abort records are there too. Without auditd, the kernel writes audit records to its own log, which vpsfort reads with ufw or oom on. Not scored twice: failed logins at Dovecot (dovecot) and Postfix's SASL (smtp, smtps, submission) through PAM aren't scored when that app is in [sources] apps, which scores its own lines. Alerts that PAM's line and the audit record both make (the same failure, password, account or group change) are one alert: they share a key, and the second within a minute says nothing.
44.breadcrumbs: vpsfort: the daemon » PAM, account changes and auditd
44.title: PAM, account changes and auditd

45.body: vpsfort is made for servers, but half of it watches the machine itself, and that half is as useful on a Linux desktop: deploy/vpsfort-desktop.toml (sudo ./install.sh --template desktop; Fedora: desktop-dnf) turns it on and leaves the firewall alone. Behind a home router nothing reaches a desktop from the internet, so there is nobody to score or ban. On: new or changed crontabs, timers and their scripts, SSH keys, sudoers, PAM, systemd units, /usr/local/bin ("Cron watch"); package programs and libraries against the package database, new set-uid programs ("Package and set-uid check"); programs running from /tmp, /dev/shm, memory or a deleted file, and shells or network tools talking out ("Process watch"); failed su, sudo, polkit and console or screen-lock logins, new accounts and admins, changed passwords ("su and sudo", "PAM, account changes and auditd"); pending security updates; low disk space and memory. With ClamAV or YARA installed, [antivirus] scan_changed scans every changed file ("Scans of changed files"). Off: blocking (mode = "shadow"), blocklist feeds, the cluster, the exposure watch (desktop apps open and close listeners all day), quiet-log warnings (a laptop sleeps), the digest. SSH reachable from the internet (a forwarded port, a public address): then it is a server for that port. Set mode = "enforce", add your SSH names' canaries and the SSH rate limit from vpsfort-standalone.toml, and allowlist where you log in from. Messages: alerts are in the journal (journalctl -u vpsfort), the actions log and vpsfort tui. For a message on your phone, a copy bot (XMPP client bot, Telegram, mail, Signal, Matrix) with [notify] xmpp = false ("Deployment layouts"; deploy/vpsfort-desktop.toml names the XMPP client bot's lines). A failed sudo is a high alert even when it is your own typo: it says "if it wasn't you". What a desktop does differently, and how the profile takes it: on a desktop would be the profile every new app, game or update opens new outbound connections a warning for each new (program, port) pair [procwatch] new_outbound = false: only shells and network tools talking out, and the ports miners and reverse shells use (always high) AppImages run from /tmp/.mount_* "runs from a temporary directory" (high) allow_appimages = true: not when the program is on the FUSE mount the AppImage made; a program in a directory merely named so still is a Snap or Flatpak app updated while it runs runs from a deleted file "its program file was deleted" /snap and Flatpak's /app count like /usr (on servers too) snapd writes units and timers (snap-*.mount, snap.*.service) at every refresh a high integrity alert each time [cron] exclude leaves snap-* and snap.* in /etc/systemd/system out. An intruder can hide a unit by naming it so: without snaps, delete those lines browsers talk to hundreds of servers the usual advice is to ignore them by name nothing by name: ignore_processes would also let a dropper that calls itself firefox run from /tmp unreported. Their connections are covered by new_outbound = false Flatpak's and Snap's own files (/var/lib/flatpak, /snap) are outside what the package check and the set-uid search read. ignore_ports (remote ports a game uses, say) never hides a shell's or network tool's connection: a reverse shell on port 443 is still one.
45.breadcrumbs: vpsfort: the daemon » Desktops and laptops
45.title: Desktops and laptops

46.body: Every [exposure] interval (60 s), the daemon: reads listening sockets straight from /proc/net/{tcp,udp}{,6} (no ss subprocess) and maps them to processes through /proc/<pid>/fd; reads what filters incoming traffic, and the rules that let traffic in from anywhere : ufw , when it is active (ufw status); else firewalld , when it runs: its zones (firewall-cmd --list-all-zones, re-read every 5 minutes or when a file in /etc/firewalld changes, as firewall-cmd is a Python program talking over D-Bus), with the ports of the services they name read from firewalld's own service files (/etc/firewalld/services, then /usr/lib/firewalld/services; includes followed). The default zone and zones with an interface other than loopback, container bridges and tunnels let in from anywhere: their ports, services, protocols (every port of one), a target of ACCEPT (every port), and rich rules that accept (with limit value=: rate-limited). Zones bound to sources, and rich rules naming a source, let in from those only. vpsfort's own zone holds banned sources and opens nothing; else iptables : the filter table's INPUT chain for IPv4 and IPv6 (iptables -S, ip6tables -S, the programs set in [enforce]), followed like the kernel does: rules in order, jumps into chains of their own, the chain's policy. Rules for some sources only (-s, --match-set), for loopback or container/tunnel interfaces, for states other than NEW, and for source ports don't count; limit, hashlimit, recent and connlimit rules mark the port as rate-limited. A match it doesn't know makes an ACCEPT count and a DROP not, so exposure is over- rather than under-reported. iptables counts as a firewall only if INPUT drops by default or something it reaches drops for everyone: fail2ban's per-address rejects alone don't make one. A socket on [::] takes IPv4 connections too, so it is reachable when either family lets it in (e.g. policy ACCEPT (IPv6) when only IPv4 is filtered); else nftables chains of their own on the input hook (other than the filter tables iptables-nft keeps for iptables), read as nft -j prints them (src/nftrules.rs): the base chains in priority order and the chains they jump to, rules in order (tcp dport and sets, meta l4proto, ct state, iifname, ip saddr for source-limited rules, verdict maps, limit for rate-limited), the chain's policy; an accept ends one base chain only, so a listener is reachable when no base chain drops it. A match this reader doesn't know makes an accept count and a drop not, as with iptables; a chain whose name nft can't be handed safely counts as filtering and is passed through. Before 2026-11-03 these chains were noticed, not read ("nftables, rules not read" in an older daemon's report); else no firewall : the TUI's Exposure tab says so in a red box above the list, its tab and the Overview's Health panel show it, vpsfort status and the daily digest say it too; classifies every listener: state meaning local only bound to loopback or a private address (e.g. 127.0.0.53:53, the Docker bridge) blocked by ufw / firewalld / iptables public address, but the firewall doesn't let new connections in (e.g. Erlang's epmd) allowed by ufw / firewalld / iptables from some sources only closed to the internet, open to the addresses some rules name (ALLOW 7946/tcp from 3 sources: the cluster port, open to the peers; firewalld: ALLOW 6379/tcp (work) from 10.0.0.0/8); not exposed, so no new/gone alerts allowed by ufw / firewalld / iptables public and let in: really exposed allowed by ufw / firewalld / iptables, rate-limited let in by a ufw LIMIT rule (an address opening 6 connections in 30 seconds is dropped), a firewalld rich rule with limit value=, or by iptables past a limit, hashlimit, recent or connlimit rule published by docker docker-proxy listener: reachable regardless of ufw or the INPUT chain ; the tab shows the ufw rule allowing it, or none: containers blocked when there is none: connections from the internet are DNATed by Docker before ufw sees them, but a container calling the host's public address (Nextcloud's admin check of its Talk server, or anything using the public domain name) reaches docker-proxy through the INPUT chain, which ufw then blocks — the check hangs and fails no firewall public, and nothing filters incoming traffic honeypot one of vpsfort's own [ports] honeypot listeners: exposed on purpose, never alerted about; "blocked by ufw" means it catches nothing public, nftables rules not read a report from a daemon older than 2026-11-03: nftables rules of their own decided, unread The first scan is learned silently as the baseline (one info alert lists it). After that it alerts, under the exposure notification topic: New internet-facing listener: e.g. an admin panel published on 0.0.0.0 by accident. It must be seen in 2 consecutive scans. Listener gone: a service stopped or crashed. It must be missing from 3 consecutive scans, so restarts don't flap. Dead firewall rule: ufw allows a single port from anywhere, but nothing listens on it publicly (with firewalld: a single port in a zone's ports, not a service: Fedora's dhcpv6-client would always count). That's exactly the 53/udp, 853/udp and 51821/tcp rules found by hand on the VPN host. Port ranges such as the TURN/STUN relay ranges (49152:65535/udp and /tcp) are never reported as dead. Sockets opened inside them are marked dynamic : TURN servers open one per call participant, and Linux client sockets use that range too. They're listed in the TUI but never trigger new/gone alerts. Listeners with their own single-port rule, like TURNS on 5349/tcp, are still tracked normally. ufw inactive , with nothing else filtering (iptables rules of your own count). When what filters changes (ufw enabled or disabled, firewalld started or stopped, or iptables or firewalld rules read for the first time after an upgrade), the baseline is learned again, with one info alert, rather than every listener the change hid or opened reported as gone or new. A report from a daemon older than the iptables reading shows firewall not checked rather than no firewall until the daemon is restarted. A view from outside ([exposure] peer_probe = true, off by default): hourly, the node asks its direct cluster peers (a probes fact, not forwarded) to try its public TCP ports (at most 32: the listeners the watch doesn't see as local only), as the internet would, with one connection each and nothing sent; the peers answer with what they could reach. A port the firewall here should block that a peer reaches is a high system alert (a rule the watch didn't read, or something other than the firewall filtering that port), and a port open here that no peer reaches an info once a week (a provider's firewall in front of the host, or the peer's route). status and the digest show the latest answer. The peers' attempts never score here: cluster peers are protected addresses. Needs probes in [cluster] share and accept on every node. Use [exposure] ignore = ["5000/tcp"] for ports that are exposed by design through another path. The TUI's Exposure tab (6) and vpsfort status show the current table; the tab also names the firewall rule letting each listener in, the first that matches as the firewall applies them (ufw's ALLOW 5222:5223/tcp, LIMIT 9843/tcp; firewalld's ALLOW ssh (public), LIMIT rich rule 5222/tcp (public), ALLOW target ACCEPT (trusted); iptables' ACCEPT 80,443/tcp, ACCEPT 22/tcp via ssh-guard, policy ACCEPT). Dead rules are ufw's and firewalld's only. Weekly reboot / apt upgrades: for startup_grace (15 min) after vpsfort starts, no new/gone listener alerts are raised, because Docker containers come up after vpsfort. A listener must be missing from gone_after_scans (5) consecutive scans before it's reported as gone, so a service restarted by an upgrade doesn't trigger alerts. If Docker's userland proxy is disabled ("userland-proxy": false), published ports have no docker-proxy listener. Their ufw ALLOW rules would then be reported as dead; add those ports to ignore.
46.title: Exposure watch

47.body: Scheduled tasks are the classic way for an intruder to stay on a server after a reboot or a password change. Every [cron] interval (1 min), and within seconds of a change where the kernel can say so (inotify on the watched directories, src/inotify.rs: so a change undone within the minute is still seen, and an alert comes right after the write; the minute scan stays as the fallback, and the start line says how many directories are watched), vpsfort reads: crontabs: /etc/crontab, /etc/anacrontab, /etc/cron.d/*, and every user's crontab in /var/spool/cron/crontabs/ (what crontab -l shows). Each task line counts on its own; comments don't, so the header crontab -e rewrites is ignored. VAR=value lines count too, because changing PATH changes what runs; run-parts directories: /etc/cron.{hourly,daily,weekly,monthly,yearly}. Each file is a task, fingerprinted by content (SHA-256); enabled systemd timers in /etc/systemd/system/timers.target.wants/, cron's modern sibling; scripts that crontab lines run, e.g. /usr/local/bin/av_scan.sh, bash /opt/job.sh or cd /opt/app && ./run.sh, also behind sudo -u, flock, timeout, env, nice/ionice. Redirect targets, arguments and inline code (sh -c '...') are not scripts. Programs in the system's package directories (/usr/bin, /usr/lib, ...) are skipped; other files ([cron] files), the usual ways back in besides cron: authorized_keys of root and every user in /home, and /etc/ssh/authorized_keys/* (AuthorizedKeysFile /etc/ssh/authorized_keys/%u, as on the hardened hosts), /etc/sudoers(.d), /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group, sshd_config(.d), PAM (/etc/pam.d/*: one line there lets anyone in), apt's hooks (/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/*, DPkg::Post-Invoke runs as root at every package change) and dnf's actions (/etc/dnf/plugins/post-transaction-actions.d/*, /etc/dnf/libdnf5-plugins/actions.d/*), /etc/update-motd.d/* (run as root at every login), /etc/ld.so.preload, /etc/ld.so.conf.d/*, /etc/rc.local, /etc/profile.d/*, /etc/environment, /etc/bash.bashrc, root's .bashrc and .profile, module loading and device rules (/etc/modules-load.d/*, /etc/modprobe.d/*, /etc/udev/rules.d/*), /etc/init.d/*, programs installed by hand (/usr/local/bin/*, /usr/local/sbin/*: the SSH gateway's shell, vpsfort itself), and systemd units (/etc/systemd/system/*, enabled ones in *.wants/, and drop-in overrides in *.d/*.conf, which can replace a service's ExecStart); also user-level units and autostart entries (/etc/systemd/user, ~/.config/systemd/user, /etc/xdg/autostart, ~/.config/autostart), every user's shell start-up files in /home (.bashrc, .profile, .zshrc, ...) and what sshd runs at each login (/etc/ssh/sshrc, ~/.ssh/rc), at-jobs (/var/spool/cron/atjobs, /var/spool/at) and the cron.allow/at.allow files, name resolution and the host's identity (/etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/nsswitch.conf, resolved.conf, the SSH host keys, hosts.allow/hosts.deny), the scripts the network stack runs as root when a link comes up (NetworkManager's dispatcher.d, ifupdown's if-*.d, dhclient's hooks), vpsfort's own /etc/vpsfort, the loader's ld.so.conf, sysctl.conf and sysctl.d, fstab, pam.conf and security/access.conf, polkit's rules.d, logrotate's configuration (its postrotate scripts run as root), the package sources and their keys (apt/sources.list*, apt/trusted.gpg.d, yum.repos.d, pki/rpm-gpg), CA certificates added by hand (/usr/local/share/ca-certificates, pki/ca-trust/source/anchors), Docker's daemon.json and WireGuard's configs (their PostUp lines run as root). The desktop profile leaves /etc/resolv.conf out, which Wi-Fi and DHCP rewrite. Only fingerprints are kept, never contents (so no password hashes in alerts or the state file). A file root owns is hashed whole (up to 1 GB, so a change deep inside a large program shows); anyone else's only its first 16 MB, plus its size, as its owner could make it huge and change it every minute. Masked units (symlinks to /dev/null) are recorded as such. Installers announce their files: vpsfort expect-change PATH=SOURCE... records the content PATH is about to get (in expected-changes next to the state file, kept 7 days), and a change to exactly that content is logged as info instead of alerted. install.sh does this for vpsfort's binaries, scripts and units before it replaces them, and the bots' and vpsfort-web's installers for their units, and for /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group and /etc/gshadow right after they create (or rename) their system user (expect-change PATH: its content as it is now); any other content still raises the usual alert. Files of a pattern added later (or by the upgrade that introduced file watching) are learned silently, and files of a removed pattern are forgotten instead of reported as removed. A file two patterns reach under different names is watched once, under the first pattern's: on Fedora 42 and later /usr/local/sbin is a link to /usr/local/bin, and vpsfort's binary would otherwise be two alerts at every upgrade, the second unannounced. Editor swap files, .dpkg-old leftovers and dotfiles (.placeholder) are ignored; cron and run-parts don't run them either. Any user can write their own crontab, so its lines are stripped of control characters, lines are capped at 1,000 characters, and a crontab of more than 500 lines is watched as one fingerprint. Programs it names are only opened if they are regular files (a named pipe would otherwise hang the scan). Learn period: everything present during the first learn (1 day) is accepted. Changes in that time are only written to the actions log. After that, every change is reported once under the integrity admin topic and becomes the new normal: change severity new or changed task, crontab line or script high, with "the server may be compromised" if nobody here made it the same, but the file is a package's and identical to what it installed (the MD5 dpkg recorded, or rpm's digest) warning, "installed by package man-db, unmodified" a task or line removed (e.g. someone disabling the virus scan) warning A user's own changes have an hourly budget: a change any local account could have made (it owns the file, the link to it, or a directory above it: its crontab, its scripts, its authorized_keys) counts against that account. After 5 such alerts in an hour, the rest of the hour's are only logged (the TUI's Alerts tab, the actions log), and one more alert says so; so one account changing its crontab every minute can't use up the hour's integrity messages. What only root can change is never held back. Process watch alerts share the same budget, by the user a process runs as. Package lookups read dpkg's database (/var/lib/dpkg/info/*.list, *.md5sums, status) line by line, and only for files that changed. Running dpkg-query -S / dpkg --verify instead would load every package's file list and hash whole packages, all counted against vpsfort's memory limit. With package_manager = "dnf", rpm's database (SQLite, not text) is asked instead: rpm -qf for the owners of the changed files, then rpm -q for those packages' file digests; %config files count as dpkg's conffiles do. New and changed lines are listed in the alert (+ ... / - ...). So your own edits produce a message too, which confirms the watch works. vpsfort integrity prints everything that is watched, with package origins.
47.title: Cron watch

48.body: With [antivirus] enabled = true, vpsfort reads the log of scheduled ClamAV scans (checked every minute) and reports, under the integrity topic: infected files (critical): each path: Signature FOUND is listed; a scan that didn't finish (high): no summary written, or an exit code beyond 2. Exit 137 means it was killed, usually out of memory (clamscan loads ~1-1.5 GB of signatures); no finished scan for stale_after (warning, daily, 36 h by default): the timer/cron job stopped running or keeps dying; signatures older than 7 days (warning): freshclam isn't working. Clean scans are only logged ("virus scan finished ...: 2813 files, nothing found"), and vpsfort status shows the last one. Only runs newer than the last reported one count. On the first read of an existing log, only its newest run is news. install.sh ships the scan as vpsfort-avscan.timer (daily at 02:30 ± 10 min; Persistent=true catches up after a reboot). It runs /usr/local/sbin/vpsfort-avscan, which: uses clamdscan when clamd runs (clamav-daemon, or Fedora's clamd@scan), otherwise clamscan; runs at nice 19 with idle I/O, and with OOMScoreAdjust=900, so if memory runs out the scan dies (and is reported) rather than ejabberd or a database; wraps each run in marker lines with UTC times and the exit code, and indents the scanner's output, so a file name with line breaks can't forge a marker. Scan paths and excludes are in /etc/default/vpsfort-avscan (/etc/vpsfort/yara, the YARA rules, is skipped by default: see "Scans of changed files"). The timer is enabled only when [antivirus] is enabled and ClamAV is installed. Plain clamscan --stdout output appended by your own job also works: point log at it (dates are read as UTC).

49.body:
[antivirus] scan_changed scans every file the integrity watches report new or changed, right after the report, with "clamav", "yara" or "both" ("none", the default: no scans). Independent of enabled (the scheduled scans' log): [antivirus]
scan_changed = "both"
yara_rules = ["/etc/vpsfort/yara"] # .yar/.yara files, directories of them, or one compiled .yarc What is scanned: new or changed crontabs, scheduled tasks and the scripts they run (a script that comes with a new crontab line too), files of [cron] files (SSH keys, sudoers, systemd units, /usr/local/bin, ...), package files that differ from what the package manager installed, new or changed set-uid programs, and programs running from a temporary or deleted file (as they run: /proc/<pid>/exe). Not what vpsfort's own installer announced. A file reported again (a change every minute) is scanned again; up to 200 files go to one scan, up to 1,000 wait (more are dropped), and the queue isn't kept across restarts. A local user's own files (their crontab and the scripts its new lines run, files they can change, their processes) go to at most 20 scans an hour: any account can change its files every minute, and each scan may load a gigabyte of signatures. What it reports: each infected file is a high integrity alert, malware in /tmp/.x/kworker: ClamAV: Unix.Trojan.Mirai-1; YARA: SUSP_ELF_Miner (it was scanned because: process kworker (pid 4242, ...) runs from a temporary directory ...), once a day for the same file and finding. One in a local user's own file counts against that user's hourly budget of 5 alerts (see "Cron watch"), so a pile of test signatures can't flood the admins; every hit stays on record. A scanner that fails (not installed, rules that don't compile, out of time) is a warning, once a day. Each scan is on record (TUI, actions log), not sent: scanned 3 of 3 changed files with ClamAV (clamd) and YARA (2 rule files): nothing found, with every file's result. ClamAV: while clamd runs (its socket clamd_socket, /run/clamav/clamd.ctl; Fedora's is /run/clamd.scan/clamd.sock), files go to it with clamdscan --fdpass: clamd keeps its signatures loaded, and reads root's files through the descriptors vpsfort passes. Otherwise clamscan runs, loading its signatures for each scan (1-1.5 GB, half a minute and more). clamdscan reads clamd's configuration from its own default place (clamd_config names another); Fedora's clamd reads /etc/clamd.d/scan.conf, which its clamdscan isn't told about, so that file is used when it is there and the default isn't (the scan script does the same). YARA: yara --scan-list with every rule file, each in a namespace of its own (the same rule name in two files is no error), or one compiled file (yarac rules.yar rules.yarc, then yara_rules = ["/etc/vpsfort/rules.yarc"]: much faster with large rule sets). Rule sets decide the alerts: start with a curated one (e.g. YARA Forge's core set), not every community rule (some flag admin tools). The rule files are malware fragments by design: ClamAV flags them (a Forge file as Html.Downloader.Satan), and YARA would match its own strings, so the files of yara_rules are never scanned here, and the nightly scan skips /etc/vpsfort/yara (AVSCAN_EXCLUDE; keep the rules there, or add their place to it). YARA rules also work inside ClamAV: .yar files in ClamAV's database directory (/var/lib/clamav) are used by clamscan and clamd, a hit reads YARA.Rule_Name.UNOFFICIAL (ClamAV supports part of YARA: no modules). Memory: vpsfort's unit is limited to 128 MB, which clamscan and large YARA rule sets exceed. They run as a transient service of their own (systemd_run, /usr/bin/systemd-run --wait --pipe), with MemoryMax=scan_memory (2G), RuntimeMaxSec=scan_timeout (30 min), nice 10 and idle I/O; systemd_run = "" runs them inside vpsfort's limit (small YARA rule sets only). clamdscan itself needs little. Hostile names: only regular files are scanned, up to scan_max_mb (100 MB): not devices (/dev/zero, /dev/random, /dev/urandom, or links to them, whose reads never end), named pipes or sockets. Each file is checked again right before each scanner reads it, so one swapped for such a link while ClamAV ran isn't handed to YARA. The scanners open the files by name themselves, so a swap in the moment between the check and their reading can't be ruled out: scan_timeout then ends the scan, reported as a failed scanner. Names with control characters are not scanned (they would break the scanners' file lists; the scan's record says so). Results are matched to the names vpsfort asked about, so a file named x: Eicar FOUND can't report another one.

50.body: Weekly ([verify] interval, the first pass a quarter of an hour after the first start), vpsfort checks what a rootkit replaces: Package files: every program and library a package installed under dirs (/usr/bin, /usr/sbin, /usr/lib, /usr/libexec, and their pre-merged-/usr aliases; not /usr/lib/firmware) is hashed and compared with the MD5 dpkg recorded (/var/lib/dpkg/info/*.md5sums), like debsums. With package_manager = "dnf": with the digest rpm recorded (SHA-256 on current Fedora and RHEL), like rpm -Va, asking rpm -q 25 packages at a time so rpm's lock is never held for long; %config and %ghost files are left out, and a file two architectures' packages share (i686 and x86_64) may match either. Files moved aside with dpkg-divert are left out, and a mismatch is checked again after the pass (an upgrade may have run meanwhile). New mismatches are high ("reinstall: apt install --reinstall <package>", or dnf reinstall <package>); the first pass reports what it finds as a warning, once. Set-uid and set-gid programs under suid_roots (/usr, /opt, /home, /root, /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, /srv, /etc, /boot; not /var/lib/docker), seen through init's root (/proc/1/root), since the service's own /tmp is private: learned on the first pass, then a new or changed one is high (a warning if dpkg installed it unmodified), a removed one only logged. Any user can make set-uid files of their own: a pass keeps at most 10,000 owned by root and 1,000 owned by others (hashing only the first MB of those), names at most 20 changes one by one and the rest in one more alert, and says ( high ) how many it left out. Cost: it reads at most max_rate_mb (20) MB a second, and drops what it read from the page cache, which would otherwise count against the service's memory limit. A server's package files are a few GB: some minutes a week. vpsfort status and the TUI's Health panel show the last pass.
50.breadcrumbs: vpsfort: the daemon » Package and set-uid check
50.title: Package and set-uid check

51.body: Every [procwatch] interval (60 s), from /proc: Outbound connections: TCP connections this host opened (to a port not listening here, to a public address), by program and remote port: curl to 443, beam.smp to 5269 (federation). The pairs are learned for learn (3 days); after that a new pair is a warning, once, and becomes normal. A shell or network tool talking out (bash, sh, nc, socat, telnet: a reverse shell) and any connection to a port miners and reverse shells use (suspicious_ports: 3333, 4444, 14444, ...) are high , always. Containers' network namespaces are read too, through one of their processes (/proc/<pid>/net/tcp is that namespace's, socket inodes are global): a connection out of a container is named with the container's id from its cgroup. Programs running from where nothing should run: /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, memory only (memfd:, except runc starting a container), or a program file deleted after start outside the package directories (an upgrade replacing /usr/sbin/sshd is the patch status's business). High , a warning for a process in a container; once a day per program. ignore_processes and ignore_ports leave programs (by /proc/<pid>/comm name) and remote ports out. A process that doesn't run as root counts against its user's hourly budget of 5 alerts, shared with their own crontab and files (see "Cron watch"): the rest of the hour's are only logged, and one more alert says so. Three more baselines , learned for the same learn and then reported once each: kernel modules (/proc/modules; kernel_modules): one loaded that was never seen is high , since a rootkit lives in one (so does a driver an upgrade brings: lsmod, modinfo); the desktop profile turns this off, where every device plugged in loads one. Containers (containers), read from Docker's own files under docker_dir (/var/lib/docker/containers: no docker command, so no Go program inside vpsfort's memory limit): a new container running is a warning, and one that is privileged, on the host's network or PID namespace, mounts /, /etc, /root, the Docker socket and the like, or adds a capability as good as root (SYS_ADMIN, SYS_MODULE, SYS_PTRACE, ...) is high ; a known container that gains such a thing is high too, while a recreated one (an update: new image, same name) is no news. WireGuard peers (wireguard_peers, through wg show all dump, wg): a new peer on an interface is high , a new way into the VPN unless you added it. A WireGuard interface inside a container (wg-easy's) isn't seen, as the container's connections aren't. status shows each baseline's size.
51.title: Process watch

52.body: Every [patches] interval (6 h): pending upgrades (apt-get -s dist-upgrade, a simulation that takes no lock, run in a transient unit of its own with systemd-run so apt's cache isn't charged to vpsfort's memory limit; security ones by name), a newer kernel in /boot than the one running, /run/reboot-required, and programs still running a library or program an upgrade replaced (from /proc/*/maps: they keep the old code until restarted). What needs doing goes into the daily digest's "Needs attention" (3 security updates pending (openssl, libssl3, ...): apt upgrade, kernel 6.12.48+deb13-amd64 is installed but 6.12.9+deb13-amd64 runs: reboot), and vpsfort status and the TUI's Health panel show it. No alerts of its own. apt = false skips apt. Started without systemd (by hand), vpsfort runs apt itself. With package_manager = "dnf", dnf instead: dnf --cacheonly --quiet check-update, then with --security (exit status 100: updates pending), from the metadata dnf-makecache.timer keeps current, in a transient unit with MemoryMax=1G (dnf's metadata is larger than apt's cache); apt = false skips it too. Fedora has no /run/reboot-required: there the newer kernel in /boot and the stale programs say it.
52.title: Patch status

53.body: Every [ssh_audit] interval (1 h, the first five minutes after start) sshd's settings are checked as sshd itself applies them: sshd -T for the global ones, and sshd -T -C user=...,addr=203.0.113.1 for root and the gateway users, so Match blocks count as they do for a login from the internet (a Match Address for the LAN doesn't excuse the internet). The config files are parsed too, Includes in order, to say which file each setting comes from and which lines it overrides: the classic is a cloud image's sshd_config.d/50-cloud-init.conf saying PasswordAuthentication yes in front of sshd_config's own no (the message names both lines, and the fix says to set ssh_pwauth: false for cloud-init, which would otherwise write the file again). When sshd -T fails (no host keys readable, a broken config), the settings come from the files over OpenSSH's defaults and the report says so. Nothing is changed. It reads the files, as sshd will at its next start or reload, not the running daemon: an edit counts as soon as it is saved, so run sshd -t && systemctl reload ssh (sshd on Fedora) before trusting a clean report. A setting written otherwise than sshd shows it is quoted with its line ("LoginGraceTime 600s, written 10m in ..."), and cloud-init's own setting is suggested only where cloud-init is installed. The layout is detected (profile = "auto"), or set: standard (most VPSs): root with a password from the internet (high), passwords accepted at all, naming the accounts that have one (a warning; a note when no allowed account has a password), PAM's keyboard-interactive password prompt counts too, a key first (AuthenticationMethods publickey,password) doesn't; PermitEmptyPasswords, a second uid-0 account, LogLevel too low for vpsfort to see failed logins, StrictModes no, host-based logins, PermitUserEnvironment, GatewayPorts, weak ciphers, MACs and key exchanges, DSA and short RSA host keys, host keys readable by others (Fedora's ssh_keys group is fine), config files and /etc/ssh writable by anyone but root, and every allowed account's key files and .ssh directories writable by others (high for root, or with StrictModes no). Notes, not alerts: X11Forwarding, PermitTunnel, MaxAuthTries above 6, a long LoginGraceTime, PermitRootLogin yes while only keys work, an AuthorizedKeysCommand. hosting panels (cPanel/WHM, Plesk, DirectAdmin, HestiaCP, VestaCP, CyberPanel, aaPanel, ISPConfig, Webmin; found by a file each installs): the same checks, and the fixes say where the panel changes them (cPanel: WHM's SSH Password Authorization Tweak, after adding root's key). gateway (hardening/harden-vps.sh, or the same set up by hand): detected when a user AllowUsers or the su_group names has a ForceCommand, or AllowUsers is set with no root login and pam_wheel limiting su to an existing su_group. On top of the standard checks, each piece of the layout: no root login at all, no passwords (high, not a warning), AllowUsers set and naming no one else, each gateway user's sessions forced into the wrapper, the wrapper root's and not writable by others (nor its directory), running nothing but su and the sftp server, the user's keys in a root-owned file outside its home, each key line starting with restrict, port forwarding only local and only to 127.0.0.1 (PermitOpen), no agent, X11, socket or tun forwarding, a home the user can't write (only ~/xfer), a locked password, not in a sudo group, pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su (the group it names, which must exist and have no other members), root with a password (or the su stage leads nowhere), port 22 (a note). harden-vps.sh's leftovers too: a rollback timer still armed (ssh-harden-rollback-*.timer: the old config comes back when it fires) and backups in /root/ssh-harden-* readable by others. The first reading tells everything at once (an alert when there is a warning or worse; only logged otherwise). Then a new or worse problem is an alert (host integrity topic), with the watched settings that changed since (changed: passwordauthentication: no -> yes); settings that change without a new problem, and problems fixed, are one info message; high problems still open are told again every remind (7 days). The daily digest lists the open warnings and high problems under "Needs attention" and the summary as SSH: gateway (gabc...): no problems; vpsfort status and the TUI's Health panel show the summary. vpsfort ssh-audit (as root, without the daemon) prints every problem with its id and fix (--all with the notes, --json for scripts); ignore = ["x11-forwarding", "gateway-port"] hides problems by id (an id covers its per-user and per-file forms). Changes to the files themselves (sshd_config, key files, the wrapper) are the cron watch's alerts, as before. The kernel's sysctls ([sysctl_audit], hourly, src/sysctlaudit.rs) are checked the same way: forwarding (a note where a VPN, container or bridge interface exists, a warning otherwise), ICMP redirects and source routing, rp_filter, SYN cookies, ASLR (kernel.randomize_va_space, high), kptr_restrict, dmesg_restrict, Yama's ptrace_scope, unprivileged BPF, kexec_load_disabled, SysRq, perf_event_paranoid, unprivileged user namespaces, the protected symlinks, hardlinks, FIFOs and regular files (high for the links), suid_dumpable, the BPF JIT's hardening, userfaultfd, tty line discipline autoloading. The first reading tells everything; then a new or weakened one is an alert with the values that changed, fixed problems and changed values are told, high ones reminded every remind (7 days). vpsfort sysctl-audit prints the problems with the sysctl -w command and the key = value line that keeps the setting after a reboot in /etc/sysctl.d/90-hardening.conf (--all with the notes; ignore = ["kernel.sysrq"] hides a key). The file takes only such lines: a pasted sysctl -w command there is ignored at boot. To apply and keep every fix at once: vpsfort sysctl-audit --all | sed -n 's/^ *fix sysctl -w \([^;]*\);.*/\1/p' | tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/90-hardening.conf && sysctl --system. A sysctl the kernel shows only with CAP_SYS_ADMIN (net.core.bpf_jit_harden) is a note in the daemon's reading, which runs under the unit's capability bound, and is read by the command in a root shell; status, the TUI's Health panel ("Kernel") and the digest carry the summary. A tenth of what Lynis checks, with no benchmark or score.
53.title: SSH audit

54.body:
vpsfort abuse-report turns the bans of a time window into a report for the abuse desks of the networks they came from. It works without the daemon: it reads actions.jsonl and its rotated copies, including the gzipped ones. vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml abuse-report # last 7 days, top 50 sources
vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml abuse-report --since 30d --contacts -o /root/abuse.txt
vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml abuse-report --ip 13.204.36.0/24 --json Per source: first and last time seen, the number of incidents, the activity in plain words ("connection attempts to closed ports of commonly attacked services: TCP/23 (Telnet)", "SSH probing / login attempts"), and up to 25 log lines with full UTC timestamps. With [geo] on, it also gives the country and network owner. A network ban lists the addresses involved and what each did. Bans from now on keep the latest evidence lines of a network's worst members; older network bans recorded only the member addresses. Order: repeat offenders come first. --min-events 3 (the default) leaves out sources with less evidence, such as a single blocked packet. --top 50 is the default; --all lists every source. --contacts: looks up each network's abuse mailbox via RDAP (rdap.org, which forwards to the right registry). It makes about one request per second, with one request covering a whole network. The report is then grouped into one section per mailbox, each starting with a short "Hello, ..." ready to paste into an e-mail. Withheld: account names, except non-existent ones the attacker tried (invalid user oracle); the names of decoy (canary) accounts; internal scores; and bans received from other cluster nodes. Those other nodes have the evidence, so run the report there too, or merge the reports (below). One report for both servers. Each server only has its own evidence; a peer's report is just counts and points. To combine them, export a JSON report on each server without filtering, then merge on one of them: # on the VPN host
vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml abuse-report --json --all --min-events 1 -o /root/abuse-vpn.json
# copy it to the XMPP server, export there too, then merge
vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml abuse-report --json --all --min-events 1 -o /root/abuse-xmpp.json
vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml abuse-report --merge /root/abuse-xmpp.json /root/abuse-vpn.json --contacts -o /root/abuse.txt The merged report has one entry per source: incidents are added up, and every log line says which server it hit ((to 12.37.48.86) connection attempt to closed port TCP/23 (Telnet)). --min-events, --top, --ip and --contacts apply after merging, so a source seen a little on each server still counts in full. The same report given twice (same server and period) is skipped with a warning instead of doubling every count. Weekly, to the admin's phone. vpsfort-abuse-report.timer (Mondays 06:00 UTC, installed and enabled by install.sh) does the above on its own: the VPN server sends its JSON report to its cluster peers with vpsfort cluster-send-report (gzip-compressed, one message over the encrypted cluster link, never stored or forwarded as a fact; the peer writes it to [cluster] inbox, default /var/lib/vpsfort/inbox, mode 0600, and never parses it), and the XMPP server waits for it (up to 15 minutes), merges it with its own and puts the text report in the admin bot's outbox. The bot sends it to the admin as an OMEMO-encrypted file (vpsfort-xmpp-bot's README, "Weekly abuse report"); vpsfort-tg-bot, as a file encrypted to the admin's OpenPGP key. ABUSE_REPORT_ROLE=auto in /etc/default/vpsfort-abuse-report picks the role: relay on a Telegram relay node (below), else merge where a bot's outbox exists ([notify] bot_outbox, else /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/outbox, and [notify] tg_outbox), else send when there are cluster peers, else off; off also turns the timer off. A server without peers merges at once (just its own report). Nothing stays behind: work files are in /run and removed on exit, the peer's report is deleted once merged (an unmerged one after 7 days; on a send node, which never merges, at its next run), and the bot deletes the outbox file once sent. A missing peer report is named in the job's output (journalctl -u vpsfort-abuse-report) and the report then covers the servers it has; add vpsfort-abuse-report.service to [sources] services to be told when the job fails. systemctl start vpsfort-abuse-report # now, as root: on the VPN server first, then the XMPP server
vpsfort cluster-send-report /root/abuse-vpn.json # by hand: to the peers' inbox as abuse-<node>.json.gz --merge reads these gzip files directly. Times are UTC throughout, which is what abuse desks expect. The report doesn't say whether the firewall actually blocked anything, so it is also accurate for a server in shadow mode.
54.title: Abuse reports

55.body: Three operator tools for the days something is being changed on purpose: vpsfort quiet 2h holds the admins' messages back for a while (1 minute to 30 days; vpsfort quiet off ends it early): a planned upgrade or a move that would otherwise flood the channels. Decisions are still made, logged, shown in the TUI and shared with the peers; only the sending waits, and nothing is sent later for the time that passed. By default the topics the host says about itself are held (system, exposure, integrity, digest, protected, false_positive, registration); --topics integrity,exposure names others, and users' own warnings (account_attack, brute_force, compromise, new_network) are never held unless their topics are named. --note "kernel upgrade" goes into the actions log. The window survives a restart of vpsfort (an upgrade restarts it in the middle of one), status shows it, and an info message marks its start and its end. vpsfort explain <address or network> prints everything the daemon knows about one address: its scores and evidence, how many times this network was banned and when last, the bans and operator allowlist entries covering it (a wider network's too), the services it logged in to lately, why it is never banned if so, its place, and the latest decisions and alerts naming it; --json for scripts. vpsfort status --json prints the daemon's whole snapshot the same way (what the TUI and the web console read). vpsfort baseline export FILE writes the learned baselines of the state file (- for stdout): the cron and file fingerprints, the package and set-uid check, the process watch with its modules, containers and WireGuard peers, the exposure listeners, the accounts' networks and providers, and the SSH keys per account. vpsfort baseline import FILE , with vpsfort stopped, writes them into the state file of a reinstalled or cloned host (its own file is kept for everything else), so it starts without the learning day of the cron watch, the three days of the process watch and the week of the accounts, and reports what the first host would have reported. The file holds account names, their networks and the host's file fingerprints: it is written readable by its owner only, and is for your own hosts.

55.title: Quiet windows, explanations and baselines

56.body: (This is about nftables; the iptables, ipset and firewalld backends heal the same way: see "Firewall backends".) On Debian and Ubuntu, /etc/nftables.conf begins with flush ruleset. Any systemctl restart nftables, or a package upgrade that triggers one, silently deletes vpsfort's table and every ban. In enforce mode the daemon checks for the table every 30 s. If it's gone, it recreates it, re-adds all active bans with their remaining time, and raises a high system alert. A single change the firewall program refuses (a ban, unban or allow that nft, ipset, iptables or firewall-cmd fails on: a busy kernel, a set deleted a moment ago, the program missing after an upgrade) is not lost either. The decision stands in the actions log and at the peers; the change itself is kept and tried again at the same 30 s check, bans the start-up restore couldn't put back included. A later decision about the same network replaces a waiting one, and an unban of a ban that never got in has nothing to undo. When a change fails a second time (so for more than 30 s), a high system alert says how many changes wait and what the program said, repeated hourly while it goes on; an info message says when the failures are over. Changes wait for at most 7 days (10,000 at most). vpsfort status, the TUI's Health panel (Enforce), the daily digest's "Needs attention" and the web console show how many wait and how many attempts failed since the start. The state file and the actions log are watched the same way. A state save that fails (the disk full, the file's owner changed by hand) is tried again after 10 minutes instead of an hour, and once saves have failed for an hour a high system alert says so (repeated every 6 hours, an info when they work again): after a restart vpsfort would otherwise lose what it learned since, without anyone knowing. A line that can't be written to the actions log is reported the same way, since the abuse reports and the console's reports rest on that log; the file is opened again for the next line, in case the descriptor is what went bad. vpsfort's own files are checked at start and once a day (vpsfort self-audit prints the same): the cluster key (and its .next/.prev during a rotation), the node key, the XMPP API password file, the journal verification key and the WAF keys must be readable by their owner only; the config (readable by others: a warning, or high when it holds the cluster key inline), the state file and the actions log must not be readable by everyone nor writable by anyone else; /etc/vpsfort, the state directory, the inbox and the feeds', WAF and geo caches must not be writable by others (a planted file there is loaded); the bots' outboxes may be written by their group (root:bot, sticky, by design) but never by everyone; the binary must be root's and not writable by others; and every one of them must belong to the user the daemon runs as. Each problem is a system alert with the mode and the fix, repeated weekly while it stays.
