56.title: Self-healing firewall table

57.body:
[[ratelimit]] entries cap new connections per source address in the kernel, from the first packet, before any score reacts: [[ratelimit]]
ports = ["5222/tcp", "5223/tcp"]
rate = "30/minute" # n/second, n/minute or n/hour
burst = 30 They live in a second chain, rl, at prerouting priority mangle . That's after conntrack, so only new connections count, and still before Docker's DNAT, so Docker-published ports are limited too; UFW's limit rules never see those. Allowlisted and operator-allowed addresses are exempt, and so are private, CGNAT, loopback and link-local sources (Docker containers calling the host's own published ports, VPN clients): vpsfort never bans those either. Per-source state lives in dynamic sets (rl0_4, rl0_6, …), and vpsfort status shows how many packets each entry dropped. Enforce mode with nftables only; the ufw and iptables backends ignore them. install.sh dry-runs the full ruleset with nft -c against the kernel.
57.breadcrumbs: vpsfort: the daemon » Kernel rate limits
57.title: Kernel rate limits

58.body: vpsfort can't tell "no attacks" from "not seeing logs" by scores alone, so [silence] raises a system warning when an enabled source: logs nothing for its threshold (defaults ufw = "2h", ejabberd = "6h", ssh = "2d", Nextcloud AIO off: nextcloud_aio, called nextcloud until 2026-10-26). Measured on the Sep–Oct month: UFW and ejabberd were never quiet for 3 h outside an outage; sshd often was for a day. Typical causes: ufw logging off, ejabberd stopped, or a unit renamed. An info alert follows when lines return. an app's log ([sources] apps) logs nothing for its time in [silence.apps], by its key in [sources.app_logs]: nginx_access = "2h", nextcloud = "7d". None by default: a busy site's access log is never quiet for hours, while nextcloud.log at the default loglevel holds only warnings and errors and can be quiet for days. Counted by the log's first pattern, which reads all its lines (the Patterns tab shows them too). logs, but no line can be tied to an address for blind_after (6 h, at least blind_lines = 200 lines). This catches ejabberd's hide_sensitive_log_data (5 days in that month) or a log format vpsfort no longer understands. Silence is measured from the later of the last line and the daemon's start, so a reboot or a stopped service never counts as silence. The checks run in the live daemon only, not in replay. A heartbeat ([heartbeat] url, off by default): vpsfort fetches the URL every every (5 minutes), with curl as for the feeds, so a service outside (healthchecks.io, Uptime Kuma's push monitors, a cron monitor of your own) notices when this node, or every node, goes dark: the cluster's peers only cover each other. Only the node's address reaches that service; the URL, which may hold a token, must be https:// and is never shown whole (status says https://hc-ping.com/…). A failed ping is logged once and then hourly, and three in a row are in the digest's "Needs attention". The host's names ([dns] names = ["example.org", "nextcloud.example.org"], off by default): once an hour each name is resolved through the system's resolver and compared with this host's addresses. A name that resolves elsewhere is a high system alert (a record changed at the registrar or the DNS provider, a hijack or a takeover of the domain, sends users, federation and mail elsewhere while the server runs on, with nothing in its logs; or the host moved); one that doesn't resolve is a warning. Both repeat every 6 hours while they last, and status lists the names. Not for a host behind NAT, whose public name never resolves to its own addresses. Out-of-memory kills ([sources] oom = true, the default): when the kernel kills a process for lack of memory (Out of memory: Killed process 785891 (clamscan) ... anon-rss:920752kB), a system alert names the process and its size. It's high, or a warning for a virus scanner, which [antivirus] reports as well. A kill for exceeding a unit's or container's own limit (Memory cgroup out of memory, e.g. vpsfort's MemoryMax) is told apart. On a 2 GB host without swap, the nightly clamscan was killed this way every day for weeks without anyone noticing. Disk and memory ([resources], on by default): every minute vpsfort reads df -Pk for the disks paths (each filesystem once; default /) and /proc/meminfo plus /proc/pressure/memory. A filesystem under 10% free raises a warning, under 5% a high alert; memory gets a warning when less than 10% stayed available for 15 minutes, or when tasks spent 10% of the last 5 minutes stalled waiting for memory (pressure stall information). Each alert repeats at most every 6 hours. status shows the latest reading. This comes before the out-of-memory kills below: on a host without swap, a shortage that lasts is the warning sign. The clock , once an hour, the same way: /run/systemd/timesync/synchronized (timesyncd leaves it once it is), else timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized (the kernel's own flag, which chrony and ntpd set too; [resources] timedatectl). A clock that isn't synchronised is a warning once a day and a line in the digest's "Needs attention" and in status: the cluster refuses messages more than max_clock_skew off, the web console's one-time codes drift, and every time vpsfort records is wrong. Failed services ([sources] services = ["vpsfort-xmpp-bot.service"], empty by default): vpsfort also follows systemd's own messages about these units (journal match UNIT=<name>, accepted only from PID 1) and raises a high system alert when one ends unsuccessfully (a non-zero exit status, a signal, a timeout, a watchdog kill, ...) and is not started again within service_restart_grace (default 2 minutes; keep it longer than the units' RestartSec): service vpsfort-xmpp-bot.service failed (exit-code, exit status 78/CONFIG) and was not restarted: it is down (for the bot, a wrong password or setting, after which RestartPreventExitStatus=78 keeps it down). A failure that systemd recovers from on its own (Restart=: "Scheduled restart job"), or that someone starts again in that time, says nothing. When systemd gives up restarting a unit (Start request repeated too quickly), the alert comes at once. Each at most once an hour per service. Clean stops and restarts (systemctl restart) say nothing. Restart loops that systemd never gives up on are not reported. Journal integrity. When journald no longer has the position vpsfort saved (journal files vacuumed, rotated away or deleted while lines were unread), vpsfort reads the last initial_lookback instead and raises a high system alert: expected after a downtime longer than journald keeps logs, otherwise someone may have removed evidence. [journal] verify_every (off by default) runs journalctl --verify and raises a high alert when an archived journal file fails: damaged, or, with verify_key_file (the verification key journalctl --setup-keys printed, for Forward Secure Sealing), changed after it was sealed. Files journald is still writing are left out (checked while they change, they can fail without anything wrong). Know what the key gives away: journald derives every sealing key from the verification key, so whoever reads it can seal edited entries of any past period too. Kept in verify_key_file on the server itself, it catches only an intruder who doesn't look for it; for a real guarantee keep the key elsewhere and verify copies of the journal there (journalctl --verify --verify-key=... --file=...). journalctl also takes it on its command line, where every local user can read it (ps) while the check runs, unless /proc is mounted with hidepid=invisible. vpsfort says so in a warning when it starts with the key set (at most once a week). The unit is Type=notify with WatchdogSec=2min. vpsfort reports READY=1 and pings the watchdog from its main loop, so if that loop ever hangs (a stuck nft or ejabberdctl call, a deadlock), systemd restarts it. vpsfort status shows the age of the last line per source.

59.body: Every vpsfort node can exchange what it learns with the others directly over TCP. No VPN or other infrastructure is needed, and nodes can be on different providers. What is shared ("facts"): fact effect on the receiving node bans the address/subnet is banned here too for the origin's duration, capped at max_remote_ban, tagged from peer <node> unbans a ban lifted at the origin (e.g. a false positive: a banned address then logged in) is lifted here too reports points a node scored for an address since its last sync, counted here × report_factor (0.5). An address that probes every server a little still adds up to a ban trust operator allowlist entries (vpsfort allow). Login trust is no longer shared: older nodes still send it, and it is ignored notices admin messages relayed to a node that delivers them (XMPP, or a copy bot). Kept for a peer that can't be reached for [cluster] notice_ttl (24 h; was an hour) within 2 MB in all, so a relay node down for the night still gets them, each saying how late it is log_digests once a day, from 00:05 UTC, the SHA-256 of the previous day's lines of the node's actions log, and how many there were. The receiving node keeps it (120 days per peer; the first word about a day stands, a later one can't rewrite it) as tamper evidence: a root intruder who edits the log on the node can't edit the copies the peers hold. vpsfort log-digests [node] on a peer prints what it holds; vpsfort log-digest --day D on the node hashes that day again, so the two can be compared mirror every line of the node's actions log, at the next sync, to the one direct peer [cluster] mirror_to names (its node id), which appends them to <mirror_dir>/<node>.jsonl (/var/lib/vpsfort/mirror, 0700; rotated once at mirror_max_mb, 64) with a marker line where batches are missing (the mirror was unreachable for an hour, or a restart) or the origin had to drop lines (more than 1,000 or 256 KB in one sync). The hashes prove an edit; the mirror keeps the lines, so what a wiped node decided is still somewhere. vpsfort mirror on the peer lists what it holds, status shows both sides, the self-audit checks the directory probes a node's request to its direct peers to try its public ports from outside, and their answers ([exposure] peer_probe; "Exposure watch") Rules that keep it safe: Facts refused for their signature are an alert (high, system, once a day per origin): a node broken into or a stolen cluster key sending facts in another node's name, or a node whose key changed or isn't pinned here; status counts them. Only peers may connect (allow_only_peers, default on): connections from any address the peers don't resolve to are dropped unread. Peers named by host name are resolved again every 10 minutes (every minute while a lookup fails), and the listener, the engine and the nftables allowlist follow. While no peer resolves at all, every connection is refused, never accepted. Local protections always win. Allowlisted, private and cluster-peer addresses are never banned by peer facts. Peers are added to the nftables allowlist automatically. Evidence is never echoed back. Peer-reported points are not re-reported. A ban a node decides itself, based partly on peer reports, is shared as that node's own decision. History stays local. A node starts sharing only after catching up with its journal, so replayed history isn't broadcast as fresh evidence. How it works: Every fact has a unique id (origin node, time-based sequence). Nodes apply each fact once and forward it to their own peers up to max_hops (3), so full meshes, chains (A↔B↔C) and stars all work, without loops or double counting. share is what a node sends: its own facts and the ones it forwards. Every sync_interval (10 s) each node sends its peers the facts learned since the last send. Every full_sync_every (10 min), or after a failed delivery, it resends everything, so restarted or temporarily unreachable nodes catch up. Empty messages double as heartbeats. A peer that stays unreachable for 5 minutes raises a system alert, at most hourly. Security: Each message is one TCP connection. The sender first offers a fresh X25519 key in a hello sealed under the shared key; the receiver answers with one of its own, both derive the message's key from the two (HKDF-SHA-256, the shared key as salt), and the message goes out under it: XChaCha20-Poly1305 , pure-Rust crypto, a random 192-bit nonce each. Only a holder of the shared key takes part, and once both sides have dropped their fresh keys nobody can read a recording of the message, not even with the shared key: a key that leaks later gives away nothing said before ( forward secrecy , as the web console's agent protocol has it). A peer running an older version doesn't answer the hello; the sender then sends the message the old way, sealed under the shared key alone ("LGC1"), says so once in its journal and in status ("plain frames"), and tries the exchange again every 10 minutes. [cluster] forward_secrecy is "prefer" (that), "require" (refuse the old way both ways, once every node is current) or "off". Without the key, nobody can read or inject facts. Tampered, foreign or garbage connections are rejected and logged. Messages whose timestamp is more than max_clock_skew (5 min) off are rejected, so nodes need roughly correct clocks (systemd-timesyncd is enough). Time zones don't matter: all timestamps are Unix time (UTC), and the daemon reads journald's UTC timestamps. Times shown in the TUI, status and the logs are UTC. Replaying a recent message is harmless, because facts are de-duplicated. Without node identities, every key holder is fully trusted. A compromised node can ban or trust addresses on the others, under any node's name (with identities, under its own only: below). max_remote_ban bounds how long its bans last there: the built-in default is 1 day, while the templates use 30 days, because both nodes are yours. A capped peer ban isn't renewed while the origin's longer ban continues; the address is then banned again only on local evidence. Peer bans wider than this node bans itself (v4_wide_prefix, or v4_prefix without growth; IPv6 v6_prefix) and allowlist entries wider than /16 (IPv6 /32) are ignored. A peer's suspicion report adds at most one ban threshold of points, relayed notices take at most 2 MB of memory at once (16 KB each), and each connection must deliver its message within 30 s. Protect /etc/vpsfort/cluster.key like a root password, and rotate it if it may have leaked (see below). Except peers you limit (peer_accept): peer_accept = { "203.0.113.10:7946" = ["notices", "files"] } lets what arrives from that peer's address be notices and cluster-send-report files only, whoever's facts they are (its own or forwarded); the rest is dropped, counted in vpsfort status and logged once per kind. The limit goes by the connection's source address, not the node name in the message, which any key holder can write, so it needs allow_only_peers (the default). Use it for a node that is more exposed than the rest, such as the Telegram relay node below: broken into, it still holds the key (it can read every fact), but can't ban, unban or allowlist anything on the others. Its files are written under the node name it first used, never one an unlimited peer uses, so it can't replace another node's weekly report. Node identities (optional, below): each node signs the facts it originates and the files it sends with an Ed25519 key of its own, and the others take a node's facts only with its signature. A broken-into node, or anyone who stole the cluster key, can then speak only for itself, not for the others; and a node is dropped by deleting its public key, without a new cluster key. At most 8 concurrent incoming connections, 30 s per message, 1 MB per message, 32 files in the inbox (a report merged later is read up to 64 MB unpacked): even 8 messages at once (each also decrypted into a copy) stay far inside the memory limit. A large sync (a full resend of thousands of bans) is split into messages of at most 512 KB, sent in order over one connection thread per peer. Run the same version on all nodes: an older node's large full sync can exceed the new 1 MB limit. Setup (what the deploy scripts do for you): deploy.sh generates deploy/cluster.key once on your Mac (vpsfort cluster-keygen, mode 0600, git-ignored) and ships it to every node. install.sh installs it as /etc/vpsfort/cluster.key unless one exists. In each node's [cluster]: enabled = true, a unique node_id, listen = "0.0.0.0:7946", and peers = the other nodes' ip:7946. install.sh runs vpsfort cluster-ufw-rules, which opens 7946/tcp only for the configured peers (ufw allow from <peer> to any port 7946 proto tcp). A peer that is still a documentation address (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24, 2001:db8::/32, 3fff::/20: a template's example nobody replaced) gets no rule, and the command says so. Check it with vpsfort status (per-peer delivery status and nodes heard from) or the TUI's overview (Cluster: node1 - 1/1 peers ok). Bans from peers show (from peer vpn) in their message, and origin in actions.jsonl.

60.body:
With one shared key, the node name on a fact is only a claim: any key holder can write any name. Node identities make it a proof. Each node gets a signing key of its own, and every node pins the others' public keys: vpsfort cluster-identity --out /etc/vpsfort/node.key # on each node, as root: creates the key (0600), prints its line [cluster]
identity_file = "/etc/vpsfort/node.key"
nodes = { node1 = "6h0w…=", vpn = "pQ3k…=", tg = "Zf1c…=" } # the same on every node
require_signatures = true What is signed: each fact by the node it comes from, over its origin, sequence number, time and content (Ed25519, pure Rust). The signature travels with the fact when other nodes forward it (the hop count is outside it, as forwarders change it), and with full resyncs. cluster-send-report files are signed by their sender, over its name, the time sent, the file name and content. The shared key still encrypts and authenticates every message, as before. What is checked: a fact whose origin has a key in nodes is taken only with a valid signature from that key; otherwise it is dropped, counted in vpsfort status ("facts refused for their signature") and logged once per origin. A file under a pinned name must be signed by it, and then needs none of the peer_accept name rules above: it is that node's report, whichever peer it comes through. With require_signatures = true, facts and files from nodes not in nodes are refused too; without it, they are taken unchecked, as before (nodes then protects the pinned names only: a node broken into could still invent a new name). Dropping a node: delete its line in nodes on the others (with require_signatures) and restart them. Its facts and files are refused from then on, though it still has the cluster key: it can still read what the others share, and send heartbeats. Rotate the cluster key too (below) when that matters, or when the node is still in peers. Rolling it out: older versions ignore the signatures and still read every message, but leave them out when they forward a fact. So first update every node; then set identity_file on each (signing only: nothing is refused yet); then add nodes everywhere; and set require_signatures last. A node's own entry in nodes must match its identity_file (vpsfort refuses to start otherwise), so one nodes list fits every node. A new key for one node: cluster-identity --out a new file, put its public key in nodes on the others, then point identity_file at it and restart the node. Its facts sent in between are refused, and resent with the new signature only if it originates them again. What it doesn't cover: the node name on a heartbeat (vpsfort status's "nodes heard from") is still a claim; and a node can still be trusted with what it says itself, within the limits above (max_remote_ban, peer_accept). Rotating the key (deploy/rotate-cluster-key.sh on your Mac). Swapping the key on one node and then the next would leave a gap in which the two can't read each other, and facts sent in it are lost: a sender can't tell. So vpsfort also accepts the keys in <key_file>.next and <key_file>.prev from peers, while always sending with key_file, and the rotation goes in three rounds, each done on every node before the next. Like deploy.sh, the script only copies files (the step's script, and for start the new key) into a private, freshly created /tmp/vpsfort-rotate.XXXX on each node (over SFTP only, so hardened hosts whose SSH user may run no remote command work too); you then paste the printed command into a root shell there, as with deploy.sh: it copies the files into a private directory of root's, checks them against hashes computed on your Mac (so the SSH user can't swap the script root runs), and runs the step (no sudo needed): ./deploy/rotate-cluster-key.sh start node1 vpn # then paste the printed command into a root shell on each node # new key -> /etc/vpsfort/cluster.key.next (accepted, not used yet)
./deploy/rotate-cluster-key.sh switch node1 vpn # ... rotate.sh switch: sends with the new key; old one -> cluster.key.prev
./deploy/rotate-cluster-key.sh finish node1 vpn # ... rotate.sh finish: cluster.key.prev removed, only the new key works Each root step restarts vpsfort, prints the node's key fingerprints (vpsfort cluster-key-id: the first bytes of the key's SHA-256, equal for equal keys, revealing nothing about it) and ends with OK: the new key (…) is in place., or a warning if the node holds a different key. vpsfort status and the daemon's startup line show the fingerprints too, with "rotation: also accepting …" while a .next/.prev file exists. Steps can be repeated (stage and run a step again for a node where it failed), and run in the wrong order they stop with a message. The key copies (/tmp/vpsfort-rotate.XXXX and root's) are deleted when the step runs, whatever its outcome; until then it is readable by the SSH user, as deploy.sh's copy is. deploy/cluster.key on your Mac becomes the new key when finish is staged, so deploy.sh installs the current key on new nodes. A .next/.prev file without a valid key stops the cluster on that node with a High alert instead of being ignored. Rotation needs the key in key_file, not inline as key. With node identities (above), removing one node from the cluster no longer needs it: deleting its key in nodes is enough to refuse what it says. Rotate the cluster key when the node left may still read the cluster's messages and that matters, or after a leak; node keys (identity_file) are not touched by the rotation. Key age. vpsfort status shows how old the key file is (its modification time: when install.sh or rotate.sh switch put it there), and once it is older than [cluster] rotate_after (default 180d, 0 turns it off) every node sends a Warning once a week until the key is rotated. Single server: [cluster] is off by default (enabled = false). Then no key is needed, nothing listens on 7946, no peer alerts exist, and vpsfort behaves exactly as without the feature. listen = "" makes a send-only node, for a host that can't accept incoming connections. It still pushes its facts to the others, but it only learns from nodes it can reach and receives nothing back.
60.title: Node identities

61.body: To get admin messages on Telegram without the XMPP server ever connecting to Telegram, run vpsfort-tg-bot on a separate small VPS that joins the cluster (deploy/vpsfort-tg.toml, node id tg): On the relay node: [notify] xmpp = false with tg_outbox: no ejabberd, no users' warnings; every admin message (its own and the relayed ones) goes to vpsfort-tg-bot, which sends it with XMPP account names replaced by pseudonyms. share = ["notices"] and relay_notices = true: its own alerts and digest also go to the XMPP admin, and it passes nothing else on. It accepts the others' bans for its own firewall. [sources] services = ["vpsfort-tg-bot.service"] makes a failed bot a system alert, and a bot that leaves messages unsent past bot_stuck_after raises one too; both reach the XMPP admin through the relay. On the XMPP node: the relay node in peers, peer_accept = { "<tg>:7946" = ["notices", "files"] }, and relay_notices = true: its admin messages still go out over XMPP (and vpsfort-xmpp-bot) as before, and as notices to the relay node. On the VPN node: the relay node in peers and peer_accept = { "<tg>:7946" = ["notices"] }. It relays its admin messages already ([notify] is off there). The weekly abuse report: the relay node's timer runs in role relay (auto picks it with xmpp = false and cluster peers): it sends its own JSON report to the XMPP node (ABUSE_REPORT_SEND_TO), waits for the merged text report (ABUSE_REPORT_RELAY_WAIT_MIN, 60) and puts it in vpsfort-tg-bot's outbox ([notify] tg_outbox). If none arrives (a cluster without an XMPP server, or its ABUSE_REPORT_FORWARD_TO unset), it merges its own and the peers' reports itself; set ABUSE_REPORT_ROLE=merge there to skip the wait. On the XMPP node, ABUSE_REPORT_PEERS="vpn tg" waits for its report, and ABUSE_REPORT_FORWARD_TO="<tg>:7946" sends the merged text there (cluster-send-report --name abuse-report --peer …, written to the relay node's inbox as abuse-report-xmpp.txt.gz, deleted once handed over). Telegram then sees the relay node's address only. In the alerts and digests vpsfort-tg-bot replaces the servers' own addresses and host names (certificate targets, peer addresses in cluster warnings) with their node ids (SERVER_NAMES), and the abuse report, which names the servers' addresses for the abuse desks, goes only as a file encrypted to the admin's OpenPGP key (vpsfort-tg-bot's README). Relayed notices live an hour: if the relay node is down longer, what was relayed meanwhile doesn't reach Telegram (it still reached the XMPP admin). Deploy vpsfort with these settings to every node before you set them: older versions reject unknown keys.

62.body:
vpsfort-web shows the whole cluster on one HTTPS page for its admins (one or several, all equal): every node's bans, alerts, decisions, offenders, places, peers, certificates, disks and updates, with what needs attention first, every node's abuse report of the last day or week split per network owner (each part ready to mail), and /metrics for Prometheus. It only reads. It is a program of its own, under a user of its own, and never holds the cluster key: each node's vpsfort-web (its agent ) hands that node's data to the console, sealed with a separate web key that can't make a ban. vpsfort's part is one read-only socket: [console]
socket = "/run/vpsfort-console/console.sock"
group = "vpsfort-web" # vpsfort-web's group: it may connect [sources]
apps = ["vpsfort-web"] # ban addresses that guess the console's password or probe it The socket answers snapshot (what the dashboard shows), digest (today's so far) and abuse 24h / abuse 7d (abuse alone: 7d); unban, ban, allow, feeds clear, digest send and every other command get error: read-only socket without reaching the daemon. The control socket stays root's. An abuse report is abuse-report's, live: this node's own bans of the window from the actions log (also its rotated copies), each source's activity in the report's words, its country and network from [geo], its first 25 log lines worded for an abuse desk, and how many more. At most the 1000 most persistent sources, ranked among the first 20,000 the window holds (it is built inside the daemon's memory limit; a flood's further sources are only counted); no RDAP lookups (the weekly report makes those). It is built beside the main loop (reading a week of the log takes a moment and holds up nothing), one at a time, two requests waiting at most, and handed out again for a minute. With actions_log off there is none. vpsfort makes the socket's directory its own at start (root, mode 0750, the group above; a directory someone else made is refused), the socket mode 0660. The directory's name must start with vpsfort and not be the control socket's. Without the group (vpsfort-web not installed) the console socket stays off and vpsfort says so at start; everything else runs as before. The snapshot carries vpsfort's version and, in stats.hours, events and bans per hour over the last 7 days (since vpsfort started: they aren't saved), for the console's longer charts and its table of differences between nodes. The snapshot's geoblock names the countries [geoblock] blocks (countries, only_countries, as ISO codes) and its AS numbers, so the console's map hatches them. Prometheus without the console: [metrics] textfile = "/var/lib/prometheus/node-exporter/vpsfort.prom" makes the daemon rewrite that file every every (60 s) in the exposition format, for node_exporter's textfile collector (--collector.textfile.directory; the directory must exist). The daemon writes it through a temporary file it makes afresh each time and renames into place: a link someone put in that directory, which is node_exporter's, not vpsfort's, under either name is never written through. About 60 series, named as the console's /metrics names them (vpsfort_enforcing, vpsfort_active_bans{origin,kind}, vpsfort_bans_total, vpsfort_cluster_peer_up{peer}, vpsfort_cert_expiry_timestamp_seconds{target}, vpsfort_disk_free_ratio{mount}, vpsfort_unapplied_changes, vpsfort_clock_synced, ...), so vpsfort-web's deploy/prometheus-rules.yml fits either; nothing in them names an attacker's address or an account. vpsfort unban 11.148.51.11 # or a subnet: vpsfort unban 11.148.51.0/24
vpsfort ban 198.51.100.7 --for 30d --note "mail scanner" # or a subnet; 1d by default
vpsfort allow 203.0.113.7 --for 7d --note "temporary access"
vpsfort allowed # list entries with time left
vpsfort disallow 203.0.113.7 In the TUI, on the Offenders , Bans , Events (a ban decision) or Alerts tab (an alert about an address): u unbans the selected entry (after a y confirmation), b asks for a number of days to ban it (1 unless you type another number), and a asks for a number of days to allowlist it (7 unless you type another number, 365 at most as the daemon keeps them; the end date is shown); the command goes to the daemon in the background and its answer shows in the footer. The Bans tab lists the operator allowlist under the bans. A saved snapshot or a decision log is read-only: both keys say so instead. Ban bans an address or network until the time given (365 days at most), as if vpsfort had decided it: in the firewall, the actions log, and shared with the peers (who apply it like any peer ban, capped at their max_remote_ban). It counts as an offence, so a later automatic ban of it starts higher on the ladder. Refused for this host, cluster peers, allowlisted addresses and host names, operator allowlist entries (vpsfort disallow it first), a network with any of those or a recently logged-in address inside, an address inside a banned network, and networks wider than vpsfort's own widest ban (use a blocklist feed for those). Banning an address already banned replaces that ban. In shadow mode it is decided and shared, not applied, and the reply says so. Unban lifts the ban and also clears that address's score and offence history, so it isn't re-banned the next second, and a later ban starts again at 1 hour. Unbanning an address inside a banned subnet is refused with a hint: unban the subnet, or allowlist the address. Allow lifts every ban inside the network and protects it until it expires: never scored into a ban, never banned by peers. In nftables it goes into the oper4/oper6 sets with a kernel timeout, accepted before feeds and bans, so it works even for an address inside a banned subnet. With the ufw backend nothing is added to ufw (an allow from rule would open every port to that network, past your own rules): an address inside a banned subnet stays blocked until that subnet is unbanned, and vpsfort allow says so. Cluster: both are shared, so peers follow the operator's decision. Peer allowlist entries are capped at max_remote_ban. All commands talk to the daemon over /run/vpsfort/vpsfort.sock, which is root-only, so use sudo. Allowlisted host names. [allowlist] hosts = ["home.example.dyndns.org"] allowlists what the names resolve to, like nets: never scored into a ban, never banned by peers, accepted before the drops in nftables (and iptables). They are resolved at start and every 10 minutes (every minute while one fails, keeping the addresses known so far; a warning says which name fails). A newly listed address's ban is lifted and its score forgotten; an address the name no longer resolves to is an address like any other. Whoever controls the name's DNS controls the entry, so use a name whose DNS is yours. vpsfort status shows what they resolve to.
62.title: Web console (vpsfort-web)

63.body:
[feeds]
enabled = true
urls = ["https://www.spamhaus.org/drop/drop.txt", "https://www.spamhaus.org/drop/dropv6.txt", "https://iplists.firehol.org/files/firehol_level1.netset"]
refresh = "24h" Download: every refresh period, with curl (falling back to wget). Shelling out keeps the binary free of a TLS library. A redirect must stay on https (--proto-redir =https in the default fetch, also used for geo databases and abuse contacts; add it to a fetch of your own). The last good copy of each list is cached in cache_dir, so a failed download keeps the previous list instead of emptying it. Failures raise a daily warning. Formats: plain CIDR lists, Spamhaus cidr ; SBL… lines and Spamhaus JSON lines. Sanitising: private and bogon ranges are dropped; FireHOL level1 lists 10.0.0.0/8, 127.0.0.0/8 and 172.16.0.0/12, which would break loopback and Docker. So are prefixes wider than /8 (IPv4) or /19 (IPv6), and anything overlapping your allowlist or cluster peers. Nested entries are merged. Loading: into the separate nftables sets feed4/feed6 (ipset: <iptables_chain>-feed4/-feed6), in one atomic transaction (lists of up to 10,000 networks; a longer one is emptied, then filled 10,000 at a time), after the allowlist accepts and before vpsfort's own bans. A feed can never block your allowlisted addresses, peers or operator allowlist. More than max_entries (100,000) networks is treated as a broken feed, and a refresh covering more than max_growth (2) times the address space of the last accepted load (plus a /16) is refused too: the last accepted list (<cache_dir>/accepted.txt) stays loaded, and a system alert says why. After an intended change (a new feed URL), delete that file once. Networks wider than min_prefix_v4 (/12) or min_prefix_v6 (/24) are never loaded: one bad entry must not drop a whole provider at the prerouting hook, where only the static allowlist, peers and operator entries are exempt. Whole networks (ASNs): asn_urls = ["https://www.spamhaus.org/drop/asndrop.json"] (Spamhaus ASN-DROP: hijacked and criminal networks; JSON lines, AS64500 ; ... text or plain numbers) adds every address block the [geo] network database gives those ASNs, under the same limits as the other lists (min_prefix_*, max_entries, protected addresses). It needs [geo] with an asn_url; until the database is loaded the ASN lists are left out (vpsfort feeds says so) and a refresh follows once it is. A list built from other URLs than the last accepted one (accepted.txt records which) is an intended change, which the growth check doesn't refuse. One-step removal: vpsfort feeds clear empties the sets immediately (until the next refresh); [feeds] enabled = false plus a restart keeps them empty. vpsfort's own bans are untouched either way. vpsfort feeds shows per-list status. Feeds are only applied with the nftables, ipset or firewalld backend in enforce mode (firewalld: the ipsets vpsfort-feed4/-feed6 as sources of vpsfort's zone, like [geoblock]'s, at most 50,000 networks per list, and [waf] lists the same way in vpsfort-waf4/-waf6); in shadow mode they're downloaded and counted only.
63.title: Blocklist feeds (optional)

64.body:
vpsfort reads what it sees in logs; a WAF sees inside web requests (SQL injection, path traversal, a CVE probe in a header) that no log line here shows. [waf] closes that gap the other way round: the WAF decides, vpsfort blocks the address at the firewall, for every port and not only the web server's, and with a cluster on every node. CrowdSec's formats are built in; any other app that gives out the addresses it blocks works through a generic format. [waf]
enabled = true
refresh = "1m" [[waf.sources]] # CrowdSec's own detections (its AppSec WAF, scenarios, cscli)
name = "crowdsec"
format = "crowdsec"
url = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/decisions?type=ban&origins=crowdsec,cscli"
api_key_file = "/etc/vpsfort/crowdsec-bouncer.key" # from `cscli bouncers add vpsfort`; chmod 600
action = "ban" [[waf.sources]] # CrowdSec's community blocklist: tens of thousands of addresses
name = "crowdsec-capi"
format = "crowdsec"
url = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/decisions?type=ban&origins=CAPI,lists"
api_key_file = "/etc/vpsfort/crowdsec-bouncer.key"
action = "list" Where from: one of url (read with [waf] fetch, curl), file (a file another program writes) or command (a program and its arguments, no shell, 60 s at most). api_key_file sends its key in the header api_key_header (X-Api-Key, CrowdSec's; Authorization with Bearer <token> in the file for a token). curl gets it on its stdin (-H @-), never on its command line, where any local user could read it; a key file other users can read is refused, and so is a key sent over plain http to anything but loopback. Formats (format): crowdsec: told apart by shape: the local API's decisions (/v1/decisions, or /v1/decisions/stream?startup=true: without startup=true the stream lists only changes, and is refused), cscli decisions list -o json (alerts holding decisions) and -o raw (CSV), or the blocklist mirror's plain list. Only the Ip and Range scopes are addresses (Country, AS, Username are left out), simulated decisions are left out, and durations (3h59m56s) are taken as relative, so the CrowdSec host's clock doesn't matter. plain: one address or network per line, # and ; comments (fail2ban, a blocklist file, anything exported as a list). json: the entries at the dotted path items (arrays on the way are walked into: decisions finds every decision in a list of alerts; JSON lines work too), their fields named by ip_field (default ip), duration_field, until_field, type_field, origin_field, reason_field, as dotted paths. A list of strings is a list of addresses. csv: the same fields by header name or column number (from 1); delimiter, header. regex: every match of pattern on a line, with the groups ip, duration, until, type, origin, reason (linear-time, like [[patterns]]). E.g. fail2ban-client banned ([{'sshd': ['192.0.2.1', ...]}]) with pattern = "'(?P<ip>[0-9a-fA-F.:]+)'". A duration is a Go duration, a number of seconds or 90s/12h/7d; until is a Unix time (seconds or milliseconds) or an ISO 8601 date. Without either, a decision lasts while it is listed. Any other app is one more format: a Format variant in src/waf.rs whose parser hands each entry's fields to Parsed::add, which checks them the same way for every format. Filters: types (default ["ban"]: captcha and throttle are for an HTTP-layer bouncer; entries without a type always count) and origins (CrowdSec: crowdsec, cscli, CAPI, lists, console; empty: all). action = "ban" (for a WAF's own detections, up to max_bans, 10,000, per source): each decision becomes a vpsfort ban for as long as it lasts (default_ban, 4 h, when it doesn't say, renewed while listed; max_ban, 7 d, at most), with the reason waf <name>: <scenario>, category waf in the digest, in the TUI and the actions log, and shared with the cluster (share = false keeps it here). It is refused like an operator ban for allowlisted, peer and own addresses, networks wider than vpsfort's own bans, and also for an address someone logged in from lately: a WAF's false positive must not lock out a user. When the WAF drops the decision (cscli decisions delete), the ban is lifted, here and at the peers. A source that can't be read leaves its bans alone: they end on their own, in the kernel. vpsfort unban lasts only until the next read while the WAF still lists the address: delete the decision there, or vpsfort allow it. These bans work with every backend. action = "list" (for blocklists): the networks of all such sources go into the sets waf4/waf6 (ipset: <iptables_chain>-waf4/-waf6), after the feeds' and before vpsfort's bans, sanitised as the feeds are (bogons, protected addresses, wider than min_prefix_v4/_v6, more than max_entries in all) and replaced in one step when they change. nftables and ipset only. vpsfort waf clear empties them until the next read. Failures: a source that can't be read, or gives out something that isn't a list (an HTML login page served with status 200, JSON cut short), keeps its last good decisions (cache_dir, with absolute end times: list entries still end when their decisions do). A system warning says so, once a day; vpsfort waf, the TUI, the digest and vpsfort-web show each source's state, and vpsfort-web's metrics have vpsfort_waf_source_error. Timing: decisions are read every refresh (1 min); a new ban is in the firewall within that. The first read waits until vpsfort has caught up with the journal.

65.body:
[geoblock]
enabled = true
countries = ["CN", "Russia"] # ISO codes or names
only_countries = [] # e.g. ["UA", "DE"]: every other country is dropped
asns = [64500] # networks by AS number Source: the [geo] databases vpsfort has loaded anyway (DB-IP's lite databases, or your own in their columns), so there is nothing to download and no second database in memory. The list is computed when they load (at start and after the weekly refresh) and loaded into the firewall; only its sets hold it afterwards. Computing it costs about 1 MB beyond the databases themselves, the United States included (the ranges are merged while they are read, measured with the test real_geoblock_sizes), and it goes into the firewall 10,000 networks per command, so the commands for a whole list are never in memory at once. The lite data places some addresses in the wrong country, and a network's addresses can move between monthly releases: this is coarse, not a curated list. What is dropped: the addresses the country database places in countries; with only_countries, those it places in any other country (addresses it places nowhere stay reachable); and the address blocks the network database gives asns. All three can be combined. Unknown country names or codes are refused at start (vpsfort print-config checks), and so is a country both blocked and the only one let in. Never dropped: the allowlist, this host's addresses, the cluster peers (as configured at start) and private or special-purpose ranges are cut out exactly, not by leaving out a whole block (an IPv6 address keeps its whole /64, the databases' granularity). Neighbouring ranges merge before they become CIDRs. With DB-IP's lite databases of autumn 2026 (computed in a few milliseconds): China is 15,040 networks (8,331 IPv4 + 6,709 IPv6), Russia 22,983, China, Russia, Iran and North Korea together 41,152, everything but Ukraine 27,690 (the other countries' neighbouring ranges merge), the United States 251,826. More than max_entries (200,000; raise it for the United States) is refused with a warning, and what was loaded before stays. Only some ports: ports = ["22/tcp", "5222", "5223"] closes just those local ports to the blocked countries and networks ("5222" is both protocols): a web site stays open to the world while SSH and XMPP don't. nftables (tcp dport { ... } ip saddr @geo4 drop) and ipset (-p tcp -m multiport --dports) only; firewalld's zone drops everything from its sources, so ports is ignored there with a warning at start. Where: nftables: the sets geo4/geo6, dropped after the allowlist, operator allows, whitelisted ports and replies to the host's own connections, before the feeds and bans. ipset: <iptables_chain>-geo4/-geo6, one rule each. firewalld: the ipsets vpsfort-geo4/-geo6, sources of vpsfort's zone (whitelisted ports stay open; on a change only the difference is sent, and after a reload they come back with the bans). firewalld takes thousands of entries slowly while vpsfort waits, so it takes at most 50,000 networks: for more, use the nftables or ipset backend. Not with ufw or plain iptables; in shadow mode it is computed only. Effects: dropped traffic never reaches the firewall's log, so blocked countries make no events, bans or alerts. Cluster peers don't share it (each node has its own [geoblock]). vpsfort status shows what is loaded (geoblock (CN): 8331 IPv4 + 6709 IPv6 networks, computed ..., active in nftables), or why not. enabled = false and a restart empty the sets again.

66.body:
[digest]
enabled = true
at = "07:00" # UTC
certs = ["example.org:5223", "example.org:5222/xmpp", "nextcloud.example.org:443"]
cert_warn_days = 21 One XMPP message to the [notify] admins each day, flagged with ⚠ in the subject when something needs attention. It covers: Needs attention: certificates expiring within cert_warn_days or failing to check, failing cluster peers, failing feeds, dead ufw rules, and the period's warning-or-worse alerts. Bans by cause: tripwire, port scan, ssh, xmpp, subnet, from peers, cluster evidence. Top offenders with their current ban, alert counts by topic, and event counts. Exposure, certificates, cluster, feeds and the operator allowlist. Certificates are checked every 6 h against the live endpoints with openssl s_client (/xmpp = STARTTLS on 5222), so a failed ACME renewal is caught before clients see it. An expiring certificate also raises its own alert: warning under 21 days, high under 7. An endpoint that gives no certificate is checked again after 1, 2 and 4 minutes before it is reported, so a service still starting after a reboot raises no alert. cert_files (e.g. ["/opt/ejabberd/database/ejabberd@localhost/acme/live/*"], * allowed in the file name) adds the certificates on disk. If one of them covers an endpoint's hostname and expires more than a day later than the certificate actually served there, vpsfort warns: renewed, but not in use: point certfiles at it and reload . That's exactly the manual step after each renewal being missed. Old certificates left on disk are ignored. ejabberd's own certificate log lines become admin alerts as they happen (system topic, so the VPN node relays them too): ejabberd logs alert Storing certificate for … in PATH (debug level) info: certificate renewed , with the new DANE TLSA 3 1 1 value (SHA-256 of the public key, via openssl x509 -pubkey | openssl pkey -pubin -outform der) Certificate in PATH … will expire in a week / has expired warning / high Failed to request certificate … Challenge failed for domain D … warning, with the cause: nothing answered on port 80 , or redirected to https (port 80 must reach ejabberd's ACME handler without a redirect) DANE ([digest] dane = true, the default, with dig installed): each live endpoint's certificate is compared with the TLSA records published for it (_5223._tcp.example.org): when 3 1 1 records exist and none is the certificate's public key, a warning says so once a day, with the value to publish; status and the digest show it. Without dig, or without any 3 1 1 record, nothing is said. With DANE, a renewal can change the key, so the safe order is: A certificate renewed alert arrives, carrying the new 3 1 1 value. Publish that TLSA record next to the old one. Wait for the DNS TTL to pass. Point certfiles at the new file and reload ejabberd. The renewed, but not in use check stops warning once the switch is done. If ejabberd's log level is lowered below debug, the "Storing certificate" line disappears. The cert_files disk check still notices the new file. vpsfort digest previews today's digest so far; vpsfort digest --send sends it now. After a restart the period continues; the first period after installation starts at installation. Hosts without ejabberd (the VPN node): [notify] is off there, so with the cluster on and notices in share, the digest and all admin-topic alerts are relayed as cluster facts. The XMPP node delivers them to its admins, prefixed with the origin node ([vpn] vpsfort daily digest); its own admin messages carry its name the same way ([xmpp] vpsfort daily digest, [xmpp] vpsfort: system). XMPP clients such as Conversations and Monal don't show a message's subject, so every admin message repeats it, with that tag, as the body's first line. Relayed messages bypass admin_topics and are rate-limited per message.
66.title: Daily digest (optional)

67.body: With [geo] enabled = true, addresses are labelled "Germany / Hetzner Online GmbH (AS24940)" in new-login alerts and their user notices, ban messages, compromise alerts, the TUI's Offenders tab ( where column and details), status, replay and the digest's top offenders. vpsfort geo [--download] <ip>... looks addresses up by hand. The TUI's Countries tab (7) lists the countries with active bans or tracked offenders, most offenders first, under an All countries row. The port histogram (local ports probed, TCP and UDP together, from addresses that aren't allowlisted or trusted; the counts are kept in the state file across restarts and halved once a day, so a probe from a week ago weighs 1/128 of one from today) and the network (ASN) list follow the selected row: select Germany and both show only Germany's traffic, a network present in several countries counting only its addresses there. The histogram for All countries works without [geo]. Ports are named from the daemon's configuration first ([ports] names = { "51820/udp" = "WireGuard" }, then [xmpp] c2s_ports as "XMPP client" and the cluster port as "vpsfort cluster"), then from a built-in list of well-known services (Telnet, RDP, Web HTTPS, STUN/TURN, ...); tui --actions has no daemon configuration, so it uses only the built-in names. The Map tab (8) draws active bans as red triangles and addresses that logged in during the last hour as green circles, both growing with the count, at their coordinates when a city-level database is loaded (see Cities and coordinates below; the addresses at one place grow one marker) and else at the country's capital (z zooms on Europe, where capitals crowd together, and back): the free country database names countries, not towns. A subnet ban counts once, located by its first address. Nothing leaves the server per lookup. Two databases are downloaded weekly into /var/lib/vpsfort/geo/, and lookups happen in memory: DB-IP IP to Country Lite (~4.5 MB gzipped). The country is geolocated per address range, not just where the network is registered, which matters for VPN exits and cloud regions. DB-IP IP to ASN Lite (~7 MB). It gives the network owner's real name, e.g. "Cloudflare, Inc.". Both are free, need no account, are updated monthly, and are licensed CC BY 4.0, so the digest carries the credit line "IP locations: DB-IP.com". iptoasn.com 's ip2asn-combined.tsv.gz (public domain, 9 MB) also works for asn_url; it names networks by registry handle ("HETZNER-AS"). A database of your own: country_url and asn_url take any https source (DB-IP's commercial downloads are such URLs), and fetch any command that prints the file (the URL is appended; {month} is optional). The files are read as they are, gzipped CSV: DB-IP's commercial IP to Country (start,end,continent,country) replaces the lite country database with no conversion, and the columns of its city lite, IP to Location, IP to ISP and IP to Location + ISP files are known too (the country, never the continent; from the ISP files the AS number and the organisation name, the ISP's name where that is empty). A header row, when a file has one, names the columns (country or country_code, city, latitude, longitude, asn or as_number, organization_name, name, isp_name), so IPinfo's CSVs read as well; without one the layout is told by the columns' count and content, and a file in no known layout is refused with a message that says so. MMDB files are not read: that format is looked up in place, so the whole file would sit in memory next to the ranges (DB-IP's IP to ISP MMDB is 465 MB), and MaxMind's databases (MMDB, or CSVs keyed by GeoName ID) therefore still need an export to these columns. The credit line is shown for DB-IP's free data only. Sizes: DB-IP's commercial IP to Country has 1.2 million ranges and costs about what the lite one does. Its IP to ISP (13.7 million rows, 1.1 GB) and IP to Location (41 million rows) files are far beyond a 128 MB unit and are refused, so the lite network database (or iptoasn's) stays the network half. A database with more than [geo] max_ranges (2,000,000) ranges is refused; raising it allows a bigger one, with the unit's memory limit raised to match (a range takes 16 bytes for IPv4 and 24 for IPv6, about twice that while it loads): the drop-in is under "Memory" below, and the daemon warns at start when the bound exceeds the unit. Cities and coordinates: a city-level database (DB-IP's city lite, its IP to Location, or a CSV whose header names city, latitude and longitude) adds the city and the range's coordinates to what is kept: labels read "Germany, Nuremberg / Hetzner Online GmbH (AS24940)" in alerts, bans, the TUI's details and the digest, and the TUI's and the web console's maps draw each ban and login at its coordinates (to a hundredth of a degree), at the capital only where the database has none. The status snapshot carries the located places (world.spots, at most 1,000, the most bans first; the rest draws at the capitals), so a console reading an older node, or a node without coordinates, draws it as before. DB-IP's city lite has 7.8 million ranges (660 MB as CSV, about 120 MB gzipped): with max_ranges = 8000000 and the unit at MemoryMax=512M (the drop-in under "Memory") it loads, taking an estimated 150 MB in memory and up to twice that while loading; not in the default unit, where it is refused before anything is read. A network pinned by places keeps neither city nor coordinates (the database was wrong about it). Cost: about 1.2 million ranges load in under a second and take about 40 MB of memory. IPv6 is kept at /64 granularity. Wrong countries: the lite data places some networks where they are registered, not where they are used (a server in Georgia on addresses registered in Latin America shows as Brazil). [geo] places = { "198.51.100.0/24" = "GE" } pins such networks to the right country (an ISO code or a name; the most specific network wins), ahead of the database: in labels, accounts' countries and the counters. [geoblock] keeps the database's own ranges. New-login alerts by provider: an account's networks are still learned per /16, but a login from a new /16 of a provider (ASN) the account already used is no news. Mobile carriers and VPN services hand out addresses from many /16s, so this removes most of the noise for your VPN users. Failures: each download must decompress and parse before it replaces the previous copy. A failed refresh raises a daily warning and keeps the old data, and without any database the labels simply don't appear.

68.body:
vpsfort warns the affected user, and admins, over XMPP with ejabberdctl send_message chat <from> <to> <subject> <body> (mod_admin_extra). It doesn't use announce_send_all, which would message everyone. Configure it in [notify]: topic user admins when account_attack ✓ ✓ about 20 failed logins on one account from 3+ addresses within an hour brute_force ✓ ✓ an address is banned after failed logins on that account compromise ✓ ✓ a successful login right after failures/suspicious activity from the same address new_network opt-in – a login from a /16 never seen for that account (after the 7-day learning period) registration, false_positive, protected, system – ✓ new account, a banned address that later logged in, an allowlisted/trusted address crossing the threshold, ejabberd hiding IPs exposure, integrity – ✓ listeners/firewall drift; new or changed cron jobs, infected files, failed or missing virus scans Shadow mode: only admins are messaged (users_in_shadow = false). Rate limits: one message per recipient, incident and account every 6 h; an attack alert and the bans it triggers count as one incident. Admin alerts without an account (system, exposure) are de-duplicated by their message. At most max_per_hour (30) messages per hour to users in total, and the same again for admins per topic , so a flood of account alerts can't silence system or compromise alerts. Languages: users get their messages in English, French, German, Polish, Russian or Ukrainian. [notify] language = "en" sets the default, and [notify.languages] overrides it per account, by user name (alice = "uk") or full JID ("alice@example.org" = "ru"). Names like "russian" work too. Plural forms and ban durations are translated as well ("заблокирован на 6 часов"); place names from [geo] stay in English, and admin messages are always English. notify-test <jid> sends the test message in that account's language. Only the recipient's own account is mentioned. When one address attacked several accounts, each user's message names only their own. Only real accounts are warned. User notices go only to accounts vpsfort has seen log in successfully. An attacker failing logins against made-up names on your domain can't make the server message them or use up the hourly budget; admins still get the alert. Sending: happens in a background thread with a 20 s timeout per ejabberdctl call, so a slow ejabberd never delays detection. Use CTL_OVER_HTTP (ejabberd 25.03 and later). By default every ejabberdctl call starts a second Erlang VM: tens of MB and about half a second each, counted against vpsfort's memory limit. With CTL_OVER_HTTP, ejabberdctl sends each command over a local Unix socket using curl instead (measured on the XMPP server: 0.15 s, a few MB). Add a listener to the existing listen: list, and an entry under the existing api_permissions: section (YAML keeps only one copy of a repeated key, so don't start a second one): listen: - port: "unix:ctl_over_http.sock" module: ejabberd_http tag: "ctl_over_http" unix_socket: mode: '0600' # the ejabberd user and root only request_handlers: /ctl: ejabberd_ctl
api_permissions: "console commands over http": from: - tag: "ctl_over_http" who: all what: "*" Then set CTL_OVER_HTTP=ctl_over_http.sock in ejabberdctl.cfg, restart ejabberd, and check that time ejabberdctl status answers in well under a second. curl must be installed. …but send vpsfort's messages through ejabberd's HTTP API. ejabberdctl over that socket loses messages and garbles text, so vpsfort doesn't use it for messages: It puts its arguments into JSON without escaping them, so ejabberd rejects every message with a line break or a quote (HTTP handler crashed: exception error: {invalid_byte,10} in ejabberd.log), which is nearly every alert and the digest. ejabberdctl still exits successfully, so vpsfort logged them as "notified". ejabberd's /ctl handler re-encodes each argument byte by byte, so anything beyond ASCII arrives garbled ("→" as "â" and two boxes; Cyrillic and emoji alike), whoever sends it. The REST API (mod_http_api) keeps text intact, but only over TCP: on the Unix socket it answers every call with 400 Bad Request. So add a listener on loopback that serves only /api, with a permission that allows only send_message: listen: - port: 5285 ip: "127.0.0.1" module: ejabberd_http tag: "vpsfort_api" request_handlers: /api: mod_http_api
api_permissions: "vpsfort notifications": from: - tag: "vpsfort_api" who: all what: send_message and set api = "127.0.0.1:5285" in [notify]. Every local process can reach that port, so it can send messages as the server, or as any account, and nothing else. Better: let only a dedicated account call it. Create vpsfort@example.org with a long random password, put the password in /etc/vpsfort/xmpp-api.password (root, mode 0600), set api_user = "vpsfort@example.org" and api_password_file = "/etc/vpsfort/xmpp-api.password" in [notify] (vpsfort then sends HTTP Basic authentication), and grant the command to that account instead of to all: api_permissions: "vpsfort notifications": from: - tag: "vpsfort_api" who: user: "vpsfort@example.org" what: send_message The from parameter of send_message is still free, so whoever holds that password can send as any JID; the file is root's only. If an existing api_permissions entry for mod_http_api allows the loopback ACL (the stock "http access" one does), it grants local processes every command on this listener too; remove loopback from it unless something relies on it. Without api, vpsfort can use ctl_socket = "/absolute/path/ctl_over_http.sock" (posts proper JSON to /ctl: line breaks and quotes work, non-ASCII is garbled and logged as a warning), else ejabberdctl. notify-test sends two lines with quotes and arrows, so all of this is visible in a test. XMPP accounts are messaged over XMPP; Nextcloud accounts through Nextcloud's own notifications (the bell, which its apps and e-mail reminders carry) when [notify] nextcloud_occ names the occ command: ["docker", "exec", "--user", "www-data", "nextcloud-aio-nextcloud", "php", "occ"] for AIO, ["sudo", "-u", "www-data", "php", "/var/www/nextcloud/occ"] for a Nextcloud of your own. vpsfort runs occ notification:generate with the subject and the text in the account's language ([notify.languages] by user name), under the same rules as XMPP users (the topics of user_topics, only accounts seen logging in, one message per incident every 6 hours, the hourly budget). SSH and other accounts go to admins only. Admin messages encrypted through the admin bot. With bot_outbox set (the XMPP server's /opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/outbox), messages to admins (alerts and the digest) go to the XMPP admin bot (vpsfort-xmpp-bot), which sends them OMEMO-encrypted and keeps them out of the server's archive. vpsfort puts each message in the outbox as a file (alert-*.msg, given to bot_user) and looks every 10 s. A message the bot hasn't taken within bot_grace (2m), one it refused (addressed to someone other than its admin), and one it started sending and never finished is claimed back and sent the usual way above, unencrypted, with a last line saying why. If the outbox is missing, messages go the usual way at once. Users' warnings always go the usual way. vpsfort also tells the admins when another file waits in the outbox longer than bot_stuck_after (1h), i.e. a weekly abuse report the bot can't send. notify-test --bot <admin> sends a test through the bot and waits for it. The bot's side is in vpsfort-xmpp-bot's README, "Alerts from vpsfort". The VPN host has no bot: its alerts reach the XMPP server through the cluster and go out from there. A copy on Telegram (optional). With tg_outbox set (vpsfort-tg-bot's /opt/vpsfort-tg-bot/outbox; unset by default, and then nothing goes to Telegram), every message to the first of admins (alerts, the digest, relayed VPN alerts, the bot warnings below) is also put in the Telegram bot's outbox, in the same file format and given to tg_user (vpsfort-tg-bot). vpsfort-tg-bot sends it to the admin's Telegram chat with XMPP account names replaced by pseudonyms. The XMPP way is unchanged, so there is no fallback for the copy: it waits until vpsfort-tg-bot sends it (vpsfort-tg-bot drops alerts older than a day). When copies wait longer than bot_stuck_after, vpsfort tells the admins the XMPP way, at most once per bot_stuck_after. Users' warnings never go there. notify-test --telegram puts a test there and waits up to a minute for vpsfort-tg-bot. The weekly abuse report goes there too (the job reads tg_outbox). The bot's side is in vpsfort-tg-bot's README. A copy by mail (optional). mail_outbox (vpsfort-mail-bot's /opt/vpsfort-mail-bot/outbox) and mail_user (vpsfort-mail-bot) work exactly like tg_outbox and tg_user, next to them or instead: every message to the first of admins (all admin messages with admins empty or xmpp = false) goes there too, and vpsfort-mail-bot mails it through the local Postfix or any SMTP server, the whole mail (subject included) OpenPGP-encrypted to the recipients' keys. No fallback; a mail bot that sits on copies longer than bot_stuck_after is reported over XMPP and to the Telegram bot (and the other way round). notify-test --mail puts a test there and waits up to a minute. The weekly abuse report goes there too. The bot's side is in vpsfort-mail-bot's README. A copy on Signal or Matrix (optional). signal_outbox/signal_user (/opt/vpsfort-signal-bot/outbox, vpsfort-signal-bot) and matrix_outbox/matrix_user (/opt/vpsfort-matrix-bot/outbox, vpsfort-matrix-bot) work exactly like tg_outbox, next to the others or instead. vpsfort-signal-bot sends through signal-cli while the safety number with the admin is the one it pinned; vpsfort-matrix-bot sends Olm/Megolm-encrypted to the devices the admin verified. Both send OpenPGP files instead when that isn't possible (or keep the copies waiting without an OpenPGP key). A bot that sits on copies longer than bot_stuck_after is reported over XMPP and to the other copy bots. notify-test --signal and --matrix put a test there and wait up to a minute. The weekly abuse report goes there too. The bots' sides are in their READMEs. A copy to a push service (optional). push_outbox/push_user (/opt/vpsfort-push-bot/outbox, vpsfort-push-bot) work exactly like tg_outbox: vpsfort-push-bot sends to ntfy, Gotify or any webhook, sanitized as for Telegram (none of them encrypts end to end), files only OpenPGP-encrypted (and not to Gotify, which takes none). notify-test --push puts a test there and waits up to a minute. The bot's side is in vpsfort-push-bot's README. A copy over XMPP from a host without ejabberd (optional). xmpp_outbox/xmpp_user (/opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot/outbox, vpsfort-xmpp-bot) work exactly like tg_outbox, for vpsfort-xmpp-bot in client mode (BOT_MODE=client): with an account on any XMPP server it sends the admin (any server too) OMEMO-encrypted messages and files, and OpenPGP files when OMEMO can't reach the admin (or keeps them waiting without an OpenPGP key). For a VPN server, a relay node or the desktop profile (deploy/vpsfort-desktop.toml names the lines). Not with bot_outbox: one vpsfort-xmpp-bot per host. notify-test --xmpp-client puts a test there and waits up to a minute. The bot's side is in vpsfort-xmpp-bot's README ("Client mode"). Admin messages on Telegram only. With tg_outbox and admins empty, admin messages go to vpsfort-tg-bot only and never over XMPP, while users are still warned over XMPP. A Telegram bot that leaves messages unsent is then raised as a system alert instead (journal, actions log, peers with relay_notices). Without ejabberd on the server, use xmpp = false instead. vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml notify-test you@example.org # on the server: one real test message
vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml notify-test --bot admin@example.org # the same through the admin bot (OMEMO)
vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml notify-test --telegram # a test through the Telegram bot (vpsfort-tg-bot)
vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml notify-test --mail # a test through the mail bot (vpsfort-mail-bot)
vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml notify-test --signal # a test through the Signal bot (vpsfort-signal-bot)
vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml notify-test --matrix # a test through the Matrix bot (vpsfort-matrix-bot)
vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml notify-test --push # a test through the push bot (vpsfort-push-bot: ntfy, Gotify, a webhook)
vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml notify-test --xmpp-client # a test through the XMPP client bot (vpsfort-xmpp-bot, BOT_MODE=client)
vpsfort -c vpsfort.toml replay --notify week.json # preview what would be sent (sends nothing) On the Sep–Oct month this would have sent 6 admin messages and no user messages; no account was attacked that month.

sudo vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml tui # live dashboard over the Unix socket
vpsfort replay --year 2026 weekly.log # offline: same pipeline, never touches the firewall
vpsfort replay -v --snapshot snap.json *.log # with evidence; then: vpsfort tui --file snap.json
vpsfort tui --actions actions.jsonl* [vpn.jsonl ...] # the state at the end of decision logs (read-only)
vpsfort print-config # effective configuration (all defaults)
vpsfort config-diff [--against old-defaults.toml] [--all] # what an upgrade means for your config file
vpsfort geo [--download] <ip>... # country / network owner from the offline database
vpsfort integrity # watched cron jobs/timers/scripts, recent virus scans
sudo vpsfort ssh-audit [--all] [--json] # sshd's settings against this host's layout, with fixes
sudo vpsfort self-audit # the modes and owners of vpsfort's own files (keys, config, state, outboxes)
vpsfort sysctl-audit [--all] [--json] # the kernel's hardening sysctls against good practice, with the line to set
vpsfort canary-check # accounts that can log in over SSH here but [canary] ssh matches (exit 1 if any)
vpsfort mirror # the peers' actions logs mirrored here ([cluster] mirror_to names this node on them)
vpsfort status --json # the daemon's whole snapshot (what the TUI and the console read)
vpsfort explain <ip|net> [--json] # scores, evidence, bans, allows, logins, place, recent decisions of one address
vpsfort quiet 2h [--topics a,b] [--note ...] / quiet off # hold the admins' messages back (decisions go on)
vpsfort baseline export FILE / import FILE # the learned baselines, for a reinstalled or cloned host (import with vpsfort stopped)
vpsfort log-digest [--day YYYY-MM-DD] # the hash of one day's actions log (what the peers get each night)
vpsfort log-digests [node] # the peers' daily log hashes this node holds (tamper evidence)
vpsfort abuse-report [--since 7d] [--contacts] [-o file] # evidence per attacker, for abuse desks
vpsfort cluster-send-report <file> # a JSON abuse report to the peers' inbox
vpsfort replay --state state.json *.log # also write the state file the daemon would keep
vpsfort print-nft [--no-tripwires] # ruleset installed in enforce mode
vpsfort status # plain-text summary: bans, cluster, exposure, offenders
vpsfort unban <ip|net> / ban <ip|net> --for 1d / allow <ip|net> --for 7d / disallow <ip|net> / allowed
vpsfort test-pattern [--pattern NAME] [-v] <file>... # what the [[patterns]] find in log lines
vpsfort expect-change PATH=SOURCE... # announce a watched file's new content (installers)
vpsfort feeds [status|refresh|clear] # blocklist feeds
vpsfort waf [status|refresh|clear] # decisions of WAFs: CrowdSec, ...
vpsfort digest [--send] # preview / send the daily digest
vpsfort cluster-keygen # new random cluster key
vpsfort cluster-identity --out /etc/vpsfort/node.key # this node's signing key; prints its line for [cluster] nodes
vpsfort cluster-key-id [--file deploy/cluster.key] # fingerprints of the keys in use (compare nodes)
vpsfort cluster-ufw-rules # ufw commands opening the cluster port to peers only replay accepts journalctl short output and journalctl -o json. To test new rules against real traffic first: journalctl -u ejabberd -u ssh -k --since -7d -o json > week.json && vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml replay week.json TUI keys (? shows them all; the footer shows the ones that work on the current tab): 1-9/Tab/←→ switch tabs (Overview, Offenders, Bans, Events, Accounts, Exposure, Countries, Map, Alerts, and 0 Patterns when [[patterns]] are configured) · ↑↓ select · PgUp/PgDn/Home/End page, first, last · Enter opens the details of the selected address, ban, decision or alert under the list (evidence, whole message, tracked addresses in a banned subnet; ↑↓ move on to the next row) · / filters the rows by any text in them (an address, a country, a signal; ↑↓ pick a row while it is typed, Enter keeps it, Esc clears it) · o sorts Offenders (danger, last seen, address) and Bans (newest, time left, address) · s cycles the minimum severity on Events and Alerts · t cycles the topic on Alerts · u unban · b ban for N days · a allowlist for N days · z zooms the map on Europe · PgUp/PgDn scroll the networks on the Countries tab · p pauses · r refreshes now · q or Ctrl-C quits (Esc doesn't). The cursor stays on the same address when a refresh re-sorts a list. The Overview's Health panel shows the cluster peers, blocklist feeds, certificates, disk and memory, the last virus scan and the cron watch, coloured by how they are doing; the footer shows the node, the mode (ENFORCE/SHADOW) and how fresh the data is (red when the daemon stopped answering). Snapshots load in the background, so the keys never wait for a busy daemon. In an 80-column terminal, less important columns (fast/slow scores, place, signals) are left out before addresses are cut, and the tab bar glues each number to its name (4Events). Alerts (9) lists the latest 50 alerts, newest first, however many bans came after them (the Events tab keeps the last 500 decisions, mostly bans, so on a busy day an alert scrolls out of it within hours): time, severity, topic (suspicious login, account under attack, exposure change, host integrity, system, ...), the accounts concerned and the message; its details add whether the address is still banned, the note sent to the user and the evidence. The tab bar and the Overview count the high and critical alerts of the last 24 hours in red. Patterns (0, only with [[patterns]] configured) lists each pattern with its kind, lines read from its unit or file, matched lines, last match, addresses, the lines it matched without an address in group ip, its port and where its lines come from; for the selected one it shows the 20 busiest addresses (lines, last seen, banned or how dangerous now) and the latest 5 lines without an address. tui --actions <file>... reads decision logs (/var/log/vpsfort/actions.jsonl and its rotated .gz copies, also ones copied to another machine, or the logs of several servers together) without the daemon and shows the state at their end: the bans still active then, the decisions, and per country and network the active bans, the sources banned during the period, their evidence lines and the ports in them. Nothing is re-scored. The tabs are Overview (period, bans per cause, from which peer, bans per hour), Bans, Events, Countries, Map, Trends and Alerts (the log's latest 500); scores, accounts and the exposure scan aren't in the log. Trends (6) shows bans per day over the whole log (as many recent days as fit) and a table of weeks (Monday to Sunday, UTC), newest first: bans, the change from the week before, distinct sources, and the three countries and networks most bans went to. Use it after a tuning change, e.g. a new slow_threshold, to see whether it cut the noise or let more through; merge rotated copies (actions.jsonl*) to cover more weeks. Places come from the [geo] database when it's set up on that machine, else from the ban messages, which name the place for bans decided on that server and for bans received from peers. Given several logs, a decision logged twice counts once: the same line in two files, or a ban received from a peer whose own log, with the original ban, is among the files (within 5 minutes). What's still banned at the end is worked out per log, so an unban in one log never ends another server's ban.

70.body:
Without a Rust toolchain: every version tag vpsfort-v<version> gets its bundle, vpsfort-<version>-<commit>-<arch>.zip for each architecture (x86_64-linux-musl, aarch64-linux-musl for arm64, armv7-linux-musleabihf for 32-bit ARMv7 with hardware floating point), as an asset of the tag's GitHub Release (see "Releases" in the repository README ); CI also keeps one for every commit as a workflow artifact (they expire and need a GitHub login), and scripts/bundle.sh builds it locally. It holds the static binary, everything deploy.sh copies to a server, the config templates in configs/, SHA256SUMS, and install.sh. Download and verify (on your machine, then copy the zip over, or on the server): take the zip for the server's architecture (uname -m: x86_64, aarch64, or armv7l for armv7) from the GitHub Release of the version's tag, with the GitHub CLI or from the Releases page (each crate's releases are tagged vpsfort-v<version>): arch=x86_64-linux-musl # the server's: aarch64-linux-musl (arm64), armv7-linux-musleabihf (32-bit ARM)
gh release download vpsfort-v0.6.1 --repo makhort/vpsfort --pattern "*-$arch.zip*" # the zip, its .sha256 and .sigstore.json
sha256sum -c vpsfort-*-$arch.zip.sha256 # the download is intact (macOS: shasum -a 256 -c)
gh attestation verify vpsfort-*-$arch.zip --repo makhort/vpsfort --source-ref refs/tags/vpsfort-v0.6.1 gh attestation verify (after gh auth login) checks the signed build provenance: that this repository's CI built exactly this zip from that tag. With --bundle vpsfort-*-$arch.zip.sigstore.json it checks the attestation attached to the Release instead of fetching it from GitHub. Only a public repository's releases have one (GitHub offers attestations for private repositories only with Enterprise Cloud). On the server (unzip comes with apt install unzip, or dnf install unzip): arch=x86_64-linux-musl # as above: aarch64-linux-musl, armv7-linux-musleabihf on ARM
unzip vpsfort-*-$arch.zip && cd vpsfort-*-$arch
sudo ./install.sh --template vpsfort-standalone.toml # a new server: only puts /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml in place (Fedora: vpsfort-standalone-dnf.toml)
sudoedit /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml # allowlist, [notify], [cluster] node_id and peers, ...
sudo ./install.sh # installs and starts vpsfort (in shadow mode) Templates (configs/, --template takes the file name, or the short one: tg for vpsfort-tg.toml): vpsfort.toml for an XMPP server (the default), vpsfort-standalone.toml for a host with SSH and UFW only, vpsfort-desktop.toml for a Linux desktop or laptop (--template desktop; "Desktops and laptops"), vpsfort-tg.toml for the Telegram relay node; each with a -dnf variant for Fedora and RHEL (vpn-dnf for vpsfort-standalone-dnf.toml; vpsfort-dnf.toml is the default on a host with dnf and no apt). A finished config can go in at once: sudo ./install.sh --config my.toml. Upgrades: run sudo ./install.sh from the new bundle. Your config stays; the matching template (by [cluster] node_id and package_manager) lands next to it as vpsfort.toml.new, and config-diff shows what the new version changes. The previous binary stays as /usr/local/bin/vpsfort.prev. Cluster key: the first node whose config has [cluster] enabled gets a new /etc/vpsfort/cluster.key. Copy it to the others (as root, mode 0600) and install them with sudo ./install.sh --cluster-key FILE. What it checks: root, Linux, systemd, and that the bundle's binary runs here (the bundle's TARGET names its architecture). It copies the bundle into a directory only root can write and checks every file against SHA256SUMS there, so a non-root owner of the unzipped files can't swap them in between; then it runs the same install.sh as deploy.sh (below). ./install.sh --check only checks the files. SHA256SUMS catches damaged files, not a forged bundle: that is what the attestation (above) is for.
