71.body:
The same release has a package per architecture, for the distribution's package manager instead of install.sh: vpsfort_<version>-1_<arch>.deb (amd64, arm64, armhf; Debian, Ubuntu and their derivatives) vpsfort-<version>-1.<arch>.rpm (x86_64, aarch64, armv7hl; Fedora, RHEL and its rebuilds) and vpsfort-<version>-r0.<arch>.apk (x86_64, aarch64, armv7; Alpine, with OpenRC: below), each with its .sha256 and .sigstore.json, downloaded and verified as the bundle above (--pattern "*.deb*", "*.rpm*" or "*.apk*"). CI keeps them for every commit as workflow artifacts, and scripts/package.sh builds them locally (cargo install cargo-deb cargo-generate-rpm --locked once, and python3 for the .apk, which scripts/apk.py at the repository's root writes; none needs dpkg, rpm or apk-tools, so it runs on macOS too; --target aarch64-unknown-linux-musl or armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf for the ARM ones). Or from the signed apt and dnf repository on GitHub Pages, once it is set up (the repository README, "Deployment"), where apt upgrade and dnf upgrade then bring new versions. sudo apt install ./vpsfort_0.6.1-1_amd64.deb # Debian, Ubuntu; Fedora, RHEL: sudo dnf install ./vpsfort-0.6.1-1.x86_64.rpm
sudoedit /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml # a new host: the template is in place, nothing runs yet
sudo vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml print-config > /dev/null && sudo systemctl enable --now vpsfort vpsfort-abuse-report.timer Paths: /usr/bin/vpsfort (the bundle: /usr/local/bin), /usr/bin/vpsfort-avscan and /usr/bin/vpsfort-abuse-report, the units and timers in /usr/lib/systemd/system, the config templates in /usr/share/vpsfort/templates (vpsfort.toml, -vpn, -tg, -desktop, each with a -dnf variant: on a new host copy another one over /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml). /etc/vpsfort, /etc/default/vpsfort-avscan, /etc/default/vpsfort-abuse-report and /etc/logrotate.d/vpsfort are the same as the bundle's; the last three are the package's config files (dpkg asks about them on an upgrade only if you changed them; rpm keeps yours and saves the new one as .rpmnew). Nothing starts on its own. A new host gets the template (vpsfort-dnf.toml where dnf is the package manager, else vpsfort.toml) as /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml: its names and addresses are examples, so vpsfort isn't enabled or started until you run the lines above. The timers are yours to enable too (vpsfort-abuse-report.timer; vpsfort-avscan.timer with [antivirus]); once enabled they stay enabled across upgrades. Upgrades: the config stays; the matching template (by [cluster] node_id and package_manager, as install.sh picks it) lands next to it as vpsfort.toml.new, and config-diff against the previous version's defaults is printed. vpsfort is restarted only if it was running and the config is valid for the new version (print-config accepts it); otherwise it keeps running the previous version and the install says what to fix. The cluster port is opened for the peers as install.sh does (ufw, or firewalld's rich rules; plain iptables rules are only printed). Over a bundle or deploy.sh install: the package takes it over. The bundle's binaries under /usr/local (vpsfort, vpsfort.prev, the two helper scripts) and its units in /etc/systemd/system (they would shadow the package's) are removed, what was enabled is enabled again on the package's units, and the config, the cluster key, the state and the timer settings stay; then vpsfort is restarted if it was running. Where the bundle's /etc/default/vpsfort-avscan or vpsfort-abuse-report differs from the package's, dpkg asks what to do with it (D shows the difference, N keeps yours), and rpm keeps yours and saves its own next to it as .rpmnew. The integrity watch reports each removed file as a warning once (/usr/local/bin and /etc/systemd/system are watched by content; the new paths are the package manager's, covered by the weekly package check). Replacing the config: when a terminal is there, the install asks whether to replace the config with this version's template (the old one kept as vpsfort.toml.old); Enter, a timeout of a minute, no terminal or DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive keep it. VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace (or keep) answers without asking: sudo VPSFORT_PACKAGE_CONFIG=replace apt install ./vpsfort_*.deb. After a replacement vpsfort keeps running with the old config until you edit the new one and restart it. Rollback, removal: rollback is installing the previous version's package (apt install ./vpsfort_<old>.deb --allow-downgrades, dnf downgrade ./vpsfort-<old>.rpm); there is no vpsfort.prev. apt remove vpsfort (dnf remove) stops and disables the service and timers and keeps /etc/vpsfort, /var/lib/vpsfort and /var/log/vpsfort; apt purge vpsfort removes them too, cluster key and state included (rpm has no purge: delete them by hand). dpkg-reconfigure vpsfort (rpm: dnf reinstall ./vpsfort-*.rpm) runs the post-install step again. Alpine (apk, OpenRC): apk add --allow-untrusted ./vpsfort-<version>-r0.x86_64.apk puts the same files in the same places, with the OpenRC script /etc/init.d/vpsfort instead of the unit (supervised by supervise-daemon, started again 5 seconds after a crash, vpsfort's own messages in /var/log/vpsfort/daemon.log; the unit's sandboxing and capability bound have no equivalent there) and, instead of the timers, /usr/share/vpsfort/periodic/vpsfort-abuse-report and vpsfort-avscan to link into /etc/periodic/weekly/ and /etc/periodic/daily/ (busybox crond runs them; the settings stay in /etc/default/). The package is unsigned, hence --allow-untrusted: sha256sum -c and the attestation verify it. Alpine has no journal: a new host gets vpsfort-alpine.toml as its config, which follows /var/log/messages instead ("Requirements", Alpine) and turns off what needs apt or dnf ([patches], [verify]) and systemd ([sources] services). The install scripts are POSIX sh: a first install puts the template in place and starts nothing; an upgrade keeps the config, saves the new template as vpsfort.toml.new and restarts a running vpsfort when the config is valid, then runs canary-check. Then rc-update add vpsfort default && rc-service vpsfort start. apk del vpsfort stops it and keeps /etc/vpsfort, the state and the logs. Not yet run on an Alpine host: CI installs the package in an Alpine container.

72.body:
Deploy in shadow mode (the default), next to the existing cron jobs: ./deploy/deploy.sh # on the Mac: tests, builds the static binary, copies to the ssh host given (or deploy.sh's default)
# then paste the command it prints into a root shell on the server UFW logging must be on for firewall signals (ufw logging low). Review for 1–2 weeks using vpsfort tui and /var/log/vpsfort/actions.jsonl. Look for "likely false positive" and "crossed the ban threshold" (protected-address) alerts, and tune weights in /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml. Enforce: set mode = "enforce" and run systemctl restart vpsfort. Then check: nft list table inet vpsfort # rules + ban sets with remaining timeouts The table hooks at prerouting right after connection tracking (priority mangle - 1), so it runs before UFW's chains and Docker's DNAT; your ALLOW rules can no longer shadow the bans. Allowlisted networks get an explicit accept in that table too, and so do replies to the server's own connections. Rollback: set mode = "shadow", restart, then nft delete table inet vpsfort. Retire the Python pipeline: remove /etc/cron.d/log_analyzer and /etc/cron.d/daily_log_analyzer. Keep daily_cleanup (ejabberd DB maintenance). Done on both servers in 2026-10; the Python files are gone from this repo too (see the git history). Delete, never reorder, the old auto-generated UFW deny rules (blocked_*, ejabberd_*). They sit below the ALLOW rules, so they never matched traffic to open ports: in Sep–Oct 2026, 4,438 XMPP connections and 106 SSH sessions came from addresses they "deny". Several of them also cover your own users. In that month, people logged in from 12.209.15.0/24, 13.149.62.0/24, 13.235.62.0/24, 11.165.47.0/24, and 12.19.56.0/24. Making those rules effective would lock those users out.
72.title: Rollout

73.body: Upgrading: install.sh keeps your /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml and saves the new template next to it as vpsfort.toml.new. Before replacing the binary, it saves the old version's defaults (print-config without a config file). After installing, it runs: vpsfort -c /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml config-diff --against <old defaults> That lists unknown options (typos, or removed ones; the daemon refuses to start with them), new options with their defaults, changed defaults (marked as unaffected if your file sets the option), and whether the file is valid. Run it by hand any time; without --against it lists the sections your file doesn't set, and --all lists every option. The bots' new names (2026-10-17): xmppbot is now vpsfort-xmpp-bot (/opt/vpsfort-xmpp-bot, vpsfort-xmpp-bot.service) and tgbot is vpsfort-tg-bot (/opt/vpsfort-tg-bot, vpsfort-tg-bot.service, user vpsfort-tg-bot, the new default of tg_user). Deploy this vpsfort first (its abuse report unit may write to the new outboxes), then each bot: the bot's install.sh moves its old install over and rewrites the old outbox paths, tg_user and unit names in vpsfort.toml and /etc/default/vpsfort-abuse-report (keeping a copy of each), then restarts vpsfort. The bots' READMEs have the details. Rolling back: the replaced binary is kept as /usr/local/bin/vpsfort.prev (a package install: the previous version's package instead, "Install from a package"). vpsfort --version shows the git commit a binary was built from (plus ", modified" for uncommitted changes), and git checkout <commit> && ./deploy/deploy.sh rebuilds any earlier version. After a reboot vpsfort re-applies everything that lives only in the kernel: active bans, operator allowlist entries and blocklist feeds. It resumes the journal from its saved position. If journald no longer accepts that position, for example because old journal files were vacuumed, it falls back to initial_lookback instead of retrying forever. Events from history are scored on their own timestamps, and anything carrying wall-clock time (exposure scans, cluster messages, Nextcloud's live logs) waits until the backlog is processed.

73.title: Restarts, reboots and upgrades

74.body:
The unit runs as root with a capability bound of nine (CapabilityBoundingSet in vpsfort.service): NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW for nft, ipset, iptables, ufw and wg, NET_BIND_SERVICE for honeypot ports below 1024, DAC_READ_SEARCH and SYS_PTRACE for other users' crontabs, scripts and keys and for /proc/<pid>/fd, exe and root, DAC_OVERRIDE for the metrics textfile in node_exporter's directory and files the bots own, CHOWN, FOWNER and FSETID for the outboxes' files and the console socket's group. A bug in a parser can't load a module, mount, reboot or change the clock with these. Transient units (systemd-run: apt, dnf, the scanners) are started by PID 1 and keep their own capabilities. The unit runs with MemoryHigh=112M and MemoryMax=128M (child processes included). Measured peaks: scenario vpsfort with [geo] a month of real traffic (Sep–Oct, ~210k records) ~10 MB ~50 MB synthetic flood: 280,000 sources, no bans ~37 MB ~66 MB synthetic flood: 450,000 sources, 222,700 bans in 42 h ~80 MB ~115 MB The patch status's apt-get -s (or dnf check-update) runs in a transient unit of its own (systemd-run), outside this limit; the weekly package check drops what it reads from the page cache as it goes. systemctl status vpsfort shows a peak that includes page cache (journal and geo files read at start), which the kernel reclaims under the limit rather than killing anything. The floods are far beyond what's possible from UFW: its log rules are rate-limited to about 3 lines a minute (the real month had 141,772, which is exactly that). Per-address state is about 600 bytes, and [scoring] max_tracked_ips (50,000) bounds it. The real month peaked at about 4,200 addresses over two days. When the cap is reached, the least suspicious 20% are dropped (banned ones last, and they stay banned). The geo database is released before a weekly reload, so two copies never coexist. If memory is ever tight, [geo] enabled = false saves 30–40 MB. A bigger geo database needs a bigger unit. The 128 MB are sized for DB-IP's lite databases (about 1.2 million ranges together, 40 MB); DB-IP's commercial IP to Country (1.2 million ranges on its own) still fits, about 10 MB more. A city-level database (DB-IP's city lite: 7.8 million ranges, with a city and coordinates per range) or anything else beyond [geo] max_ranges (2,000,000) does not: a range takes 16 bytes (IPv4) or 24 (IPv6), and about twice that while it loads. Raise the two together, the bound in vpsfort.toml and the limit in a drop-in that survives upgrades (install.sh replaces vpsfort.service, not vpsfort.service.d/): systemctl edit vpsfort [Service]
MemoryHigh=448M
MemoryMax=512M then systemctl restart vpsfort (the cron watch reports the new drop-in once, as it does any unit change). Reckon with 32 bytes per range allowed plus 64 MB for the rest: max_ranges = 8000000 is about 310 MB. At start the daemon compares that estimate with its cgroup's memory.max and logs a warning when max_ranges was raised beyond what the unit holds; DB-IP's IP to ISP and IP to Location editions (13.7 and 41 million rows) are beyond any sensible unit and are refused by the bound.
74.title: Memory

75.body: path purpose /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml configuration (deploy/vpsfort.toml is the annotated template; the package keeps the templates in /usr/share/vpsfort/templates) /var/lib/vpsfort/state.json journal cursor, bans, repeat offenders, trusted IPs, per-account networks, providers and SSH keys, the cron/file, package, set-uid and outbound-connection baselines. Gzip-compressed JSON (zcat state.json | jq .; older plain-JSON files are still read). Saved at most every 10 min when something changed, hourly otherwise, and on stop. After a crash the journal is replayed from the saved cursor, and bans live on in the kernel, so nothing is lost. After the Sep–Oct month the file was 95 KB (539 KB before), which is at most ~14 MB of writes a day instead of ~150 MB. An unreadable file is renamed to state.bad-<time> (not overwritten), and a high system alert says what was lost /var/lib/vpsfort/geo/ offline country and network databases ([geo]) /var/log/vpsfort/actions.jsonl audit log of every ban, unban and alert (rotated weekly by /etc/logrotate.d/vpsfort, 12 weeks kept). A ban decided here carries signals (what the source did, per signal, as data) and the place; a peer's ban carries the place this node knows and up to 3 of the peer's evidence lines /var/log/vpsfort/actions.jsonl.index the log's hourly index: for each hour with a decision, the offset of its first line, so a reader of the last day or week (the console's abuse report) starts there instead of parsing months. Advisory: its header names the log file (inode), a fresh one starts after a rotation (also when the log is truncated in place, as logrotate's copytruncate does), and an entry is used only if a line of that hour really starts at its offset /run/vpsfort/vpsfort.sock snapshot socket for the TUI (root only) /run/vpsfort-console/console.sock read-only snapshots for vpsfort-web ([console]; root and its group) /etc/vpsfort/cluster.key shared cluster key (mode 0600; same file on every node) /var/lib/vpsfort/feeds/ last good copy of each blocklist feed /usr/local/sbin/vpsfort-avscan, /etc/systemd/system/vpsfort-avscan.{service,timer} (the package: /usr/bin/vpsfort-avscan, /usr/lib/systemd/system/) the daily ClamAV scan ([antivirus]); settings in /etc/default/vpsfort-avscan /var/log/vpsfort/avscan.log scan results read by vpsfort (rotated monthly) /usr/local/sbin/vpsfort-abuse-report, /etc/systemd/system/vpsfort-abuse-report.{service,timer} (the package: /usr/bin/vpsfort-abuse-report, /usr/lib/systemd/system/) the weekly abuse report for the admin bot; settings in /etc/default/vpsfort-abuse-report /var/lib/vpsfort/inbox/ reports peers sent with cluster-send-report (mode 0700; deleted once merged) /var/lib/vpsfort/file-positions.json where each followed log file ([[patterns]] file, [sources] apps, audit_log) was left: inode and offset, saved every 30 s and at stop, so a restart reads the lines written meanwhile (a rotation during the downtime from the new file's start; a position older than a day is left alone). A followed log is read at its own path only: a symbolic link, a pipe or a device there is not read (said once in the journal), since a service's user who owns the log directory (postgres, mysql, redis do) could otherwise point root's reader at any file of the host /var/lib/vpsfort/mirror/<node>.jsonl ([cluster] mirror_dir) the actions log of each peer that names this node in mirror_to, as it sends it (mode 0600 in a 0700 directory; .1: the previous copy) [metrics] textfile (e.g. /var/lib/prometheus/node-exporter/vpsfort.prom) Prometheus metrics for node_exporter's textfile collector, rewritten every minute; off by default
75.title: Files

76.body:
The project is a git repository. scripts/ci.sh runs what CI runs: cargo fmt --check, clippy with warnings as errors, the tests, cargo audit (fails on known vulnerabilities, unsound code and yanked versions of dependencies; unmaintained ones are only reported; offline it uses the advisory database already on disk), cargo deny (the repository's deny.toml: permissive licenses only, crates from crates.io only, two versions of one crate reported but not refused), the static musl build, and a parse check of every config template. deploy/deploy.sh runs it before every deployment, scripts/install-hooks.sh makes every git push that touches vpsfort/ run it, and .github/workflows/vpsfort.yml runs it on GitHub. ./scripts/ci.sh # all checks (~1 min); VPSFORT_SKIP_AUDIT=1 skips cargo audit and cargo deny
cargo test # tests only
cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl # static Linux binary from macOS (rust-lld, see .cargo/config.toml)
cargo build --release --target aarch64-unknown-linux-musl # the same for arm64; armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf for 32-bit ARM
TARGET=aarch64-unknown-linux-musl ./deploy/deploy.sh ... # deploy to an arm64 server (ci.sh builds $TARGET)
cargo install cargo-audit --locked # once, for the dependency check
./scripts/install-hooks.sh # once: git push runs ci.sh (skip: git push --no-verify) Fuzzing. fuzz/ holds three cargo-fuzz targets. records feeds arbitrary input in every log format vpsfort reads (journal JSON, syslog lines, Nextcloud's JSON log) through the parsers and the decision engine, then lets a day pass for their timers. Attackers shape those lines (user names, request paths, banners), so nothing in them may panic, hang or grow without bound. actions_log feeds a decision log (actions.jsonl as peers and older versions wrote it, or a damaged rotated copy) through what reads it back: the dashboard's log view (tui --actions) and the live abuse report. log_index feeds a forged or damaged hourly index (below) against a log and checks that a reader is never sent into the middle of a line or past the end. The targets' code is src/fuzzing.rs. tests/fuzz_smoke.rs runs them on stable over the seeds in fuzz/seeds/<target>/ (made-up lines with documentation addresses) and fixed mutations, so cargo test and ci.sh keep them working (the first run of actions_log found an overflow on an impossible time). The real search needs nightly: rustup toolchain install nightly --profile minimal && cargo install cargo-fuzz --locked # once
cargo +nightly fuzz run records fuzz/corpus/records fuzz/seeds/records -- -dict=fuzz/records.dict -max_total_time=600 -max_len=8192 The same for actions_log and log_index (no dictionary). New inputs collect in fuzz/corpus/ and crashes in fuzz/artifacts/ (both git-ignored; replay a crash with cargo +nightly fuzz run records <file>). Don't seed it from the month of real logs: the corpus would hold real addresses. The first run (2026-10-16: 630,000 inputs in 2 minutes) found nothing.
76.title: Development

77.body: tests/real_nft.rs enforces on a real kernel with the real nft, as root: the ruleset the daemon writes (chains, sets, the kernel tripwire rules, a rate limit, a whitelisted port) is what the kernel takes, bans and operator allows land in their sets with their time left, an unban removes one, a feed loads, and the table deleted (as nft flush ruleset does) is rebuilt with the bans still active. It uses a table of its own (inet vpsfort_ci) and runs only with VPSFORT_REAL_NFT=1 as root; CI runs it on its x86_64 and arm64 runners, and then the installed daemon in enforce mode: an operator ban in the set, the table deleted and back within 30 s with the ban, an unban. Every other enforcement test uses a stand-in nft. tests/layouts.rs runs the daemon itself in each deployment layout ("Deployment layouts"): the vpsfort binary with a stand-in journalctl (attacks stamped now), a stand-in nft recording every ruleset, a stand-in ejabberd API, the bots' outboxes and peers on 127.0.0.1. It needs to bind 127.0.0.1 (a sandbox that forbids it fails these tests). It found that every relayed alert of the same kind after the first was dropped for 6 hours ([vpn] vpsfort: password guessing blocked for one attacker, then nothing for the next); fixed 2026-10-17. Replays of the servers' own logs (kept out of this repository) showed: One week of ejabberd logs (August). One month of all three sources (Sep 11 – Oct 11), about 210k records. This replays in about 1 s and produces 185 bans of 93 distinct targets: 54 subnets, and hosts whose main trigger was UFW port scanning (83) or XMPP TLS/silent-connection probing. None of those targets ever authenticated successfully, and no user address was banned. The only failed logins that month were 8 expired FAST tokens from real users. Formats seen in the real logs and handled: OpenSSH 10 sshd-session lines. kex_exchange_identification resets without [preauth]. ejabberd hidden_by_ejabberd. This triggers a high alert, because client IPs were hidden from Sep 27 to Oct 2 (hide_sensitive_log_data), which blinds XMPP detection. FAST (mod_auth_fast) and SQL-backend logins. In-band registrations. UFW TCP/UDP/ICMP/GRE blocks, including from Docker bridges.
77.title: Validation

78.body: Five nodes run live in enforce mode: one Ubuntu 22.04 (the VPN host, kernel 5.15), three Debian 13 (the XMPP and Nextcloud server, kernel 6.12, since mid-October 2026 after a shadow-mode period, and two more that joined in late October 2026) and one Fedora 44 (the test server below, which stayed on). Every node signs its facts and pins the others' keys, and one web console shows all five. Below, "both hosts" means the VPN host and the XMPP server, and "another node" one of the Debian nodes that joined later. Everything listed here was seen on these servers; what has only been seen in tests is under "Not yet verified".

79.body: Live journald input on both hosts: follow, resume from the saved cursor after restarts, and per-source "last log line" ages in vpsfort status. A source gone quiet : the warning after 2 h without SSH lines and 6 h without ejabberd lines ("detection for it is blind - is sshd running and logging to the journal?"). Bans in nftables on both hosts (nftables 1.0 on the VPN host): table, sets, timeouts, and shadow-mode bans restored when enforcing began. Allowlists with overlapping entries, which used to make the setup fall back to ufw. Bans after connection tracking (the bans chain), on another node: IPv4 bans drop traffic, and so do IPv6 bans, including /64 subnet bans (8 bad addresses in subnet, distributed probing) with the addresses inside shown as banned; subnet bans grew from a /24 to a /22. The server's own connections to a banned address get their replies: ping reached two addresses banned there while their bans ran, and curl to a banned address's web server got its answer (308 Permanent Redirect, Caddy) with the ban 40 minutes from its end. Self-healing on the VPN host: after nft delete table inet vpsfort, the table came back within 30 s with all its sets and chains (bans, allowlists, operator allows, blocklist feeds, rate limits), every active ban re-added with its remaining time, and a high system alert reached the admin. Kernel rate limits on the VPN host: the rl chain loads, and status reads its drop counters. SSH canary accounts : real probers trying canary names on the VPN host were banned. Blocklist feeds on both hosts: Spamhaus DROP (v4 and v6) and FireHOL level 1 download, about 4,700 networks after dropping overlaps, active in nftables. The 13 skipped entries are private or reserved ranges (FireHOL lists e.g. 10.0.0.0/8), networks wider than min_prefix_v4/v6, and anything overlapping this host, a cluster peer or the allowlist. Geo database downloads (DB-IP lite) and readable places in bans and alerts. Operator controls over the control socket: an allow / allowed / disallow round trip (unban uses the same path).

80.body: Facts between nodes in both directions, the same ban list on every node, and repeat offences escalating across nodes: an SSH canary prober was banned on one node and the ban escalated on the other. Node identities : every node signs its facts and pins the others' keys with require_signatures = true (vpsfort status with four nodes: "3 node keys pinned, others refused"), and bans flow between them as before. Forward secrecy between the real nodes : after a restart, each of the four peers answered the key exchange (cluster: peer <address>:7946 answers key exchanges: forward secrecy on). A node that stops answering : the "cluster node is not responding" alert while one server was reinstalled. Relayed messages : the VPN node's alerts relayed through the cluster to the XMPP admin account, and its daily digest to the Matrix room of another node.

81.body: Exposure watch with real /proc/net and ufw status: Docker-published ports recognised as bypassing ufw, and dead-rule alerts debounced while containers are recreated. On another node both directions of a port change: a new listener (new internet-facing listener 0.0.0.0:7948/tcp (vpsfort-web, allowed by ufw)) and an allow rule with nothing behind it (ufw allows 7949/tcp from anywhere, but nothing listens on it publicly). Process watch on another node: 3 outbound (program, port) pairs learned, then new outbound connections reported (the Matrix bot's first connection to port 443, and curl as root). Certificate checks with openssl, including Let's Encrypt's 6-day certificates on the Nextcloud endpoint (judged by their own lifetime). Cron watch, antivirus results and out-of-memory alerts : the learn period, change alerts with dpkg origins, the vpsfort-avscan timer, and kernel OOM kills (which uncovered weeks of clamscan being killed for memory, and freshclam being disabled). Scans of changed files (scan_changed): on the VPN host a changed sshd_config scanned with clamscan; on another node (scan_changed = "both") a new file in /usr/local/bin scanned with clamscan and YARA (Debian's yara 4.5, YARA Forge's core set compiled with yarac to one .yarc): scanned 1 of 1 changed files with ClamAV (clamscan) and YARA (1 rule file): nothing found, both through systemd-run. su alerts on the XMPP server: su from the SSH gateway user to root, and between root and the ejabberd account (the database cleanup script), each with the account's last SSH login and its place; and the warning for a switch that succeeded after a failed attempt (su to root by <user> on pts/0 succeeded after 1 failed attempts, the admin's own typo of the su password), with the account's last SSH login. A canary login on another node: the gateway user had been left out of [canary] except, so its SSH login raised the critical LOGGED IN to canary account alert and banned the admin's address (the failed su right after was reported too, as if it wasn't you, someone has <user>'s login); the admin came back through the provider's console. Now vpsfort canary-check and the installers warn about such an account first ("Canary accounts"). Account changes : vpsfort-web's installer creating its user and group was reported (new account vpsfort-web (UID ...), shell /usr/sbin/nologin (useradd)); with the installers announcing their files, the agent's install on the VPN host logged /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group as announced. The package and set-uid check with dpkg : no file differs from its package's checksums, 17 set-uid programs. The patch status with apt-get -s after an upgrade: the old kernel still running. The SSH audit on the VPN host (OpenSSH 8.9p1, a provider's cloud image with password and key logins): ssh-audit found root's password login from the internet (high) and passwords accepted, with the setting traced to cloud-init's sshd_config.d/50-cloud-init.conf:1 in front of sshd_config's own PasswordAuthentication no (named as ignored), and two notes (LoginGraceTime 600, X11Forwarding yes). After the fixes it suggested and a reload, it found no problems, and the daemon's next reading logged them as fixed (fixed: login-grace, root-login, x11-forwarding, with the changed settings as evidence). On another node, vpsfort ssh-audit as root against its harden-vps.sh gateway (OpenSSH 10.0p2): sshd -T and sshd -T -C per user worked, the gateway user was detected, and no problems were found; the daemon's own first reading came 5 minutes after the restart, as an info alert that was only logged (SSH audit (gateway (...)): no problems), and status showed it under "ssh audit". The sysctl audit's fixes on the XMPP server and the Fedora node: its sysctl -w commands, applied as printed (8 warnings and 6 notes on Fedora), left no problems, and the daemon's next reading logged them as fixed (sysctl audit: fixed: dev.tty.ldisc_autoload, kernel.kexec_load_disabled, kernel.kptr_restrict, ...). Watchdog: the units run as Type=notify with WatchdogSec=2min, without watchdog restarts.

82.body: The XMPP admin account : system, exposure and integrity alerts, the daily digest, and the VPN node's alerts relayed through the cluster. The XMPP bot (bot_outbox) on the XMPP server: admin messages reach the admin OMEMO-encrypted, while users' warnings still come from ejabberd in plain text. After an ejabberd restart the bot was back online about two minutes later. The Matrix bot (matrix_outbox) on the Fedora node (xmpp = false), through matrix.org to Element X, end-to-end encrypted and without warnings: notify-test --matrix, real alerts (a source gone quiet, new outbound connections), the VPN node's daily digest, and the weekly abuse report (abuse-report-2026-11-02.txt, 51 KB, 50 sources, covering two nodes) as an encrypted attachment that Element X decrypted and opened in its file viewer. Element X showed the room as the bot makes it (encryption on, named vpsfort with its topic, the admin invited). Its event details show the file encrypted with AES-256-CTR with the key inside the Megolm-encrypted event, and list the bot's identity as unverified (the admin never verified the bot account) without a warning in the timeline. The mail bot (mail_outbox): notify-test --mail and a digest (digest --send) went through the outbox and a real mail server, and GnuPG decrypted them and verified the bot's signature. Real alerts (a source gone quiet, new listeners, a cluster node not responding) and the weekly abuse report arrived PGP-encrypted, decrypted and read in Proton Mail on Android.

83.body: The apt repository on GitHub Pages , on the XMPP server (Debian 13): apt update checked the signed InRelease against the key downloaded from the Pages site, whose fingerprint matched the one in the repository's README, and apt install vpsfort installed 0.6.0. The package taking over a bundle install of an older version there, while vpsfort ran: the bundle's binaries under /usr/local and its units in /etc/systemd/system went (each reported once by the integrity watch as removed), the config stayed (config-diff: valid for this version; the template saved next to it as vpsfort.toml.new), dpkg asked about the bundle's two /etc/default files (D showed each difference, N kept them), and the service restarted as /usr/bin/vpsfort on the package's unit, enabled, with both timers; the new unit links were logged as announced by an installer, accepted. The state across that restart : the 223 active bans with their remaining times and offence counts, 1,227 scored addresses, the trusted logins, the earlier alerts and the baselines came back from the state file, and all four peers answered within ten seconds. The dnf repository , on the Fedora node (Fedora 44, dnf5, kernel 7.2): dnf imported the key from the Pages site (its fingerprint matching the README's) and checked the signed package, and dnf install vpsfort took over that node's bundle install the same way: the bundle's units and binaries gone, the config kept with the -dnf template next to it, firewalld's rich rules for the peers already in place, the service restarted on the package's unit, its 205 bans back and all four peers answering. The bundle's /etc/default/vpsfort-avscan and vpsfort-abuse-report stayed, with the package's versions saved as .rpmnew (rpm's way with files it doesn't own yet). vpsfort's own files after both takeovers : vpsfort self-audit found no problems on either node, with the modes and owners the packages set and the config, keys and state the bundles left.

85.body: All fixed the same day: an OPENPGP_KEY file left at mode 0600 stopped the Matrix bot at its start (Permission denied; it needs the 640 its README gives); a gateway user missing from [canary] except banned the admin at the next SSH login, with nothing warning about the list before (now vpsfort canary-check, run by the installers, the daemon's daily check, and the alert's own advice); the installers' new system user raised high alerts for /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group (the installers now announce them); vpsfort-web check failed on an AGENT_ALLOW list with blanks when config.env was sourced in a shell, as the docs said (the commands now read the file themselves, as systemd does); two SSH audit messages: the fix named a cloud-init setting on a host without cloud-init, and LoginGraceTime was shown in seconds while the file said 10m; an empty console socket setting was refused; no way to correct a country the geo database gets wrong (now [geo] places); the XMPP bot never came back after an ejabberd restart (a session it could not resume; it starts a new one now); the console's filters were drawn below their tables; the package's upgrade wrote the new template vpsfort.toml.new without announcing it, so every upgrade raised a high integrity alert for it (the .deb/.rpm, bundle and Alpine installers now announce it, and the package also a replaced config and its .old copy); the package repository's instructions saved the signing key with the shell's umask: under a strict one, apt's unprivileged _apt user could not read it and refused the repository as unsigned (the key is installed with mode 0644 now); the TUI's Overview called the decisions of the running process "In all", which read as if the state had been lost after a restart (now "This run"); the sysctl audit's fix read "sysctl -w <key>=<value>, and the same line in /etc/sysctl.d/90-hardening.conf", so the command itself went into that file, where it is ignored at boot: the settings would have been lost at the next reboot (the fix names the key = value line now, and the README gives a one-line command that applies and keeps every fix); the packages' question whether to replace the config went to the install's output, which dnf holds back until a scriptlet ends: under dnf the install looked hung for the question's whole minute, then kept the config (the question goes to the terminal itself now, in all eight packages).

86.body: The Fedora node's first evening, following TESTING-fedora.md : a Fedora Cloud VPS, Fedora 44, x86_64, kernel 7.2.10, firewalld 2.4.4 (nftables underneath), rpm 6.0.2 and dnf5, NetworkManager, SELinux disabled by the provider's image. Installed from the x86_64 release bundle with the vpsfort-standalone-dnf.toml template, real scanners on the public address, and a VPN as the probe (exits in Brazil, the Netherlands and Argentina). Verified: Install from a bundle on a new server: the template first, then the install (the bundle's binary checked to run here); upgrades from later bundles kept the config. firewalld's log lines (firewall-cmd --set-log-denied=unicast): filter_IN_public_REJECT lines became port-scan and tripwire signals; real scanners were banned on their first tripwire hit, in shadow and in enforce mode. The exposure watch reading firewalld's zones: sshd allowed by firewalld [ALLOW ssh (public)]; a test server blocked, then allowed after --add-port, then a dead rule once it stopped; a rich rule for one address shown as allowed from some sources only; the baseline after the startup grace and a "listener gone" alert. rpm and dnf (package_manager = "dnf"): package origins in the cron watch (package pam, package openssh-server; /etc/pam.d/sudo flagged MODIFIED and back); the package check matched 7,472 files against rpm's digests and learned 14 set-uid programs, and a byte appended to /usr/bin/tree raised the high alert with dnf reinstall as the fix; the patch status ran dnf check-update and saw the newer installed kernel (7.2.11 while 7.2.10 ran) and 9 programs on replaced libraries. The firewalld backend: vpsfort's ipsets, its zone (target DROP) and the forwarding policy made with one reload; bans restored at start; an operator ban dropped the probe (its SYNs logged as filter_IN_vpsfort_DROP and not counted again), and it connected again after unban; bans lifted on time, as firewalld's entries don't expire; after firewall-cmd --reload and after systemctl restart firewalld, all bans back within 30 s, with the high alert. nftables next to firewalld: vpsfort's table, its sets with kernel timeouts and the kernel tripwire rules loaded on kernel 7.2; firewall-cmd --reload left the table untouched (firewalld 2.4 removes only its own). The ipset backend: the sets and their rules for IPv4 and IPv6, a ban with its kernel timeout, blocklist feeds loaded into vpsfort-feed4 (with the ASN-DROP networks), and the chain rebuilt within 30 s after iptables -t mangle -F vpsfort. Honeypot ports: 22 and 23 set as honeypots, tried with nc from the VPN's exit nodes. Blocking by country (ipset backend): Brazil and the Netherlands came to 32,358 IPv4 and 104,957 IPv6 networks, loaded a second after the geo database; exits in both countries timed out with no ban made, one in Argentina connected; enabled = false emptied the sets. Memory: 47-59 MB peak, under the unit's 128 MB; 80 MB with Brazil and the Netherlands blocked (the list is computed and loaded in a fraction of that since, see "Blocking countries and networks"). The canary lockout warning: an upgrade's installer ran vpsfort canary-check after the config check and again after the restart, and listed root (a key file in /root, the canary list ["*"]) with the except line to add. It listed operator too, which has no shell and only shares /root: no longer counted ("Canary accounts"). The sysctl audit: 30 sysctls read, 8 warnings and 5 notes in status, and the first reading's warning alert (redirects accepted, rp_filter off, kptr_restrict, ptrace_scope, suid_dumpable). net.core.bpf_jit_harden could not be read under the unit's capability bound and raised an alert of its own: a note now. The unit's capability bound and the kernel module baseline: an upgrade ran whole under the bound (the nftables table, firewalld's rich rules, the journal, the bots' outboxes); a module loaded afterwards (ip_set, by an ipset list in a root shell) raised the high "never seen before" alert within a minute. Files an installer announces: the bots' and the console's units were logged as announced by an installer, accepted; a bot's logrotate rule, which its installer did not announce, raised the high integrity alert: the installers announce it now. Found by this run , all fixed the same day: a bundle could carry an older binary under a newer commit's name (bundle.sh reused what was built); status asked nftables for rate limits under other backends; a failed start (a [verify] interval under 1h) logged its reason only at info priority; the package count read 0 after a restart; the feeds status named nftables under ipset; a first install warned it couldn't announce its files; the patch status left out the other pending updates when something needed attention; and /usr/local/sbin (a link to /usr/local/bin on Fedora 42 and later) made every upgrade two integrity changes.

Standard pieces that other means cover are not listed. Blocking: the plain iptables backend (backend = "iptables") on a host; the ipset backend, which shares its chains, has run; what a honeypot connection sent (honeypot_capture) in a real ban's evidence and an abuse report: the capture and its wording are tested against a local connection; the removal of the old raw-priority chain at the first start after an upgrade (the upgraded node wasn't checked; Fedora was a new install); a change the firewall program refused being kept and tried again, with its alert ("Self-healing firewall table"): the firewall programs on the servers have not refused one yet; the same for a state save or an actions log write that fails for an hour; the cluster link's fallback to plain frames for an older node, and forward_secrecy = "require"; the self-audit of vpsfort's own files finding a problem on a server: it ran clean on two nodes, whose files have the modes the installers and packages set; the clock warning on a host whose clock isn't synchronised; the container and WireGuard peer baselines on a host (the tests read Docker's files and wg show output as the hosts write them), and the new watched files of [cron] files reporting a change; the actions log mirrored to a peer ([cluster] mirror_to), a notice held for a peer down longer than an hour and delivered late, a fact refused for its signature raising its alert, and a followed log file resumed after a restart (file-positions.json) on a server; Alerts not yet seen on a host: sudo (no host has sudo; su was seen) and new-SSH-key alerts; PAM failures and auditd alerts (account changes were seen), and which of the three forms of audit records a given journald writes; SSH password guessing (ssh_auth_fail): SSH is key-only on the hosts, so only synthetic tests cover it (ssh_invalid_user and canary probes occur for real); the built-in patterns for common services ([sources] apps) on a host that runs one of them: the vpsfort-web patterns read its live journal (the Patterns tab counts the lines) but have matched nothing, as no login failed; the current versions' formats have not been checked against a real log either; patterns of your own on a live journal, the journal position alert and journalctl --verify; an infected file's alert, and clamdscan --fdpass through clamd; the SSH audit's alert for a new problem or a weakened setting, the TUI's SSH line, a gateway with something wrong, Fedora's OpenSSH, and cPanel's and Plesk's layouts; node identities: a fact refused for its signature, a node dropped from nodes, and a cluster where older versions forward signed facts; the bot fallback: a message the bot doesn't take (bot stopped, no trusted admin device) going out unencrypted after bot_grace. 88.body: UFW-only evidence (blocked packets) can carry forged source addresses, TCP tripwire hits included. A forged hit can't ban an address that logged in within trust_ttl (nor through a peer), and bans never drop replies to the server's own connections. It can still ban other addresses for an hour, and a subnet that holds no protected address, so an attacker who forges packets can block outsiders from reaching this server. Bans of a forged source cost the attacker nothing. Honeypot ports ("Honeypot ports") rule them out for the connections they take, and lower a blocked SYN to half a ban.

89.body: A read-only web console for a vpsfort cluster: every node's bans, alerts, decisions, offenders, countries and networks, cluster peers, certificates, disks, updates and integrity checks on one HTTPS page, with what needs attention first, and every node's abuse report of the last day or week, split per network owner and ready to mail. For one admin or a few, all equal. /metrics gives the same in Prometheus' format for Grafana. It only reads . Nothing in it can ban, unban, allow or change a setting: those stay on the servers, over SSH, as vpsfort unban … and the TUI. every node the console's node ┌────────────────────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ vpsfort ── console socket ──► agent│ ◄── TCP 7949 ───│ console ── HTTPS 7948 (TLS 1.3) ──► browser│ │ (root) read-only, 0660 vpsfort-web vpsfort-web password + one-time code │ └────────────────────────────────────┘ request sealed │ + its own node's vpsfort (socket) │ with the web └──────────────────────────────────────────┘ key; reply under a fresh X25519 key One binary, two roles, each switched on by a setting: the agent (AGENT_LISTEN, on every node) hands its node's vpsfort data to the consoles; the console (CONSOLE_LISTEN, on the node or nodes you choose) asks the agents in NODES and its own vpsfort, and serves the page.

9.body: vpsfort is one static Rust binary for a self-hosted Linux server. It does what usually takes four or five separate tools: It bans attackers in the kernel firewall seconds after they show themselves. It watches the host for the ways intruders stay in. It notices when its own view goes dark : a log source that stops, a firewall that was flushed, a scan that was killed. It tells the admins over end-to-end-encrypted channels (or sanitized, to a push service), and warns the users whose accounts are under attack. It shows the whole cluster on one read-only HTTPS page, and to Prometheus (vpsfort-web, optional). Several servers share what they see over an encrypted peer-to-peer link. There is no central server and no vendor in between: the web console only asks the nodes, with a key of its own that can't make a ban. journal ─► vpsfort ─► nftables / firewalld / ufw / iptables / ipset ◄── encrypted cluster link ──► vpsfort on other nodes │ ├─► vpsfort-xmpp-bot ─► XMPP, OMEMO-encrypted ├─► vpsfort-tg-bot ─► Telegram, pseudonymized, files OpenPGP-encrypted ├─► vpsfort-mail-bot ─► e-mail, PGP/MIME-encrypted ├─► vpsfort-signal-bot ─► Signal (signal-cli), else OpenPGP files ├─► vpsfort-matrix-bot ─► Matrix, Olm/Megolm-encrypted, else OpenPGP files ├─► vpsfort-push-bot ─► ntfy, Gotify or a webhook, sanitized, files OpenPGP-encrypted └─► vpsfort-web (read-only socket) ─► the cluster on one HTTPS page, /metrics for Prometheus What one install covers, and what you would otherwise run: vpsfort part usually done with scoring and banning, subnet bans, tripwires, honeypots, canary accounts; built-in sources for common web, database and mail servers fail2ban, sshguard, CrowdSec country and network (ASN) blocking CSF CC_DENY, ipset scripts with a GeoIP list ban sharing between your servers, blocklist feeds CrowdSec, CSF cluster, ipset scripts a WAF's decisions (CrowdSec, or any app with a list) enforced at the firewall CrowdSec's firewall bouncer cron and persistence watch, package and set-uid check (dpkg or rpm), process watch AIDE, debsums, rpm -Va, rkhunter, Wazuh FIM listeners compared with firewall rules, dead rules, Docker bypass Lynis, external port scans, by hand patch status (apt or dnf), certificate checks apticron, dnf-automatic, needrestart, an uptime or certificate monitor SSH hardening audit (sshd's effective settings, key file permissions, a su/sftp gateway's layout) Lynis, ssh-audit, Wazuh SCA quiet log sources, OOM kills, disk, memory, failed units Monit, Netdata, Prometheus daily digest, weekly abuse report; live abuse reports per network owner with the e-mail ready; an attacker's evidence as a link for its hosting provider Logwatch, AbuseIPDB scripts, by hand a read-only web console for the cluster, a REST API, Prometheus metrics Grafana with exporters, the CrowdSec Console, Wazuh's dashboard Key numbers (measured, from the README): ~10 MB static binary with no runtime dependencies (the optional web console is another ~4 MB). ~10 MB RAM for a real month of traffic (~50 MB with the offline geo database). The hard limit is 128 MB, and it held in a synthetic flood of 450,000 sources. A real month of logs (~210,000 records) replays through the full engine in about one second : 185 bans of 93 targets. No address that ever logged in was banned. Tripwire ports banned about 7,500 scanners on first contact in that month.
