91.body: Its own key, never the cluster key. vpsfort's cluster key lets its holder ban, unban, allowlist and trust addresses on every node. A web console is the part of a system most exposed to the network, so it must not hold that key: the agents and the console share a separate web key (32 random bytes, vpsfort-web keygen), and a stolen web key reads status data, nothing more. It cannot forge cluster facts, and the console can't ask an agent for anything but reading (snapshot, digest, abuse_24h, abuse_7d). An agent says what it answers; the console asks older agents for snapshots and digests only (an agent refuses a request it can't read, and vpsfort bans an address that sends many of those). The agent protocol (src/wire.rs), one request and one reply per TCP connection: The request is sealed with XChaCha20-Poly1305 under the web key (as the cluster's messages are), with its time (refused beyond 5 minutes of clock difference), a random id (refused if seen again) and a fresh X25519 public key. The reply is sealed under a key derived (HKDF-SHA-256) from a second fresh X25519 key and the console's, with the web key as salt and the request id and both public keys bound in. Only a holder of the web key can make or read it, it answers that one request only, and once both fresh keys are gone nobody can read a recorded reply, even with the web key (forward secrecy). The cluster's own link does the same since its key exchange (vpsfort's README, "Cluster"); snapshots name accounts and addresses. Frames are bounded (4 KB requests, 16 MB compressed replies, 64 MB uncompressed); an agent takes 8 connections at once, 2 per address, 10 seconds for a whole request, and only from AGENT_ALLOW. Memory follows what is kept: long lists (every active ban of a flood) are cut to their newest few thousand while parsing, their full lengths kept. The console: HTTPS, TLS 1.3 only (rustls with ring), with a self-signed certificate made at install (compare its fingerprint with the browser's once) or a Let's Encrypt one (read again when it changes). Older clients (TLS 1.2 only) are refused. Admins, two factors each: admin and any others you add, all equal (no roles). Each has a password (Argon2id, passwd [--user NAME]) and a one-time code from an authenticator app (TOTP, RFC 6238, totp-setup [--user NAME] shows a QR code); each code works once, and only for its admin. TOTP=off leaves the passwords alone. Or a passkey (WebAuthn: a security key, the phone's, the browser's keychain), registered on the "Your account" page (up to 10 per admin, kept in STATE_DIR/passkeys/<admin>.passkeys, vpsfort-web passkeys and remove-passkey on the server): the login page offers "Log in with a passkey" for an account that has one. A passkey that checked its holder (a fingerprint, a face, the key's PIN: the user-verification flag) is the login on its own, without the password or the code; one that was only touched (a security key without a PIN) stands in for the code beside the password, and the page says so. A password that is given must still be right. The console checks the answer itself (src/webauthn.rs): the challenge it issued for that account, the origin, the site's hash and the user-presence flag in the authenticator data, the signature (ECDSA P-256 or Ed25519, with ring) and a signature counter that must grow (a cloned key is refused). Attestation is not checked (the key is the admin's own). Passkeys need the console reached by a host name, not an address: localhost through an SSH tunnel works. Every attempt costs the same Argon2 check (one at a time), whichever factor is wrong and also for an account that doesn't exist, and the answer doesn't say which. Five failures from an address within 15 minutes lock it out for 15 minutes, and vpsfort bans it (below); ten failures at one account from anywhere lock the account for 15 minutes, except for addresses it was logged in to from (the admin's own) and for a login with the account's current one-time code (a guesser can't produce one), so a guesser spread over many addresses is stopped without locking the admin out, even from a new address. With TOTP=off the lock holds for every unknown address. Proof of work before each login (LOGIN_WORK, default 20 bits; 0 off): the page's JavaScript (web/work.js, in a Web Worker, plain SHA-256) must find a nonce such that SHA-256(challenge ‖ nonce) starts with that many zero bits, about 2^20 hashes, and the console checks it with one hash before any Argon2 runs. That's under a second on a laptop and a few on a phone, solved while you type; a guesser pays it for every guess. The difficulty ramps with failures lately (15 minutes): each failure from the address adds a bit (up to 6: 64× the work), every 3 failures at the account from anywhere adds one (up to 4), every 50 failures from everyone adds one (up to 3), capped at 28 bits. A challenge is signed by the console (a key made at start), good for 5 minutes, works once, and one solved before the difficulty rose is refused (428 with a fresh challenge: the page solves it and tries once more). A challenge is for the address and account it was issued to (both in its signature), so one solved cheaply for an account with no failures can't be spent on the one under attack; nothing is kept for challenges handed out and not used, so asking for them costs the console nothing. vpsfort-web check times a solve. Nothing fingerprints the browser and no cookie is set for it: Mullvad or Tor are treated like anyone else; a browser without JavaScript or Web Workers can't log in, which was true already. Sessions are named by a random 256-bit cookie __Host-lgw (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict); 30 idle minutes or 12 hours end one, and so does removing its admin (remove-admin), at its next request. 8 per admin, 64 in all. An admin sees their own sessions (address, browser, times) and can end the others; after a login the page says when that admin last logged in, from where, and how many failed attempts at the account came since. The sessions (as the cookies' digests), these records, the lockouts and the failure counters are written to STATE_DIR and read back at start, so a restart (an upgrade, or a crash an attacker provokes) neither resets a lockout nor logs every admin out; without a STATE_DIR they live in memory. Read only , and only for this site's pages: the API answers GET; login and logout take JSON (a form from another site can't send it) and check Origin; requests another site's page makes (Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site) are refused. The page is a few files compiled into the binary (web/: app.js the views, dom.js building and patching the page, core.js what it works out), no libraries, nothing from other hosts. Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; ..., no inline script, no framing, no-store; connect-src adds RDAP's servers (rdap.org and the five registries) for the abuse-mailbox lookup below. Everything a node sends (log lines, account names, a peer's notices) goes into the page as text (textContent), never as HTML. A small HTTP parser of its own (src/http.rs): no chunked bodies, no proxy requests, no folded headers, one Host and one Content-Length, 16 KB of headers, 8 KB bodies; anything else is refused and the connection closed. 64 connections at once, 12 per address, 30 seconds per request and 10 minutes per connection however busy (a few addresses can't hold every slot by sending a byte every 29 seconds). CONSOLE_ALLOW drops other addresses before TLS. Privilege separation. vpsfort runs as root; vpsfort-web as its own system user, under a sandboxed unit (ProtectSystem=strict, no capabilities, MemoryDenyWriteExecute, 128 MB at most), writing only its own state (STATE_DIR, the admins' passkeys among it). It reaches vpsfort only through vpsfort's console socket ([console] in vpsfort.toml): root's directory, mode 0750, group vpsfort-web, which answers snapshot, digest and abuse 24h / abuse 7d and refuses every other command before the daemon sees it. The control socket, the cluster key and vpsfort's state stay root's. What a break-in would give. The console broken into: everything the page shows, read only; the web key. An agent's node broken into: the web key, and with it the power to show the console false data (what a node reports is displayed, never acted on: the console has nothing to act with). Neither gives a ban, an unban or the cluster key. vpsfort watches it. vpsfort-web writes to the journal: login failed from <address>: … (with the account tried, if it can be one: nothing else a stranger types reaches the log), console: unknown path from <address>: GET /.env, refused connections, agent requests without the web key. With [sources] apps = ["vpsfort-web"] vpsfort scores them (25 points a failed login, 40 a probe for secrets, 20 a refused connection) and bans the address like any other attacker, on every node through the cluster.
91.title: Security design

92.body:
On every node of the cluster (the console's too): Install it (from a release bundle, below, or ./deploy/deploy.sh <host> from a checkout). The first run puts /opt/vpsfort-web/config.env in place and creates the user vpsfort-web. The web key , once, on one node, then the same file to every other node's /opt/vpsfort-web/web.key: /opt/vpsfort-web/vpsfort-web keygen --out /opt/vpsfort-web/web.key
/opt/vpsfort-web/vpsfort-web key-id # the same fingerprint on every node vpsfort's console socket, in /etc/vpsfort/vpsfort.toml, then systemctl restart vpsfort: [console]
socket = "/run/vpsfort-console/console.sock"
group = "vpsfort-web" And in [sources], apps = ["vpsfort-web"] (with your other apps) to ban password guessers. In config.env: AGENT_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:7949, and AGENT_ALLOW the console node's address. Open the port to that address only: ufw allow from 203.0.113.10 to any port 7949 proto tcp (firewalld: firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family=ipv4 source address=203.0.113.10 port port=7949 protocol=tcp accept'). The console's own node needs no agent: the console reads that node's vpsfort through VPSFORT_SOCKET, so AGENT_LISTEN stays empty there and 7949 needs no rule. On the console's node, also: In config.env: CONSOLE_LISTEN, and NODES the other nodes' agents (vpn.example.org:7949, 198.51.100.20:7949). Either: CONSOLE_LISTEN=127.0.0.1:7948, reached through SSH: ssh -L 7948:127.0.0.1:7948 <host>, then https://127.0.0.1:7948 (a hardened SSH gateway needs PermitOpen 127.0.0.1:7948 for its user); or CONSOLE_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:7948 with CONSOLE_ALLOW the networks you work from, and the port opened to them in the firewall. vpsfort's exposure watch reports the new listener once. The admin's login: /opt/vpsfort-web/vpsfort-web passwd # asked twice, not shown; 12 characters at least
/opt/vpsfort-web/vpsfort-web totp-setup # scan the QR code, or add the otpauth:// link It then asks for the code the app shows and writes the secret only when it matches: if the scan didn't take, nothing is written and you run it again. More admins, the same way, each with their own password and codes (they log in with their name in "Account"; admin is the default): /opt/vpsfort-web/vpsfort-web passwd --user alice
/opt/vpsfort-web/vpsfort-web totp-setup --user alice # alice scans it with her own app
/opt/vpsfort-web/vpsfort-web admins # who can log in
/opt/vpsfort-web/vpsfort-web remove-admin alice # her sessions end at once No restart needed: the console reads the files at each login. bash /opt/vpsfort-web/install.sh again (a package install: dpkg-reconfigure vpsfort-web, or dnf reinstall the rpm; it starts nothing, so finish with systemctl enable --now vpsfort-web): it sets the files' owners and modes, makes the self-signed certificate if there is none, and starts the service once nothing is missing (until then it lists what is). Check it: /opt/vpsfort-web/vpsfort-web check # reads config.env itself, as the unit does check reads every file and asks this node's vpsfort and every agent in NODES once. Open the console. The browser warns about the self-signed certificate once: compare the SHA-256 fingerprint it shows with vpsfort-web fingerprint (install.sh prints it too) before you accept it. A console without vpsfort (a host that only aggregates the nodes and serves the page): VPSFORT_SOCKET=, CONSOLE_LISTEN and NODES, no agent, and skip step 3. Every node shown is then an agent's. One thing is missing there: with no vpsfort on that host, nothing bans password guessers at its console from the journal; the lockout above still applies, so keep CONSOLE_ALLOW narrow (or the console on 127.0.0.1 behind SSH). Two consoles: both in each agent's AGENT_ALLOW. A node without the console: CONSOLE_LISTEN= (the default).
92.title: Setup

93.body: variable default meaning NODE_NAME vpsfort's [cluster] node_id, else the host name this node's name in the console VPSFORT_SOCKET /run/vpsfort-console/console.sock vpsfort's [console] socket; empty without vpsfort WEB_KEY_FILE /opt/vpsfort-web/web.key the web key, the same on every node AGENT_LISTEN empty (no agent) where the consoles ask for this node's data, e.g. 0.0.0.0:7949 AGENT_ALLOW required with an agent the consoles' addresses or networks; any: the web key alone decides CONSOLE_LISTEN empty (no console) where the console serves HTTPS, e.g. 127.0.0.1:7948 CONSOLE_ALLOW empty: every address addresses or networks that may reach the login page NODES empty the other nodes' agents, host:port, separated by commas or blanks TLS_CERT, TLS_KEY /opt/vpsfort-web/tls.crt, tls.key PEM certificate chain and key; read again when they change LOGIN_WORK 20 bits of proof of work before a login (ramps with failures; 0: off) RDAP_LOOKUPS on the console looks up abuse mailboxes (rdap.org, HTTPS with the system's CA bundle) when an admin asks; off, or when it can't get out, the admin's browser asks rdap.org itself PASSWORD_FILE /opt/vpsfort-web/admin.password admin's Argon2id hash (passwd) TOTP, TOTP_FILE on, /opt/vpsfort-web/admin.totp one-time codes for every admin (off: passwords only); admin's secret (totp-setup) ADMINS_DIR /opt/vpsfort-web/admins the other admins: <name>.password, <name>.totp (passwd --user, totp-setup --user) METRICS_TOKEN_FILE unset a token that reads /metrics without a login (Prometheus) REFRESH_SECS 10 how old the nodes' data may get while a page is open SESSION_IDLE_MINUTES, SESSION_MAX_HOURS 30, 12 when a session ends EXPECTED_VERSION unset the vpsfort-web release every node should run (0.5.0): a node on another gets a row on the Overview. Nothing is downloaded or checked online STATE_DIR /var/lib/vpsfort-web where the attention history, the nodes' digests, the admins' marks, the share links, the lockouts and failure counters, and the sessions are kept across restarts (the unit's StateDirectory); empty: in memory only (a restart then forgets the lockouts and logs every admin out) HISTORY_DAYS, DIGEST_DAYS 7, 14 how long the attention history keeps a problem that went, and how many days of each node's digests are kept The console asks the nodes only while someone looks (a page open, a Prometheus scrape): an idle console sends nothing. A slow node's answer shows with the next refresh; one that doesn't answer shows as down, with the reason and its last data, and is asked less and less often (twice the wait after each failure, up to a minute) until it answers again. The page asks for what its tab shows (/api/v1/cluster?only=...), not the whole cluster document every time.
93.title: Settings (/opt/vpsfort-web/config.env)

94.body:
vpsfort-web run (the unit does)
vpsfort-web check settings, files, this node's vpsfort and every agent, once
vpsfort-web keygen [--out F] a new web key (or metrics token); F mode 0640, never overwritten
vpsfort-web key-id the web key's fingerprint (and a rotation's .next/.prev keys)
vpsfort-web gen-cert --name console.example.org --name 203.0.113.10 [--force]
vpsfort-web fingerprint the certificate's SHA-256 fingerprint, as browsers show it
vpsfort-web passwd [--user NAME] [--stdin] an admin's password (a new NAME: a new admin)
vpsfort-web totp-setup [--user NAME] [--force] [--no-confirm] their one-time codes' secret: a QR code, the otpauth:// link (also without a label, for password managers) and the secret in groups; written only after a code from the app matches, so a failed scan leaves nothing behind (--no-confirm writes at once, for scripts)
vpsfort-web admins the admins, and whether each can log in
vpsfort-web remove-admin NAME remove one (not admin): files gone, sessions end
vpsfort-web passkeys [--user NAME] an admin's passkeys (registered on the "Your account" page)
vpsfort-web remove-passkey --user NAME --id ID remove one (a lost key) Rotating the web key (deploy/rotate-web-key.sh, as vpsfort's rotate-cluster-key.sh): the agent also answers requests sealed under <WEB_KEY_FILE>.next and .prev, while the console sends with WEB_KEY_FILE, so the key changes in three rounds without a moment in which the console can't ask an agent: start (the new key as .next on every node), switch (it becomes the key, the old one .prev), finish (the old one goes). Each round copies the files over SFTP and prints the command to paste into a root shell on each node, which checks them, installs the key and restarts vpsfort-web; key-id and check show a rotation in progress. Share links made before switch end with it (they are signed with the key).
94.title: Commands

95.body: Overview: nodes up, active bans (and how many distinct addresses), bans and events in the last hour, alerts in 24 hours, tracked addresses; Needs attention (a node without data, a failing cluster peer, differing cluster keys, shadow mode, a certificate running out, a full disk, security updates, infected files, changed package files, feed errors...); events and bans per minute over three hours, per node (also as a table); a card per node. Alerts, Activity (every decision), Bans (per node, or one row per address with the nodes that ban it), Offenders (scores, evidence, accounts with failed logins): filters, sorting, details on click, a column chooser (kept per browser), CSV and JSON. On Alerts and Activity, Merge folds the same alert or decision on several nodes (a peer's ban relayed to each; a cron's ten su lines within a minute) into one row with every node and a ×N count; rows carry their severity as a left edge, and rows newer than your last look are tinted, with their count in the header ("12 new"). World: countries, networks and ports, all nodes added up. Every list folds: the Countries picker shows the top 15, a country's Networks and Busiest ports the top 10 each (a big country has dozens of networks; a port scan lists hundreds of ports), with "Show all N" under each and the full lists on a search; each scrolls inside its card, so picking a country shows its networks and ports side by side with the picker on a desktop, and above it on a phone, with the country's figures as a chip in the filter row and a link to the map. Map: the TUI's map, drawn properly. Countries from Natural Earth (public domain) in the Equal Earth projection, the whole world or Europe. ▲ sized by active bans, offenders or events, at the addresses' coordinates where a node's geo database is a city-level one (one marker per place, "Germany, Nuremberg" on hover) and at the country's capital for the rest (the free databases name only the country; a node without coordinates, or an older one, draws as before); ● where addresses logged in during the last hour; countries [geoblock] blocks hatched, with the nodes that block them and whether it is in force. Hover for the figures; a click opens the country on World. web/world.json is made by scripts/world-map.py. An address's page (#/address/<address or network>; every address or network shown is a link, also inside log lines and messages): the bans covering it on every node, its scores, the decisions and alerts naming it, whether a node trusts or allows it, its entry in the last week's abuse report, and who runs its network (RDAP). Abuse: every node's abuse report merged ( To send turns it into the checklist: networks not yet mailed, most bans first, with Copy, Mail and Mark mailed on each row and nothing else), for the last 24 hours or the last 7 days (each button shows how many networks it has), one row per network owner (by AS number, else by name): its countries, sources, bans, log lines, the nodes that banned them and when last seen. A click opens its sources: what each did, in the words of the weekly report, and its first log lines marked with the node they hit. Copy puts that network's part on the clipboard as an e-mail to its abuse desk ("Hello, the following addresses in your network ... attacked our servers"), .txt saves it as a file, Mail looks up the network's abuse mailbox (RDAP) and opens the e-mail in your mail program, addressed and with a subject (a report too long for a mail link goes in part, the rest saved as a .txt to attach). The text names the attacked servers by their public address, never by the nodes' names. The mailbox lookup: the console asks rdap.org (one a second, kept a day, following a registry's redirects only to public host names); if it can't (RDAP_LOOKUPS=off, no way out from its host) the page asks rdap.org itself, which then learns the address asked about and the admin's address. The console follows a registry's redirects only to rdap.org and the five registries (*.arin.net, *.ripe.net, *.apnic.net, *.lacnic.net, *.afrinic.net), and only to their public addresses. Only plain e-mail addresses are taken from RDAP (the network's owner writes it, and may be the attacker). Mark mailed remembers a network as reported, shown on its row; "Hide those already mailed" leaves out its sources for 30 days. The marks (mailed networks, problems seen) are kept by the console in STATE_DIR, so every admin and browser sees the same and a restart keeps them; this browser's copy stands in while the console has none. CSV : one line per source. Sources with fewer than 3 log lines are left out unless you ask, as in the weekly report. Each node builds its report from its actions log when asked (vpsfort keeps it a minute, the console too); the page asks again every 5 minutes or on "Again". A node's page starts with what changed since the console's previous snapshot of it ("+3 bans, 1 new alert, new listener on 0.0.0.0:7949"), then vpsfort's mode and figures, log sources, the cluster as that node sees it (peers, facts, key), certificates, disk and memory, updates, cron, antivirus and package checks, listening services, blocklists, the allowlists, patterns, today's digest so far, that node's abuse report (as on Abuse), and its whole snapshot as JSON. Overview also has sparklines under the bans and events tiles (the last 3 hours), the activity charts over 3 hours (per minute), 24 hours or 7 days (per hour, from vpsfort's hourly figures since its start), node cards you can pin to the top (★, per browser), Needs attention as a queue (click a problem once seen: it dims, "3 unseen of 8" in the header), and Nodes side by side : each node's vpsfort and vpsfort-web versions, mode, firewall, thresholds, cluster key and which watches are on, the cells that differ from most nodes marked; click two nodes to see only what differs between those two. Your account (your name in the header): this session, the login before it, your sessions with "Log out the others", your passkeys (add one: the browser asks the security key or the phone; remove one), this browser's settings (colours, notifications, the node legend, the saved views, the keys), and Console health : what vpsfort-web check prints, on the page: the certificate's expiry (a warning under 14 days), the web key's id, the admins, the proof of work, the sessions open, every node's state and vpsfort-web version. Attention history (Overview, under Needs attention): the problems of the last 7 days as the console saw them appear and go, with how long each lasted. Kept in STATE_DIR (/var/lib/vpsfort-web, the unit's StateDirectory), so a restart keeps it; with STATE_DIR empty, in memory. A changing count ("3 high or critical alert(s)") is one problem. A node's digests: "Past days" on a node's page shows the last two weeks' digests as the console kept them (each day's when it was shown, and every node's 15 minutes before midnight UTC: the console's only traffic to the nodes while nobody looks), in STATE_DIR across restarts. Snapshot saves the node's snapshot alone, as vpsfort tui --file reads it; Export JSON on the Overview saves everything the console has (the merged view and every node's snapshot) for a ticket. Share links (an address's page): "Share link" makes a link to that page that needs no login, for handing the evidence to the address's hosting provider: it opens that address's data only, read-only like everything here, and ends when it expires (24 hours, 3 days or a week; a week at most). Its holder is a stranger to the cluster and sees what the weekly abuse report would, no more: the bans covering the address, the ban and unban decisions about it with their evidence, and its scores. Account names are withheld as the abuse report withholds them ("failed password login (account name withheld)"), anything with an @ becomes [account], internal points go, and the alerts about the host, the users notified, the admin's notes, and what the nodes trust or allow are left out altogether; the nodes are numbered, not named, in fields and texts alike; no abuse report, no RDAP, no other page, every link plain text. One address may open shared pages 30 times a minute (429 beyond); a wrong, expired or hammering request is logged with the address first (share link refused from …), and vpsfort's vpsfort_web_share pattern bans an address that keeps trying. The link carries the address and its expiry, signed with the web key (on a console without one, a key made at start: its links end with a restart). The links made are listed on the account page (who made it, for which address, until when; in STATE_DIR across restarts), and any admin can end one early there: it is refused from then on. Making and ending one is logged. Re-offended: a network marked mailed whose sources were banned again after the mark shows "seen again: N" on Abuse, so you can tell which reports worked. Saved views: ★ in the header saves the tab you are on with its filters ("alerts · level=high q=ssh"), in this browser; the same menu lists them for one click back. Keys: / the tab's search, g the address box, 1–8 the tabs, j/k the next and previous row, Enter opens it, Esc leaves a box, ? shows the list. Never while typing. The node legend under the header (on the tabs with node chips) says which colour is which node; "hide" there, and the Account page brings it back. Times: a table cell shows the time (today's as a time, this year's with the day, older with the year) and, within a day, how long ago; the full date is in the tooltip. Every table of the Alerts, Activity, Bans and Offenders tabs exports as CSV or JSON (the rows as filtered, all of them). CSV cells that would start a spreadsheet formula (=, +, -, @) get a ' first: log lines and network names come from strangers. The page refreshes in place: only what changed is redrawn, so the scroll position, rows opened, text selected and the focus stay, and charts and the map are redrawn only when their data changes. While text in the page is selected, refreshes wait ("held" in the header) so it can be copied. A tab left in the background asks again when shown; data older than three refreshes shows in red in the header; the tab's title counts what needs attention (high or critical). Filters and settings (not searches) are remembered in the browser. / jumps to the page's search box. The header's search box takes an address or network and opens its page, or searches the open tab. Each tab keeps its scroll position and opened rows while you look at another. If the console stops answering, the page says so with how old its data is, tries again with backoff (up to a minute) and offers "Try now". Printing a page (an abuse report, a node) gives black on white without the header or buttons. A tab's filters are in its address (#/alerts?level=high&q=ssh), so a link shows another admin the same. 🔔 in the header turns on browser notifications of new critical problems while a console tab is open; ◐ picks light, dark or the system's colours. On a phone, tables turn into cards.
95.title: The page

96.body: JSON over HTTPS, GET, with the session cookie (log in with POST /api/login {"user": "admin", "password": "...", "code": "123456", "work": {...}}, Content-Type: application/json; without user: admin; work is the challenge from /api/v1/session?user=… with the nonce found, see "Proof of work" above; without it, or with one too easy for the failures since, 428 and a fresh challenge). path /api/v1/session {"logged_in": …, "user": …, "totp": …, "node": …, "work": {"salt", "difficulty", "expires", "mac"}} (needs no session; ?user=NAME for that account's difficulty) /world.json the Map tab's countries and capitals (public data, needs no session) /api/v1/cluster everything below in one document; ?only=alerts,history only those parts (and nodes, totals, attention, refresh_secs) /api/v1/overview nodes, totals, attention /api/v1/{attention,alerts,actions,bans,offenders,accounts,world,history,nodes} one part; list entries carry node and node_id; world also has by_country (each country's networks and ports), geoblock (what each node blocks) and port_names /api/v1/nodes/<id> one node: its summary, what needs attention, its whole snapshot (_cut gives the full length of lists cut short) /api/v1/nodes/<id>/digest {"text": …}: that node's digest so far /api/v1/nodes/<id>/digests {"digests": [{"day", "text"}, …]}: the last 14 days' digests of that node the console kept (each day's when shown, and every node's 15 minutes before midnight UTC) /api/v1/attention/history {"problems": [{"level", "text", "nodes", "first", "last", "gone"}, …]}: what needed attention in the last 7 days, with when it appeared and went (gone null: still there); a count in the text is left out, so a changing count is one problem /api/v1/check the console's own health: version, certificate (fingerprint, not_after, days_left), web key id, admins, TOTP, proof of work, sessions, every node's state and version /api/v1/export everything as one JSON file (a download): the cluster document and each node's whole snapshot (vpsfort tui --file reads a node's snapshot) POST /api/v1/share {"net": …, "hours": 1–168} → {"path": "/#/share/<net>?t=<token>", "expires": …}: a link to that address's page that needs no login (see below) /api/v1/share the share links made that haven't expired (id, net, by, made, expires, ended); POST /api/v1/share/end with an id ends one early /api/v1/address/<net>?share=<token> the address's data for a share link's holder: that address only, until the link expires /api/v1/abuse/{24h,7d} every node's abuse report merged: nodes (each with sources, or error), sources, providers (key, asn, name, countries, bans, events, first, last, nodes, sources with activity, evidence, omitted, members) /api/v1/nodes/<id>/abuse/{24h,7d} the same for one node /api/v1/address/<address or network> bans, actions, offenders, trusted, allowed naming it or overlapping it, each with its node /api/v1/rdap/<address> {"abuse": [...], "network": ...}; 502 with "fallback": true when the console can't look up /api/v1/sessions this admin's sessions; POST /api/v1/sessions/end-others ends the others /api/v1/marks the admins' marks (networks marked mailed, problems seen) as the page keeps them, and kept: whether the console stores them; POST replaces them (an object, 256 KB at most) /api/v1/passkeys this admin's passkeys (id, name, added, alg, logins and last_used as the console counted them, sign_count: the authenticator's own counter, 0 for passkeys that sync) and the relying party id; POST /api/v1/passkeys/begin gives the registration options, /finish takes the browser's answer (challenge, id, clientDataJSON, attestationObject, name), /remove an id. At the login, /api/v1/session?user=NAME carries passkey (the request options) for an account that has one, and POST /api/login takes passkey: {id, challenge, clientDataJSON, authenticatorData, signature} instead of code /metrics Prometheus' text format Times are microseconds since 1970 (UTC), as in vpsfort. Node ids are 0 for this node and 1, 2, ... for the entries of NODES.
96.title: API

vpsfort_memory_{total,available}_bytes, vpsfort_memory_available_ratio, vpsfort_swap_{total,free}_bytes, vpsfort_memory_pressure_ratio{kind}, vpsfort_updates_pending, vpsfort_security_updates, vpsfort_reboot_required, vpsfort_kernel_outdated, vpsfort_processes_using_replaced_files, vpsfort_updates_checked_timestamp_seconds integrity vpsfort_av_{infected_files,scanned_files,errors}, vpsfort_av_signatures_outdated, vpsfort_av_scan_completed, vpsfort_av_last_scan_timestamp_seconds, vpsfort_verify_{checked_files,mismatched_files,setuid_programs}, vpsfort_verify_last_run_timestamp_seconds, vpsfort_cron_{tasks,scripts,files,errors}, vpsfort_cron_scanned_timestamp_seconds, vpsfort_procwatch_{pairs,outbound} exposure vpsfort_listeners{exposure}, vpsfort_public_listener{proto,port,process}, vpsfort_firewall_dead_rules, vpsfort_ufw_active patterns vpsfort_pattern_{lines,matches,unaddressed}_total{pattern,kind}, vpsfort_pattern_addresses{pattern,kind} the console vpsfort_web_logins_total{result} (ok, failed, locked_out), vpsfort_web_sessions, vpsfort_web_nodes No series names an attacker's address or an account (personal data, and unbounded); countries, networks, ports, peers and the rest are bounded by vpsfort's own caps. A family appears when the node has that part ([feeds], [antivirus], ... switched on). 98.body: path owner, mode /opt/vpsfort-web/vpsfort-web root 0755 the binary (.prev: the rollback one) /opt/vpsfort-web/config.env root:vpsfort-web 0640 settings /opt/vpsfort-web/web.key root:vpsfort-web 0640 the web key /opt/vpsfort-web/tls.crt, tls.key 0644, root:vpsfort-web 0640 the console's certificate /opt/vpsfort-web/admin.password, admin.totp root:vpsfort-web 0640 admin's login /opt/vpsfort-web/admins/ root:vpsfort-web 0750, files 0640 the other admins' logins /etc/systemd/system/vpsfort-web.service root 0644 the unit /run/vpsfort-console/console.sock root:vpsfort-web 0660 vpsfort's console socket (vpsfort makes it) /var/lib/vpsfort-web/passkeys/<admin>.passkeys vpsfort-web 0600 the admins' passkeys: public keys, written by the console at registration (the directory of the passwords is root's, and the unit may write nowhere else). With STATE_DIR= empty they go beside the password file, which the console must then be able to write. A file beside the password file is still read while the state directory has none for that admin /var/lib/vpsfort-web/ (STATE_DIR) vpsfort-web 0700 attention-history.json, digests.json, marks.json, share-links.json, lockouts.json, sessions.json (the cookies' digests only): the console's own state across restarts Logs: journalctl -u vpsfort-web.

99.body:
Every version tag vpsfort-web-v<version> gets its bundle, vpsfort-web-<version>-<commit>-<arch>.zip for each architecture (x86_64-linux-musl, aarch64-linux-musl for arm64, armv7-linux-musleabihf for 32-bit ARMv7), as an asset of the tag's GitHub Release (see "Releases" in the repository README ). Take the one for the server's architecture (uname -m) and check it: arch=x86_64-linux-musl # the server's: aarch64-linux-musl (arm64), armv7-linux-musleabihf (32-bit ARM)
gh release download vpsfort-web-v0.5.1 --repo makhort/vpsfort --pattern "*-$arch.zip*" # the zip, its .sha256 and .sigstore.json
sha256sum -c vpsfort-web-*-$arch.zip.sha256 # the download is intact (macOS: shasum -a 256 -c)
gh attestation verify vpsfort-web-*-$arch.zip --repo makhort/vpsfort --source-ref refs/tags/vpsfort-web-v0.5.1 Then on the server: unzip vpsfort-web-*-$arch.zip && cd vpsfort-web-*-$arch
sudo ./install.sh # or as root; again after editing config.env
sudo ./install.sh rollback # back to the previous version
